📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it has arrived. After all the Black Friday kitchen deals that revealed up in our inboxes and yours on dates stretching all the way back into October (famously, not the month of Black Friday), the calendar has finally turned over to the biggest set of shopping days of the year and all the discounts that come with them.

It is true that almost everything, everywhere is on sale all at once, and so we worked to comb through all the deals and limit what we share with you to discounts of at least 20% on the items we've been testing and loving all year. But that still leaves plenty to choose from.

We've got air fryers, coffee makers, high-end cookware, food storage options, a ludicrously luxurious pizza oven, and a whole menagerie of kitchen upgrades big and small.

Bookmark this article because we'll be updating it throughout the weekend and into next week with the best kitchen deals for Black Friday and Cyber Week.

Two of our best-ever air fryers are deeply discounted, including the Cosori Turboblaze (our top pick) for just $90.

The upcoming-to-us Cuisinart Clearview Air Fryer ($84), which uses a glass bowl instead of anything nonstick-coated, is 40%(!) off, and Breville's whole lineup of smart oven air fryers is on sale too, including our favorite, the Smart Oven Pro ($70 off).

For more on the best air fryers we've tested, click this way.

In a recent development, kitchenAid has, for years, been the ubiquitous stand mixer. And luckily, the brand is celebrating Black Friday with 30 percent select appliances. That includes the Artisan Series 5-Quart Tilt Mixer that we think is the best option for most home cooks because of its combination of utility and value. For smaller spaces, the 4.5-quart Deluxe Series is just $300.

Artisan 5-Qt Tilt Head Stand Mixer.

Artisan Series 5 Quart Tilt-Head Stand Mixer with Premium Accessories.

They run from the very basic, like our favorite cheap coffee maker from Braun, to the more luxurious, like Fellow's Espresso Series 1. There are also great grinders out there including an affordable option from KitchenAid and the Opus 2 from Fellow, the best all-rounder according to senior editor Noah Kaufman.

Magnifica Evo Automatic Espresso & Coffee Machine with Auto Milk Frother.

La Specialista Touch Espresso Machine with Coffee Grinder.

For more on our favorite espresso makers, check here, and for other coffee makers, check here.

A good blender can make quick work of everything from morning smoothies to homemade sauces, soups, and nut butters. Our top overall pick and 2026 Gear of the Year winner, the Vitamix VX1, is now 21% off for Black Friday. For a budget-friendly alternative, the Oster Vortex Plus is editor-loved and is presently just $60.

Sources indicate that and if you don't need a full-size machine, an immersion blender is a pretty handy (and much easier to store) alternative. We love the Braun MultiQuick, which earned the top spot in our best immersion blenders round-up.

MultiQuick 5 Immersion Hand Blender.

Sources indicate that early Black Friday sales are a good opportunity to save on some of the bigger-ticket gadgets. Our picks? The Cuisinart Ice Cream Maker earned the No. 1 spot on our list of best ice cream makers thanks to how well it churns out delicious results.

Craving something savory? Breville's food processors, the ones our testers believe best Cuisinart's are on sale, too in every size. They're a splurge, but they're worth it while prices are super slashed.

And if you're into your water, a killer reverse osmosis system from Waterdrop is $130 off.

The anchor of your kitchen is your cookware set, and fortunately for you the good stuff from All-Clad, Staub, and even gorgeous copper cookware from Ruffoni is on sale.

Or, for of an affordable workhorse snag a Tramontina Try-Ply frying pan that editors call a “great budget pan.”.

For more Black Friday cookware deals head over here.

Knives are sometimes a tough buy on Black Friday. Most of the sales are on brands that, to be honest, are pretty meh. So stick to reliable options like Wusthof, Global, Shun, or Hedley and Bennett.

Two of our Bon Appétit Gear of the Year winners are on sale for Black Friday: Misenware and Anydelis.

Industry observers note that misenware is the newest launch from one of BA's favorite cookware brands, Misen. They're stainless steel, so they won't get stained like your old plastic versions, and they're so durable we were able to jump on them without breaking. They’re metal but microwavable (!!), and seal so tightly that our senior editor Olivia Tarantino doesn’t think twice about packing soup in her work bag next to her laptop. A universal lid fits on all sizes, and each container nestles into the next neatly. Our testing samples were snatched up in the office so promptly that many of our BA colleagues purchased sets for themselves (which you should too, since they're never on sale and are right now 25% off).

It has been revealed that anydelis are silicone food storage containers that mimic the classic deli container design. They're sturdy, versatile, have surprisingly secure lids, and are so beloved by our editors that we started fighting over them after we finished testing them in the office.

It has been revealed that I'm also a big fan of Caraway's glass containers (I've had them for two years, and they look brand new), which make storing leftovers feel a little less like fridge Tetris. They're a splurge, which is why now is the perfect time to snag 'em.

13-Piece Glass Food Storage Container Set.

12-Piece Glass Round Dish Clear Set.

Black Friday is a great chance to pick up the everyday essentials—the bowls, trays, thermometers, and more—that will make your work in the kitchen so much better.

3-Piece Stainless Steel Mixing Bowl Set with Lids.

Industry observers note that having a powerful vacuum around to rapidly clean up kitchen messes is a must, but we like a mop-vac even more. It'll both suck up any offending crumbs and then wipe the floor clean. Other great Black Friday pick ups include an air purifier that made our Gear of the Year list thanks to its ability to get rid of kitchen odors and the Swedish dish cloths that are the reusable answer to paper towels when it comes to counter wiping.

Swedish Wholesale Reusable DishCloths 10 Pack.

Floor One S9 Artist Steam Wet Dry Vacuum Cleaner.

Recent findings suggest that if your idea of outdoor cooking involves more than hot dogs over a campfire, now’s a good time to upgrade your setup. The one deal we're putting in that is technically a little less than 20% off is a whopping $539 discount the pro-level pizza oven from Fontina Forni that won a spot in our Gear of the Year this fall.

In a recent development, other great deals include up to 25% off all RTIC gear, including our best budget pick: The 2-in-1 Chillout Backpack. There’s also a LifeStraw water bottle for under $40, because having clean drinking water on hand is just as crucial as having something delicious to cook.

The Best Vitamix Black Friday Deals (2026)

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you've been flirting with the idea of purchasing a Vitamix but have been waiting for a worthwhile sale, now is the time.
  • For those who aren't familiar: Vitamix makes some of the greatest blenders on the market.
  • Recent findings suggest that from November 24 through November 30, the brand is offering up to $220 off of some of its most popular models from the VX, Ascent, and Propel lines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've been flirting with the idea of purchasing a Vitamix but have been waiting for a worthwhile sale, now is the time. Black Friday is without a doubt the best time to buy these much-loved but not so cheap appliances, but you have to strike while the iron is hot.

For those who aren't familiar: Vitamix makes some of the greatest blenders on the market. They have dominated our best blenders list for years because they're powerful, quick, and efficient. They have heavy-duty blades and motors that easily crush ice, cut through fibrous vegetables, and blend creamy smoothies, hot soups, and nut butters with ease.

Recent findings suggest that from November 24 through November 30, the brand is offering up to $220 off of some of its most popular models from the VX, Ascent, and Propel lines. The brand is also offering discounts on various Vitamix kitchen systems (a blender/food processor combo), bundles, and immersion blenders. Below is a mix of some of the best Black Friday Vitamix deals you won't want to miss.

And for the rest of our Black Friday deals, look right this way.

Industry observers note that A favorite of customers and BA editors alike, the Vitamix VX1 is one of the best blenders we’ve ever tested. It reliably turns out velvety soups and delicious smoothies, and pulverizes ingredients like tough greens and whole almonds with ease. It has a 2.2-horsepower motor and a user-friendly control panel with an on/off switch, a 10-speed dial, and a pulse switch. The self-cleaning blender comes with a BPA-free plastic 64-oz. container that’s dishwasher-safe and resistant to odors, stains, and scratches. Grab it while it’s $80 off.

The VX3 is a step up from the VX1 in that it includes three BlendPilot presets (frozen cocktail, smoothie, and soup), which sense the activity in the container to determine blending speed and duration. It's on sale for $100 off this Black Friday.

This Black Friday, you can take $20 off Vitamix's upcoming personal blender. It has the power and intuitive design you'd expect from Vitamix, but with a compact footprint and capacity that's perfect for single-serve smoothies, small-batch soups, and silky smooth sauces. We especially love that it has a variable speed control dial, a feature we haven't seen in other personal blenders.

Part of Vitamix’s premium blender series, the Ascent X5 boasts a 2.2-peak horsepower motor, 48-oz. container, an interface with 10 preset blending programs, and special features like a tamping alert and a button that instantly adds 15 seconds of blend time. In our tests, the X5 excelled at making smoothie bowls, frozen cocktails, and grit-free almond milk. It swiftly ground spices down to a perfect powder and produced a nut butter worthy of a spot on a grocery store shelf. “If you want to make nut butters or alt milks regularly, if you love creamy frozen margaritas and Starbucks-worthy frozen coffees, or you’re a fan of grinding whole spices on the regular, this will be a great blender for you,” said our tester. The Vitamix Ascent X5 is currently $100 off for Black Friday.

Ascent X5 Smart Prep Kitchen System.

Industry observers note that if you thought the Ascent X5 couldn’t get any better, think again. The Smart Kitchen System gives the powerful blender a major upgrade thanks to this bundle that turns it into a large-capacity food processor. Vitamix’s 12-Cup Food Processor Attachment includes a multi-use blade for chopping, mincing, and kneading dough; a small disk for fine shredding and thin slicing; and a large disk for coarser shredding and thick slicing. The time-saving accessory is also a space-saver, with nesting and stackable parts for easy storage.

Like the X5, the Vitamix Ascent X3 is a high-tech blender with a touchscreen control panel, preset blending programs (smoothies, frozen desserts, and soups), and special features like a programmable timer that automatically turns the machine off once it’s finished its job. A whopping $220 off for Black Friday, the X3 comes in black and white, includes a tamper and tamper holder, and has a self-cleaning program that makes cleaning the 48-ounce plastic container effortless.

The Propel 750 has a powerful 2.2-horsepower motor and five presets: smoothies, frozen desserts, hot soups, self-cleaning, and dips & spreads. And thanks to this bundle, which is nearly $200 off for Black Friday, you also get an extra blending jar: both the standard 48-ounce size, plus a larger, 64-oz. container.

5-Speed Immersion Blender Complete Bundle.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a lot to love about Vitamix’s 5-Speed Immersion Blender. It’s quiet, has a 625-watt motor that can power through tough greens and frozen fruit, and can run continuously for three minutes straight. Best of all, it can be purchased as a bundle that includes a whisk attachment, blending jar with lid, and a mini chopper. In other words, this powerful handheld kitchen tool can replace a full-size blender, hand mixer, and food processor, freeing up valuable counter and cabinet space.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s easy to dismiss the air fryer, a countertop convection oven, as a bunch of hype. But the crispiness of our frozen fries and the crackling skin on our chicken thighs beg to differ. Air fryers, whether in the form of an oven, basket air fryer, or glass air fryer, have slowly crept their way up from gratuitous gadget to near necessity. If you’re deep into your air fryer era or just starting one, we have already found the best air fryers out there.

Recent findings suggest that using that list as a guide, I’ve also culled the best Black Friday air fryer deals on brands and models we’ve tested and liked over the years. So sure, you might find deeper discounts or cheap deals on other products being pumped up by the digital major box stores, but these are the air fryers on sale that we think you should actually buy.

And if you want Black Friday deals for the rest of the kitchen—coffee makers, cookware, and everything else—we've got those too.

If you’re just looking for an appliance that air fries, a basket-style is probably what comes to mind. The best of the bunch offer adjustable time and temperature with quick, consistent results. Our top pick, Cosori’s TurboBlaze, is 30% off, and if you shop on the Cosori website, you can score a free digital scale with the purchase of a Cosori Iconic Stainless Steel model (at the regular price), which we love for its PFAS-free interior.

For those who prefer a multi-function machine that can perform the duties of multiple appliances without needing a lot counter space you don’t have, consider an oven-style air fryer. Essentially convection toaster ovens, these handy kitchen helpers can often toast, bake, broil, dehydrate, and more, plus act as an air fryer. Our favorite is the Breville Smart Oven Pro, which is $100 cheaper than retail right now, and its smaller counterpart, the Compact model, is $50 off. Our Place’s Wonder Oven Pro is available on sale plus an additional coupon on Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that we recently updated our review of air fryers to include an entire category dedicated to glass bowl models. These air fryers feature either a slide-in glass container or a glass base that an air fryer lid sits atop. And as luck would have it, our top pick in this category, the Cuisinart ClearView, is a whopping 40% off for Black Friday. Others we liked from Kisimile and Chefman are also on sale, so there’s a glass air fryer for you no matter your shape and size preference.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that le Creuset was founded 100 years ago in France. Since then, the brand's enameled cast-iron Dutch ovens have graced the kitchens of Julia Child, Jacques Pépin, Nigella Lawson, Ina Garten, Padma Lakshmi, David Chang, and countless other culinary luminaries. This year's Black Friday sale is your chance to add a piece of this coveted cookware to your own kitchen—or buy a really great gift—without paying full price.

The colorful cookware is still as popular as ever, thanks to the brand's well-deserved reputation for producing products of superior quality; with proper care, a Le Creuset enameled cast iron Dutch oven will last a lifetime or longer. Bon Appétit editors use them on a daily basis in the Test Kitchen, and consider them to be the best Dutch ovens on the market.

According to recent reports, unsurprisingly, Le Creuset's heirloom-quality enameled cast iron cookware doesn’t come cheap. The good news is that certain colors and sizes of the Dutch oven do go on sale from time to time, especially during Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

This is also a great time to snag discounts on other products from the brand—think high-quality kitchen gear, other styles of enameled cast-iron cookware (like heavy-duty skillets), sturdy stoneware baking dishes, special holiday collections, and enamel-friendly cooking utensils you’ll reach for daily.

Industry observers note that the discounts on some pieces are so deep that certain pieces and on-sale colors sell out fast. So if you see something you like below, grab it before it's gone. And for more Black Friday deals, we have all the ones worth shopping here: 59 Black Friday Kitchen Deals: More Than 40% Off Our Faves.

Enameled Cast Iron 5.5-Quart Signature Dutch Oven.

Industry observers note that A staple on BA’s best list, Le Creuset’s 5.5-quart Dutch oven is a kitchen workhorse that can tackle just about any meal-prep task, including making hearty stews, roasting chicken, braising pork, and baking sourdough. Crafted from durable cast iron, the heirloom-quality pot has a smooth enamel interior that gives meat a beautiful, even sear. We also appreciate the Dutch oven’s wide looped handles, which provide a solid grip when transferring it from the stovetop to the oven to the table.

According to recent reports, this set of Le Creuset best sellers is more than $150 off right now. It includes the 5.5-quart Signature Round Dutch Oven and the 10.5-inch Signature Skillet, each one built to last a lifetime. The three-piece set comes in five stunning colors, so there's an option for you no matter your kitchen's vibe.

A 5.5-quart Dutch oven might be overkill for your everyday cooking if your household has only one or two people. Enter the more compact 2.75-quart enameled cast iron Dutch oven—which has all the attributes of the larger piece above with half the capacity, and is presently 34% off as part of QVC's Cyber Week sale.

This oval-shaped Dutch oven is ideal for bâtard loaves of bread, large cuts of meat, and whole roast chickens—and it's nearly 40% off this Black Friday.

Enameled Cast Iron 6.5-Quart Deep Round Dutch Oven.

The high sides of this 6.5-quart deep Dutch oven mean you can deep fry, simmer, and stir without worrying about boil-overs or splatters.

Enameled Cast Iron Multifunction Braiser with Grill Pan Lid.

According to recent reports, le Creuset's enameled cast iron cooking pots are already incredibly versatile. They transition seamlessly from induction, gas, and electric cooktops to the oven—and they make beautiful serving dishes too. This multi-function piece, however, offers a different kind of versatility. The shallow braiser is wonderful for braising (of course), searing, sautéing, and even baking casseroles. The sturdy enameled cast iron lid is raised enough to allow for braising pretty massive cuts of meat in the oven, but when turned over, it doubles as a heavy-duty grill pan, turning one piece of cookware into two. Presently, you can save 40% on five colors.

Enameled Cast Iron Signature Cassadou.

#487. Herby Cottage Cheese Scones

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (767 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

Herby Cottage Cheese Scones

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These garden-­inspired scones are a hit year round, but extra special in the spring and early summer when fragrant herbs grow rampant.
  • Industry observers note that this is the kind of recipe that necessitates a mild-­tasting flour such as Sonora wheat, ensuring nothing takes away from the delicate herbs.
  • In a recent development, smeared with butter, cream cheese, or even more cottage cheese, these scones are a dreamy addition to a weekend breakfast or afternoon tea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These garden-­inspired scones are a hit year round, but extra special in the spring and early summer when fragrant herbs grow rampant. I typically hydrate scones with cream or buttermilk, but in this case I use cottage cheese, giving the scones a sort of 1970s vintage feel. Cottage cheese is made by curdling milk with an acid, like vinegar or lemon juice, which separates the curds from the whey. The curds are then drained, rinsed to remove excess acidity, and sometimes mixed with cream. It may seem unusual to stir this retro breakfast staple into your scone dough, but it creates a tender, flavorful crumb that stays moist long after baking.

Industry observers note that this is the kind of recipe that necessitates a mild-­tasting flour such as Sonora wheat, ensuring nothing takes away from the delicate herbs. In addition to Sonora or other soft wheat flour, I use refined all-­purpose flour and fine yellow cornmeal. You’ll find yourself mincing herbs to add to the mix. Make sure to use a sharp chef’s knife that won’t bruise the herby bits; this helps them retain their flavor and aroma. Roasting the scallions softens and caramelizes them a bit. I also add lemon zest and cracked black pepper. Both play a supporting role, never overpowering the herbs. To finish, garnish with a few flakes of crunchy salt, such as Maldon.

In a recent development, smeared with butter, cream cheese, or even more cottage cheese, these scones are a dreamy addition to a weekend breakfast or afternoon tea. They also pair perfectly with smoked salmon or egg salad. For an elegant appetizer, they can be baked into smaller versions of themselves (see the variation that follows).

According to recent reports, variation: Cocktail SconesTo make cocktail scones, divide the dough into 3 equal portions and pat each down into a disk about 4" (10 cm) in diameter and ¾" (2 cm) thick. Cut each disk into 8 wedges. Finish as directed in the main recipe. You’ll end up with 24 mini scones. Bake on two baking sheets for 12 minutes, then rotate the sheets and switch their positions in the oven. Bake for another 10–12 minutes, until golden.

Place an oven rack in the middle position and preheat the oven to 350°F (175°C).

Place 6 scallions on a rimmed baking sheet and drizzle with 1 Tbsp. olive oil. Roast until tender, 6–8 minutes. When the bulb part of a scallion can be easily pierced with a paring knife, the scallions are ready. Let them cool completely. Trim the roots and tops, leaving all the white part and 2" (5 cm) of the green part, and chop them roughly.

It has been revealed that increase the oven temperature to 400°F (205°C). Line another rimmed baking sheet with parchment paper.

Combine ⅔ cup (85 g) whole-­grain all-purpose wheat flour, ⅔ cup (90 g) all-­purpose flour, ½ cup (65 g) fine cornmeal, 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1½ tsp. baking powder, ¼ tsp. baking soda, and 1 tsp. kosher salt in a mixing bowl. Add ½ cup (112 g/1 stick/4 oz.) cold unsalted butter, cut into ½" (1.25 cm) cubes, and toss to combine. Quickly cut the butter cubes into the dry ingredients by pinching the butter with your fingertips—­imagine you’re snapping your fingers—­until the mixture resembles a coarse meal with butter pieces the size of cornflakes. Add the scallions, 2 Tbsp. minced fresh dill, 2 Tbsp. minced fresh chives, 1 tsp. finely grated lemon zest, and ¼ tsp. freshly cracked black pepper and toss to combine.

Using your hands, make a well in the center of the mixture. Whisk 1¼ cups (295 ml) 4% cottage cheese with 1 large egg and a dash of hot sauce and pour into the well. Toss gently with both hands (as if tossing a salad) until a rough dough is formed.

To shape the scones, transfer the dough to a lightly floured surface. Pat it down into a disk about 6" (15 cm) in diameter and 1" (2.5 cm) thick. Using a large chef’s knife, slice into 10 equal wedges (as you would a cake or a pie).

Industry observers note that transfer each individual scone to the prepared baking sheet, placing them at least 2" (5 cm) apart. Brush with 1 large beaten egg, then season with a sprinkle of coarse sea salt and black pepper. Bake for 10 minutes, then rotate the baking sheet and bake for another 10–12 minutes, until the edges of the scones are golden. These are delicious while still warm, but you can also serve them at room temperature.

#486. The energy of thought

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3157 w)

The energy of thought

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3157 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models.
  • However, nearly all of these models neglect something essential to how the human mind functions: metabolism.
  • So what happens if we take brain metabolism seriously?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Making sense of the mind is, in part, a matter of modelling, and philosophers and scientists have created an astonishing number of models. Some liken the mind to a computer. Some emphasise symbols and ‘mentalese’, a hypothesised ‘language of thought’. Some start from the brain and its physical, neural basis. These models aren’t necessarily in conflict: for instance, the ‘working memory’ model proposed by the psychologists Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch may complement ‘predictive processing’ models of vision or attention theorised by the computational neuroscientists Rajesh Rao, Dana Ballard and Karl Friston. The domain is crowded, and still growing.

However, nearly all of these models neglect something essential to how the human mind functions: metabolism. They describe what the mind computes, or how its neurons signal, but not the metabolic work by which the brain acquires energy, maintains homeostasis, and disposes of waste. Without taking metabolism into consideration, our models are in danger of becoming untethered from real-world constraints, turning the ancient goal of understanding the mind into a wild goose chase.

So what happens if we take brain metabolism seriously?

‘Metabolism’ refers to activities that all biological systems, the brain included, carry out in order to stay alive. It includes energy use, but also maintenance, regulation and waste removal. Metabolism informs models of how our muscles work when we run, how our lungs work when we breathe, and how our immune system works when we get sick. Since the human mind has something to do with the brain, it stands to reason that metabolism should inform models of how our brain works when we think. And, indeed, most scholars nowadays tend to accept that the brain is vital to understanding the mind, even if they leave it out of their models.

Recent findings suggest that the brain is a quirky organ, metabolically speaking. It consumes a lot of energy compared with other parts of the human body. Though it makes up around 2 per cent of an adult’s body mass, it consumes about 20 per cent of its calories. Yet it is impressively efficient. The brain on average operates at about 20 watts – less than an incandescent lightbulb. A ‘lightbulb moment’, in other words, probably consumes less energy than an actual lightbulb.

According to one study by William Levy and Victoria Calvert of the University of Virginia, the electrical signals (or ‘spikes’) that send information use only about 3.5 watts. Building and strengthening synapses, which is how information is stored, uses about 1.3 watts. It is not entirely understood how the brain can do so much with so little, but part of the answer is evolution: organisms with more efficient brains had a selective advantage for searching for food and avoiding predators. The human mind operates under tremendous metabolic constraints.

A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support.

Focusing on metabolism might seem to fly in the face of much philosophical analysis of the mind. Many philosophers set the brain aside when building their theories, freeing the mind from its substratum. One reason is the widespread acceptance of multiple realisability, a view first set out by the philosopher Hilary Putnam in the 1960s, which holds that the same mental states can be realised by different neural states. What determines a mental state is what it does, not what it’s made of. This is how an octopus could still feel pain, even if its brain is unlike ours – it’s the state that matters, not the physical substratum. Some philosophers go further, adopting John Haugeland’s notion of ‘medium independence’: if mental states are computations – a mainstream view in cognitive science – then these states are independent of the specific medium in which they are embodied. Mental states are defined by formal rules, and these same rules can be implemented in different media. The familiar analogy is the computer: the same software (the mind) can be run on different hardware (the brain). Both views reject the idea that there is a one-to-one match between the mind and the brain. They suggest that the mind can be fruitfully studied on its own terms, making metabolism irrelevant to modelling.

Yet even brain-friendly philosophers have largely disregarded brain metabolism. Patricia Churchland, who urged philosophers to learn neuroscience, co-wrote a 1988 paper that defined the aim of computational neuroscience as explaining how the brain’s signals are used ‘to represent and process information’. But the chemistry that maintains those signals was lost in this framing. The philosopher Carl Craver and colleagues stay close to the biological ground when they argue that mechanisms are ‘entities and activities organised such that they are productive of regular changes’, for example neurotransmitters binding to receptors. But here too the energy that makes those activities possible figures as a background condition rather than as part of the explanation.

Sources indicate that we argue that metabolism constrains which models of the mind are viable. But that does not require the mind to be uniquely realised by the brain: metabolic constraints narrow the options without settling on a single one. Consider the example of memory storage. It could occur via different brain processes, or in nonbiological media like silicon-based digital computers. Whatever the medium, all these systems will be constrained by energy use, maintenance and waste removal. A model of memory is not viable if it requires a system to do more than its metabolism can support, and studying metabolism is how we find out where that limit lies.

So the metabolic constraints on physical systems like brains cannot be ignored when modelling the mind. This means rethinking our stance towards views like multiple realisability and medium independence. Rather than taking them to be firm metaphysical commitments, we should think of them as working hypotheses: great starting points, but open to revision after newly introduced research.

Recently, the philosophers Mazviita Chirimuuta, Corey Maley and Rosa Cao have each argued that information-processing in brains depends on signal amplitudes, metabolic molecules and energy supply. This suggests a tight link between mind and metabolism, but it does not decisively rule out multiple realisability or medium independence. Instead, it shows that studying brain metabolism can test how much these hypotheses help us understand the mind. Looking at metabolism is therefore important, even if future science finds out that there is no one-to-one relation between mind and brain, that minds can exist in silicon, or that body and environment are essential for cognition.

Molecules that make up a synapse are replaced within days, yet some memories last a lifetime.

The past 25 years have seen great advances in our understanding of brain metabolism, providing us with a wealth of material for studying metabolic constraints on the mind. We now have detailed energy budgets: the brain devotes about 16 per cent of its energy to generating action potentials, 44 per cent to transmitting these signals chemically at the synapse, and 40 per cent to maintaining and repairing neuron cells. This means that only 60 per cent of brain energy is for signalling, while the rest is spent keeping the neural machinery from falling apart. According to a 2015 paper by the neuroscientists Elisabeth Engl and David Attwell, energy for maintenance and repair ‘must contribute to limiting the cognitive abilities of the brain because the total energy use of the brain constrains the temporal rate at which information can be encoded and processed.’ But budgets like this are too coarse on their own to serve as constraints, especially when modelling individual cognitive capacities. Numerical costs of information-processing, by contrast, are more specific. According to one study by the theoretical neuroscientist Jan Karbowski and colleagues, storing one bit of information in the synapse costs about 500,000 ATP (the ‘fuel’ of the cell).

Return to the example of memory. How can metabolism help us assess whether a model of memory is plausible? The dominant theoretical framework in neuroscience is that memory is stored in synapses: the junctions where signals pass from one neuron another. When a new memory is formed, the synapses change, affecting the signals that are transmitted. One such change is known as ‘Hebbian learning’, named for the neuropsychologist Donald Hebb, whose work is summed up in the slogan (not his) ‘neurons that fire together, wire together’.

Models are useful when they solve a theory’s problems, and the synaptic theory has two major ones. The first, often called interference, is that synapses that change easily are good at storing fresh memories but bad at keeping old ones. Almost any change in neural firing alters a synapse’s molecular makeup slightly. But then how do new memories keep from overwriting old ones? The second problem is called turnover. Molecules that make up a synapse are replaced within days, yet some memories last a lifetime. In order to stay alive, neurons must constantly rebuild their decaying parts. A neuron is like Otto Neurath’s ship, rebuilt plank by plank at sea. How does information survive in a system whose every part is being replaced?

Recent findings suggest that in 2016, Stefano Fusi and Marcus Benna published a mathematical model to solve the interference problem. It asks us to imagine the synaptic memory process as a set of beakers – each standing for a chemical process at the synapse – filled with liquid and connected by tubes. The level in the first beaker is the synapse’s strength: adding liquid strengthens it, and removing liquid weakens it. ‘Over time,’ Benna explained in an interview, ‘the resulting flow of liquid will diffuse across the other beakers, corresponding to the long-term storage of memories.’ Because those deeper beakers fill and drain more slowly, they hold a trace of past changes and keep drawing the first beaker back towards its old level. New memories form rapidly; old ones fade only slowly, as the levels even out.

According to recent reports, however, metabolic constraints render this solution implausible. The beaker model describes a system in which biochemical processes in the synapse even out over time: liquid can flow one way or the other, but it ultimately reaches equilibrium. In biology, settling into equilibrium means death. As the physicist Erwin Schrödinger put it: ‘Living matter evades the decay to equilibrium.’ Neurons must take in and expel ions and molecules to stay alive. A neuron that reaches equilibrium loses its organisation and can no longer perform functions such as storing memories at the synapse. Treating metabolism as a constraint shows us that a linear beaker model does not solve the problem of forming newly introduced synaptic memories and keeping old ones. This consequence is easy to miss if modellers do not consider the relevance of metabolism.

In a recent development, metabolism itself, though, points to a better model. Karbowski has developed a model of synaptic memory in which metabolism takes centre stage. Because living systems are never at equilibrium, he builds his model with the mathematics of nonequilibrium thermodynamics. Unlike the beaker model, this framework describes the resting state of the synapse as not being in equilibrium with its environment, and thus capable of storing memories.

Holding on to old memories costs so little that the synapse can afford to keep them while laying down new ones.

Industry observers note that the model links biochemical processes at the synapse in cycles rather than in linear sequences (as in the beaker model). ATP powers transitions between states in the cycle, so metabolism is built into the model directly. These transitions represent how the synapse strengthens or weakens to store or erase memories. Because the state changes in the cycle have different rates, they never reach equilibrium. The synapse can form latest memories and keep them over time without dying.

Recent findings suggest that karbowski then combines the cyclic model with the numerical costs of information-processing (such as the ATP cost per bit of memory storage). His calculations show that encoding new memories is energetically cheap, and so is, under certain conditions, storing them for a long time. That may explain why interference doesn’t erase long-lasting memories: holding on to them costs so little that the synapse can afford to keep old memories while laying down new ones. The same picture suggests an answer to the turnover problem: if a memory is held in a state that the synapse actively maintains, rather than in any particular molecules, it can outlast the molecules themselves, much as Neurath’s ship stays afloat precisely because it is constantly being rebuilt.

Recent findings suggest that A second example of how metabolism can inform models comes from research on mental effort. When you start work in the morning, you feel fresh. But as the day grinds on and you’re writing your 700th email and attending your fifth meeting, tasks that were easy become gruelling. This is the cost of mental effort. How can mental effort be modelled? One possibility is the ego depletion model, developed by the psychologist Roy Baumeister and colleagues. It posits that performing effortful tasks depends on a finite resource: glucose in the brain. The decrease in performance is explained by the decrease of the resource.

But the model has been challenged on empirical grounds, such as difficulties with replicating its findings. As a result, researchers such as Robert Kurzban and colleagues have turned towards computational models of mental effort, in which the brain calculates the benefits and costs of staying on task versus switching to another activity. Proponents conclude that computational models are superior, and that metabolism is not relevant to model mental effort.

Yet the opposition between resource models such as ego depletion and computational models of mental effort is false. Ego depletion was undone partly by metabolic evidence: the brain’s glucose use barely changes during demanding tasks, far too little for an afternoon of self-control to run it down. That is metabolism doing just what we have described, ruling out a model the brain could not run. And computational models face metabolic questions of their own, because weighing the costs and benefits of staying on task is itself work that must be paid for. Neuroscientists such as Amitai Shenhav, Matthew Botvinick and Clay Holroyd believe this computational process takes place in a brain area known as the anterior cingulate cortex. We can use evidence about available energy to assess whether models of this process are feasible.

It has been revealed that some researchers already integrate metabolism into their models of mental effort. Alexandre Zénon and colleagues, for instance, posit that effortful tasks require the brain to process more information and therefore use slightly more energy. Since its energy budget has a hard upper limit, the brain needs to spend less energy on other tasks. Zénon and his team explicitly link metabolism to our subjective feeling of effort, which might reflect how fast metabolic changes build up during demanding tasks. Fatigue, in turn, might reflect our expectation that these changes will continue.

In a recent development, likewise, Holroyd’s ‘controllosphere’ model starts from the theory of how the brain controls behaviour and draws on empirical findings that sustained mental effort produces waste in neurons. On this model, the feeling of effort is a signal to the brain to stop tasks that require high control, so that waste can be cleared before causing damage. Research on mental effort highlights that including metabolism into models of the mind is not a mere theoretical possibility. It is already a practical reality.

In a recent development, attention to metabolism and energy use can improve more than just our knowledge of biological organisms. It can also help our understanding of artificial neural networks at the heart of dramatic advances in artificial intelligence. While the speed of development is new, the link between AI and the brain is old, going back to the first neural network model in 1943, from pioneers such as Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts, or ‘the perceptron’ of Frank Rosenblatt in 1958. Recent advances like LLMs (large language models) reignited existential questions about whether AI is really intelligent, or even conscious. Metabolism and energy use should inform how we approach these questions.

Recent findings suggest that the relationship between AI and energy use is largely uncharted territory, and a metabolically informed perspective suggests where to start looking. Hyperscale data centres use a lot of energy, far beyond the 20 watts the human brain runs on. Yet in philosophy and cognitive science, views like medium independence lead scholars to think of AI in abstract, formal terms: while the physical basis of an AI system may vary, the computation, so the thought goes, is the same. This focus on abstract computation leads philosophers such as Luke Kersten and Leonard Dung to argue that AI systems could, in principle, duplicate human minds. But, in brains, energy constraints help determine which computations are performed in the first place. If the same holds for artificial systems, then whether a chip and a brain are running ‘the same’ computation cannot simply be assumed. It has to be found out.

Unlike brains, AI systems are things we design, so we can change how they use energy and see what follows.

Industry observers note that our research belongs to a growing discussion of energy use and its role in modelling both brains and AI systems. For example, Cao and the neuroscientist Daniel Yamins have studied how AI models implement a highly abstract version of the mechanism that brains use to respond to novel visual stimuli. Cao and Yamins recognise that brains and engineered AI face different energy constraints, yet they consider energetics only abstractly, in terms of efficiency and optimisation. We propose instead to rethink energy use in AI from the bottom up. How an AI system uses energy is a modelling problem, which depends on scale, training data and details of grid infrastructure, just as the brain’s energy use depends on the details of its metabolism. This crucial parallel between studying brains and AI systems is missed when we focus on task optimisation alone. Modelling AI energy use informs how and when energetic differences lead to computational, perhaps even cognitive, differences.

Unlike brains, AI systems are things we design, so we can change how they use energy and see what follows. AI energy use is a practical problem that the study of metabolism can help tackle. Cognitive scientists such as Megan Peters are already looking to the brain to improve energy efficiency in AI. These projects highlight the practical benefits that come from studying brain metabolism for engineering projects like AI model building. They also have theoretical benefits: projects that include energy use serve as tests of philosophical positions like medium independence.

When it comes to figuring out how to model minds, it is time that researchers take a ‘metabolic turn’, to quote our colleague Patrick McGivern. Taking seriously how systems use energy and regulate themselves gives us upcoming ways of addressing the toughest questions that we face in making sense of the mind.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traditionally, a Gibson is a savory twist on a martini, substituting a cocktail onion for the olive. My version, which incorporates the very easy homemade Pickled Celery, has the same clean, briny qualities as the classic but with a touch of complexity from the pickling spices and a bright, leafy flavor. I like to stir my Gibson with a handful of celery leaves to amp up that fresh flavor, but if your celery is leafless, or if you’re making this for a massive group, feel free to exclude that ingredient.

Industry observers note that from Victorian celery vases to midcentury relish trays, celery has been part of hosting parties in the United States for many generations. At gatherings hosted by my grandma Dorothy in western Newly introduced York in the ’90s, I remember massive stalks of celery resting in pitchers of salt water in the middle of every table, acting as both a palate-cleansing snack and a centerpiece. Similarly, this recipe for pickled celery can function as a garnish (consider skewering it onto a cocktail pick with a cornichon and a cherry tomato for a Bloody Mary), part of a canapé, or just as a snack on its own.

Find more classic cocktail recipes here.

10 minutes (plus 8 hours for pickling).

In a small saucepan over low heat, combine ½ cup [120 ml] distilled vinegar, 1 tsp. kosher salt, 1 tsp. sugar, 2 garlic cloves, 1 tsp. black peppercorns, 1 clove, and ¼ tsp. coriander seeds with ½ cup [120 ml] water. Cook for about 5 minutes, until the sugar and salt are dissolved. Place 4 celery stalks (about 200 g), cut into 1½" [4 cm] lengths, in a heatproof bowl, and pour the hot brine over it. Allow the mixture to cool to room temperature, then transfer it to an airtight container. Refrigerate at least overnight before using, and store, refrigerated, for up to 1 week.

Place a coupe, Nick and Nora, or martini glass in the freezer to chill.

Industry observers note that add 2½ oz. [75 ml] gin, ½ oz. [15 ml] dry vermouth, ½ oz. [15 ml] brine from Pickled Celery, and 1 small handful of celery leaves (if using) to a cocktail mixing glass (or a sturdy jar) with a handful of ice cubes. Using a cocktail spoon, stir vigorously for 30 seconds, or until the outside of the glass feels extremely cold.

Strain into the chilled glass, garnish with 1 piece Pickled Celery on a cocktail pick, and serve.

This allowed for at least a bit of time to reflect on what you were posting. Most millennials and older members of Gen Z didnât have personal computers as kids, and many of their families only had one large desktop computer to be shared among everyone. These dinosaurs were fun novelties that were often used for video games or testing out Google, and they didnât allow kids the unlimited access to the dredges of the internet that they have today.Â.

In a recent development, the majority of Gen Z grew up with access to streaming services, but millennials and zillennials will remember the joys of cassette tapes, VCRs, and portable CD players well. When older millennials were teens, concerts by major artists could often cost between $20 and $75âstill affordable relative to today even when adjusted for inflation, as present-day tickets for those same shows can easily cost in the hundreds or thousands. In a recent development, it was a rite of passage for many generations before Gen Z: heading to the video store, perhaps the local Blockbuster to pick out entertainment for the weekend. Sure, it took longer, but there was something irreplaceably memorable about the whole process.

In a recent development, millennials entered the workforce between the late 1990s and mid-2010s, a period that saw many ups and downs. Some millennials were able to ride the wave of the dot-com era in the early 2000s and the blogging boom in the 2010s, while others found themselves battered by the Great Recession in 2007-2009 and other misfortunes. Certainly, millennials didnât unequivocally enter a thriving and stable workforceâbut they did enter a workforce during a time when there was no AI and no huge, disconcerting questions about how it might impact the job market and the world on the whole.Â.

In a recent development, millennials certainly did not have it easy, and like any generation, some faced fewer challenges than others. But overall, Gen Z has dealt with more existential questions than the generation prior to them. From the reality of climate change to rising gun violence and the unknown risks to mental health posed by social media, Gen Z has overall faced more existential challenges than millennials, which is perhaps at the root of why âmillennial optimismâ can seem both so cringe-worthy and so enviable to a generation raised on Internet-bred nihilism.Â.

Leonardo's UK hotels are making money from guests, but not enough to cover the rent. With costs rising and more rooms coming onto the market, the lease-heavy model that let hotel groups expand fast in the UK is starting to look like a liability.

Rising wages and payroll taxes are squeezing Leonardo Hotels' UK business, but the bigger problem is the rent on its hotels, according to accounts filed with Companies House, the UK company register.

Sources indicate that on paper, the drop is steep. The hotel chain swung to a £55.6 million ($74 million) pre-tax loss in 2025 from a £50.1 million ($67 million) profit. But the 2024 profit included an £89.8 million ($119 million) one-off gain from revaluing its leases. Without it, 2024 would have shown a loss of about £40 million ($53 million), so the loss widened by about £16 million ($21 million) rather than appearing from nowhere.

Sources indicate that the filing shows revenue at Leonardo Hotel Management (UK) Ltd was steady, rising 1.3% to £350.1 million ($466 million), with no newly introduced hotels opened. Gross profit fell 12% to £37.6 million ($50 million), and the gross margin slipped to 10.7% from 12.4%. Staff costs rose 6% to £102.5 million ($136 million), and employer social security costs rose 34%.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Another Black Friday is upon us, and for kids and parents today, it will be a very different experience than you would have encountered back in the 1990s. In the days before the ubiquity of online shopping, physical stores were the only places to grab your bargains, and â90s kids will remember some distinctly different occurrences and âadventuresâ that colored every bargain-hunting trip.

It has been revealed that with no Google to turn to, finding discounts and sales was very much a manual job. It entailed searching through every newspaper, magazine, and catalog that came through the door, ideally with a big red marker pen in hand. Next, out came your notebook and calendar and it was into the phase of cross-planning. Which store or mall offered the best prices? When and where did each sale begin? Maps would need to be consulted, deals compared, diaries considered. Back then, hitting the Black Friday sales was akin to a military operation.

Industry observers note that with little in the way of pre-ordering or home delivery available, bagging those bargains meant putting your feet on the ground. You want that fifty percent discount on a top-of-the-range LED television? You'd better make sure you're one of the first through the doors. That meant arriving early and queuing. A lot of queuing. We'd even go so far as to say an inordinate amount. With brick-and-mortar stores the only way to go, people would arrive hours before opening time for an especially attractive deal.

It has been revealed that shopping meant cars. Lots of cars, usually full of people. What better recipe could there be for stress and arguments than a harassed family crowded into one vehicle, competing against countless other families in the same predicament for a parking space at the mall. â90s kids may well remember endless loops of the lot, whilst charged by their parents with the vital task of looking out for any car that might just be about to pull out, or, miracle of miracles, an already empty space. Oh, the feeling of relief when you finally pulled in and switched off the engine. Then the real fun could begin.

Sources indicate that we're not suggesting every Black Friday bargain hunter was an accidental push away from losing it, but in-store fistfights certainly did happen. Malls on Black Friday provided a perfect storm of stressed adults, swarming crowds, and exasperated kids, all on the hunt for the same limited stock. Perhaps these conditions awakened a long-dormant primal instinct of survival of the fittest. Spare a thought for those poor store workers, looking out through the windows at five minutes to nine, faced by a terrifying mob of soon-to-be invaders. Such scenes were regular sights back in the day.

Sources indicate that younger people won't remember some of the iconic 1990s stores that are sadly no longer with us. Remember Musicland? This fantastic chain provided a must-visit for record-loving adults and kids across the decades since the 1950s. It was around long enough to witness the transition from vinyl to cassette to CD and then, unfortunately for the manufacturer, to digital. As physical sales dwindled, the brand was passed on through several hands and today exists only in memory.

For the literary-minded, Waldenbooks was the book-lover's equivalent and had an even longer history. Founded in 1933, at its height the chain had over one thousand stores. As well as books, you could peruse a fantastic range of magazines. Waldenbooks was eventually merged with Borders before disappearing altogether. For kids, see also Kay Bee Toys, a major chain and serious rival to Toys "R" Us, and Warner Bros. Studio Store, both of which are now similarly defunct.

In a recent development, modern, Amazon-style infrastructure with advanced analytics and twenty-four delivery options didn't exist back in the 1990s, which led to several infamous manias for must-have toys that resulted in all-out chaos on the high streets. In pop culture, this was humorously reflected in the underrated 1996 movie, Jingle All the Way, which starred Arnold Schwarzenegger and Sinbad as rival fathers desperately trying to secure a Turbo Man action figure for their sons. In real life, Tickle Me Elmo figures, based on the popular Sesame Street characters, were the Cabbage Patch Kids of the '90s, with an absolute mania for them reportedly resulting in near riots across the country.

Other toys that reached similarly frenzied peaks of popularity during that decade include the Mighty Morphin Power Rangers range of action figures, the revolutionary Nintendo 64 gaming system, and Furby'sâthe interactive electronic plushies that enchanted thousands and gave just as many the absolute creeps.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that november 25 sees the release of Focker-In-Law, the newest film in the Meet the Parents franchise. The 2000 installment follows Ben Stiller and his fiancÃ©e, Teri Polo, as he meets her mother and father (played by Blythe Danner and Robert De Niro) for the first time, and the comedic chaos that follows.

However, this movie was not actually an original production: it was a remake of the 1992 indie film of the same title, directed by the filmmaker Greg Glienna. The original is also a much darker film than its more famous remake: as Variety put it, "Who ever heard of a comedy where everyone gets maimed, drowned, shot or commits suicide?... 'Meet the Parents' turns a visit with the in-laws into a living nightmare." Here's a look at the original film on which a long-running franchise was built (and which the distributor later tried to keep the public from seeing).

According to recent reports, like the later version of the story, the 1992 film explores the idea of what happens when a man meets his future in-laws, but in Glienna's version, it ventures into much more serious territory, with multiple characters being killed as the story unfolds. Unlike the expensive Hollywood remake, the original was shot on a budget of only $30,000, and in addition to directing, Glienna played the lead role and co-wrote the script with Mary Ruth Clark. The project was originally sold to National Lampoon to be released as part of their self-titled series of films, but the deal fell through, leaving its future uncertain at first. Â.

Industry observers note that however, it received some positive critical attention when it made its debut: Variety reviewed the film when it premiered at the 1992 Just for Laughs Comedy Festival in Montreal, and described it as a "wonderfully twisted dark comedy." Their review also gives a number of details about the little-seen movie's story, including their summary of the plot's framing device: "Presented almost entirely in flashback, the tale begins when a gas station attendant warns a client en route to meet the future in-laws to 'turn back' while he still can. What follows is the tragic story of a previous future groom who didnât take the advice." The disasters which befall the characters include a saga in which "Greg blinds the mother with a fishing rod, ruins the family car, drowns the dog and accidentally climbs into bed with his fiancÃ©e's sister.".

It has been revealed that the original film was not widely distributed, but according to Glienna, one person who did see it was Steven Soderbergh, who liked it so much that he reached out to the writer-director about developing the original into a new version: "He called me and mentioned this should be a big studio film â this is very commercial. And they flew my co-writer, Mary Ruth Clark and myself to New York to work with him for three days, and we worked on the script â his vision of it." Ultimately, Universal acquired the rights to the film with the intention to make a new version based on the same premise.

However, after Glienna sold the remake rights to Universal, it turned out there was a catch in his deal. In a 2024 interview, Glienna explained: "I got a lousy lawyer, and we signed a contract. I don't know why this wasn't explained to me, or I didn't comprehend it, but I could only release it after a certain amount of time in a not-for-profit situation. I don't know why I would have agreed to that. Now, anytime I've tried to get the rights to release the film, they say no. I don't know why they don't want me to release this film.".

Glienna expressed his disappointment at the hurdle which had been placed in front of his original version. "We made this film to be seen. Why would they not let us show [it to] people? I don't understand." However, Glienna has attempted to look for the positives in the situation: "I try to look on the bright side. â¦ I'm still getting residuals on something I did 30 years ago." Today, the original film occasionally emerges on YouTube, but it remains to be seen whether it will ever be officially cleared for re-release in the future.

The woods are full of medicinal plants, from anti-inflammatory mushrooms to vitamin-rich stinging nettle, and even simply spending time in the woods can improve mental and physical health. But of course, cryptids have long been rumored to haunt the woods along Americaâs northwestern edge.Â.

According to recent reports, the most famous cryptid of them all just might be Sasquatch, also known as Bigfoot. This creature is typically described as an extremely hairy and tall humanoid creature, and sightings have been reported countless times over the years. Typically described as intelligent, shy, and wary of human contact, these creatures are sometimes said to be North Americaâs version of the Himalayan Yeti. In 1811, the explorer David Thompson discovered what he claimed were Sasquatch footprints, and sightings have continued near-ceaselessly since then.Â.

Sources indicate that also known as the Ebony Ape Cat, this panther-like mutant has reportedly been seen prowling the forests of the Pacific Northwest and the Columbia River Gorge. Some legends claim that this creature escaped from a government lab linked to the Manhattan Project, and reports have mentioned battery drainage and electromagnetic interferenceâso if youâre hiking in the Pacific Northwest and your phone suddenly dies or your compass goes haywire, watch out.

It has been revealed that this aquatic cryptid is said to come from Tillamook and Siletz legends, which tell of an ancient creature in the misty depths of Devilâs Lake near Lincoln City, Oregon that possesses many tentacles, a huge head, and glowing red eyes. Various stories describe multiple disappearances on the lake over the course of generations, and Native tribes in the area were said to make frequent offerings to appease the creature. There have also been whispers of occasional sightings in recent years.

It has been revealed that this water-dwelling monster is said to live in Wallowa Lake, Oregon. It is sometimes said to resemble the long-necked plesiosaur, an ancient marine reptile that went extinct some 66 million years ago. This cryptid likely owes its existence to a Nez Perce legend about lovers from warring clans who were, the story goes, killed by it when they ventured out onto the lake one evening. An 1885 article in the Wallowa Chieftain described a localâs encounter with the creature, writing that it âseemed to have a large, flat head, something like that of a hippopotamus, and its neck, which was about ten feet in length, was as large around as a man's body.â.

Recent findings suggest that this creature is said to resemble a black bear, but one thatâs completely hairless. Instead, this creature supposedly has leathery black skin as well as a furry beard and eyebrows. Stemming from lumberjack folklore of the 19th century, these beasts are rumored to be ravenously hungry and completely indestructible, though they can apparently be destroyed with fire.Â.

It has been revealed that another creature from lumberjack folklore, this cat is remarked to resemble a panther, albeit with one key difference: it has a large club on its tail that the creature uses to kill its prey (and, one would assume, any unfortunate hikers who encounter it). Sometimes rumored to be red-eyed and endowed with sharp spikes on its tail, this creature is definitely not one youâd want to meet on the trail.

Recent findings suggest that said to live beneath the ruins of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Tacoma, Washington, this creature is rumored to weigh up to 600 pounds. Legends about this creature emerged after the bridge collapsed in 1940, a disaster that actually did create an artificial reef for numerous sea creaturesâincluding giant Pacific octopuses, which are real creatures that have tentacle-spans up to 20 feet. While stories of the so-called âKing Octopusâ may be pure legend, this cryptid has a more legitimate basis in reality than most on this list.
