#473. Breaking: The pretendian wars

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4470 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Aeon ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The pretendian wars

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4470 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that what does it mean to belong to an ethnic community or group?
  • I am an Indigenous studies scholar in the US, and I study and wrote a book about self-indigenisation.
  • Anthropologists also, of course, study Indigenous people.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what does it mean to belong to an ethnic community or group? And who gets to decide? From an Indigenous American perspective, people are ‘Indigenous’ because they have family and clan-based ties to the community. When those ties don’t exist, stories fill the gap. But what if those stories are unverifiable? Or what if people take on ‘identities’ based on ‘knowledge’ that turns out not to be true, what then? How do they benefit from those narratives, whether true or not? Self-indigenisation based on self-identification describes people who claim to ‘be’ Indigenous, even when there is ample evidence that they have no Indigenous ancestry or lived experience as Indigenous people. It is a growing phenomenon in the United States and Canada as well as in other countries. Explaining why people pretend to be Indigenous when they aren’t is complicated, especially in light of the fact that the United Nations accepts self-identification as one criterion for indigeneity. However, in places where self-indigenisation has become egregious, it usually comes down to the fact that they perceive benefits, both material and psychological. The way it plays out varies from place to place, but there are commonalities across difference.

I am an Indigenous studies scholar in the US, and I study and wrote a book about self-indigenisation. I am an American Indian person, someone who comes from a long line of people who have been colonised. So mine is in part an insider perspective. As Native people, our experiences and cultures are unambiguous to us, if not always well known to others. They are well recorded in our families’ oral histories and usually in mountains of documentation, given that Indians are arguably the most documented ethnic group in the history of the US. Beginning with the earliest European settlers, missionaries and colonists kept track of the lives of Indigenous people for reasons including religious conversion, treaty negotiations, and census enumeration.

Anthropologists also, of course, study Indigenous people. The kinds of knowledge produced from external perspectives can vary widely from that which Indigenous people produce about themselves. Sometimes they conflict, but on occasion anthropologists’ research has helped tribes to recover lost knowledge. Both have their place. Anthropologists who study Indigenous cultural identity use the term ethnogenesis to describe how the identities of ethnic communities are formed or understood, and how they can change over time. Even Indigenous studies researchers recognise that, contrary to popular thought, Indigenous communities don’t remain static and unchanged over vast expanses of time. A popular tendency to misconceive of Indigenous people as gripped in terms of ‘authentic cultures’ doesn’t account for historical processes, including colonisation. History has imposed seismic changes on all Indigenous peoples, especially those who were in the way of foreign invasion and conquest. Expectations of cultural authenticity, then, can be a trap that doesn’t allow for peoples to experience history, to change with changing times.

In our modern world, there are of course many ways that cultures have evolved, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous. This blending of cultures through intermarriage has resulted in a blurring of lines that has made it difficult to make distinctions based on social constructions of race and ethnicity. Around the world, the questions are about what Indigeneity is and who decides, and how those questions are answered will vary. Laws and custom vary by country, and people will also make their own determinations. That mentioned, there is also the very real phenomenon of ethnic fraud, the wrongful claiming of Indigeneity by people without any demonstrable connection to a historical Indigenous community. In extreme examples, these claims are based on flagrant lying.

Some anthropologists have identified a phenomenon they refer to as neo-Indianism. It was first named by Jacques Galinier and Antoinette Molinié, whose book The Neo-Indians: A Religion for the Third Millennium (translated from French by Lucy Lyall Grant, 2013) examined the rise of a upcoming kind of Indigenism in Latin America where New Age rituals were invented for tourist consumption at Teotihuacan in Mexico, Cuzco in Peru, and other archaeological sites. Misrepresented as traditional Indigenous religion, the general public was unaware of the ruse even as it became a global industry. Similarly, there are growing instances of fake Aboriginal individuals in Australia. The same is happening in Aotearoa (New Zealand) among the Māori. Nowhere, however, is the problem of ethnic fraud more prevalent than in the US and Canada, where it is called ‘pretendianism’.

The Boy Scouts of America blatantly relied on playing Indian to build its movement under the guise of ‘honouring’ Native people.

Pretendianism is sometimes known by the more benign-sounding term cultural appropriation, which describes an array of offensive behaviours, such as sports mascots or events with inappropriate names and imagery, Halloween costumes, or the flagrant, unauthorised use of Native spirituality and culture, such as pipe ceremonies and sweat lodges, just to name a few. In Germany, for example, there is an entire subculture dedicated to the fetishisation of Native Americans, which perpetuates harmful, inaccurate stereotypes. If we understand Nativeness conceptualised as a spectrum, then cultural appropriation, ethnic fraud and pretendianism can be understood as existing on the extreme end, at which claims to Indigeneity are objectively illegitimate.

Recent findings suggest that the noted American Indian studies scholar Philip J Deloria coined the term ‘playing Indian’ with his seminal 1998 book of the same name, in which he traced a history of Americans’ penchant for adopting the dress and cultures of Native Americans for a variety of reasons, ranging from frivolous to serious and even politically motivated. The Boy Scouts of America, an extremely popular hobbyist club for children that romanticised America’s frontier days, blatantly relied on playing Indian in the early 20th century to build its movement under the guise of ‘honouring’ Native people. More than a century earlier, the 1773 Boston Tea Party, in which colonists costumed in Indian garb, was clearly a political incident that contributed to the incitement of a revolution. Many, many examples can be given of how the cultures of Native Americans are claimed for reasons that most Native people find offensive.

Pretendianism takes cultural appropriation to the next level when it goes beyond playing Indian to becoming Indian. People ‘become’ Indian when they claim to ‘be’ Indian with no connection to a tribal community, or little to no evidence of Native ancestry. It often begins with an individual who at some point in life transforms their identity claims from white (but sometimes other races or ethnicities) into Native American, based on family folklore or nothing at all, hence ‘race-shifting’, the term used in Australia. When those people have children and raise them with that mythology, pretendianism becomes generational. Amid many legitimate tribes who wrongfully lack political recognition by the US federal government, there are also hundreds of fake tribes that sprouted up in the 20th century. The majority of them claim to be Cherokee, but there are numerous others claiming to be Chumash, Shawnee, and more.

In a recent development, the work of Darryl Leroux shows how in Canada pretendianism is most prevalent in the east with a proliferation of ‘Abenaki’ groups. Faux Abenakis are also a problem in the state of Vermont, with four groups whom the state politically recognises but who have virtually no documentation to back up their claims of Abenaki descent. There are also dubious Metis and Inuit groups in Canada.

Grey Owl turned out to be Archie Belaney, a British-born white man with no Indigenous ancestry.

There are many pretendians whose names or faces you may recognise, emerging predominantly from the film industry. Perhaps most familiar is Iron Eyes Cody, who became best known as the ‘Crying Indian’ in the 1971 anti-littering commercial. Cody was not just an American actor who played Native American characters, he was an imposter of the highest order with a detailed but wildly false story about being Cherokee and Cree, which he wrote about in a 1980 autobiography. In 1996, a Latest Orleans Times-Picayune article revealed his true identity as the son of Italian immigrants. Born Espera Oscar de Corti, his film career began in the 1920s and spanned eight decades, with more than 200 film credits.

In Canada, the early 20th-century ‘Apache’ conservationist Grey Owl turned out to be Archie Belaney, a British-born white man with no Indigenous ancestry. Both Belaney and Cody married Native women, which doubtless helped legitimise their false claims. The same was true for James Young Deer, a silent-film actor, director and producer who rose to fame working for the Pathé Frères film company. Young Deer falsely claimed to be Winnebago/Ho-Chunk, and married the actual Ho-Chunk actress Lilian St Cyr.

Industry observers note that grey Owl. All images courtesy Library and Archives, Canada.

Born Archibald Belaney in Hastings, England.

Sources indicate that more recent exposures include Sacheen Littlefeather and Buffy Sainte-Marie. Littlefeather is best known as the ‘Native American’ woman who rejected an Oscar on behalf of Marlon Brando at the 1973 Academy Awards, ironically in the name of accurate representation of Native people in the film industry. I knew her for a decade before she died in 2022, and I document this story in detail in my book. A year after Littlefeather’s death, a bombshell story broke in the Canadian media that the rock-and-roll legend Buffy Sainte-Marie – who had risen to fame for her fiery Indian activism upon which her music was based – had fabricated a story about being born to a Piapot Cree family, adopted out, and raised by a white family. The evidence was overwhelmingly convincing that none of it was true.

It has been revealed that there are many other examples of high-profile people who long claimed Native identities but with thin or non-existent evidence. In Canada, they include the celebrated author Joseph Boyden, the influential children’s rights lawyer Mary Ellen Turpel-LaFond, the prominent academic Carrie Bourassa, and the filmmaker Michelle Latimer, to name a few. In some of these cases, awards and honorary doctorates have been rescinded after investigations revealed their façades. In the US, one example stands out for the attention it received in the political arena. In a dramatic misstep, the Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren in 2018 released the results of a DNA test in response to a challenge by the president Donald Trump about her claims to being Cherokee. The test showed that there was ‘strong evidence’ that she had a Native American ancestor six to 10 generations in the past. The Cherokee Nation, however, responded as it had for many years about her claims, that it had no record of Warren’s kinship to them, and that DNA does not always translate to Native identity or tribal belonging.

Industry observers note that pretendianism tends to be concentrated in entertainment, academia, publishing, government contracting, environmentalism and, increasingly, social media. In the US, the high-profile academics Ward Churchill and Andrea Smith, who lost their tenured professorships, have sparked intense debates about what it means to claim Native American identities with little or no evidence of connection to a tribal heritage. In another high-profile case, the University of California Berkeley professor Elizabeth Hoover drew the ire of Native American scholars after confessing that she had been wrongly claiming to be Mohawk throughout her career.

Recent findings suggest that it’s safe to say that, in the US and Canada, no other non-white ethnicity is as commonly falsely claimed as the Indigenous identity. Explaining why is not as simple, however, and researchers continue to offer compelling and sometimes provocative answers. There is no single explanation, and even in the cases of Canada and the US, both former British colonies and neighbouring North American countries, there are different factors and nuances. And there is likely more than one point of origin, historically and geographically, which would mean a potential variety of reasons for why people ‘became’ Indian at certain moments in time.

That remarked, there is an explanation that fits within the long history of the US’s colonialism and American Indian policy. This perspective can help us understand the motivations of those who fraudulently become ‘Indian’ and the social landscape of various eras. It shows us that, for example, pretendianism is not just a matter of personal and individual pathology – it’s systemic, which explains why it is continually perpetuated.

In a recent development, one point of pretendianism’s origin is in the late 19th century, when the US, under the ideology of manifest destiny, was engaged in the violent dispossession of Native Americans. With the 1887 passage of the General Allotment Act came the brutality of boarding schools, family separation, forced religious conversion, and the allotment of Native lands. The boarding schools were tools of forced assimilation. Land allotment accomplished these objectives by confining Native Americans to reservations, and encouraging a sedentary life of farming and industry.

Native people could earn money based purely on performing being Indian and the skills associated with it.

Sources indicate that all aspects of assimilation meant to move Native Americans into a cash-based capitalist economy. Boarding schools and land allotment forced a shift in their fundamental way of life, one in which everything is commodified, a concept previously unknown in Native life.

Sources indicate that by the 1920s, federal policymakers had recognised that assimilation was a catastrophic failure because it produced widespread poverty and all manner of social ills in reservation communities. Farming and ranching often proved to be unviable on many reservations. But there was one way that Native people could earn a lucrative living in the late 19th century: performing in the Wild West indicates that were sweeping the country. The majority of Native Americans who were recruited to Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West show and others were veterans of the Plains Indian wars. For decades, the US had been fighting wars of aggression against Plains and other tribes in the west to force them on to reservations, thus freeing up vast tracts of land for settlers. Militarily defeated and succumbing to the US’s policy of Americanisation, many Indians went from prisoner-of-war camps to the Wild West shows. For the first time, Native people could earn money based purely on performing being Indian and the skills associated with it. This is the historical moment when Nativeness became a commodity, a way to make money from who one was, ethnically.

Industry observers note that the US film industry has deep roots in the Wild West shows. Westerns were a prominent thematic genre of the early films, at a time when the US was contemplating the closing of the frontier. No longer a military threat, Native peoples became highly romanticised as Americans lamented the ‘vanishing Red Man’ in film. It was a natural progression, then, when the Show Indians became Movie Indians. It wasn’t long before people of other races and ethnicities began passing themselves off as Native Americans to obtain roles. The War Paint Club was the first Native American advocacy group, formed in 1926 to combat problems like fair representation and Native American roles for Native Americans in the industry.

In this way, Southern California became ground zero for the normalisation of Native ethnic fraud. Throughout the 20th century, other circumstances arose expanding opportunities to falsely claim Native American heritage based on no more than a family rumour, or simply the desire to profit financially. They included loose land-claims processes; changes in census rules that allowed for self-identification, and the reduction of the negative stigma of being Native American. In addition, a US government federal relocation programme in the 1950s led to urban Native American population centres where people with false claims could blend in as Native without community accountability; and a budding New Age industry that capitalised on all things Native American. California was the centre for all of these.

Sources indicate that people are often mystified when they learn about the pretendian phenomenon; why would someone want to claim a heritage they weren’t born into? Identity commodification, coincident with the growth of Hollywood, gives us a conceptual tool to understand its historical particularity. Over the previous century, the opportunities for material gain associated with this ethnic fraud have only grown, and they show up in several specific spheres: film and entertainment, academia, publishing, government contracting, and environmental activism.

According to recent reports, it’s not difficult to see why film and entertainment would attract opportunists looking to capitalise on an ethnically ambiguous appearance, paired with a convincing story. Iron Eyes Cody and Buffy Sainte-Marie were of Italian ancestry, and performativity is a key aspect of pretendianism. The ability to pass as Native American can be a door-opener, especially in casting rooms, but in other spaces as well. Yet, even when one does not ‘look’ stereotypically Native, a good story can compensate.

Fraudulently obtaining government contracts not only siphons away resources, it sows distrust and suspicion.

Stories help how many academics and authors deliver a compelling performance, regardless of whether they can pass as Native based on looks. In higher education, the ability to use words convincingly gives a leg up in competitive job markets, sometimes at the expense of actual, verifiably Native people. In academia, there is always caution about violating anti-discrimination laws, so hiring committees steer clear of asking about a person’s Native heritage, even when entire careers are built on identity claims. Such was the case with Elizabeth Hoover, whose environmental research in Mohawk communities was facilitated by her supposed Mohawk heritage.

In a recent development, in the publishing world, a gifted storyteller can cash in on the experiences of Native people. There are many books on the market by authors who co-opt Native culture, Native aesthetics, even Native trauma as though they are their own. In Canada, Boyden won many top Canadian book awards, honorary degrees and prestigious teaching appointments for his novels and short stories about Native life, based on his supposed lived experience. But Boyden was another fraudster, not a First Nations person, and is one of many examples of people who absorbed valuable resources meant for legitimate Indigenous people. Thanks to deep investigative journalism, his lack of Indigenous heritage was exposed in 2016. Boyden has since unconvincingly defended himself as having a small amount of Indigenous ancestry.

Industry observers note that native identity fraud also occurs in government contracting. In 2019, the Los Angeles Times conducted an investigation revealing that, since 2000, more than $300 million had gone to 12 companies claiming membership in three fake Cherokee tribes under federal, state and municipal programmes for minority businesses. One of the businesses turned out to be owned by the brother-in-law of the then-Congressional representative for California, Kevin McCarthy. Fraudulently obtaining government contracts does a double harm. It not only siphons away resources, it sows distrust and suspicion toward legitimate tribally affiliated businesses.

Industry observers note that since the rise of the environmental movement in the 1970s, there has been a marked surge in Native American cultural appropriation, including patterns of Native becoming. During the US presidency of Joe Biden, we saw an elevation in influence of Indigenous cultural knowledge related to climate change resilience strategies up to the highest levels of policymaking, including the White House. The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, the Inflation Reduction Act and other legislation that privileged green energy, environmental justice and Indigenous knowledge in climate resilience projects brought material benefits to Native communities through unprecedented levels of funding for environmental and energy projects. But fraud dilutes its effectiveness.

The surge in funding coincided with a proliferation of Indigenous conservation and environmental nonprofit organisations. In many cases, Indigenous conservation groups were led by legitimately Indigenous people. But when grant programmes are opened up to groups who are not federally recognised tribes, there tends to be far less scrutiny about who the leaders are of an ‘Indigenous led’ group. The same is true in the philanthropy world. Private funders are often ill-equipped to make those kinds of determinations and sometimes fear that enquiring about them is rude or even illegal. Too often, the result has been the distribution of grants (in the environmental sector and beyond) to people or groups posing as Native, but with no verifiable Native American heritage.

There are other ways that posing as an Native American can be lucrative. Again in California, for example, where there is a proliferation of groups that call themselves ‘tribes’. Some are more legit than others, and there is no law prohibiting a group from calling itself a tribe. One group known as the Northern Chumash Tribal Council (NCTC) near San Luis Obispo, for instance, began as a ‘cultural monitoring’ group, overseeing the development of sensitive sites where there might be Native American human remains or other burial items. Contracts for cultural monitoring can command hundreds of thousands of dollars and, while laws allow only the ‘most likely descendants’ to monitor a site, they are notoriously lax. Fred Harvey Collins, the founder of NCTC, also went on to lead an effort to establish a national marine sanctuary, garnering significant attention and massive cultural and financial support. However, a legal battle involving his ancestry revealed in 2017 that he possessed no Native American heritage.

Claiming to be Native allows one to distance oneself from America’s violent past.

Sources indicate that not everyone who dubiously calls themselves Native American does it for financial gain. In the US and Canada, it is wildly common to hear people talk about having ‘Indian blood’ or a mysterious Native American ancestor somewhere in the family tree, with no evidence whatsoever to back up the family lore. Sometimes, commercial DNA tests will suggest trace amounts of Indigenous ancestry in the distant past (recall Warren’s case), but as the scholar Kim TallBear has shown in Native American DNA (2012), from a Native standpoint, without a tribal community or family ties, DNA isn’t enough to legitimately call oneself Native American, and certainly not with any legal standing.

So what’s in it for them – what are the benefits of untruthfully claiming Native American heritage?

Industry observers note that there are psychological, affective benefits to thinking one has a linkage, however distant, to the ‘original Americans’. Who, after all, is more ‘American’ than Native Americans? In another strand of reasoning, claiming to be Native allows one to distance oneself from America’s violent past. If one is the colonised, they must not be coloniser. Self-indigenising is a way to be absolved of responsibility for the crimes of colonialism and maintain the fiction of familial innocence.

It has been revealed that ultimately, though, in a country founded on the rights to private property and free speech, identity is perceived as a personal possession, something one can claim at will. In the US, there is a strong common belief that a person can be whoever and whatever they say they are, regardless of facts or evidence.

Recent findings suggest that native people have come to see the stakes of pretendianism as higher than ever. When university and entertainment jobs, contracts and grants meant for actual Native Americans are taken by people with no connection to legitimate tribal communities, it constitutes stealing resources from the descendants of people who have already been victimised by centuries of theft and loss. Money that is meant to help mitigate those patterns of erasure is unintentionally rendered a tool of more erasure.

At the same time, determining who is Native is not always a simple or easy task. There is a wide, grey area on the spectrum of Nativeness, where people can be legitimately Native American and not be an enrolled member of a federally recognised tribe. Confusion and fear about how to determine who is legitimately Native in our institutions has contributed to the perpetuation of pretendianism. There is growing recognition that something can and must be done to ensure that the resources meant for Native people go to Native people.

In a recent development, in the US, this has long been acknowledged in the art world. Since 1935, the Native American art market has been governed by the Indian Arts and Crafts Board, a US government agency within the Department of the Interior. It was originally set up to encourage the growth of the market, promoting economic self-sufficiency of ‘federally recognised American Indians and Alaska Natives (Indians)’. In 1990, US Congress passed the Indian Arts and Crafts Act, a truth-in-advertising law with strict requirements that anyone selling art as ‘Indian’-made should be enrolled in a federal or state-recognised tribe, or be a certified artisan of the tribe. It is meant to ensure authenticity, in turn guarding the commercial value of Indian-made art. While the law is widely viewed as deeply flawed for the ways it excludes documented Native people and simultaneously includes people from state-recognised groups, it does act as a bulwark against fraud.

Wrongly claiming Native American heritage is akin to stolen valour, especially when leveraged for financial or professional gain.

In a recent development, the art world is virtually the only realm of social life with regulatory guardrails against Native ethnic fraud. Aside from this, those addressing the issue with the most urgency are in universities, particularly in Canada. There, a few colleges have implemented verification processes for admissions and scholarship applications. In the US, fears about violating race-based anti-discrimination laws present significant obstacles to implementing similar verification procedures.

Sources indicate that scholars push back against these fears by emphasising that Native Americans are more accurately understood as a political group than as a racial group by virtue of their sovereignty. Verification involves questions about relationships to claimed tribal communities, not questions about race. It’s not unlike asking for proof of military service for those who seek a veteran’s benefits. Wrongly claiming to be a veteran is called stolen valour and can lead to legal consequences. Wrongly claiming Native American heritage is akin to stolen valour, especially when it is leveraged for financial or professional gain. At the very least, it should not be rewarded.

It has been revealed that the pretendian wars that Indigenous people are fighting in the US and abroad are aimed at spreading awareness that wrongful Native-claiming is not a harmless frivolity. Valuable resources are being diverted from those to whom they are intended. In some cases, it is a criminal offence, and more needs to be done to guard against it. It should be just as socially unacceptable to illicitly claim Native American heritage as it is to illicitly claim to be a military veteran. People with unsubstantiated stories about Native American heritage should seriously rethink those claims before perpetuating them. They should do the research to find out the truth, but if no evidence is found, they should stop repeating the story. They should also remember that DNA tests showing Indigenous ancestry do not substitute for kinship; this is how belonging is determined in most tribal communities. Until then, Native people are sounding the alarm bells with urgency and determination.

Madeleines are small sponge cakes baked in molds shaped like seashells with the signature bump, la bosse, proudly protruding from the top. In a recent development, as much as I love a plain madeleine, I adore a citrus-scented one. My first madeleine, my Proustian moment, was not at a lovely Parisian pâtisserie. No, my family and I were visiting some of my mother’s friends in Paris and not knowing what they were, I grabbed a bag of lemon madeleines in a local supermarket, simply because I thought the seashell-shaped cakes were the prettiest thing I had ever seen. I could have inhaled them all in an afternoon if I had been allowed.

Seasonal citrus zests—lemons, of course, yuzus, blood oranges, mandarins, or a medley of several—find their way into my madeleines, but the tart-sweet, fruity, floral flavor of Cara Cara oranges is my favorite. Dusting the still-warm madeleines with floral and citrusy coriander-scented powdered sugar just before serving sends them over the top.

Sometimes, all the letters in certain words or phrases can be reshaped to form something completely different, but still readable. This is known as an anagram, defined by Merriam-Webster as âa word or phrase made by transposing the letters of another word or phrase.âÂ.

One of the most famous lines from William Shakespeareâs Hamlet is, âTo be or not to be: that is the question, whether tis nobler in the mind to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune.â Anagram expert Cory Calhoun found that all the letters in this phrase can be reshaped into the sentence: âIn one of the Bard's best-thought-of tragedies, our insistent hero, Hamlet, queries on two fronts about how life turns rotten.âÂ.

Literature is filled with examples of words and phrases that can be rearranged into oddly similar or relevant words and phrases. In Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets, it is revealed that the student Tom Marvolo Riddleâs name is an anagram for I Am Lord Voldemort. Vladimir Nabokov created his character Vivian Darkbloom with an anagram of his own name, and Samuel Butlerâs novel Erewhon takes its title from an anagram of the word nowhere.Â.

Another famous anagram appears in Stephen Kingâs The Shining, in which the child protagonist Danny writes the word REDRUM on a bathroom mirrorâa word that, of course, is an anagram for murder.

Anagrams have also appeared in beloved movies. The film October Skyâs name is an anagram of Rocket Boys, the book on which it was based. In the film The Matrix, the station between the real world and the false one is named Mobil, which is an anagram for limboâa word that refers to the realm in between heaven and hell, or any kind of liminal space between two different realities.

The Lebanese architect Lina Ghotmeh is known for works that preserve memories of the past but are built for the future. These notably include her design for the Estonian National Museum (completed in 2016), which transformed a former Soviet airfield, and Stone Garden (completed in 2020), an apartment building in her home city of Beirut, whose facade openings, filled with greenery, evoke bullet scars and shelling. This short documentary from the London-based director Stephen Pook deconstructs Ghotmeh’s approach to architecture, revealing how her designs and thoughtful use of materials are born of a process in which history matters as much as the physical environment. In particular, the film focuses on her aesthetics and philosophy in the context of another work that demands deep sensitivity to the past and a vision for the future: her redevelopment of the Western Range at the British Museum in London, which constitutes about a third of the iconic museum’s total gallery space.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that my earliest dessert obsession was the malted milkshake, which I indulged in every time I had enough babysitting money. My oldest, best friend, Toi, was equally obsessed with Whoppers, and we both wondered why malted sweets were so good. Turns out, the secret is in the combination of malted barley, wheat flour, and evaporated whole milk that gets toasted to caramelize the sugars contained in it.

Industry observers note that this cake is my latest malted creation. Layering the malted vanilla and chocolate batters so they create a striped pattern isn’t just an aesthetic choice. Doing so really does keep the flavors distinct. Starting off in a cold oven allows the cake to bake evenly without overbrowning and results in a smooth, fine, melt-in your-mouth crumb. For extra malted flavor, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with malted vanilla syrup in several additions, letting the syrup sink in after each addition.

I originally made this syrup to give my milkshakes that nostalgic, malt-shop flavor. But honey, it’s no one-hit wonder. It is a beautiful sweetener and is terrific when brushed on top of still-warm Striped Malted Pound Cake.

According to recent reports, I also drizzle it over roasted fruit and mix it into buttercreams, glazes, and frostings. For breakfast, I stir it into coffee or lattes, smoothies, yogurt, and oatmeal. And it’s got savoy game, too. Try it on a dinner plate, spooned over roasted sweet potatoes or carrots alongside roasted chops or chicken.

More delicious loaf cake recipes this way.

Makes one 9x5" loaf, 12 to 16 servings.

Grease a 9x5" loaf pan with softened butter or cooking spray. Dust the pan with all-purpose flour, shaking out any excess.

In a medium bowl, whisk together 1¾ cups / 220g all-purpose flour, 1⁄4 cup / 34g cornstarch, 1⁄2 tsp. fine sea salt, and 1⁄2 tsp. baking powder.

In a stand mixer fitted with the paddle, combine 16 Tbsp. / 2 sticks / 226g unsalted butter, at room temperature, 1¼ cups / 273g granulated sugar, and 1⁄4 cup / 37g malted milk powder. Beat, starting on low speed and increasing to medium-high speed until lightened in color and fluffy, 5–7 minutes, scraping down the sides of the bowl once or twice.

On medium-low speed, add 3 large eggs, at room temperature, one at a time, scraping down the sides of the bowl after each one is incorporated.

Add one-third of the flour mixture and beat on the lowest speed until just combined. Add 2 Tbsp. heavy cream and beat on low speed until just combined. Add another one-third of the flour mixture, beating until combined, and another 2 Tbsp. heavy cream to combine. Add the remaining one-third of the flour mixture and beat until the batter is smooth, scraping down the sides of the bowl as necessary. Mix in 1½ tsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract and 1½ tsp. whiskey or bourbon (if using).

Transfer 1½ cups of the batter to a medium bowl. Sift in 3 Tbsp. unsweetened cacao powder or cocoa powder and add the remaining 1⁄4 cup heavy cream, stirring to form a smooth chocolate batter.

To create the striped layers, drop 1 cup of the vanilla cake batter into the center of the loaf pan and then drop ½ cup of the chocolate batter on top of the vanilla batter. The alternating layers do not have to totally cover each other and let the layers spread naturally. Continue to drop those same-size portions of batter directly on top of each other, alternating the vanilla and chocolate, until all the batter is used. The batter should have spread to the corners, but if not, gently rap the pan on the counter to help it even out. Smooth the top with a small offset spatula.

Place the cake in a cold oven and set the temperature to 300°F. Bake until the loaf is golden, its top is slightly cracked, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean, 1 hour 20 minutes–1 hour 30 minutes.

Let the cake cool in the pan on a wire rack for 10 minutes, then run a knife around the edges to release it. Invert the cake onto a wire rack, reinvert, and cover the warm cake loosely in plastic wrap until completely cooled. If desired, use a pastry brush to brush the top of the cake with ½ cup Malted Vanilla Syrup several times, letting the syrup sink in after each addition. The cake will keep, wrapped in plastic at room temperature, for up to 5 days.

It has been revealed that in a small saucepan, combine ⅓ cup / 73g granulated sugar, ½ cup / 120g water, 2 Tbsp. malted milk powder, and pinch of fine sea salt. Cook over medium heat until bubbling, whisking until the sugar and malt powder dissolve and the mixture becomes glossy, slightly thickened, and evenly beige, 2–3 minutes.

Remove from heat and whisk in 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or pure vanilla extract. Let cool slightly before using. This will keep in a covered jar or airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 1 week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As people who write about food and kitchen gadgets for a living, Bon Appétit editors are constantly surrounded by a wide range of products. Between our own purchases and the endless stream of samples sent our way, it means there’s always something new coming across our desks and into our homes. Each month we round up the standouts we tested or bought ourselves that changed the way we cook and eat.

This month, holiday-ready martini glasses, turmeric-laced bone broth, and digestion-friendly tea.

Read on for all the products we obsessed over in November.

This summer, I spent a week in Paris with my family and gloriously found myself eating steak frites on more than one occasion. Besides the perfectly cooked bavette and thin, crisp fries, I was enamored with the bistro aesthetic—down to the super-sharp and sleek steak knives I used for each meal. When I came across Made In Cookware’s set, I knew it was a sign that I, too, could adopt this sophisticated French look. These knives are manufactured in Thiers, France, a region known for knife-making, which speaks to their aesthetic and craftsmanship. I love that they’re non-serrated; the sharp edges maintain the integrity of meat and can be sharpened once dull. These steak knives are also full tang, which means they’re constructed with a single rod of stainless steel from tip to handle. And speaking of the handle—the feature that attracted me to this set in the first place—they come in several materials, including olive wood, black polymer, and (my pick) pearlescent acetate. — Melissa Knific, contributing editor.

What is a martini glass if not a tiny birdbath for my olives? These Year and Day glasses are my favorite kind: classic and elevated, but durable. They’re great for anything you’d serve up, and the best part is that I can set them in the dishwasher at the end of the night. —Casey Hendricks, executive director of audience development.

A woman in her late 20s who starts her mornings with a mug of bone broth as the weather gets cold—I know I’m a cliché. But this chicken bone broth from Fond, specifically the turmeric and black pepper variety, truly does start my day off on the right note. There’s eight grams of protein per cup, sure, but my favorite part is that it’s made without alliums (like garlic and onion) so it’s especially kind to my tummy. Instead, the broth gets its flavor from carrots, turmeric root, celery, lemon juice, cracked black pepper, and thyme. All the vegetables Fond uses are organic and they use 100% pasture-raised chicken, so it’s as close to making my own bone broth at home as I can get, without having to simmer a pot for 18 hours. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

M6HG Instant Hot Countertop Reverse Osmosis Water Filter.

In a recent development, there were a couple of things happening at my house at the same time: First, my wife’s lovely and enormous collection of houseplants continued growing; second, we decided to get a water softener to fight against the notoriously hard water in my part of Newly introduced Jersey. Those two things don’t go together well because softened water and its added sodium can be bad for plants long term. A reverse osmosis system is one way to fight against that, but we didn’t have the budget (or really the need) for a whole-home RO system, nor did we have the space under our sink for one of those. Enter Waterdrop’s countertop RO. The M6HG has an autofilling pitcher that makes plant care convenient, but it’s also turned out it’s getting more use than our fridge filter for drinking. Water comes out a chilly 48 degrees and measures precisely to 4, 8, or 16 ounces (which my kids love for some reason). It also dispenses at 77℉, 113℉ (supposedly good for baby formula), 131℉, 149℉, 167℉, 185℉ (for delicate tea), and 203℉ (for French press or pour-over coffee). Oh yeah, it’s on major sale for Black Friday. — Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor.

In a recent development, I never grew up with advent calendars, but I can totally see what the fuss is about. My family and I take such joy opening up a window of surprise every morning. Since the advent calendars in our home are usually food-related, we’ll enjoy the treat together later in the evening, with varying degrees of jostling, depending on what it is. Well, looks like the 2026 holiday season will be another one of us throwing elbows because we have our hands on BonBon’s magnificent Lighthouse Advent Calendar. No paper windows here! The cool Swedish confectionary’s calendar is actually a long tower filled with 24 individually wrapped, numbered mini bags of vegan gummies. The daily candy should be a mix of BonBon’s exclusive new flavors as well as its beloved classics. I think my Swedish husband and daughter are already losing their minds (it’s only November) and I’m already fearing for our next dental visit, but it is giving this exceptionally fast holiday season a good reason to stop and appreciate a fun, sweet moment every day. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food director.

Sources indicate that ’Tis the season for...soup. My Dutch oven and I have been on a tear making favorites like white chicken chili, chicken-lentil soup, and tons of minestrone. In my attempt to “be frugal,” I’ve been bringing my soups to work for lunch in my, yes, ludicrously capacious bag, and more specifically, my 20 oz. insulated thermos by Hydroflask. It’s truly the perfect size for a lunch-appropriate portion and keeps my soup warm from morning until around 1 p.m. when it’s time to eat between meetings. It’s completely leak-proof which is crucial for a soup commute. And, it’s dishwasher safe, so when I come home after work, I can just throw it in the dishwasher to use all over again the next day. A small investment for a considerably more delightful desk lunch. —June Kim, executive editor.

Limited Edition Peppermint Mocha Barista.

Industry observers note that I’m not really a pumpkin spice latte girl, but a peppermint mocha is a seasonal drink I can definitely get behind—so when I heard that Táche, the brand behind my favorite pistachio milk, had come out with a Peppermint Mocha flavor, I was very eager to try it. Sure enough, it was love at first sip. It tastes deeply chocolatey thanks to the addition of Dutch-processed cocoa, and has just enough peppermint flavor to feel festive and balanced without veering into toothpaste territory. I’ve been mixing it with a shot of espresso over ice to make an easy peppermint mocha latte, but to be honest with you, my favorite way to enjoy it is straight up, chilled and poured into a glass. —Alaina Chou, commerce writer.

In a recent development, I’m often hesitant to use pre-made, packaged products when it comes to cooking. One could say I’m a bit of a control freak, but I’m not opposed to a shortcut, especially when it’s after 7 p.m. on a weeknight and I still need to get dinner on the table.

Enter Gymkhana Butter Masala Mild Simmer Sauce. The London-based, two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant recently launched a line of sauces, marinades, and chutneys inspired by its iconic dishes. I paired the butter masala sauce with cubed paneer that I quickly broiled, topped everything with fresh cilantro, and served it alongside basmati rice.

Sources indicate that the sauce is rich, complex, and packed with flavor, yet all it requires is a quick reheat. Dinner came together in less than 30 minutes and tasted like something I’d order at a restaurant. Needless to say, I’ll be stocking up on a few more jars. —Ali Inglese, executive producer.

According to recent reports, I’ve absolutely been loving this soothing tisane (aka herbal tea!) from La Vie tea. Produced in the French tradition—and primarily sourced directly from French gardens!—these delicate blends are all made from herbs, flowers, and spices as opposed to tea leaves. The digestion-friendly blend I’ve been enjoying is mostly ginger, fennel, and chamomile, with notes of orange and cinnamon—I’ve been parked on the couch with a huge mug of this brew after many a hearty dinner this month. I’m looking forward to dipping into the lavender-scented “Calm” blend ahead of the forthcoming hectic holiday season! —Rebecca Firkser, test kitchen editor.

I’m a complete nut for ice cream. Regardless of the season, I’m always ready to pop a pint open for dessert (or a mid-day pick-me-up, let’s be honest). And I can say unequivocally that Graeter’s is my favorite ice cream of all time. Even Oprah agrees with me. She named it her favorite too back in 2002. And thanks to the modern miracle that is dry ice, you can have the best ice cream on the planet sent straight to your door. This option is available year-round, allowing you to pick your own flavors in packs of six or twelve pints (get the Coconut Chip if you know what’s good for you). But if you want to get in the holiday spirit, start with the Holiday Pack. It offers an assortment of seasonal flavors as well as the always in-demand, Black Raspberry Chip. Whether you’re treating yourself this year or shopping for that impossible-to-buy-for friend, this small-batch ice cream from the Buckeye State is the way to go. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on the northwestern tip of France's Noirmoutier Island, behind the 19th-century Church of the Sacred Heart, a small cemetery overlooks the Atlantic Ocean. Beyond its stone walls stretch the waters of the Bay of Biscay, with the tiny island of Le Pilier visible on the horizon. Many of those buried here were sailors and fishermen whose lives were intimately connected to the sea.

Among the traditional graves stands a striking row of white Commonwealth headstones, commemorating the victims of a largely forgotten maritime tragedy.

On June 17, 1940, as British troops and civilians were being evacuated from France, German aircraft bombed the British troopship HMT Lancastria off the coast of Saint-Nazaire. The ship sank within minutes, taking thousands of lives in one of the deadliest maritime disasters of World War II.

In the following days, the Atlantic currents carried the bodies of victims onto the French coastline, including the shores of Noirmoutier.

Today, the cemetery contains 40 Commonwealth war burials, 22 of them unidentified. Most were victims of the Lancastria disaster.

Overlooking the very ocean that claimed so many lives, L'Herbaudière's marine cemetery remains a peaceful yet poignant reminder of the island's maritime heritage and the tragedies of war.

The cemetery is located on Avenue Mourain, behind the Church of the Sacred Heart (Église du Sacré-Cœur), in the village of L'Herbaudière, approximately 5 kilometers (3 miles) northwest of Noirmoutier-en-l'Île. Parking is available near the church. The Commonwealth war graves can be found in the southern corner of the cemetery. Take some time to admire the beautiful views over the Atlantic Ocean and the nearby island of Le Pilier. As this is an active cemetery, visitors are asked to remain respectful of the graves and those paying their respects.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday hasnât always been about filling shopping bags to the brim and taking advantage of online deals.

Sources indicate that according to History, the first Black Friday had nothing to do with clothing discounts or shoppers fighting over the latest retail items. The date wasnât even close to Thanksgiving.

So, what really happened on the first âBlack Friday,â and how did it evolve into a shopping holiday that spurs Americans to camp outside stores and relentlessly add to their online shopping carts?Â.

Letâs flip back a page or two in American history and see what we can find!Â.

According to recent reports, the first Black Friday was on September 24, 1869, otherwise known as the crash of the U.S. gold market.Â.

In a recent development, two devious Wall Street financiers, Jay Gould and Jim Fisk, let greed consume them and decided to buy as much gold as they could get their hands on, drive up its price, and sell it for a greater profit. This wasnât the first time the deceitful pair had resorted to such schemes. According to PBS, one year earlier, they âused stock fraud and bribery to keep Cornelius Vanderbilt from taking control of the Erie Railroad.â.

It has been revealed that connected to President Ulysses S. Grant through his brother-in-law, Abel Rathbone Corbin, Gould and Fisk put a bug in the Commander-in-Chiefâs ear, persuading him not to sell more gold so its value would rise. With Corbinâs approval, General Daniel Butterfield became assistant treasurer of the United States and promised to keep Gould and Fisk privy to the government's gold transactions.Â.

In a recent development, when Grant discovered what Corbin, and therefore Butterfield, was doing behind the scenes, he âordered the sale of $4,000,000 in government gold.â This decreased the price of gold from $160 to $133 and sent the stock market tumbling down. Investors immediately panicked, brokerage houses went bankrupt, and the market fell 20 percent, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of Latest York.

Investors who had borrowed money to buy gold at the higher price suddenly couldnât repay their loans, and Corbin was among them. Gould, however, was savvy enough to sell his gold before the collapse. He ended up controlling the Union Pacific Railroad, Western Union Telegraph Company, and the Manhattan Elevated Railroad. His partner, whom he hadnât told of his sales, wasnât so lucky.

Three years after the first Black Friday, Fisk was shot and killed by financier Edward Stokes, ironically, during a dispute that involved money. Neither Gould nor Fisk ever served time behind bars for the scandal that caused the first Black Friday.

According to recent reports, the term was reborn in the 1950s, when tourists traveled to Philadelphia in droves on the Friday after Thanksgiving for the annual ArmyâNavy football game. Police officers worked extra shifts to manage the crowds, according to History. Shoplifters contributed to the chaos by stealing from stores, demanding more attention from law enforcement.

From then on, Philadelphia referred to the day as âBlack Friday.â In 1961, local officials tried to rename it âBig Friday,â but it didnât catch on. Then, in the 1980s, retailersÂ reinterpreted Black Friday as a day when stores moved from red (operating at a loss) to black (making a profit) through extensive holiday discounts.Â.

It has been revealed that though we've held on to this version of Black Friday for decades, its story began with the U.S. gold market crash of 1869 and Philadelphiaâs hectic ArmyâNavy weekend in the â50s.Â.

Today, the beloved shopping holiday isnât even contained to a single day. It now spans online and in-store sales that begin weeks in advance and continue for days afterward. In 2026, we can be thankful that Black Friday has nothing to do with stock market crashes and lawless shopping chaos.

#462. Latest Update: Chile Is Getting a Massive Upcoming National Park in 2027

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1238 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Matadornetwork ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Chile Is Getting a Massive Upcoming National Park in 2027

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve already hiked the W Trek in Torres del Paine, you may want to start looking a little farther south for your next trip to Patagonia.
  • Sources indicate that in early November 2026, conservation nonprofit Rewilding Chile signed an agreement with the Chilean government to donate an additional 55,186 acres of land toward the creation of Cape Froward National Park (Parque Nacional Cabo Froward).
  • In a recent development, the park is expected to be officially established by the end of 2027, though you can already hike and camp in parts of the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve already hiked the W Trek in Torres del Paine, you may want to start looking a little farther south for your next trip to Patagonia. Chile is planning to establish a upcoming national park in 2027, at the southernmost point of mainland South America, about 40 miles south of Punta Arenas.

Sources indicate that in early November 2026, conservation nonprofit Rewilding Chile signed an agreement with the Chilean government to donate an additional 55,186 acres of land toward the creation of Cape Froward National Park (Parque Nacional Cabo Froward). That brings the upcoming park’s total acreage to about 452,000 acres, creating a park 50 percent larger than originally planned when it was introduced in March 2024. For comparison, that’s nearly twice the size of Washington’s Mount Rainier National Park.

In a recent development, the park is expected to be officially established by the end of 2027, though you can already hike and camp in parts of the area. But getting there is a bit more complicated than visiting most of Chile’s national parks, especially if you want to stand on the actual cape: there are no roads to it, and hikers have to time their river crossings with the tides.

A humpback whale off the coast of Cape Froward. Photo: Suzie Dundas.

Sources indicate that by November 2025, Rewilding Chile had donated more than 314,000 acres to the project. The November 2026 agreement adds another piece of private property to the project, and the government is contributing about 82,500 acres of state-owned conservation land, roughly 13,000 more than it originally promised.

According to recent reports, one of the remaining steps before the park is official is a consultation with Indigenous peoples of the area, whose ancestral territory includes Cape Froward. Those discussions, which cover how creating the park could affect their traditional customs, practices, and relationships with the land, are expected to run through March 2027.

Cape Froward will also become the southernmost mainland stop on Chile’s Route of Parks, a roughly 1,700-mile tourism and conservation route through Chilean Patagonia that starts near Puerto Montt.

A huemul deer in Chile. Photo: JGacituaCL/Shutterstock.

Recent findings suggest that one of the main reasons for establishing the park is to protect the huemul, an endangered species of deer native to Chile and Argentina. There’s a depiction of one with a condor on Chile’s national coat of arms, though they’re becoming less common to see in the wild. Cape Froward is one of the species’ last remaining habitats.

The area is also close to an endangered ruddy-headed goose refuge, and its forests have Guaitecas cypress trees, which are the southernmost naturally occurring conifer species in the world.

Protecting the land can also help fight climate change. The park contains lots of wetland areas, which have accumulated layers of partially decomposed vegetation over thousands of years. That means there are large amounts of carbon stored in the ground, and draining or damaging that land would release it into the atmosphere, contributing to climate change.

There are historical and cultural reasons for protecting Cape Froward, too. The Kawésqar people have lived and traveled by canoe in the region for thousands of years, and naturalist Charles Darwin spent time exploring the Brunswick Peninsula during his voyage on the HMS Beagle in 1834.

Industry observers note that the closest city is Punta Arenas, which has direct flights from Santiago. Many Americans headed to Patagonia fly to Punta Arenas before driving north to Puerto Natales, the closest town to popular Torres del Paine National Park. To get to Cape Froward, you’ll head in the opposite direction, for about 45 miles (roughly 90 minutes) until the road ends near Punta Árbol.

The main draw for backpackers is the trek to the Cruz de los Mares, a large metal cross on a hill above Cape Froward marking the southernmost point of mainland South America. The full out-and-back trip can take about a week, much of it spent hiking along rocky beaches and crossing rivers that may be impassable at high tide. Outfitters in Punta Arenas like Chile Nativo run guided expeditions, sometimes covering some of the distance by boat.

Industry observers note that for a more moderate outing, hike to the San Isidro Lighthouse, built in 1904 and accessible via a 3.5-mile each-way walk along the coast from a trailhead at the end of Route 9. Much of the hike is along the beach, where it’s possible to spot dolphins and other marine mammals in the strait. For a more challenging hike, take the 7.4-mile round-trip route up Mount Tarn, a roughly 2,700-foot mountain that Charles Darwin summited in February 1834. The route passes through muddy forests before climbing above the tree line, with views toward Tierra del Fuego on clear days.

According to recent reports, hikers on Mount Tarn. Photo: Pax Multimedia/Shutterstock.

In a recent development, it’s also worth spending a day on the water. Humpback whales migrate to southern Chile from December to April to feed, and boat tours from the Punta Arenas area visit nearby Francisco Coloane Marine Park. Local outfitters also offer guided sea kayaking expeditions along the Brunswick Peninsula, including multiday trips to some of the more isolated stretches of coastline.

November through March is generally the best time to visit, with particularly long daylight hours in December and January. Even in summer, temperatures can drop close to freezing overnight, and strong winds can complicate both hiking and boat travel. Snow is always possible.

Unlike Torres del Paine, Cape Froward doesn’t have a network of refugios where you can buy dinner or rent a sleeping bag. Rewilding Chile has plans for trails, designated campsites, restrooms, and a shelter near the cape, though travelers shouldn’t expect all of those facilities to be ready when the park is officially established. For now, Punta Arenas is the best place to base yourself, stock up on supplies, and arrange guided trips.

Industry observers note that cape Froward isn’t the only national park project worth keeping tabs on over the next year. Several other countries are working on newly introduced park designations, and in some cases, you can already visit the proposed parks.

Ocmulgee Mounds, Georgia: Georgia could finally get its first national park. In November 2026, a bill to redesignate Ocmulgee Mounds National Historical Park in Macon cleared the House Natural Resources Committee. The existing park is free to visit and has hiking trails, a museum, and earthen mounds built more than 1,000 years ago. The bill still needs to pass both chambers of Congress, and if it doesn’t pass before the current session ends in early January 2027, it dies.

Sources indicate that seal River Watershed, Manitoba, Canada: Four First Nations are working with the Canadian and Manitoba governments to protect a roughly 12.4-million-acre watershed in northern Manitoba. The proposal could include a national park reserve in the area inhabited by polar bears, wolves, and caribou. Much of the area is unreachable by road but is popular for wilderness canoeing.

Great Koala National Park, Fresh South Wales, Australia: This one is actually expected to open before the end of 2026, making 2027 its first full year. The New South Wales Parliament passed legislation in October to add roughly 440,000 acres to its national park system, bringing the project to more than 1.17 million acres. The newly protected forests are home to an estimated 12,000 koalas, who will now have additional protections.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Historians actually now doubt that some of the most brutal methods of execution attributed to centuries past were real.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Humans have experimented with a lot of different execution methods over the years, with the most commonly used these days being lethal injection, electrocution, and hanging. But in the past there were many more ways of carrying out lethal punishmentâsome of which are as strange as they are horrifying.

Historians actually now doubt that some of the most brutal methods of execution attributed to centuries past were real. For instance, the brazen bull (which involved someone being placed inside of a hollow bronze bull and then a fire being lit underneath it) and the blood eagle (cutting open a personâs back and pulling their lungs out to create wings) both fall into the likely-fictional category. But there are other gruesomely creative execution methods from history that were definitely realâincluding the five examples below.

Sources indicate that volcanoes have caused thousands of accidental deaths throughout history, with pyroclastic flows and explosive blasts being the most common ways people are killed by them. But from the early 17th century to the early 19th century, Mount Unzen in Japan was also deliberately used to brutally execute people.

It has been revealed that during Japanâs Edo period, the Tokugawa shogunate feared the spread of Christianity and so essentially put the country under lockdown. Any Christians who were discovered were tortured and ordered to abandon their religion, and anyone who refused was executed in a rather unusualâand very painfulâway. They would be taken to Mount Unzen, a volcano located at the western tip of Japan, and thrown into its bubbling hot springs. Although it was a fairly fast deathâno one could survive long in the acidic boiling waterâit would have been agonizing.

For hundreds of years, elephants were trained to carry out public executions in South and Southeast Asia. The huge animals would place one of their massive feet on the condemned personâs head or torso to quickly crush them to death. But there were a few otherâfar cruelerâways that elephants could carry out the death penalty. In 1850, British diplomat Henry Charles Sirr described elephants in Sri Lanka âbeing taught to prolong the agony of the wretched sufferers by crushing the limbs, avoiding the vital parts.â The huge animals could also tear a person limb from limb with the aid of their trunk, or they could cut a person to death with the aid of blades that were fitted onto their tusks or feet. The practice of execution by elephant started dying out during the 17th and 18th centuries, when European countries began colonizing South and Southeast Asia.

Itâs often thought that people were executed at sea by being made to walk the plank, but this punishment was surprisingly used very rarely, and the reality was actually much worse. Some sailors were subjected to the horrors of keelhauling, which was invented by the Dutch and was used from around the mid-1600s to the mid-1800s.

It has been revealed that A line of rope would be looped around the shipâs keel, and the victim would be tied to one end and then dropped into the sea. Those on deck would then pull the other end, dragging the poor person across the keelâwhere they would be cut and bludgeoned by barnacles, ringbolts, and chains. This process would often be repeated multiple times; according to William Falconerâs An Universal Dictionary of the Marine (1780), âit is continued till the culprit is almost suffocated for want of air, benumbed with the cold of water, or stunned with the blows his head received by striking the shipâs bottom.â Although not always intended to be fatal, in practice the punishment would often end in death.

A particularly gruesome account of keelhauling, which occurred aboard the Egyptian vessel the Mehemet Ali, was described in 1882. Two sailors were subjected to the punishment and the news correspondent aboard wrote that âthe nose of one wretch was torn almost away, one ear was gone, and the shreds of the clothing he had worn clung to him only where they were held by his bonds. He was blood literally from head to foot. His companionâs condition was equally horrible.â Both men were unconscious and the reporter assumed they were dead.Â.

Recent findings suggest that during Thirty Yearsâ Warâwhich lasted from 1618 to 1648âSwedish soldiers gained a reputation for a particularly disgusting way of killing their German enemies: Schwedentrunk, which in German translates to âSwedish drink.â A funnel would be forced into the victimâs mouth and then a huge quantity of foul liquid (which was also sometimes boiling hot) was poured down their throat. Liquids used included dirty water, urine, and manure.

As you can imagine, schwedentrunk was an incredibly painful way to die, with the personâs intestines usually being filled to bursting. If they didnât burst, then bacterial infection was likely to finish the person off. âSo growing sicke, and their bellies swelling like a Tun, they have died by leysure with the greater torment,â wrote Philip Vincent in The Lamentations of Germany (1638).

The wheel is one of humanityâs most vital inventions, but itâs not only been used for good. The breaking wheel was a torture and execution device that dates back to Ancient Rome and was still sometimes used up until the 19th century. There were a variety of ways in which the wheel could be used to kill someone. Some executioners would drop the wheel itself onto a victim to break their bones, but most often the condemned person was tied to the wheelâeither across the spokes or bent around the rim. From there they were usually beaten to death with a cudgel or hammer, and sometimes a fire was also lit beneath them.

Someone tied to the breaking wheel could be put out of their misery with just one or two blows, but some people suffered many more than that. In 1581, German serial killer Peter Niersâwho was convicted of a staggering 544 murdersâwas subjected to a deliberately prolonged death, receiving 42 blows over the course of two days.

Sources indicate that the breaking wheel is also known as the Wheel of Catherineânamed after Saint Catherine of Alexandria, who at the start of the 4th century was sentenced to die on the wheel. It broke when she touched it, though, which was believed by some to be an act of divine intervention, and she was beheaded instead.Â.

#459. The Hidden Spiegeltent in Chicago, Illinois

The Hidden Spiegeltent in Chicago, Illinois

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (342 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These round wooden dance halls, lined with mirrors and stained glass, went from fair to fair.
  • Rapp & Rapp designed it, with the Oriental Theatre movie palace on the lower floors.
  • High above the theater, the architects put a large hall for Masonic meetings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spiegeltents were made to travel. These round wooden dance halls, lined with mirrors and stained glass, went from fair to fair. They went up fast and came down fast. The one on Randolph Street is not going anywhere. It was built indoors, on the 14th floor of a Loop building.

The building opened in 1926. Rapp & Rapp designed it, with the Oriental Theatre movie palace on the lower floors. The theater is now the James M. Nederlander Theatre. The whole building stands on the site of the Iroquois Theatre, where a fire in 1903 became one of the deadliest in American history.

High above the theater, the architects put a large hall for Masonic meetings. It sat empty for decades. Later it was turned into offices, and a dropped ceiling hid the room completely. When the building was converted into the Cambria Hotel, workers took that ceiling down and found the old hall again, steel bow trusses and all.

In 2019 the tent came over from Belgium in pieces, about 4,000 of them. Belgian tent builders put it together inside the hall, the traditional way, with no nails. It is about 72 feet across. From the hall, it looks like a small circus parked under factory trusses. Inside, there is carved wood, stained glass, velvet and mirrors everywhere. The mirrors are not just for looks. They let guests see around the posts that hold up the roof.

Since October 2026, the tent has been the home of Kermess by Circensia, which kept it right at the center of the room.

The tent is on Floor 14 of the Cambria Hotel Chicago Loop, at 32 W Randolph St. Go in through the hotel and take the elevator up. There are no walk-in visits and no tours. The only way in is with a ticket, booked ahead through Kermess. The current show, Premonitions Inc., is for guests 21 and over. Right next door are the Nederlander Theatre and Couch Place, the alley tied to the 1903 Iroquois Theatre fire.
