It has been revealed that questions from attendees. Answers by Skift Intelligence.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Yes — premium has moved past hype into standard U.S. airline revenue architecture, and it’s now at the crowded end of its growth curve. Premium cabins generated $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue, in 2024, and U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy. The open question is no longer demand. It’s whether every carrier scaling premium at once dilutes the yields that made it work. 12.

The behavior behind it is capital, not talk. United ordered more than 250 aircraft with more business class and premium economy, Delta is spending $1 billion on new Delta One suites arriving in early 2027, American is flying retrofitted 777-300ERs, Alaska is adding business class on widebodies and select narrowbodies plus its first premium economy, and JetBlue is launching domestic first class 345.

The results follow the spend. Delta’s premium cabins hit 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024, with premium revenue up about 57% over that stretch to $6.9 billion 6. Delta held a 9.5% operating margin through the fuel shock on fares, premium mix, loyalty, and non-flying revenue 7.

In a recent development, premium is also being unbundled, which is the clearest sign it has become normal pricing infrastructure rather than a flagship product. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, extending segmentation it already applied to Polaris and Premium Plus 8. United CFO Michael Leskinen noted “all of society is becoming more premium,” citing hotels, cruise lines, and car service 9.

The front cabin keeps growing but stops being one product. Tiered business fares let carriers sell the seat to price-sensitive buyers without discounting the full experience, which protects yield as capacity rises.

In a recent development, skift Research’s main caution is oversupply rather than demand weakness. If carriers scale premium simultaneously, especially long-haul, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to trade up and dilute the premium.

Recent findings suggest that with jet fuel averaging $4.50 a gallon and domestic fares up about 32% year over year, carriers without premium and loyalty levers are the exposed ones. Deutsche Bank expects American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier to lose money in 2026.

It has been revealed that premium demand in the U.S. is structural, built on a K-shaped income recovery and self-funded leisure travelers rather than corporate accounts alone. What’s cyclical is the return on it, and that depends on how much premium seating the industry adds from here.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Industry observers note that the U.S. market supports two fully funded premium airlines today — Delta and United — and a contested third seat that American, Alaska, and JetBlue are all spending into at the worst possible moment. Premium demand is real and large, but Skift Research warns the risk ahead is oversupply, not weak demand. Fuel at record levels is deciding who can keep paying for the buildout. 921.

According to recent reports, premium cabins generate $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue, and Delta drew 50% of passenger revenue from premium in the second quarter 3. United has grown premium seat capacity 46% since 2019, closing on Delta’s lead 5. The economics behind the third seat are much weaker: Deutsche Bank expects Delta, United, Southwest, and Allegiant to be profitable in 2026, while American, Alaska, JetBlue, and Frontier lose money — American and JetBlue by roughly $1 billion pretax each 2.

Sources: Q3 margins and revenue growth 6; American’s results 1; Alaska’s losses and premium initiative 78; JetBlue’s first class 2.

Two carriers are monetizing premium; three more are buying the seats and hoping the returns arrive. Skift Research classifies premium as a peaking trend whose main forward risk is yield dilution if everyone scales at once — which is close to what is happening now.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Loyalty cash isn’t going away — Delta took $8.2 billion from Amex in 2025 and Air Canada just had Aeroplan valued at C$10 billion, more than the airline itself. But the economics are less proven than the headline numbers suggest, the regulatory and AI risks are real, and premium cabins are now the faster-growing engine at $188 billion, or 24% of global passenger revenue. 135.

Industry observers note that two things are true at once. The cash from banks is enormous and disclosed; the net profit behind it is not. United CEO Scott Kirby pushed back on the “credit card company that happens to fly planes” framing, arguing analysts count what banks pay for miles but ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers — “Nobody counts the cost,” he said 1. Skift’s review of filings found American collected $6.2 billion from card and other partners, while United doesn’t publish total bank cash at all, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 7.2% of passenger miles in 2019 to 10.3% in 2025 1.

It has been revealed that the clearest structural alternative is premium. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as a peaking trend airlines should scale now, with over 70% of travelers saying they would trade up and Delta’s premium revenue up nearly 50% since 2019 10. American’s Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 6.

The loyalty engine is being stress-tested from three directions at once: disclosure (nobody highlights the net), regulation (uncapped U.S. interchange fees that the Credit Card Competition Act would put at risk), and discovery (AI making fares and benefits easier to compare). None of those kill it. All three argue against treating card remuneration as the only growth story.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

American has closed a lot of product gaps on paper and almost none of the financial ones. Its premium seat mix is already high — roughly 30% of seats generating about 50% of revenue 4 — but Delta converts premium and loyalty into profit at a scale American doesn’t approach 1.

CEO Robert Isom now calls American a “premium global airline,” a label adopted in press releases in December 2025.

Premium drove roughly two-thirds of Delta’s passenger-revenue growth, and Delta expects premium revenue to pass main cabin by 2027.

American’s chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate returns that fund the next round of investment and pay down debt, and that network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty “all have to be working in concert” 2 3. That is the condition American hasn’t met yet.

In a recent development, american is closing the product gap on a timeline that runs into the early 2030s while Delta compounds the loyalty and margin advantage now. The risk is crowding: with United, Alaska, and most major international carriers expanding premium cabins at once, they compete for a finite pool of travelers willing to pay up, and yields come under pressure.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

Recent findings suggest that the premium shift is real and durable, but it is late in its growth, not early. Skift Research classifies premium air travel as “peaking” — a trend to scale now, with oversupply rather than demand weakness as the main risk. It runs as long as capacity discipline holds and the wealth effect behind it holds. The thing that ends it is airlines all expanding the front of the plane at once, diluting yields. 12.

The evidence for durability is in the revenue, not the rhetoric. Premium cabins generated $188 billion in 2024, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 1. Delta’s premium cabins reached 50% of passenger revenue in Q2 2026, up from 45% in Q1 2024 3. Air Canada’s premium share has gone from about 20% a decade ago to roughly 30%, with a 35% target by 2030 4. The addressable market widened beyond corporate accounts: Skift Research found more than 70% of travelers say they would trade up, with self-funded leisure travelers driving the growth 1.

The supply response is where the clock starts. U.S. premium capacity is up 33% since 2020 against 16% for economy 1. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft 5. Virgin Atlantic is taking refurbished 787s from 192 economy seats to 127 and removing its onboard bars for more premium seats 67. Turkish Airlines is adding premium economy in 2028, leaving Qatar and Etihad among the few long-haul holdouts 3. Alaska is adding premium economy for the first time even after fuel wiped out first-half profit 8.

Sources indicate that unbundling the front cabin keeps yields up without adding seats. United is selling domestic First and Business as Base, Standard, and Flexible fares, following Delta, JetBlue, Etihad, Air France, KLM, and Qatar. Air Canada has unbundled business and premium economy and sells legroom in economy.

ZS’s Kunal Shah remarked the opportunity sits in midscale and low-cost brands: $20 of added ADR on a $100 room night is a 20% revenue gain that mostly drops to the bottom line. That widens the pool rather than crowding the same high-yield travelers.

In a recent development, premium is now a baseline revenue assumption rather than a stopgap, so the question is no longer whether it lasts but who gets squeezed when everyone’s retrofits land at once. The carriers that survive the dilution will be the ones segmenting inside every cabin instead of just adding seats at the front.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

In a recent development, no contradiction. American removed international first class from its 777-300ERs to fit 70 Flagship Suites per aircraft — trading a handful of ultra-premium seats for far more business class inventory. The math favors density at the top of the cabin: premium seats are about 30% of American’s fleet and generate roughly 50% of revenue, and premium revenue grew 22.9% in Q3 versus 19.5% in main cabin. 758.

American revealed the first class removal back in 2022, framing it then as paying for a 30% increase in premium seats on the 777s and a 63% increase on the 787-9s 8. The retrofitted 777-300ERs now flying carry 70 business class seats 4. International first class had already been abandoned by Delta, United, KLM, Air Fresh Zealand, and Latam, on the view that improved business class delivers better returns for the space 9.

Recent findings suggest that the real tension is financial, not strategic. American cut its 2026 outlook twice and now expects a full-year loss of $1 to $1.60 per share, with Q3 revenue up 19.3% to $16.3 billion wiped out by a $1.9 billion fuel increase 5. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion 4. Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that premium spending has to generate the returns that fund further improvements and pay down debt 3.

Eliminating first class is how American funds business class scale — the question is whether a carrier losing money this year can out-invest Delta and United for the same premium travelers.

Industry observers note that the industry is moving the same direction. British Airways is cutting 52 seats from each A380 to lift premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft, while reducing first class from 14 suites to 12 6. Virgin Atlantic is replacing its onboard bars with more premium seats 2. Skift Research puts premium cabin revenue at $188 billion, or 24% of global airline passenger revenue 6.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

Sources indicate that tilting schedules toward high-yield local traffic in New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago is a margin repair, not a differentiator. Those are exactly the markets Delta and United defend hardest, and American is attacking them with the weaker balance sheet. The local-market tilt only differentiates if it is paired with the reliability and premium product American has promised but not yet delivered fleetwide. 12.

Sources indicate that chief commercial officer Nat Pieper told Skift Aviation Forum that American is tailoring schedules toward higher-yield local markets in New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago, while leaning on alliance partners to extend global reach 1. Local traffic — passengers starting or ending a trip in the hub city — pays more than connecting traffic, so the mix shift lifts unit revenue without adding seats. That matters now because fuel, not demand, is the problem: third-quarter revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion while fuel expense rose 67.5%, leaving a $269 million net loss 4.

It has been revealed that the local-market tilt is a yield lever American controls, which is why it is being pulled. The uncertainty is whether it can hold corporate and premium local share in three cities where it is the number two or number three carrier, while slowing growth to protect 2027 profitability.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

New York is where the gap between the big three is clearest, and Skift’s reporting indicates three different postures rather than three comparable expansion programs.

In a recent development, american’s disclosed JFK plans are schedule and product additions, not a terminal program. Summer 2027 brings JFK–Nice and more Heathrow flying alongside fresh Philadelphia and Charlotte transatlantic routes.

Delta co-financed its own Terminal 4 expansion with the Port Authority’s broader $18.9 billion JFK overhaul, giving it fixed infrastructure control at the airport.

In a recent development, united has no JFK slot portfolio of its own. The Blue Sky partnership with JetBlue, cleared by the DOT in July 2025, gives it borrowed access from Terminal 6, plus a net-neutral swap of eight Newark timings.

In a recent development, american’s JFK position sits inside a broader catch-up effort. It earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion and United’s $3.3 billion, and is on track to lose money in 2026 1. Its Latest York investment is showing up in aircraft and cabins — the A321XLR with 20 Flagship Suites, the 777-300ER with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seating — rather than in gates 21.

Delta’s advantage is structural. Its Terminal 4 expansion let it consolidate all JFK flying in one facility, within an $18.9 billion airport redevelopment that also produced the fresh Terminal 1 and Terminal 6 34.

United’s return is the newest variable. Seven daily round trips is small, but it ends an absence at JFK and comes without United buying slots 5. United’s CFO stated this week that the Blue Sky relationship stops short of a deal, pointing to JetBlue’s nearly $10 billion debt load 6.

Industry observers note that skift’s coverage does not include a disclosed long-term American gate or terminal program at JFK comparable to Delta’s Terminal 4 investment. Treat American’s JFK strategy as route and product-level on the current record.

This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

Shares are gross cash from bank partners, not profit.

Recent findings suggest that allegiant CEO Greg Anderson put the number on the record himself: co-branded credit cards are about 5% of Allegiant’s revenue, against roughly 15% at the legacy carriers and above that at Alaska and Southwest 1. He called closing that gap the airline’s biggest revenue catalyst, with more detail promised at an investor day 1.

Industry observers note that apply that 5% to Allegiant’s actual revenue base and you get the realistic dollar figure. The company posted $962 million in revenue in the quarter ended July 2026 and $943 million in the prior quarter, a run rate near $3.7 billion including Sun Country, which Allegiant bought for $1.5 billion and closed in May 1. That implies roughly $175 million to $190 million a year in card remuneration. The program had 600,000 cardholders and first-quarter remuneration up 9% 1. For context, Allegiant’s chief marketing officer mentioned the Bank of America deal brought in $100 million in 2022, just over 4% of $2.3 billion in revenue 2.

Industry observers note that the structural reason leisure carriers sit at 4% to 6% rather than 15% is spend frequency. Sun Country’s then-CMO estimated a typical customer flies once every 12 to 18 months, which is why discounters pitch the card as a way to stay relevant between trips 8.

Sources indicate that treat 5% to 7% of total revenue as the realistic planning band for a primarily-leisure U.S. carrier, and 10% to 15% as the legacy ceiling Allegiant is aiming at rather than a near-term forecast. Also note these are gross cash from banks, not margin — United’s Scott Kirby argues analysts count the payments and ignore the cost of carrying award passengers, and no carrier discloses that cost 3.

This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

Sources indicate that points stop being a moat once an agent can price them. What holds a member is what an algorithm can’t compare: recognition at the property or gate, reliable operations, and redemption the member can actually get. Skift Research found loyalty affiliation ranked last as a reason to trust an AI recommendation, while 83% of U.S. travelers say better personalization would make them switch programs. 21.

Sources indicate that the pressure is already measurable. Skift Research found 44% of U.S. travelers book outside their preferred program because prices are cheaper elsewhere, and 55% would follow an AI tool to a better deal 1. Among business travelers, consistently good service outranks rewards as a reason to return, 46% to 15%, and 62% say they are likely to switch for a better price or experience 3. Card programs have also taken the top of the rankings: 32% of travelers named credit cards and banks the most rewarding loyalty programs, ahead of hotels at 26% and airlines at 20% 4.

Recent findings suggest that the open question is whether recognition and service can be made legible to an agent. Google’s agentic hotel booking passes along only name, payment, occupancy, and property, keeping the conversation that produced the booking — which leaves the differentiators that matter most invisible at the moment of choice. AI referrals still sit below 2% at Booking and Marriott, per Bernstein, so the terms are being set while volume is small.

This question was addressed to Tiffany Funk, Head of Flying Blue, Air France KLM Group and Gilbert Ott, Director of Loyalty, oneworld.

For airlines, yes — so far. Card-spend status converts bank payments into the industry’s highest-margin revenue: Delta took $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, and co-brand operating margins run 35–50%. For travelers, the trade is worse: status is more crowded and benefits thinner. And the whole model rests on uncapped U.S. interchange fees that Congress could change. 23.

In a recent development, the shift is now structural, not experimental. Delta made Medallion Qualifying Dollars the sole status metric from 2024, earned through flying, co-brand card spend, and bookings 5. American collapsed everything into Loyalty Points earned by flying, card use, or partner purchases, and told Skift the pandemic revealed loyal members who had never flown with the airline 6. Southwest is the latest: from January 1, 2027, cardholders earn one tier qualifying point per dollar spent under new silver, gold, and platinum tiers, with lounges built alongside Chase 4.

Industry observers note that the profitability of spend-based status is asserted more often than it is proven. United CEO Scott Kirby argues analysts count the cash banks pay for miles and ignore the cost of carrying more than 50,000 daily award passengers: “Nobody counts the cost.” Skift’s review of filings found United does not publish total cash received from banks, and MileagePlus award flights rose from 6.1 million in 2019 to 10.9 million in 2025, or 10.3% of passenger miles.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Recent findings suggest that no cut has happened, and none is imminent. The Credit Card Competition Act was reintroduced in January 2026 after a Trump endorsement but still has not had a floor vote, and the $38 billion Visa/Mastercard settlement compresses standard rates while leaving premium tiers — the ones funding travel rewards — largely untouched. The risk to travel’s co-brand economics is Congress, not the courts, and the industry is betting Congress never acts. 1.

According to recent reports, U.S. interchange — the merchant-paid fee on each card swipe — remains uncapped, unlike in the EU, UK, and Australia 1. That single condition underwrites travel’s most profitable business line. Delta collected $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, about 14% of adjusted operating revenue, American took $6.2 billion from co-brand and other partners, and Morgan Stanley estimates co-brand operating margins at 35-50%. 12.

Industry observers note that where caps landed, rewards shrank. The EU and UK capped credit interchange at 0.3% in 2015, and no European airline collects anything close to $8 billion from a card partner 1. Australia’s Reserve Bank cut its cap to 0.3%, effective October 2026 and said explicitly it was setting the level so issuers could no longer use interchange to fund rewards 1. The U.S. has run its own version: the Durbin Amendment capped debit interchange in 2011 and debit rewards largely disappeared 1.

Industry observers note that the lobbying tells you what’s at stake. Airlines for America runs a “Protect Our Points” campaign, and the card and banking industry has spent roughly $200 million opposing swipe-fee reform 1.

According to recent reports, nothing in the current reporting points to a cut in the near term — the bill has been reintroduced three times without a vote, and the settlement spares the premium tiers. But the downside modeling the industry works from doesn’t contemplate reform at all: Morgan Stanley’s three paths for the travel co-brand market by 2035 ($100B, $60B, $40B) all assume the fee structure stays intact.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

It has been revealed that neeleman’s current playbook is the opposite of the airline JetBlue became. At Breeze he avoids the Big Four entirely, flies thin routes no one else serves, and judges flying by trip cost rather than cost per seat. JetBlue today is losing money in exactly the overlapping markets he claims he would never fly, and only now shifting toward Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, and cheaper terminals. 15.

This is a counterfactual, so treat what follows as analysis, not reporting: no one has reported what Neeleman would do at JetBlue. What can be grounded is the strategy he runs now and the position JetBlue is in.

According to recent reports, neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum this month that small U.S. airlines fail when they fly head-to-head with United, American, Delta, and Southwest, and that he “would never run an airline that’s overlapping those guys” 13. He pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the cautionary case: as Spirit moved to bigger planes it landed in the majors’ markets, and the majors added seats that cost them less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1. He said chasing CASM “got Spirit to die,” and that Breeze looks at trip costs instead, generating 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1.

Industry observers note that jetBlue, meanwhile, posted a $257 million third-quarter net loss on $2.8 billion of revenue, cut its 2026 margin guidance to negative 4.5% to negative 6.5%, and watched bonds backed by its TrueBlue program trade at distressed levels amid Chapter 11 speculation 4. CEO Joanna Geraghty called that a “significant disconnect between the narrative and the bond market” and reaffirmed operating profitability in 2027 5.

The parts of JetBlue’s current initiative that most resemble Neeleman’s thinking — smaller-market growth out of Fort Lauderdale, premium seats, cheaper terminals including Spirit’s former LaGuardia slots — are the parts arriving last. BlueFirst won’t be fully installed until late 2028, and fuel at $4.64 a gallon in the fourth quarter is the squeeze in the meantime.

In a recent development, one caution on the counterfactual: Neeleman’s founder-era JetBlue was a single-fleet, point-to-point, cost-advantaged carrier in a market that no longer exists. His own argument now is that the majors have gotten “so much better at what they do,” with credit card revenue, international networks, and loyalty programs a newly introduced entrant cannot attack directly 3. A Neeleman-run JetBlue in 2026 would face the same math every other mid-size U.S. carrier does.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Industry observers note that the delivery crunch Skift has reported runs through the A320neo and 737 Max lines, where meaningful narrowbody slots are scarce until roughly 2033. Breeze doesn’t order from either. It flies the 137-seat A220-300, a separate Airbus program with far more room, and had about 44 firm A220s on order as of late 2025 with roughly 15 due in 2026. That gives Breeze growth capacity most U.S. carriers can’t buy right now. 13.

According to recent reports, the squeeze is real but line-specific. Skift’s Farnborough coverage put meaningful A320neo and 737 Max positions out of reach until about 2033, with widebodies tight into the mid-2030s, and lessors — not airlines — placing the biggest orders to absorb that risk 1. Skift Aviation Forum framed manufacturers as one of five counterparties now deciding which airlines absorb the fuel shock, with the same roughly-2033 horizon 2.

According to recent reports, breeze’s queue position sits on a different program. Cirium data cited by Airline Weekly in December 2025 revealed 44 operational A220s, six grounded for geared turbofan engine inspections, and 44 more on firm order, with David Neeleman saying about 15 would arrive in 2026 3. The A220 backlog has grown since — AirAsia’s 150-aircraft, $19 billion order in May 2026 pushed the program past 1,000 total orders and made it the largest single firm order for the type 4. That tightens the line over time, but Breeze’s positions were already contracted.

Breeze can keep adding thin, exclusive routes while A320neo and 737 Max operators wait.

Neeleman noted Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM and generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic.

Pratt & Whitney geared turbofan inspections have taken A220s out of service, which can cost Breeze more utilization than a slot queue would.

The commercial read matters more than the queue. Neeleman told Skift Aviation Forum in November 2026 that Breeze has posted four consecutive profitable quarters with a fifth expected, that it avoids the Big Four’s markets, and that it is pushing premium seating from about 41% to 45% of the cabin 5. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 5. He also pointed to Spirit, which shut down in May, as the carrier that moved to bigger aircraft and landed in the majors’ markets 5.

Industry observers note that scarce A320neo and 737 Max slots cap industry capacity through roughly 2033, which keeps fares firm — and Breeze gets that pricing benefit without being stuck in the same queue, because it buys from a different Airbus line. The constraint on its growth is engine availability and demand in thin markets, not a place in the order book.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Neeleman manages to trip cost, not CASM, and flies A220s and E190s on routes the Major Four skip.

Operating margin of 0.1% excluding aircraft sale-leaseback gains; adding first class and Starlink.

Neeleman mentioned majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat.

According to recent reports, the practical case for Breeze is that it usually isn’t a choice between carriers. Skift Research found Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, and Neeleman mentioned the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 1. The alternative on most of those city pairs is a connection on a major or a drive.

In a recent development, the second difference is product. Breeze is a low-cost carrier that sells extra legroom, first-class-style seating, and free Wi-Fi, and it’s pushing premium seating from about 41% of total seats to 45% 17. That premium lean is now industry-wide — premium cabins generated 24% of global airline passenger revenue in 2024, about $188 billion 4 — but Breeze built it in from the start rather than retrofitting late, as Frontier and JetBlue are doing now 58.

Industry observers note that reliability on thin routes is the third. Breeze flies dedicated aircraft carrying maintenance crews and spare parts, which Neeleman noted helps prevent cancellations on routes with few frequencies 2. On a once- or twice-weekly route, a cancellation can mean days, not hours.

Breeze is privately held and does not publicly report full financial results, so the four consecutive profitable quarters are the tech giant’s own disclosure 1. Low frequency cuts both ways — fewer flights means fewer rebooking options. And Breeze has no interline agreements of the kind that would get you onto another carrier if things go wrong, which is the structural cost of a network built on routes nobody else flies.

According to recent reports, breeze’s advantage is route selection, not price. The reason to pick it is that it flies nonstop where the majors connect you — and it has stayed out of the head-to-head fights that killed Spirit and are keeping Frontier’s margins near zero.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Recent findings suggest that low likelihood over the next few years. Breeze’s profitability rests on being the only airline on nearly 90% of its routes, and Neeleman has stated directly he would never run an airline overlapping the Big Four. Big-city flying would put Breeze against carriers whose seat costs are less than half what Spirit paid — the dynamic he blames for Spirit’s death. Expect large metros as spokes, not battlegrounds. 13.

It has been revealed that breeze already touches large airports — Fort Lauderdale is one, where it expanded alongside JetBlue, Frontier, and Allegiant after Spirit’s May shutdown 6. The distinction that matters is whether Breeze flies into massive cities on routes the majors also serve. On that, the strategy points the other way: 83% of third-quarter routes were exclusive to Breeze in late 2025 3, and Skift Research found it was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year 1.

The key uncertainty is what the IPO does to the growth story. Neeleman pushed a likely listing to 2027, and public-market investors tend to reward scale and recognizable markets. If Breeze needs a bigger growth narrative to price a deal, large metros are the obvious place to find one — and the place its cost structure is least suited to.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Industry observers note that breeze keeps trip cost low by flying a small, efficient airplane on routes nobody else serves, then filling it with premium seats and bundles so the flight clears its cost at low frequency. The durable part is the aircraft and the monopoly network. The fragile part is labor and fuel, which rise with age and scale — and the fix Neeleman is reaching for is more revenue per trip, not a lower cost base. 12.

Neeleman told the Skift Aviation Forum that Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — cost per available seat mile — and said chasing the per-seat metric “got Spirit to die” 1. The logic: a smaller jet costs less to operate per departure, so a thin market can support it even when the seat-mile math looks worse than a major’s 2. Spirit’s error, in his telling, was upgauging into the majors’ markets, where the majors added seats costing less than half what Spirit paid per seat 1.

Recent findings suggest that breeze’s real defense is revenue, not cost. Premium seating is moving from about 41% of the total toward 45%, and Neeleman aims a Priceline-style model starting next year that takes a commission on the real estate and spending its fresh routes create in small markets. Both raise revenue per trip rather than lower cost per trip — the admission that a startup cannot out-cost the Big Four.

This question was addressed to Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines.

Sources indicate that american can be a premium player at 200M+ passengers, but not a premium leader on Delta’s terms. Its premium mix already works — about 30% of seats generate roughly 50% of revenue, and Q3 premium revenue rose 22.9%. The constraint is that a mostly domestic, Sun Belt-weighted network of that size dilutes yield faster than cabin retrofits lift it. American earned $111 million last year against Delta’s $5.1 billion. 321.

Scale is not disqualifying by itself. American’s premium revenue grew faster than main cabin last quarter, 22.9% against 19.5% 2. The problem is what the rest of the airline costs. Revenue rose 19.3% to $16.3 billion in the third quarter while operating costs rose 19.7%, leaving a 1% operating margin against Delta’s 9% and United’s 7% 6.

In a recent development, the catch-up list is real and expensive: Starlink on every mainline jet from 2027, seatback screens returning, A321XLR Europe routes in summer 2027, 777-300ERs with 70 business class seats, a 40% increase in narrowbody premium seats, and Citi as sole co-brand card issuer 13. At least 50 revealed changes since early 2025 1.

The unresolved question is whether premium spending generates enough cash to fund the next round. American’s CCO Nat Pieper said consistent service, network, and loyalty revenue have to produce returns that pay for further improvements and reduce debt — and that reliability is the precondition. Skift’s reporting does not yet show those returns at scale. 45.

Network, customer experience, premium revenue, and loyalty all have to be working in concert.

— Nat Pieper, Chief Commercial Officer, American Airlines, at Skift Aviation Forum 5.

This question was addressed to Drew Wells, EVP and Chief Commercial Officer, Allegiant.

It has been revealed that allegiant, now merged with Sun Country, serves 42 markets from Fort Lauderdale but only marginally targets former Spirit routes — Nashville, Indianapolis, Louisville, Norfolk, and Atlantic City. It is instead adding unique markets no one else flies, expanding the airport’s destination menu.

JetBlue is Fort Lauderdale’s largest carrier and treats it as the third leg of a stool with Fresh York and Boston, adding Mint transcons, domestic first class, and a possible lounge.

The short answer: Allegiant mostly doesn’t compete with JetBlue at FLL head-to-head. It competes around it.

After Spirit shut down in May 2026, JetBlue, Frontier, Breeze, and Allegiant all added capacity at Fort Lauderdale 1. JetBlue went after Spirit’s routes directly, launching 11 newly introduced Fort Lauderdale routes on Spirit’s shutdown weekend plus a status match for Free Spirit members 3. Allegiant took a different line: of its 42 Fort Lauderdale markets, only five — Nashville, Indianapolis, Louisville, Norfolk, and Atlantic City — were Spirit cities, and it is chasing unique markets instead 1.

That reflects the two models. Allegiant flies low-frequency leisure routes from smaller cities where it is often the only nonstop, so it avoids the daily-frequency, loyalty-driven markets JetBlue serves. JetBlue’s Fort Lauderdale is built around Northeast traffic, Caribbean and Latin connections — more than 20 routes to Latin America — and premium: Mint lie-flat on transcons to Los Angeles and Las Vegas, with management calling the city “Florida’s biggest premium market” 1. JetBlue is also adding its BlueFirst domestic first class and weighing a Fort Lauderdale lounge 4.

Sources indicate that fort Lauderdale seats excluding Spirit were scheduled up a combined 40% year over year in the fourth quarter of 2026. If demand doesn’t absorb that, the thin unique routes Allegiant favors are the easiest to cut — and JetBlue, which is funding startup losses on newly introduced routes while chasing a turnaround, has the most capital at risk.

This question was addressed to Sara Nelson, International President, Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, AFL-CIO.

Recent findings suggest that customer experience and labor-as-cost coexist only when the service promise matches the cost model. The carriers now cutting hardest — KLM, Icelandair, Alaska — are protecting margin under a fuel shock, not reinventing service. The real test is where the cuts land: outsourced ground and contact-center work, and regional crews paid about half mainline, is where the customer actually meets the airline. 326.

Industry observers note that the fuel shock is forcing the trade-off into the open. Jet fuel was up 102% year over year in mid-September, and record revenue has not covered it 4. American grew revenue 19.3% in Q3 and still posted a 1% operating margin because costs grew 19.7%; Delta and United each slipped about two points 6. Carriers that already settled significant contracts — United’s five-year flight attendant deal carries a 31% pay increase and $741 million in retroactive pay — are paying for premium service with loyalty and premium-cabin cash, not by squeezing crew 45.

The unresolved question is whether outsourcing the customer-facing layer — catering, ground handling, contact centers — indicates up in the service metrics airlines sell against. KLM has disclosed the cost target and the job moves; it has not disclosed a service standard tied to them.

This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

Recent findings suggest that india’s fleet orders are not the binding constraint — ground and crew capacity are. Mumbai is rationing international slots to rebuild a terminal, new airports rather than bigger ones are being asked to absorb growth, and tighter pilot duty rules exposed how thin airline crew buffers were. The result: capacity now gets added where slots and crews exist, not where demand is. 1167.

According to recent reports, mumbai International Airport told 46 airlines it would pull 265 of Terminal 2’s 770 weekly international departure slots from October 25 to house domestic flights displaced by the Terminal 1 rebuild — IndiGo losing 74 weekly departures, Air India 33, Emirates and Etihad 10 each 1. The ministry intervened, Adani agreed to leave winter slots untouched, and traffic balancing was pushed to the summer 2027 schedule 23. IndiGo and Air India Group then agreed to phase international flying to Navi Mumbai through July 2027 4. The relief valve carries its own friction: Navi Mumbai is 45 km away with no direct metro link expected before 2031, and charges INR 1,225 in passenger fees against INR 615 at Mumbai 4. Adani’s airport CEO expects one or two foreign carriers to suspend Mumbai service for a couple of years rather than split operations 5.

Recent findings suggest that indiGo canceled more than 1,200 flights after latest crew rostering rules collided with thin staffing and system congestion, and the DGCA opened a probe 6. The meltdown deepened — the government rolled back night-flying rules, capped fares, and fined the airline, and it cost IndiGo both profit and its CEO 789. The regulator has since shown it will flex duty rules when airspace disruption lengthens sectors, temporarily relaxing pilot duty-time limits in April 2026 10. Regulators also tied summer schedule approvals to aircraft actually on the ground rather than projected deliveries, forcing airlines to cut planned flying 11.

Skift’s reporting has tracked recruitment to beat an air traffic control officer shortage, with 796 ATC positions created alongside the fleet build-out 12, and CAPA has called for airspace redesign to carry 8–10 times current traffic 13. The sharper near-term airspace problem is geopolitical: Pakistani and Iranian closures pushed IndiGo to suspend Copenhagen and cut UK flying 14, and have hit Delhi harder than Mumbai, moving Air India’s Europe and North America flying toward Mumbai with Bengaluru under study as a third hub 15.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Sources indicate that the A220 is what makes Breeze’s network possible: small enough to open thin city pairs no one else serves, long-legged enough to fly them transcon, and cheap enough per trip that Breeze can sit on routes with no nonstop competition. The same airplane caps it. At 137 seats, its unit costs can’t match a densely configured A321neo, so Breeze can’t follow demand into major, contested markets without losing the economics that work. 12.

Breeze was the sole operator on nearly 90% of its routes last year, according to Skift Research, and CEO David Neeleman estimates the airline generates 80% to 90% of its own traffic 2. He remarked Breeze looks at trip costs rather than CASM — “that’s what got Spirit to die” — and pairs the smaller aircraft with premium seating and bundles to make thin routes work 23.

Charleston, Providence, Hartford, Akron-Canton, Albany, Rochester, Memphis — cities where the Massive Three lean on aging regional jets and rivals have pulled seats.

The A220’s range lets Breeze link overlooked eastern cities to Los Angeles, San Francisco, San Diego, and Orange County, plus Las Vegas and Phoenix.

Airline Weekly reported Breeze chases yield premiums instead, and avoids competing against densely configured narrowbodies.

The A220 is a bet that U.S. majors keep upgauging and keep leaving mid-size cities to aging regional jets. That thesis has held. The risk arrives when Southwest’s 737 Max 7 — comparable in size and unit cost — finally shows up in volume, or when a thin market Breeze created attracts a larger airplane.

This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

The core of Porter’s 2021 case still stands: a 132-seat jet with low trip costs lets it hold daily frequency and keep fares up on routes bigger aircraft can’t fill profitably. What fuel has broken is the financing side. Jet fuel roughly doubled in 2026, Canada has lent money to Porter, Transat, and Flair, and the growth-at-pace ambition behind the 80-aircraft order now runs on borrowed room. 156.

The original bet, made in July 2021, had three legs: the E195-E2 was picked over the A220 specifically for lower trip costs; its near-3,000-mile range opened nonstops other carriers only served via connections; and 132 seats against Air Canada and WestJet’s 169-174-seat 737-8s meant Porter could fly thinner markets 2. A fourth leg came with the 2022 product reveal — all-economy with PorterReserve, a premium-economy-light product, rather than following rivals downmarket 3.

Industry observers note that fuel has not invalidated the aircraft choice — it has validated it. Smaller gauge is the right shape for a cost shock, because the fare you need per seat falls with the seats you have to sell. What fuel broke is the balance sheet assumption underneath the order: that Porter could scale a national network on its own money.

Trip-cost economics and frequency — the revenue-side argument for small gauge is stronger at $4-plus fuel, not weaker 1.

Self-funded expansion; Porter is now among the Canadian carriers taking government loans 5.

Breeze, which protects economics with low trip costs and routes with limited nonstop competition 4.

This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

According to recent reports, low-cost carriers are genuinely loosening single-fleet discipline — AirAsia on regional jets, Avelo on the E2, IndiGo on widebodies. But slot scarcity isn’t the driver. The reporting points to revenue, not runway access: matching aircraft size to what a market will actually pay, and chasing premium and long-haul revenue the A320/737 can’t reach. Slot-constrained airlines do the opposite — they upgauge within one fleet. 123.

According to recent reports, the behavior behind the trend is real and spread across more than one region and one type of player. AirAsia’s Tony Fernandes is negotiating with Airbus and Embraer for regional jets, explicitly breaking from the single-type model to serve smaller destinations at higher frequency 2. Avelo ordered up to 100 Embraer E195-E2s alongside its all-Boeing 737 fleet, becoming the first U.S. carrier to commit to the type 3. IndiGo has 60 A350-900s on order, with the first now slipping to the second quarter of 2028 4. Flyadeal has weighed widebodies for high-volume pilgrim and worker routes 7.

In a recent development, what those cases share is a revenue argument, not a capacity-access one. At Skift Aviation Forum, Embraer’s Arjan Meijer pointed to a widening gap between 76-seat regional jets and narrowbodies, and argued that lower per-seat costs can be wiped out by the revenue consequences of flying more seats than a market will absorb at a decent fare 1. Porter’s Kevin Jackson mentioned 132-seat E195-E2s let the airline hold daily service through weak periods and protect unit revenue 1.

It has been revealed that slot constraints produce the opposite response: more seats through the same number of movements, inside one fleet type. EasyJet’s growth at slot-limited Gatwick, Linate, and Charles de Gaulle has come from upgauging A319s and A320s to A320neos and A321neos — roughly 171 seats to 211 — not from adding a second aircraft family 89. British Airways is cutting 52 economy seats per A380 to lift premium cabins to 48% of capacity at Heathrow, again raising revenue per slot rather than diversifying types 10. IndiGo’s A321XLRs on Athens and Amsterdam do protect slots, but that’s a secondary benefit of a long-haul product decision 4.

Fleet simplicity still carries real weight. Cathay ruled out regional jets entirely, citing economies of scale and congested airports 6. Jackson said larger aircraft would suit some Porter routes, but a consistent E2 fleet serves the wider network strategy 1. And Willie Walsh has said IndiGo’s short-haul narrowbody core will not be reshaped to feed long-haul widebodies 5.

If fuel stays elevated and fares keep deciding margins, more LCCs follow Avelo and AirAsia into a second, smaller type to defend yield in thin markets rather than dump seats into them.

Mixed fleets raise crew, maintenance, and spares costs. If the carriers adding types can’t show unit-revenue gains that clear that bill, the discipline snaps back — Cathay’s reasoning becomes the consensus again.

IndiGo’s model — a widebody arm run alongside an untouched narrowbody core — becomes the template for LCCs wanting long-haul without contaminating short-haul costs.

According to recent reports, the single-fleet religion is loosening because LCCs are chasing revenue the A320 and 737 can’t capture — in thin markets and in premium and long-haul cabins. Slot scarcity pushes airlines toward bigger aircraft within one family, which is the opposite move.

This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

Skift’s reporting does not show a Porter plan for replacing its Q400s at Billy Bishop. What the reporting does establish is the constraint that decides the answer: the tripartite agreement bars jets at the island airport, and Ottawa declined to reopen it in 2015, killing Porter’s CS100 order and runway-extension plan. Unless that agreement changes, anything Porter flies downtown has to be a turboprop. 12.

Sources indicate that billy Bishop sits on an island in Lake Ontario with a runway of roughly 4,000 feet, restricted to turboprops — Porter’s Q400s already take a weight restriction to operate there 32. Porter’s growth since 2021 has gone the other way: up to 80 Embraer E195-E2s flown from Toronto Pearson, Montreal, Ottawa, and Halifax, with Billy Bishop kept as the separate downtown base 14. At Skift Aviation Forum this month, Porter President Kevin Jackson remarked a consistent 132-seat E2 fleet supports the airline’s network strategy, with smaller aircraft preserving frequency for business travelers through weaker periods 5.

The simplest path keeps Billy Bishop inside the existing rules: another regional turboprop type for the downtown operation, run alongside the E2 jet fleet. The cost is the fleet complexity Jackson noted the airline has deliberately avoided.

Jets downtown require a runway extension and a change to the agreement that governs the airport. Porter tried that in 2013 with a CS100 order and lost in 2015 when Ottawa declined to review it, with local opposition over noise and the waterfront.

Industry observers note that porter’s jet network already runs from Pearson and eastern Canadian cities, and Billy Bishop’s value — a downtown gate and a U.S. preclearance facility — would have to be weighed against operating a second aircraft type for one airport.

Whether the federal government reveals any willingness to revisit the tripartite agreement, and whether Billy Bishop’s U.S. preclearance facility — which Porter, as the airport’s only U.S. operator, stands to benefit from — raises the commercial value of staying downtown enough to justify a second fleet type 6.

Industry observers note that porter’s downtown problem is a regulatory one, not a fleet one. Until the jet ban at Billy Bishop moves, Porter’s only options are another turboprop or a smaller presence on the island.

This question was addressed to Arjan Meijer, President & CEO, Embraer Commercial Aviation and Kevin Jackson, President, Porter Airlines.

Sources indicate that one U.S. carrier has ordered the E2: Avelo took 50 firm E195-E2s plus 50 purchase rights in September 2025. The reason no one else has is a weight limit written into major-airline pilot contracts. Scope clauses cap the maximum takeoff weight of jets regional partners may fly, and the re-engined E175-E2 is roughly 13,000 pounds over that line — so the aircraft that would sell in volume cannot legally be flown by the airlines that would buy it. 12.

The binding constraint is weight, not seats. Pilot union contracts at the substantial network carriers restrict the maximum takeoff weight of aircraft operated by regional partners; the E175-E2 comes in at about 99,000 pounds, well above what those contracts generally permit 2. Embraer’s Arjan Meijer called that threshold a “paper limitation” set years before anyone designed an E175 around Pratt & Whitney geared turbofans 2.

SkyWest is the clearest casualty. It ordered 100 E175-E2s in 2013 on the expectation that scope would loosen; it never did, the order was not binding, and SkyWest kept buying first-generation E175s instead — including 20 more for American in early 2020 3. As of 2023, Embraer was still planning to build the older E1 alongside the E2 specifically because U.S. pilot contracts kept E1 demand alive 4.

In a recent development, the workaround is to skip the regional model entirely. Avelo is an independent ultra-low-cost carrier with no scope clause to satisfy, so it could order the larger E195-E2 outright, with deliveries from 2027 1. Porter Airlines in Canada has built a network on 132-seat E195-E2s, and its president Kevin Jackson argued at Skift Aviation Forum that the smaller gauge protects frequency and daily service through weak periods rather than chasing the lowest cost per seat 5.

This question was addressed to Robin Hayes, Chairman and CEO of Airbus in North America, Airbus.

In a recent development, skift’s reporting doesn’t show an active ME3 campaign to relaunch the A380, and the conditions that would make Airbus say yes aren’t there. Emirates’ traffic fell 22% and its seat factor dropped to 72% in the half to September 30, with fuel at 34% of operating cost. A four-engine, 500-seat jet is the worst possible aircraft in a fuel shock. Airbus is sold out on the A350 instead. Likelihood: very low. 14.

Industry observers note that the demand case the Gulf carriers once made for the A380 rested on slot-constrained airports and reliably full hubs. Both legs are weaker now. Emirates carried 21.8 million passengers in the six months to September 30, down 22%, with capacity down 17% and seat factor at 72% from 79.5%, as the U.S.-Iran war pushed connecting traffic toward Istanbul and Singapore 1. Its first-half profit fell 66% to $899 million and survived only on $1.93 billion of hedging gains; analyst Linus Benjamin Bauer remarked the core flying business was likely loss-making unhedged 1. Emirates’ growth had already plateaued before the war on Dubai airport congestion, with FlyDubai taking the expansion role 5.

What the Gulf carriers are actually buying is the answer. Emirates ordered 65 more Boeing 777Xs for $38 billion at the 2025 Dubai Airshow 2, holds more than 340 aircraft on order worth about $150 billion, and is spending more than $7 billion retrofitting existing jets rather than seeking newly introduced very-large aircraft 1. Etihad went the other way entirely, ordering 30 A321LRs and putting first class on a narrowbody 6. Qatar Airways’ Hamad Al-Khater said the airline is working with Boeing on the delayed 777X and has 138 aircraft arriving over five years 9.

Airbus has the opposite problem to an empty line. Widebody demand is running hard into supply chain, labor, and production constraints, with the A350 backlog already deep 4. Restarting a closed four-engine program would compete for the same engineers, suppliers, and slots that Airbus is using to deliver aircraft it has already sold.

According to recent reports, emirates has refitted aircraft inside a program valued at more than $7 billion, and British Airways is cutting its A380s from 469 to 417 seats to lift premium share to 48%. Existing airframes absorb premium demand without a newly introduced program.

Fleet strategy debate has centered on a possible stretched A350 rather than a latest superjumbo — a derivative Airbus can build on a line that is already running.

Emirates added 65 777Xs for $38 billion and Qatar Airways claims it is working closely with Boeing on the delayed program. The large-twin answer is already ordered, just late.

According to recent reports, the A380 keeps its fans in the Gulf and at Heathrow, but the money is going into retrofits, twins, and narrowbodies. Airbus closed the line because the orders weren’t there, and a demand picture weaker than 2019’s doesn’t reopen it.

This question was addressed to Darren Hulst, VP, Commercial Marketing, Boeing.

According to recent reports, boeing’s delivery performance to Ryanair improved because Boeing slowed itself down first, then rebuilt the system around quality and regulatory sign-off. Ryanair’s complaints have shifted from defective, late aircraft to a more basic constraint: there aren’t enough slots.

How Boeing’s Ryanair Deliveries Turned Around.

O’Leary said only 40 of 57 expected 737 Max deliveries would arrive on time, forcing frequency cuts at high-cost airports.

O’Leary stated Max jets were arriving with fewer defects, citing better fuselages shipped from Wichita to Seattle, and asked Boeing for a plan to accelerate deliveries.

The FAA acknowledged improvements in Boeing’s safety management, opening the door to higher 737 Max production, though delays still forced changes at Southwest and Ryanair.

Airline Weekly cited improving Max deliveries and a widening unit-cost advantage as Ryanair headed into a strong peak summer.

Boeing’s 737 chief Katie Ringgold stated traveled work was down about 60% in a year, suppliers were all at rate 42, and the next step to 47 a month would come in late spring or early summer 2026.

Ryanair’s last 29 Gamechanger Max deliveries were each defect-free and arrived one to two months ahead of their revised dates, O’Leary stated, praising Kelly Ortberg and Stephanie Pope.

Three things, all upstream of Ryanair.

Sources indicate that quality control at the fuselage source. Spirit AeroSystems, which builds 737 Max fuselages in Wichita, was brought back inside Boeing. O’Leary flagged better fuselage quality as early as 2024, before the acquisition closed 32.

Deliberate slowdown. Boeing cut output in 2024 to install stricter inspections and “move-ready” criteria. Ringgold said Boeing built fewer aircraft than customers needed as a result, and that those processes now show up as better quality and flow 2.

The FAA became a gatekeeper. After the January 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug blowout, the FAA capped 737 output at 38 a month and now formally approves every rate increase. Boeing was cleared to 42 in November 2025 2.

Industry observers note that the improvement Ryanair is praising is partly an artifact of lowered expectations: those 29 aircraft arrived early against delivery dates that had already slipped by roughly a year. The durable gain is defect-free handover, which cuts Ryanair’s own acceptance and rework time.

Recent findings suggest that all of Ryanair’s Max 8s have been delivered. Its 300-aircraft Max 10 order is now the live question, with first delivery scheduled for spring 2027 and running through 2034 1. Boeing certified the Max 7 in August 2026 after about a decade of delays and was targeting Max 10 certification by year-end 7.

Delivery reliability also matters more than usual right now. Ryanair cut its FY27 traffic target to 214 million passengers and reported a 15% drop in half-year profit after tax to €2.1 billion, with a €2 billion fuel bill increase coming in fiscal 2027/28 8. Newer, more fuel-efficient aircraft are one of the few cost levers that don’t require a fight with a union or an airport.

This question was addressed to Juha Jaervinen, Chief Customer Officer, Virgin Atlantic.

According to recent reports, british Airways’ A380 refit — 52 seats out, premium cabins from about 35% to 48% of the aircraft — concentrates high-yield passengers behind a single slot at a Heathrow where BA can’t simply add a flight 1. Virgin Atlantic is running the same play at Heathrow, and started earlier: economy on refurbished 787s drops from 192 seats to 127, and upcoming A330s carry 104 premium seats against 128 in economy 34.

Industry observers note that doyle called it one of BA’s most significant aircraft transformations. IAG’s Gallego stated the heavier premium configuration would not work across every IAG market.

Koster said Virgin had been underweight in premium since the A340-600 and called the shift an investment rather than a bet.

Virgin has already chosen speed of conversion over amenity: the onboard bars, among its most recognizable brand assets, are being replaced with more spacious private seats 2. That is the cleanest counter to BA adding suites — Virgin converts the square footage it was spending on social space into sellable Upper Class.

Sources indicate that the second lever is the ground product, where Virgin is investing in the JFK Clubhouse and expanded Retreat Suites against BA’s fresh Heathrow Terminal 5C lounge, due at the end of 2028 21. The third is the Delta joint venture, which Koster noted gives Virgin network and scale while leaving the challenger brand intact 3.

Virgin Atlantic isn’t being forced to respond to BA’s A380 refit — it moved first, and more aggressively relative to its fleet. The open question is yields: BA, Virgin, American, Alaska, Emirates, and Turkish are all adding premium seats into the same cycle, and Skift reporting flags crowding as the risk if supply grows faster than the pool of payers.

This question was addressed to Aditya Ghosh, Founder, Homage Ventures & Advisors.

Airlines control the single biggest lever for tier-2 and tier-3 growth — where they put seats. Crisil’s data shows capacity deployment, not demand, is what turned Hindon and Kannur into million-passenger airports. But that lever only works where an airport, a usable aircraft type, and viability support already exist, and all three are government-set. Airlines can move the needle hard on existing regional airports; they can’t create the next 100. 12.

Regional airports make up 58% of India’s airports but carry just 2-3% of domestic traffic, and that share has gone backwards — from 3.4% in the 2021 and 2022 financial years to 2.3% in fiscal 2025 1. Crisil’s read is that the UDAN scheme’s importance has been “more structural than volumetric” 1. Where airlines did add capacity, the numbers moved fast: Hindon and Kannur each crossed 1 million annual passengers in fiscal 2025 on the back of increased deployment, and Agra, Hindon, and Tezpur grew traffic 7-10x between fiscal 2020 and 2025 against 120% national growth 1.

In a recent development, two things cap what airlines can do on their own. First, fleet: only about 80 dedicated regional transport aircraft fly in India, and the government projects a need for roughly 100 a year over the next decade 2. Narrowbodies don’t make 45-to-90-minute thin routes work. Second, economics: only about 5% of Indian domestic seat capacity sits on regional routes, compared with roughly double that in the U.S. and Europe, and 68% of domestic traffic touches one of the 10 busiest airports 8.

The current cycle also works against small-city flying. IndiGo lost about INR 19 billion ($197 million) in the September quarter, with fuel up 67% against 26% revenue growth, and recovered only about 60% of the fuel increase through fares 5. Capacity under that pressure goes to dense trunk routes and international flying, not 70-seat regional hops. Akasa has named tier-2 and tier-3 cities as central to its domestic strategy 6, and Fly91 was built specifically for the gap 7, but neither carries the scale to change the national mix alone.

Industry observers note that airlines decide whether India’s existing regional airports fill up — that is a real, provable lever worth multiples of traffic at individual airports. They do not decide whether the next tier of cities gets an airport, a subsidy, or an aircraft small enough to serve it profitably, and that is where the 2-3% national share is actually set.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

In a recent development, the single highest-impact move is closing the fuel-recapture gap — pricing and capacity discipline that turns a $4.64-a-gallon cost into fare revenue. BlueFirst won’t be fully installed until late 2028, so the premium bet can’t rescue 2027. JetBlue recaptured only 50% of fuel costs in Q2 2026, and it guided to a negative 4.5% to negative 6.5% operating margin. Fuel is where the margin went. 142.

Everything else JetBlue is doing — premium cabins, Fort Lauderdale growth, lower-cost terminals, loyalty — matters, but on a slower clock. BlueFirst should add nearly five points of revenue per available seat mile, according to president Marty St. George, yet the retrofit doesn’t finish until late 2028 because of supply chain bottlenecks 31. The $1 EPS target assumes fuel near $3 a gallon; JetBlue paid $4.23 in Q2 2026 and expects $4.64 in Q4 42.

JetBlue has the right long-term initiative and the wrong timetable. The premium and loyalty build-out pays off in 2028; the fuel bill is due now, which makes pricing power and capacity cuts the only levers that move 2027.

This question was addressed to David Neeleman, Founder, Chairman & CEO, Breeze Airways.

Neither lever works alone. Fares recapture the cost only with a lag — United recovered 72% of its higher fuel costs in Q3, below its own 80%-90% guidance. The carriers holding margin are pairing price with capacity discipline and revenue that doesn’t ride on a seat: premium mix, loyalty, cargo, and at Delta, a refinery. Operations decide who survives the lag. 15.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Back in late 1944, two regiments of the 6th Marine Division were on Guadalcanal, training for an invasion of a target they didnât know yet, and they had more pressing matters on their minds: which of them had the better football team. The 4th and 29th Marines were loaded with former college stars, and according to Buzz Bissinger, whose 2022 book is the basis of Peter Bergâs fresh film, the 65 men who eventually played included three All-Americans and seven college captains, from Brown to Notre Dame to California.

On NPRâs Fresh Air, Bissinger did the 4th Regimentâs trash talk for them (âThis is the 4th Regiment. We are loadedâ), and the 29th, naturally, disagreed.

The game got set for Christmas Eve 1944, and the Marines went at it like the Rose Bowl was coming to Guadalcanal. There were printed rosters, a public-address system, radio announcers, and regimental bands, Denver sportswriter Terry Frei reported in his 2003 account, which drew on interviews with surviving players. It was played on the 29thâs parade ground, which was covered in coral and gravel as well as dirt, and had no grass. The game was supposed to be touch football, but the Marines, being Marines, turned it into tackle. âFifteen hundred Marines came, drunk. No one cared. Gambling, no one cared,â Bissinger said, and no one was wearing pads or helmets.

The players included Wisconsinâs two-time All-American end Dave Schreiner, captain of the 4th; Purdue fullback Tony Butkovich, the first-round draft pick of the Cleveland Rams; Notre Dameâs 1942 captain, George Murphy; Schreinerâs Wisconsin teammate Bob Bauman; and John McLaughry, a former Brown star who had played for the Upcoming York Giants. Frei notes that the 4thâs backup quarterback was an East St. Louis native named Hank Bauer, who later played and managed in the major leagues. A Marine combat correspondentâs United Press dispatch called the whole thing âthe Mosquito Bowl football classic,â and the name stuck.

It has been revealed that after all that, the score was 0-0. Thereâs even a dispute about the last play: Bissinger notes a field goal was blocked, while Frei and History.com say the 4thâs quarterback, Bob Spicer, made an interception at the end. The Marines wanted a rematch, but the 4th Regimentâs commander, Alan Shapley, refused, telling them, as Bissinger put it, that if they were going to get killed or hurt, he wanted it to happen in combat and not in a football game. Since nobody won, all the bets were a push.

By the middle of March 1945, the division had shipped out, and on April 1, the Marines landed on Okinawa. The battle lasted 82 days, and 15 of the 65 Mosquito Bowl players were killed in it, according to History.com; Schreiner, Bauman, and Butkovich were among them. On May 15, Murphy led a platoon of the 29th up Sugar Loaf Hill, and after the men ran out of grenades, he ordered a withdrawal on his own initiative. The Armyâs official history of the campaign records what happened next: âCovering the men as they pulled back down the slope, Murphy was killed by a fragment when he paused to help a wounded Marine.â Schreiner was shot on June 20 and died the next day, hours before the island was declared secure. He was 24 years old.

That fall, Time ran a short piece on the divisionâs football players. âWhen it headed for the Pacific, the 6th Marine Division boasted enough football talent to line up three all-star teams,â it remarked. âNow, on the way back, the 6th would be hard-pressed to muster one full team.â.

It has been revealed that berg, who directed the movie version of Bissingerâs Friday Night Lights, co-wrote the new film with Mark L. Smith, according to Netflix. Netflixâs Tudum lists Nicholas Galitzine as McLaughry, Bill SkarsgÃ¥rd as Bauman, Ray Nicholson as Butkovich, and Tom Francis as Schreiner. The movie opened in select theaters on October 30, 2026, and hits Netflix on November 25, with no word yet on whether it settles the last play.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The only thing that feels more like Thanksgiving than an exquisitely burnished roast turkey is the (sometimes chaotic) assemblage of loved ones seated around it. For your tablescape this year, take inspiration from the beautifully unique cast of characters that make a family a family.

According to recent reports, she just stepped off a red eye from the major city, but she looks like she came from a gallery opening—and her place setting is as bold and eclectic as her fashion sense. Bulbous postmodern ceramic plates, '90s Art Deco revival flatware from Japan, and a hand-beaded placemat are exactly the things she’d be into. The button-shaped aluminum coaster is seldom occupied, since she prefers to keep the martini glass right where it belongs: in her hand.

Piano Cocktail Glass (Set of 2).

She’s 25 going on 70. In between baking all of the pies for the major dinner, she learned lace-making from a TikTok tutorial. She sews, she antiques, and she self-publishes Jane Austen fanfic online. The cheeky cotton bottle apron and pearl-tipped doily on her table might be brand newly introduced from Gohar World, but they pair exquisitely with the pewter flatware she scored at an estate sale. Quilted floral placemats and plates adorned with dainty, hand-painted bows from The Six Bells, a store leading the revival of country cottage decor, evoke the pastoral, bucolic lifestyle she yearns for (as long as she can keep her 10-step skin-care routine).

Herzerlmuster Scalloped Placemats (Set of 2).

Sources indicate that the combo of unbridled energy and still-developing motor skills means the Gen-Alpha kids are best served by a spread of disposable and shatterproof items. And, seeing that it’ll take some clever coaxing to pull these little gremlins away from their screens, their table must match the intense digital stimuli they’re accustomed to. Loop-de-loop silly straws, melamine plates, and acrylic forks and cups in as many colors as possible are the bare minimum to keep minds forged in a Cocomelon crucible engaged for the total duration of a Thanksgiving meal. Despite the visual chaos, their table might be more tranquil than the adults’.

Prue Leith Melamine Dinnerware Set and Tumblers.

Mammut Children's Chair and Table.

Thanksgiving might be the only time you see this elusive individual, as he otherwise spends the year fussing around his DIY Earthship in the desert outside of Santa Fe. His place setting is filled with natural materials, like these Shigaraki-style earthenware plates and zero-waste Belgian linen placemats. If he starts defending his dedication to composting toilets a little too enthusiastically, fill his hand-carved wooden mug with some herbal tea and he’ll settle down fine.

Jasper Linen Placements (Set of 4).

A matriarch par excellence, she’s been holding the family together for decades. Her demeanor might be as breezy as a Big Sur afternoon, but she means business when it comes to hosting Thanksgiving. Let it be known: She had a Nancy Meyers kitchen long before Nancy Meyers picked up a camera. To steal her vibe, invest in an Italian table cloth festooned with vines, hand-painted ceramic wicker plates, and bamboo-stemmed wine glasses. Place cards, arranged for maximum harmony, should bear each name in handwritten cursive. Miss Manners would be so proud.

Wicker Hand-Painted Ceramic Dessert Plates (Set of 4).

Bamboo Balloon Crystal Glasses (Set of 2).

The Courtin family behind the Clarins skincare empire is combining what the hotel industry usually splits apart: the buildings, the brands, and the operations of a luxury hotel group, under one owner.

The family behind skincare company Clarins is taking full ownership of Evok Collection, a French owner-operator of five luxury hotels, putting its capital into hotel real estate, brands, and operations.

It has been revealed that famille C Participations, the Courtin family's investment vehicle known as FCP, mentioned Tuesday it's acquiring 100% of Evok's share capital from Zaka Investments, which had been the majority investor. FCP had invested €130 million two years ago for a minority stake.

Price and terms weren't disclosed. Family-owned Clarins produces about $2 billion in annual sales in the skincare industry.
