Forgive the Daddy Warbucks-ness of what I’m about to say, but I think it’s crucial to remember that a splurge and an extravagance aren’t quite the same thing when it comes to gifts. On one end of the spectrum, there are vapid luxury items; on the other, there are the gifts whose steeper price point is tied directly to their artistry, quality, and/or durability. While the former can be fun to window-shop, our hard-earned clams are best spent on the latter.

In a recent development, as a seasoned shopping writer, I ask myself two massive questions when mulling over a pricey purchase: What is the story behind this item? Can I picture it in my life for years to come?

It has been revealed that consider the iconic, mid-century modern Moccamaster coffee machine, which first debuted in the 1960s and has been trending on social media lately for its array of colorful, modular designs. I took the cult-fave machine for an extended test run (it’s still my daily driver), and the yellow pepper iteration made me fall in love with drip coffee all over again. The Dutch tech giant behind the appliance, Technivorm, really exercises what it calls its core tenets of “form and function,” and will service any repairs on the machines for up to five years. That is exactly the kind of lore I crave from the splurge-level items on my holiday shopping list (and the kind that will make your own design-savvy, coffee-loving giftee feel special).

If you’re reaching into your budget for gifts that last, impress, and — if you’re giving them to a family member or partner — you might be able to use yourself for years to come, the fancy gifts for food lovers start getting good. There are the major-ticket kitchen titans: a high-tech Mill food recycler, sleek Miele vacuums (post-kitchen-prep cleanup doesn’t stand a chance), and electric pizza ovens that can reach 850 degrees Fahrenheit in just 90 seconds. Sometimes “splurges” are just wise investments, especially with appliances and cookware; your giftee is going to use a well-made cutting board or top-tier kitchen knife for years or decades to come. There are also the gifts with spectacular whimsy: a stationary exercise bike that makes smoothies, a martini-lover’s menorah, a tabletop lighter that’s also an incredible conversation piece.

These gifts may be at higher price points than a classic stocking stuffer, but they’re also extra-special — we’d say, so worth it if you have the dough. If you’re looking to roll out the red carpet with splurge-worthy food and kitchen gifts, look no further.

It has been revealed that the casual gift for someone who loves food and loves to host might be nice set of chip and dip bowls, cocktail napkins, or perhaps some beeswax candlesticks. The gift of a whole dry-cured Spanish ham leg, however, is a next-level present for the most passionate entertainer in your family or friend group.

According to recent reports, no better way to pull focus at the dining table than with this copper and brass pepper mill, which East Fork indicates can literally last for “hundreds of years” when cared for properly. The 10-inch tall grinder is made in collaboration with a small, family-run company in Greece, and is actually modeled after the same mills 20th-century Greek soldiers would carry to grind coffee, a fact that finds homage in the Greek lettering inscribed on the mill.

Industry observers note that the Eater staff has tested its fare share of toaster ovens, and crowned the Balmuda as one of the best for its minimalist design and ability to not just warm but rehydrate breads and pastries; it uses a steam process to reinvigorate that day-old croissant like a wizard. This Balmuda Pro has an even more powerful heat source, and a setting called Salamander Grill Mode for giving your salmon the restaurant-grade finishing treatment.

In a recent development, the cultural martini discourse has never been stronger, or brinier. Help your giftee celebrate Hanukkah with Susan Alexandra’s dirty martini menorah. As the designer’s site proclaims, “The miracle of Hanukkah was that the olive oil that was enough only for one day of light lasted for eight days. Our favorite way of consuming olives? In a bath of vodka/ gin and a touch of vermouth!”.

Recent findings suggest that behold, a splurge that is also a cooking investment! We’ve all experienced the frustration of chopping special ingredients on a sub-par cutting board, and the moment you level up to a thick, handsome slab is one that can help give you newfound confidence and efficiency as a passionate home cook. Boardsmith’s walnut end grain cutting boards are all made to order out of a sustainably harvested black walnut, resulting in beautiful, checkerboard-like and ombré color variations. Cheese boards have never looked better, folks.

The Chicago-based luxury chocolatier Vosges is known for its intricate, decadent holiday gifts (don’t miss its lodge-inspired advent calendar), and it has curated the perfect assortment of its truffles to go with a bottle of Ceretto Barolo wine. “This is a classic Barolo,” the site explains, “[it’s] light garnet in color with Barolo’s quintessential aromas of roses, tart cherries, and hints of truffles.”.

Made in Victor, Idaho, the boutique blades of New West KniveWorks are a departure from the recent fad of making knives extra wide, favoring instead the graceful docility of a light, 8-inch steel blade and a handle made out of a durable resin composite material that will last a lifetime. In the fighting words of New West, “this precision instrument isn’t a club like Mom’s old Wüsthof Trident.” If you’re shopping for a partner who tends to their knife collection like the Crown Jewels, it’s the kind of gift that feels equal parts lifetime cooking investment and personality-forward essential tool.

Gohar World’s elevated kitchen essentials walk the line between Dalí-esque absurdity (remember when Julia Fox wore its kitchen gloves to the Grammys?) and functionality, and this metallic apron is no exception: it lends you a lacy hand (two, actually) while you’re cooking.

I really do think the Moccamaster coffee machine is the Platonic ideal of drip coffee machines; my own yellow pepper model swept me off my feet with its talent for quick, smooth brewing and its modular, chic mid-century modern design. If you love someone who loves coffee — and perhaps already owns the GOATed machine — why not invest in the brand’s powerful burr grinder? It’s certified by the European Coffee Brewing Centre (ECBC), which means it has passed a rigorous testing process for uniform grinding and quality construction.

In a recent development, imagine casually inviting your beloved over for dinner, and you serve this gorgeous Japanese wagyu ribeye steak along with an Old-Fashioned? Imperia Caviar is best known for its royal osetra, but it’s also where you can find a variety of A5 Japanese wagyu (the highest designation for beef in the country); this grade of wagyu has up to five times more intramuscular fat, which makes for an even richer, buttery flavor.

I always have a few lighters floating around my house for candles and incense, but there’s something so retro-chic about a coffee table lighter. Edie Parker, master of eccentric and surreal lifestyle [puffs chamomile pre-roll] accessories has a line of jelly-inspired tabletop lighters with all kinds of “fillings,” and the olive version is one of the most charming.

It has been revealed that unsurprisingly, we’re picky when it comes to choosing cookware at Eater — that’s why we collaborated with Heritage Steel to make the kind of cookware collection that will last a lifetime. Every frypan, lid, and pot is made out of 5-ply stainless steel, and this robust bundle includes everything you need to embark on all kinds of culinary adventures: two fry pans (8.5- and 10.5-inch), a 2-quart saucier, a 3-quart saucepan, a 4-quart sauté pan, and an 8-quart stock pot ready to simmer your most Strega Nona-worthy stews.

According to recent reports, here’s an idea: Order this massive wheel of Manchego cheese from Flamingo Estate, and ride it to victory at the Cooper’s Hill cheese rolling competition. That, or gift it to someone who can appreciate the fact that it’s sourced, per Flamingo Estate, from one of only ten cheese mongers in Spain that are still making farmstead PDO Manchego Artesano, which results in an even richer and more complex flavor.

It has been revealed that you know the big (or rather, full-size) Rocco: a $1,500 high-tech drink fridge, endorsed by Eric Wareheim and seemingly designed by someone who loves Eames chairs. This year, Rocco has launched a miniature version of its posh drink refrigerator, dubbed the Mini Mini Fridge, this 14-inch tall personal fridge fits up to 12 cans of your preferred beverages (or sheet masks; choose your journey). Unlike most mini fridges, the Mini cools down to 39 degrees Fahrenheit (the majority of countertop fridges hit 48 degrees Fahrenheit at their coldest). Kind of the dream set up for your — sorry, your giftee’s — office.

Sources indicate that atelier Sebastião Lobo crafts otherworldly flatware that’s almost too beautiful to use. This set of Calder-esque cutlery has spawned many imitations, because it’s one of the most original designs to come out of the flatware world in recent years, and a prime example of how cutlery and tableware in general got really squiggly and freaky this year.

There is nothing like devoting counter space to yet another coffee machine that requires highly specific capsules, but hey! This one is different — it brews only cold coffee. (Nitro cold brew, cold brew, and cold espresso to be specific.) Sure, it’s definitely a bit of a luxury, but then again, so is spending $7 on an iced cortado from the coffee shop every morning.

N/A drinks were created to be a more inclusive product. Only a rare few can order bottles of bubbly for over $100. The Venn diagram where these two groups overlap is small, but it exists, along with this $119 bottle of booze-free bubbly made with French Chardonnay grapes.

Recent findings suggest that in a way that I cannot quite explain, this feels like it’s targeted at the 1990s kids who grew up with Smart House and Richie Rich. This stationary exercise bike, complete with an orange slice wheel, whips up one of your favorite smoothies courtesy of your own pedaling power. As one reviewer writes, “I am 67 years old, widowed twice, and I have seen enough in this life to know when somebody has finally invented something useful. This bicycle-blender contraption has changed the direction of my spirit. Every morning I put in one banana, some frozen peaches, yogurt, a little honey, and whatever green thing is closest to expiration in my refrigerator. Then I pedal until either the smoothie is done or I start seeing little sparkles. Whichever comes first.”.

Industry observers note that khushbu Shah is the former restaurant editor at Food & Wine and the author of the cookbook AMRIKAN: 125 Recipes From the Indian American Diaspora. She lives in Los Angeles and you can follow all of her egg eating adventures on Instagram.

  • Accor’s Duncan O’Rourke told Skift that UAE city hotels cut rates 15% to 20% in August and September to protect occupancy, while Gulf resort and Holy Cities hotels ran ahead of last year.
  • For owners, lenders and investors, the 2027 question is which of those markets to underwrite, and on what recovery date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gulf travel now runs at two speeds. Pilgrimage and resort demand held through 2026, while long-haul and corporate travel fell away. Every 2027 capital and capacity plan for the region depends on which market an operator underwrites.

Accor’s Duncan O’Rourke told Skift that UAE city hotels cut rates 15% to 20% in August and September to protect occupancy, while Gulf resort and Holy Cities hotels ran ahead of last year. Then the split moved inside Saudi Arabia. After Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s airport in October, 86% of scheduled departures were canceled and Riyadh RevPAR fell 65% to $65 for the month.

For owners, lenders and investors, the 2027 question is which of those markets to underwrite, and on what recovery date.

Developers kept building. The Middle East hotel pipeline reached a record 771 projects and 188,960 rooms in the third quarter, according to Lodging Econometrics data. Saudi Arabia holds 401 projects, up 15%, and most owners are pushing ahead, though Diriyah canceled a $191 million hotel contract in November. Transactions moved the other way. Knight Frank told Skift that pre-war asking prices no longer match buyer underwriting, and investors are rerunning feasibility studies built on pre-conflict occupancy.

According to recent reports, the terms behind that pipeline are changing too. Gulf sovereign funds now expect returns and are phasing projects and selling assets to meet them. Owners are reopening hotel management agreements with operators over performance tests and when management fees get paid. Colliers’ Nicolas Nasra expects the toughest negotiating environment in a decade.

It has been revealed that forecasts disagree by most of a year. Before the October strikes, Accor expected UAE hotels back to pre-war levels by late in the first quarter of 2027. S&P Global Ratings does not expect that before the end of 2027. Since then, Accor has said regional RevPAR may fall about 12% in the fourth quarter, the region’s peak season.

According to recent reports, fourth-quarter results arrive after most 2027 budgets lock in. Every underwriting call made this month carries a recovery date the data cannot yet confirm.

Photo Credit: The new mobile app brings together six group airlines. Lufthansa Group.

Lufthansa Group has spent years bringing its airlines closer together behind the scenes. This latest move suggests Frankfurt increasingly wants to own the customer relationship, too.

Lufthansa Group is taking another step toward becoming a consumer brand in its own right with the launch of a new app that brings together six of its airlines under a single digital identity.

Unveiled on Monday, the app combines the digital services of Lufthansa, Swiss, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines, ITA Airways, and Discover Airlines, alongside elements of the group’s Miles & More loyalty program. Passengers can book flights, purchase additional services, check in, access boarding passes, and track their baggage.

While much of the functionality will be familiar to owners of the existing airline apps, Lufthansa Group chief commercial officer Dieter Vranckx described it as a logical step in developing the parent tech giant’s brand and “making it more tangible” to passengers.

His comments this week echo an earlier observation that the firm “is evolving from a group of airlines into an integrated airline group.”.

Sources indicate that indiGo calls it "disciplined growth." It's also a retreat to safer ground: Southeast Asia suits its narrowbodies while fuel is expensive and Pakistan's airspace is closed. But it's the same region where IndiGo cut six routes this summer, so the real test comes after the holiday peak.

IndiGo is adding more flights to Southeast Asia at a time when rising fuel costs and geopolitical tensions are making some of its westbound operations more expensive.

India’s largest airline will launch daily flights between Delhi and Kuala Lumpur, as well as Bengaluru and Hanoi, from Dec. 20. It will also increase Delhi–Singapore services to twice daily from the same date and Delhi–Bangkok flights to 19 a week from Dec. 28.

In a recent development, the additions give IndiGo more capacity in a region that has long been popular with Indian travelers. They also come as the airline is becoming more careful about where it deploys aircraft internationally, with higher fuel bills and airspace restrictions making some routes harder to operate profitably.

For the quarter ended Sept. 30, international capacity, measured in available seat kilometers, fell 3% from a year earlier, while domestic capacity remained broadly flat.

Industry observers note that dubai’s hotels are under pressure, but developers are still signing deals for branded residences. The main bet is on buyers, with brands delivering a healthy premium over the wider market.

Developers in the UAE are still launching branded residences, betting on long-term demand as the U.S.-Iran war that began in late February weighs on Dubai’s hotel market.

Branded residences are residential properties developed in partnership with an established brand, such as a luxury hotel operator.

Sources indicate that avenew Development has launched The St. Regis Residences at Dubai Islands with Marriott International. Dubai South has signed UK-based Cheval Collection for Cheval South Bay. And Al Seeb Real Estate Development has started main construction on Chedi Private Residences in Dubai.

Sources indicate that the launches come against a weakened hotel market. Dubai occupancy fell to 68.4% in October, down 16.5 points from 84.9% a year earlier, according to CoStar’s STR. Average daily rate dropped 28.1% to $181 and RevPAR fell 42% to $124. International visitors in the first 10 months of the year fell 38% to 9.7 million, according to Dubai’s Department of Economy and Tourism.

According to recent reports, norse Atlantic Airways is fighting for its survival after warning on Wednesday that it needs fresh funding to continue operating. In a short stock exchange filing, the Norwegian low-cost, long-haul carrier described its financial situation as “critical.”.

The organization said it had explored various strategic alternatives with its advisors and was open to discussions over a potential takeover.

Sources indicate that more immediately, Norse is in talks with selected parties to secure short-term financing. However, the airline warned that “there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution.”.

Recent findings suggest that shares in Norse plunged to an all-time low following the announcement, down more than 70% as of 1 p.m. Oslo-time on Wednesday. The manufacturer did not disclose how much money it needs or how long it can continue operating without additional funding.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that longer stays and a rise in cultural visits suggest Ramadan is becoming a more significant season in Abu Dhabi’s tourism calendar. The Department of Culture and Tourism - DCT Abu Dhabi now sees an opportunity to turn the holy month into a more deliberate travel proposition for both visitors and the global travel trade.

This sponsored content was created in collaboration with a Skift partner.

According to recent reports, ramadan has traditionally been viewed as a quieter month for travel in the Gulf. However, early data from DCT Abu Dhabi’s Ramadan 2026 season suggests that old assumptions about the holy month may be changing. The average length of stay across Abu Dhabi increased 3% year-on-year, while domestic hotel guests stayed 31% longer. Visits to cultural institutions more than doubled, rising from around 131,000 in Ramadan 2025 to over 291,000 in 2026.

Skift Studio spoke with Abdulla Yousuf, director of international operations at DCT Abu Dhabi, to explore how the emirate is making Ramadan a more intentional part of the visitor experience.

Skift Studio: How have international visitors and the travel trade traditionally viewed visiting Abu Dhabi during Ramadan, and how has that changed in recent years?

Abdulla Yousuf: Some international travelers and travel trade partners have historically viewed Ramadan as a period when activity may be lower across the region, especially regarding opening hours, dining options, and the availability of visitor experiences. We’ve collectively worked on changing that perception over the past few years. Abu Dhabi remains open during Ramadan. Our world-class hotels, cultural landmarks, theme parks, dining venues, and beaches remain open without interruption throughout the Holy Month.

Recent findings suggest that what changes during Ramadan is not operational capacity, but the emirate’s rhythm. It transforms into a culturally rich season of community and reflection during the day, which gives way to an electric, festive atmosphere after sunset. The travel trade is increasingly recognizing that Ramadan is a value-added cultural window that cannot be experienced at any other time of the year.

According to recent reports, abu Dhabi saw an increase in the average length of stay during Ramadan 2026. What do you take from that change, and what factors do you think may have influenced it?

One likely contributing factor was the timing of Ramadan within Abu Dhabi’s cooler season, when comfortable temperatures make it easier to enjoy outdoor activities, such as waterfront promenades, kayaking in the mangroves, desert adventures, and visits to heritage sites.

At the same time, Ramadan reshapes the emirate into a distinctive day-to-night journey. Calm daytime exploration of beaches, resorts, and world-class attractions transitions into evenings centered around iftars, atmospheric night markets, community suhoors, and cultural activations like Layali Nights.

Sources indicate that extended opening hours make every day feel varied, immersive, and rewarding, naturally encouraging visitors to stay longer. This variety gives travel advisors and tour operators more opportunities to build itineraries that combine relaxation, culture, and outdoor experiences, helping position Abu Dhabi as a destination worth visiting during Ramadan.

What does the 2026 data tell you about how different visitor segments are using the destination?

It has been revealed that the figures highlight two interesting trends. Visitors are spending longer in Abu Dhabi, and engagement with our cultural offering has increased significantly. The 31% year-on-year increase in length of stay among domestic hotel guests underscores the potential for Ramadan to drive longer stays in the domestic market. The increase in visits to our cultural institutions reinforces the importance of culture within the destination’s Ramadan offering.

Industry observers note that the opportunity for our international travel trade partners is in communicating this diversity more effectively. Ramadan can appeal to visitors interested in culture, family experiences, hospitality, and outdoor activities, allowing partners to tailor itineraries to different traveler interests rather than treating the Holy Month as a single type of travel experience.

What role does culture play in Abu Dhabi’s Ramadan visitor experience?

It has been revealed that culture is central to the Ramadan experience in Abu Dhabi. The Holy Month offers visitors an opportunity not only to discover our cultural attractions but also to experience Emirati traditions, hospitality, and the importance of community firsthand.

In a recent development, culture during the Holy Month is lived and shared. During the day, visitors explore landmarks such as Louvre Abu Dhabi, teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi, Zayed National Museum and Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi in Saadiyat Cultural District.

It becomes deeply communal at night, from heritage games at Al Jahili Fort and Ramadan at Qasr Al Hosn to shared iftars at Ezba Experiences, and late-night visits to Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque.

What makes Ramadan a great time to visit Abu Dhabi? What should visitors expect?

According to recent reports, visitors can expect a deeply authentic experience. First and foremost, Abu Dhabi is completely open for business. Every luxury resort, Michelin-recognized restaurant, shopping destination, and major attraction functions at full capacity with world-class hospitality.

In a recent development, after sunset, the emirate becomes remarkably vibrant. Dining evolves into a shared celebration, with iftars showcasing both global and Emirati flavors, followed by suhoors that invite people to slow down, connect, and enjoy live music, conversation, and warm hospitality late into the night. Above all, Emirati culture is rooted in generosity. International visitors are invited to sit at communal tables and build genuine connections with our community.

With Ramadan 2027 also falling during Abu Dhabi’s cooler season (February to March), visitors can combine these cultural experiences with time outdoors, whether exploring the Corniche, enjoying our beaches or discovering the desert.

In a recent development, my advice to anyone considering a visit is to embrace the distinct rhythm of the Holy Month. Ramadan offers a chance to discover Abu Dhabi at a slightly slower pace, while experiencing traditions and moments of community that make this time of year special.

Recent findings suggest that what are you hearing from tour operators and travel advisors about selling Abu Dhabi during Ramadan? Where do knowledge gaps still exist, and how does the Experience Abu Dhabi Experts Ramadan module respond to them?

In a recent development, some of the questions we encounter relate to practical considerations, such as opening hours, dining options, and the experiences available to visitors during the Holy Month. To address this, our International Operations team provides practical information and opportunities for first-hand experience of the destination. Our Experience Abu Dhabi Experts e-learning platform includes dedicated Ramadan training to help advisors better understand the visitor experience and communicate it to their clients.

We complement this with international trade engagement, including workshops in 23 markets, roadshows, and familiarisation trips that allow our partners to experience Abu Dhabi and its cultural offerings for themselves.

In a recent development, ultimately, our role is to help the travel trade move beyond general awareness of Abu Dhabi and develop a deeper understanding of the destination. The better equipped our partners are to explain what visitors can experience during Ramadan, the more confidently they can recommend it and develop relevant itineraries.

How will DCT Abu Dhabi use learnings from Ramadan 2026 to shape the destination’s approach in 2027 and beyond?

The results from Ramadan 2026 have reinforced the importance of positioning the Holy Month as a distinctive part of Abu Dhabi’s year-round visitor offering. The increases in average length of stay and cultural engagement are encouraging and provide insights as we continue developing our approach for 2027 and beyond.

One priority is to continue working with our tourism and hospitality partners to showcase the range of experiences available during Ramadan, from cultural attractions and outdoor activities to evening dining and community celebrations.

Sources indicate that our wider ambition remains aligned with Abu Dhabi’s Tourism Strategy 2030: to attract visitors year-round, encourage longer stays, and strengthen the emirate’s position as a leading global destination. Ramadan plays an important role in that ambition by offering international visitors a culturally distinctive, uniquely Abu Dhabi experience.

To learn more about Abu Dhabi, visit visitabudhabi.ae.

For decades, the companies that controlled airline distribution occupied one of the most vital positions in the travel industry. But making money from travel bookings and building a profitable technology business around them have turned out to be very different propositions. The contrasting fortunes of Amadeus, Sabre, and Travelport show just how different.

In 2000, Amadeus accounted for an estimated 26% of global GDS air bookings, compared with 34% for Sabre, including Abacus. Galileo and Worldspan, then separate systems that were later combined into Travelport, together had about 40%. By 2023, the estimates were 47% for Amadeus, 32% for Sabre, and 21% for Travelport, according to Redburn Atlantic data.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One pot, four hits of lemon: Juice (limone #1) and zest (limone #2) in the cooking water, then more juice (limone #3) and zest (limone #4) to ﬁnish. The contrast of cooked and fresh citrus yields a lemon experience as wild as it gets—at least as far as pasta goes. Crème fraîche and Parmigiano-Reggiano mellow the acid into submission, delivering a creamy yet punchy ﬁnal product just begging for forks… and maybe one more squeeze of lemon.

Sources indicate that want some protein here? Add one pound of peeled and deveined medium shrimp to the pot as soon as the pasta turns uncomfortably al dente.

More puckery, lemony dishes this way.

In a recent development, remove the zest from 2 lemons with a vegetable peeler in long, lengthwise strips. Chop the strips very fine. (You should have a heaping 2 Tbsp.) Transfer half the chopped zest to a large pot or Dutch oven. Reserve the remaining half.

Squeeze enough juice from the lemons to measure ½ cup (120 ml); reserve the remaining lemon for squeezing at the finish. Transfer ¼ cup (60 ml) of the juice to the pot with the zest and reserve the remaining juice for serving. Add 3½ cups (840 ml) water, 1 large shallot, peeled and thinly sliced, 2 Tbsp. (30 g) unsalted butter, 4 thyme sprigs, leaves stripped and stems discarded, and 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal kosher salt.

Place the pot over high heat and bring to a boil. Add 1 lb. (454 g) egg noodles. (Don’t worry if they’re not fully submerged.) Cook, stirring, until the pasta is uncomfortably al dente, 5–7 minutes. Reduce the heat to medium to maintain a lively but gentle simmer and add 1 cup (2 oz./60 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and ¼ cup (60 ml) water, stirring to incorporate and create a pan sauce. Continue cooking and adding water, ¼ cup (60 ml) at a time, until there is a generous amount of sauce pooling in the pot and the noodles are al dente, 3–5 minutes more. Add ⅓ cup (80 g) crème fraîche, the remaining finely chopped lemon zest, and the reserved ¼ cup (60 ml) lemon juice. Season with kosher salt and taste. If the only flavor you’re getting is lemon, continue salting to bring out the creaminess.

According to recent reports, serve topped with a big dollop of crème fraîche and a squeeze of lemon juice. Shower with the remaining 1 cup (2 oz./60 g) finely grated Parmigiano-Reggiano and pinches of flaky sea salt. (Yes, this is a lot of Parm! But stay with me here… it’s a vital balance to the punches of lemon.) Top with more thyme leaves, and if desired, cracked black pepper and chopped roasted hazelnuts.

Expedia Group agreed Wednesday to acquire Czech online travel agency Kiwi.com, expanding its European flight offering for consumers and B2B partners.

The companies did not disclose the price, and Expedia declined to comment on it when contacted by Skift. Kiwi generated €227 million ($264 million) in 2025 revenue.

Beguinage of Anderlecht in Anderlecht, Belgium

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that tucked away in the historic centre of Anderlecht, just a stone's throw from the Collegiate Church of Saints Peter and Guido, lies one of Brussels' lesser-known historical treasures: the Beguinage of Anderlecht.
  • Unlike traditional convents, beguinages offered women an opportunity to live in a religious community without taking permanent monastic vows.
  • The Anderlecht beguinage consists of two modest buildings surrounding an enclosed courtyard garden with an old well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that tucked away in the historic centre of Anderlecht, just a stone's throw from the Collegiate Church of Saints Peter and Guido, lies one of Brussels' lesser-known historical treasures: the Beguinage of Anderlecht. Founded in 1252, it is considered the smallest beguinage in Belgium and once provided a home to a community of just eight women.

Unlike traditional convents, beguinages offered women an opportunity to live in a religious community without taking permanent monastic vows. The beguines were typically unmarried women or widows who chose a life of prayer, work and mutual support. They followed rules of chastity and obedience but remained free to leave the community whenever they wished. This offered women a degree of independence that was relatively unusual in medieval society.

The Anderlecht beguinage consists of two modest buildings surrounding an enclosed courtyard garden with an old well. The buildings date from different periods, with sections originating in the 16th and 18th centuries. From the garden, visitors can enjoy a view of the neighbouring Gothic collegiate church.

Interestingly, the beguinage was locally nicknamed the Klaphuis, meaning 'chatterbox' in Dutch, a playful reference to the conversations that supposedly took place among its residents.

Recent findings suggest that following the French Revolution, the religious community disappeared and the buildings were converted into a hospice for disadvantaged women. They continued serving this purpose until 1928. In 1930, the complex became a local history museum, displaying archaeological finds, religious art and objects illustrating Anderlecht's past.

After decades of use as a museum, the buildings underwent an extensive restoration, completed in 2022. The restoration aimed to recover the original appearance of the complex, allowing visitors to appreciate its historic architecture. Today, the beguinage offers a rare glimpse into the everyday lives of medieval women and the history of one of Brussels' oldest communities.

Despite being surrounded by the busy streets of Anderlecht, stepping through its entrance feels like discovering a little pocket of tranquillity that has survived for almost eight centuries.

It is managed by the Erasmus House that is located close to it.

When most of us imagine the 1920s, we might think of flapper dresses and the glittery parties of The Great Gatsby. Still, amid all the upheaval and change during this decade, families were very much living out their everyday lives in America.Â.

During the â20s, rapid economic growth after World War I revved up consumer culture, and many families began buying cars, lighting their homes with electricity, and purchasing stock using credit. All this economic expansion would ultimately culminate in the Great Depression, but during the â20s, many families found themselves with access to more economic abundance than ever before. That led to some brand-newly introduced purchases, including some of the items on this list.

Industry observers note that the first radio broadcast aired on Christmas Eve in 1906, and the technology experienced rapid expansion in the 1920s. In 1921 there were just five radio stations in America, but there were 606 by the end of the decade. During this time, radio became a âpervading and somewhat godlike presence,â E. B. White wrote in 1933, that brought news, entertainment, music, and advertising to even the most rural locations. Gathering around the radio became a family ritual, and these machines often occupied special places in living rooms. Radio stars became household names, broadcasts became key parts of mornings, evenings, and holidays, and far-flung, disconnected communities now had access to breaking news and the day's newest music, among other cultural currents.

Sources indicate that thomas Edison invented the tin-foil phonograph in 1877, and gramophones were introduced in the late 1880s. These machines made their way into family homes throughout the early 20th century, and by the mid-1920s, the majority of family homes had some kind of record player. The typical 1920s model was hand-cranked and was generally kept in cabinets or cases in the parlor.Â Many of the biggest hits of the day were novelty songs, though greats like Louis Armstrong and Mamie Smith also occupied key places in many people's record collections.

Industry observers note that electric refrigerators had been invented by the 1920s, but they were too expensive for the average American family at the time and did not become popular until after World War II. Instead, most families kept perishable food in iceboxes, which were wooden cabinets that held blocks of ice in their upper chambers. An ice man would deliver fresh ice to homes multiple times per week, and families would regularly clear out the melted water from a pan on the floor.Â.

It has been revealed that in the 1920s, most houses did not have central heating or wall insulation. Instead, families relied on fireplaces, oil and coal-powered heaters, or wood-burning stoves to make it through cold winters. Wood stoves worked better than fireplaces, but still required regular maintenance and lots of firewood. Nights could get bitterly cold after the wood burned down, so many people still relied on warm clothes to stay cozy on frigid evenings.

Sources indicate that many of us might complain about laundry day today, but truthfully, our experiences have absolutely nothing on what it takes to wash clothes without a machine. Electric washing machines had been invented by the 1920s and some wealthy homes had them, but the majority of 1920s families still washed clothes by hand. âWash dayâ typically occurred once a week. Clothes would be scrubbed over a washboard before being rinsed and boiled in separate pots, then hung to dry. This had to be done on cold winter days as well as hot summer ones, and clothes would sometimes freeze on clotheslines. The day after was often set aside for ironing, which usually required another full dayâs labor.

According to recent reports, band-aids were invented in 1920, though at the time they were handmade strips that consumers had to cut. Pre-cut bandages hit shelves in 1924, and they soon became a staple in 1920s cabinets. A typical â20s medicine cabinet might have also included Vaseline, aspirin, safety razors, and thermometers, as well as some more experimental itemsâsuch as chlorine gas bombs, which were canisters of chlorine gas that users believed could help with colds when released into a room.

In a recent development, the 1920s saw a boom in vacuum cleaners, which were invented in the early 20th century. Vacuums were generally marketed to middle-class women, along with promises of freedom from the challenges of housework during an era when servants and maids had become much less common. In reality, this deviceâs popularity led to higher standards for cleanliness at home and created more work for many women. Before vacuum cleaners, rugs had typically been brought outside and beaten just once or twice a year, but vacuums (and advertisements that emphasized the dangers of dust and particles) helped create the expectation that women were responsible for single-handedly maintaining completely spotless homes.

It has been revealed that cars exploded in popularity in the 1920s, transitioning from luxury items to everyday necessities. Major companies like Ford, Chrysler, and General Motors made cars more accessible to regular people thanks to the likes of Ford's iconic Model T. In turn, cars transformed American industry, creating huge numbers of manufacturing jobs, stoking urbanization, and redefining the food industry. They altered every aspect of life for many people, making travel and leisure activities more accessible and catalyzing many cultural shifts that would define the decades to come.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’ve always loved Italian American food. Maybe because Italian and Korean cooking have traits in common: Both are homey and resourceful, and grandmothers are revered for their signature dishes made without formal recipes. This recipe was one of the first Korean Italian fusion recipes I developed, and it makes use of my two favorite secret weapons: kimchi and fish sauce. The result is the Bolognese you know and love, but with a deep, tangy twist. Fish sauce in Italian cooking is not a newly introduced idea, actually—Romans have been using salted anchovies and garum, an ancient kind of fish sauce, for centuries. For an extra-special finish, I love garnishing this with baek (white) kimchi for acidity. But it’s optional, and regular kimchi (or no kimchi) works just fine, too.

More winning pasta recipes this way.

Sources indicate that start the Bolognese sauce: Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or pot over medium-high heat. Stir in 1 medium-yellow onion, finely diced (about 1½ cups), 2 carrots, peeled and finely diced, and 3 stalks celery, finely diced, and cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions have softened and the edges start to brown, about 4 minutes. Stir in 4 cloves garlic, minced, and a pinch of kosher salt and cook for 30 seconds, then stir in 1 cup chopped kimchi and 1 Tbsp. tomato paste and cook until the kimchi pieces start to soften, about 3 minutes. Pour in ½ cup red wine, increase the heat, and simmer, stirring with a wooden spoon to dislodge any bits that have stuck to the bottom, until the wine has nearly disappeared, about 2 minutes.

It has been revealed that add the meat: Stir in 1 lb. ground beef, season with generous pinches of salt (at least ½ tsp.), and cook, breaking up the beef into small pieces with a wooden spoon, until cooked through, 6 to 8 minutes.

Sources indicate that add the tomatoes: Pour one 28-oz. can whole San Marzano tomatoes in a bowl. Using clean hands, squish the tomatoes into small pieces. Pour the tomatoes into the pot and add 1 cup beef broth or water, ½ tsp. dried Italian seasoning or dried oregano, a pinch of salt, and a few grinds of freshly ground black pepper. Bring to a simmer and lower the heat to medium-low. Gently cook, stirring occasionally, until the sauce is just thick enough to stand up on a spoon, about 20 minutes. Stir in 2 Tbsp. fish sauce and taste, then add more salt or fish sauce if needed.

It has been revealed that cook the noodles and serve: In a pot of boiling salted water, cook 1 lb. spaghetti according to package instructions, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, until al dente. Drain the noodles in a colander, then give the colander a shake to get rid of extra water. Divide the noodles among serving plates and spoon the Bolognese on top. Garnish with 1 cup chopped kimchi (white or regular; if using) and 2 Tbsp. chopped flat-leaf parsley and serve.

Do Ahead: Leftover Bolognese sauce (without the noodles) keeps in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days, or in the freezer for up to 2 months.

Cat-and-mouse team Tom and Jerry (although originally unnamed) made their debut on the massive screen way back in 1940. Deitch, however, wasnât a fanâand when the original MGM shorts were repackaged and syndicated for Saturday morning television in the 1960s, the series promptly proved controversial.Â.

Although Tom and Jerry had always had its fair share of slapstick humor, both Deitch (who initially dismissed the cartoons as âneedlessly violentâ) and American parents alike found it all a little too much to take, and so the 1960s cartoons were largely toned down.Â.

But Tom and Jerry are by no means alone in stoking controversy despite their enduring popularity, and their otherwise rather tame and unprovocative content.Â Â.

It might have been one of the most popular shows of its time, but back in the 1950s I Love Lucy saw its fair share of controversiesâsome before the first episode was even broadcast.

Recent findings suggest that real-life husband and wife Lucille Ball and Desi Arnaz had been together for almost a decade when CBS executives approached Ball to transfer her successful radio show, My Favorite Husband, to television. She and Arnaz saw it as a chance to work together, but producers thought otherwise and pushed back on Arnazâs casting before the show had even been picked up.

According to recent reports, âThe people [at Ballâs talent agency] remarked the public wouldnât believe I was married to Desi,â Ball said in a retrospective interview after the show came to an end in 1958. âHe talked with a Cuban accent, and after all, what typical American girl is married to a Latin?âÂ.

According to recent reports, even after Ball fought back against the institutional racism that Arnaz faced in even landing his role in the show, I Love Lucy continued to court controversy. When Ball became pregnant in 1952, the decision was made to write her pregnancy into the showâbut executives banned the word âpregnantâ from ever being spoken, advertisers warned never to show her pregnancy bump, and CBS even demanded each episodeâs script be ran by a priest, a minister, and a rabbi to ensure it wasnât too morally questionable.

In the end, the plotline proved one of the biggest successes in television history, with the finaleââLucy Goes to the Hospitalââwatched by a staggering 70% of television audience.Â.

In much the same way that Tom and Jerry had caused uproar when it was syndicated for the small screen in the 1960s, The Three Stooges likewise came under fire for glorifying violence when their shorts were adapted for syndication in the late 1950s.

In particular, PTA organizations and a group known as NABRTV, or The National Association for Better Radio and Television, singled the films out as âold relicsâ that were not suitable for children. In 1962, the BBC broke newly introduced ground with a short-lived satirical comedy show presented by David Frost (best known to Americans for his interviews with Richard Nixon) called That Was the Week That Was. The seriesâwhich poked fun at everyone from politicians and media figures to the prime minister and even royaltyâpromptly proved so successful with audiences that an American version followed in 1964, and ran weekly for 50 episodes.Â.

As commonplace as satire is on television today, however, back in the early â60sâand especially on the hallowed British Broadcasting Companyâthings werenât quite so open, and from its very first episode That Was the Week That Was caused outrage in the British political and media class.

Reportedly, having fielded several angry telephone calls from newspaper editors, Britainâs Postmaster General Reg Bevins, the minister then in charge of broadcasting, released a statement to the morning papers saying that he was going to âdo something about this.â When he arrived at his office, however, he found a note from Prime Minister Harold Macmillan, reading, âOh no youâre not.âÂ.

Of all the television demonstrates to fall foul of early censorship rules, the quaint and sweet NBC sitcom I Dream of Jeannie might seem like an unlikely target. The costume demonstrated Edenâs midriff, leading censors to demand that, if she is to wear it on screen, her belly-button can never be seen.Â.

As any Star Trek fan will doubtless tell you, the original 1960s series proved groundbreaking in several rather unexpected ways, with series creator Gene Roddenberry using the showâs futuristic sci-fi dressing to tackle a number of important problems, and push boundaries on several othersâincluding in the Starship Enterpriseâs noticeably international crew.

Perhaps most notably of all, though, the 1968 episode âPlatoâs Stepchildrenâ saw Captain Kirk and Lieutenant Uhura share an interracial kiss, which saw the episode banned in several U.S. states. The episode came just one year after interracial marriage was made legal in the United States.Â.

Quintessentially British surreal sketch show Monty Pythonâs Flying Circus helped to launch the international careers of all its starsâincluding John Cleese, Eric Idle, and Terry Gilliamâbut caused considerable controversy over its five-year run on the BBC.

The series (and even more notoriously, the troupeâs 1979 movie Life of Brian) faced considerable backlash at the time from religious groups, who saw much of their content as blasphemous. One notorious sketch in particular (about a cannibalistic mortician) was so shocking that its broadcast quickly led to a meeting of BBC executives who deemed the show âappalling,â ânihilistic,â and âcruel.âÂ.

Long-running sitcom All in the Family famously broke upcoming ground in the 1970s by overtly tackling a raft of taboo problems including racism, homosexuality, and the Vietnam War. The seriesâwhich related the early history of the Roman Empire, from the perspective of Emperor Claudius (played by legendary Shakespearean actor Derek Jacobi)âwas an instant hit with audiences, but caused an understandable stir with its unflinching depictions of sex, adultery, prostitution, violence, homosexuality, abortion, and even incest.Â.

In a recent development, now in its fifth decade, BBC prime-time soap opera EastEnders is one of the UKâs longest running television shows. Set around Albert Square, a neighborhood in the fictional borough of Walford in Londonâs East End (hence the name), EastEnders debuted on February 19, 1985, and immediately ran into controversy after only its first few opening minutes.Â.

Industry observers note that another now infamous British broadcast, Ghostwatch was a 90-minute Halloween special, broadcast âliveâ on the BBC on October 31, 1992. Animated series Beavis and Butt-Head caused immediate concern among parents, politicians, critics, and media watchdogs alike on its first broadcast in 1993, thanks to its crude humor and depictions of questionable behavior.

Its unflinching portrayal of life among young gay men in the â90s, including considerable on-screen nudity and sex, caused immediate controversy in the British press, with the famously conservative-leaning Daily Mail newspaper lamenting that the show âproves that we need censorship.âÂ.

Reality show mainstay Substantial Brother debuted on Dutch television in 1999; it is now franchised in more than 60 different countries, and remains in production around the world more than 25 years later.

That being said, practically all iterations of the show have faced several notable controversies over the ideaâs long runâbut when the very first edition was broadcast in the Netherlands in the 1990s, even the very idea of broadcasting every moment of contestantsâ lives to the rest of the nation in the first place caused considerable moral outrage. Nonetheless, some 10,000 people applied to be on the first Dutch series, and Massive Brother has remained a globally popular show ever since.Â.

2026 Was the Year Restaurants Went Full Midwest

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality.
  • At Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve.
  • It has been revealed that the Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s a giardinera- and tavern-style-stuffed, totally welcoming time in hospitality.

At Kyle Knall’s Milwaukee restaurant Cassis, the showstopper dish is ravioli Dauphiné, a sheet of 24 tiny squares stuffed with the Wisconsin cheese Pleasant Ridge Reserve. Topped with glazed seasonal veggies, kernels of sweet corn in summer and sliced honeynut squash in late fall, it speaks to Knall’s Midwestern-meets-French approach—one of the reasons why his restaurant earned a slot on Eater’s 2026 list of the Best New Restaurants in America.

It has been revealed that the Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, feature serious Midwest representation. The Best New Restaurants list includes Chicago’s Creepies, which also digs into that Midwest-French mashup, and Kansas City’s Akoya Omakase, which brings a distinct viewpoint to the omakase experience. Meanwhile, the pickled walleye cheeks at Rosy in Cleveland and the puffed grain toast at All Well in Chicago are among the Restaurant Dishes of the Year, and Chicago’s Bad Butter, a place best-known for its croissant take on a Chicago-style hot dog, is one of the Best New Bakeries. It even includes drinks—Culebra, a Puerto Rican spot that draws on the Latinx influences of its Chicago neighborhood, is on Punch’s Best New Bars list. Between these accolades and other national recognition, all eyes are on the Midwest right now. And that’s even before we get into the impact of the Chicago-set show The Bear, which put Italian beef on everyone’s radar, and the rise of tavern-style pizza around the country.

The Midwest has always had great restaurants, of course, but it’s undeniable that something has shifted. “People are flying into these cities rather than flying over them,” says Vinnie Cimino, the Cleveland chef who co-owns Rosy and Cordelia. “I think that word is getting out about these smaller pockets of culture and cuisine.” Some of this is attributable to diners being more willing to explore outside substantial coastal cities, but it’s also due to chefs returning home to the region. “Post-pandemic, a lot of folks moved out of larger cities and back home,” says Cimino. “Now they’re setting up shop and creating great things in the spaces that they grew up in.” David Posey, chef and co-owner of Creepies and Elske in Chicago, agrees, adding: “For a long time, it felt like we were playing catch-up with trends on the coasts. Now I think we’re less quick to follow trends and are more confident in having our own voice of what the Midwest is.”.

One of those chefs who left Newly introduced York is Knall, a Birmingham, Alabama, native who cooked at Gramercy Tavern in New York before moving to his wife’s hometown of Milwaukee in 2020. Another is Peter Hoang, who worked at his father’s Kansas City, Missouri, sushi restaurant before gaining experience in Chicago and New York restaurants. When he returned to open Akoya Omakase, he crafted menus with the audience in mind, with two omakases, priced more affordably than many at $85 and $165, as well as an à la carte menu. “My sushi is honed by Japanese techniques and sourcing,” he says. “But I interpret what I think is best for the fish, whether that’s highlighting the textures and flavors through different garnishes or using aging or salting techniques.”.

It’s not simply that these are good restaurants located in the Midwest—these restaurants are deeply Midwestern in ethos. In Chicago, David and Anna Posey, who run the Michelin-starred Elske, wanted to open a French bistro for their second venture. But as they developed Creepies with chef de cuisine Tayler Ploshehanski, David Posey claims they began expanding its focus: “We started taking flavors and adapting them to things that we’re a little more familiar with.” This means dishes that draw on the traditions of Michigan, Wisconsin, and Illinois—think tarte flambée on a tavern-style pizza crust and mussels with giardiniera. And it’s not just the food at Creepies that reflects the Midwest: “We told our designer that our inspiration board was a Midwest basement with wood paneling and low ceilings meets a bistro in the French countryside.”.

At Cordelia, Cimino leans into the traditional cuisine of Northeast Ohio, with offerings like raw-beef cannibal sandwiches and kielbasa with cabbage salad. “It’s the familiar flavors that we grew up eating, rethought into this more modern light,” he states. Meanwhile, Rosy “is a deeper dive into the culture of our region” and features dishes like Balkan cevapi and Italian cotechino cooked over live fire. The approach is drawing a wide range of Cleveland diners, from 20-somethings there for the cool, candlelit vibe to grandparents there to taste the food they grew up with. “I think that’s what the Midwest is,” Cimino says. “Being able to be that transgenerational space everybody feels welcome in.”.

That welcoming community sensibility is a key component of Midwestern restaurants. Knall counts several farmers and shoppers at the West Allis Farmers Market, where he sources for Cassis, as some of his regulars. “To me, it reveals that’s really what Midwest food is: supporting those communities,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps more than anything, it’s hospitality that sets these spots apart. “Hospitality is our biggest focus between both restaurants and maybe even more of a focus than the food,” Knall says. “To me, the way that our team makes you feel in the restaurants is such a Midwest thing.” And at Cordelia, where the slogan is “Midwest Nice,” Cimino says: “It’s welcoming you into our proverbial home.”.

Portraying a man walking away from a modern office tower block, as if to explore the surrounding community, 'Walking East' is an impressive painted metal sculpture placed directly onto the street without a plinth.

Its creator, French Hong Kong-based sculptor Polo Bourieau, cited the inspiration for 'Walking East' as 'les adventuriers du quotidien' (the daily adventurers), the everyday working people going about their day in the Kwun Tong industrial district.

Located next to a busy junction, the 5-metre tall statue becomes especially poignant during work opening, lunch and closing hours. Surrounded by commuters and workers, it looms large over the hordes, seemingly journeying with them as they attempt to navigate their daily lives and Kwun Tong's crowded streets.

According to recent reports, the statue is located at the junction of How Ming Street and Tsun Yip Street. The closest MTR exits are Kwun Tong A2 and B3.

Foods you can’t take on planes

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1563 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the best parts about travel is all of the fresh food and drink you’re exposed to.
  • Every traveler has become accustomed to throwing away bottles of water, soda, and Pedialyte (there’s nothing worse than an in-flight hangover) before going through airport security.
  • That’s the 3-1-1 rule, and it’s still in place in 2026: Each liquid has to be in a container of 3.4 ounces or less, and all of them have to fit in one quart-size bag.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the best parts about travel is all of the fresh food and drink you’re exposed to. Sometimes, you find a food you like so much that you want to take it home with you. Depending on what that food or drink is, though, it might not make it past the TSA.

Every traveler has become accustomed to throwing away bottles of water, soda, and Pedialyte (there’s nothing worse than an in-flight hangover) before going through airport security. There are some liquids with different rules, however, and some banned foods that might surprise you. The TSA has a simple rule: “If it’s a solid item, then it can go through a checkpoint. However, if you can spill it, spread it, spray it, pump it or pour it, and it’s larger than 3.4 ounces, then it should go in a checked bag.”.

That’s the 3-1-1 rule, and it’s still in place in 2026: Each liquid has to be in a container of 3.4 ounces or less, and all of them have to fit in one quart-size bag. At airports with newer CT scanners, you may get to leave that bag in your carry-on. The Department of Homeland Security has also said it’s reviewing the rule, but for now, the limits haven’t changed.

Sources indicate that if it’s not on this list, then it’s good to fly in carry-ons or checked bags, although TSA agents may ask you to take it out so they can take a look at it. These are the TSA food rules to know before you go.

Recent findings suggest that allowances: You’re allowed to bring alcohol in containers of 3.4 ounces or less (think minis) in your carry-on bag, as long as they all fit in your quart-size bag. For checked bags, you can take up to 5 liters (1.3 gallons) per person of anything between 24 and 70 percent ABV, so long as it’s in unopened retail packaging. In checked bags, anything 24 percent ABV or lower has no limit.

Prohibitions: You can’t take anything higher than 70 percent ABV in checked or carry-on bags. And even if you carry minis on, you can’t drink them on the plane.

Allowances: Formula, breast milk, juice, toddler drinks, and baby food (including puree pouches) are allowed in checked and carry-on baggage, even over 3.4 ounces, and they don’t need to go in your quart-size bag. You don’t even need to be traveling with your child to bring breast milk or formula.

Prohibitions: The only stipulations are that the amount in carry-on bags is limited to “reasonable quantities” and that you tell the TSA officer about them at the start of screening.

Allowances: All solid cheese is allowed in carry-on and checked bags, but you might be asked to take it out of your carry-on. Creamy cheese is allowed without restrictions in checked bags.

Prohibitions: You’re only allowed creamy cheese in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on bag.

Allowances: Solid chocolate is allowed in carry-ons and checked bags. Liquid chocolate is allowed without restrictions in checked bags.

Prohibitions: You’re only allowed liquid chocolate in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on bag.

Allowances: Feel free to take as many dips and spreads as you can eat in your checked bag.

Prohibitions: You can only take creamy dips and spreads in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: Completely frozen ice and ice packs are allowed in carry-on and checked bags, and so are frozen gel ice packs. Dry ice is allowed in both with your airline’s approval, up to 5.5 pounds, in a vented package marked as dry ice.

In a recent development, prohibitions: The TSA specifies that any ice that’s even partially melted or slushy (or, you know, water) has to follow the 3.4-ounce rule in your carry-on. Melted gel ice packs get the same treatment, unless they’re medically necessary or keeping breast milk or formula cold.

Allowances: Flying home from Thanksgiving? Bring all the leftover gravy you want in your checked bag.

Prohibitions: You can only take gravy in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: There’s no limit on the amount of honey you can bring in your checked bag.

Prohibitions: You can only take honey in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: Bring all the hummus you want in your checked bag.

Prohibitions: You can only take hummus in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: You can take ice cream in your checked bag. In your carry-on, stick to containers of 3.4 ounces or less, so single-serve cups, not pints.

It has been revealed that prohibitions: Got a pint? Eat it before security, because it’s not making it through. Liquid ice cream is allowed in checked bags, but you might want to just get latest ice cream at that point.

Allowances: Bring all the jam and jelly you can handle in your checked bag.

Prohibitions: You can only take jam or jelly in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Recent findings suggest that allowances: The TSA is actually very OK with you bringing your live pet lobster through security. It’s even OK with live lobsters that aren’t your pet that you initiative on eating later.

In a recent development, prohibitions: Your lobster has to travel in a clear, plastic, spill-proof container, and a TSA officer will look it over. Checked bags are fine. For carry-ons, check with your airline first.

Allowances: Bring all the maple syrup you want in your checked bag.

Prohibitions: You can only take maple syrup in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: Bring all the oils and vinegars you can handle in your checked bag.

Prohibitions: You can only take oils or vinegars in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: Any amount of peanut butter (and all other nut butters, for that matter) is good in checked bags.

Prohibitions: You can only take peanut butter in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: No limit to the amount you can bring in your checked bag.

Prohibitions: You can only take salad dressing, salsa, and sauces in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: Bring all the soup you want in your checked bag.

According to recent reports, prohibitions: To the TSA, soup is just as much a liquid as your bottle of water. You can only take soup in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: Bring all the yogurt you want in your checked bag.

Prohibitions: You can only take yogurt in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: Meat, seafood, and frozen food are allowed in carry-ons and checked bags. Stack up your checked bag with as much as you’d like to pay for.

Prohibitions: Any ice or ice packs keeping your seafood, meat, and frozen foods cold in your carry-on must be completely frozen when you go through security. Partially melted with a bit of water at the bottom? Those ice packs won’t make it through. Dry ice (see No. 6) is the safer bet.

Allowances: If you want to turn your checked bag into a weight, go right ahead.

Prohibitions: Cans can look unusual on the X-ray, which could lead to extra screening that ultimately leaves the can with the TSA agent. And anything packed in liquid, like canned fruit or vegetables, falls under the 3.4-ounce rule anyway. Better to check it or chuck it.

Industry observers note that allowances: None. This one stays home no matter which bag you pack.

Sources indicate that prohibitions: Cooking spray isn’t allowed in carry-on or checked bags. Pick up a new can when you land.

Allowances: Homemade or store-bought, bring all you want in your checked bag.

Prohibitions: Cranberry sauce counts as a spread and eggnog counts as a liquid, so you can only take them in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: Bottled juice, cold brew, and other drinks are fine in your checked bag. You can also bring an empty thermos or water bottle through security and fill it up on the other side.

Prohibitions: You can only take drinks in containers of 3.4 ounces or less in your carry-on.

Allowances: Dry and “moist” pet food count as solid food, so they’re fine in carry-on and checked bags.

Prohibitions: Wet pet food has to follow the 3.4-ounce rule in your carry-on, and there’s no exemption for prescription pet food, even for service animals.

Allowances: Powders are allowed in carry-on and checked bags.

Prohibitions: Anything over 12 ounces has to go in its own bin at screening and may need extra screening, including being opened. If you don’t need it on the plane, pack it in your checked bag.

Recent findings suggest that even foods that aren’t banned can get pulled for extra screening if they look odd on the X-ray, and the TSA officer always has the final say. When in doubt, look it up first with the “What Can I Bring?” tool on tsa.gov or in the MyTSA app. If it still seems iffy, check it, ship it, or leave it at home.

Originally published on Nov. 12, 2018, and updated on Nov. 24, 2026, with the latest information.

#430. Bolsover Town Earthworks in Bolsover, England

Bolsover Town Earthworks in Bolsover, England

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (392 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the current iteration of Bolsover Castle, in the NE of Derbyshire, is not, despite its appearance, a defensive structure.
  • Both the earlier stone building on this site and its wooden predecessor were, in contrast, both very much defensive structures.
  • It has been revealed that what we see on the ground  today is only about 1/3 of the original height.

According to recent reports, the current iteration of Bolsover Castle, in the NE of Derbyshire, is not, despite its appearance, a defensive structure. It does look  very reminiscent of the Norman white tower at the tower of London, but it is essentially a Jacobean residence dressed up for effect. However it is clear that the western and northern approaches are up steep slopes and the "keep" looks dominant on the escarpment.

Both the earlier stone building on this site and its wooden predecessor were, in contrast, both very much defensive structures. To the east and south the approach is relatively unobstructed by natural features. When the promontory at Bolsover was fortified in the 12th century  the eastern and southern defences of both the castle and the town were enhanced by earthworks and ditches with the earthworks surmounted by a wooden palisade. Bolsover was one of only 2 planned and defended towns of the 11th/12th century in Derbyshire (Castleton is the other). It was , in effect , a plantation of people of Norman descent and those Saxons who had demonstrated their acceptance of Norman rule.

It has been revealed that what we see on the ground  today is only about 1/3 of the original height. The most obvious earthwork and ditch remains are in the Hornscroft park next to the parish church but the earthwork defences, which also became the defences of the town, apparently had strength in depth with an outer ring of ditch and earthworks being identifiable to the east of the town at Oxcroft Lane (the area is known as Dyke Fields). Furthermore a local road between Bolsover and the next town to the north  (Clowne) has the local name "The Ramper" (as reflected in street names such as Ramper Avenue on nearby new developments). Local understanding is that the "Ramper" derives from the "Ramparts", a further layer of defence for the town which is now long gone. On Oxcroft lane there has also been found evidence of Roman and earlier occupation.

Industry observers note that these earthworks have long had protected status and are seen as an excellent example of medieval  town defences. Certainly  a visit to the famous castle or its historic water supply system is not complete without  a look at the real defensive  structures which pre-date it by about 300 years.

Holiday Flyers Will Forgive a Crying Baby — But Not Kids Who Do This

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (786 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving week in the US usually sends a rush of travelers through US airports, and the Sunday after Thanksgiving is usually the busiest travel day on any given year.
  • A new survey from point.me, a platform for finding flights using loyalty points, looked at how frequent flyers handle the friction that comes with a packed flight.
  • Parents dreading how their fellow passengers will respond to their crying infant can relax a little: only 2.3 percent of respondents said they would speak up about a crying baby — perhaps because everyone understands there’s very little to be done about it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving week in the US usually sends a rush of travelers through US airports, and the Sunday after Thanksgiving is usually the busiest travel day on any given year. In fact, TSA says it’s estimating it will screen more than 3 million passengers nationwide on Sunday, Nov. 29. That would put it just shy of the same Sunday in 2025, when it screened 3.13 million people — an all-time record for the agency. Those 3 million flyers will be a mix of kids, grandparents, frequent flyers, and maybe-once-a-year flyers, so some friction between travelers is all but guaranteed.

A new survey from point.me, a platform for finding flights using loyalty points, looked at how frequent flyers handle the friction that comes with a packed flight. The organization’s 2026 airplane etiquette survey talked to 2,018 travelers, more than half of whom reported flying at least five times a year. Other similar surveys have found that seat-kicking is the single most annoying in-flight behavior, but the point.me survey asked a slightly different question: not what bothers frequent flyers, but what they’ll actually speak up about.

Parents dreading how their fellow passengers will respond to their crying infant can relax a little: only 2.3 percent of respondents said they would speak up about a crying baby — perhaps because everyone understands there’s very little to be done about it.

Recent findings suggest that older kids are another matter, however. More than 80 percent of people said they would speak up about an older child kicking their seat, making it the most likely behavior on the list to get a reaction. More than half (55.5 percent) would speak up about someone playing audio without headphones, and 45.8 percent would say something to a neighbor taking over their already limited legroom.

According to recent reports, men said they were more willing to confront fellow passengers across the board. More than 85 percent of men would address a seat-kicker, compared to just 73.9 percent of women. About 60 percent of men said they would call out audio played without headphones, compared with 50.7 percent of women. Men were also more likely to step in if someone was rude to a flight attendant, at 34.7 percent versus 26.4 percent of women.

The window-versus-aisle debate has a gender split, too. Women were split almost evenly between the window (35.1 percent) and the aisle (34.8 percent), while men clearly favored the aisle (41.8 percent). Gen Z was the only age group that preferred the window on the whole, with 45 percent opting for it.

According to recent reports, but the dreaded middle seat actually wasn’t chosen as the least-favorite option. That honor went to the seat next to the bathrooms, with 41.9 percent saying it was their least favorite. The next worst seat was the middle, but not just any middle: 38.1 percent mentioned their least favorite is the middle seat of a wide-body plane’s middle row of five.

Thanksgiving flights are full of families trying to sit together, but the survey showed getting someone to swap seats isn’t a guarantee. The most popular reason people gave for agreeing to change seats was that the newly introduced one was in a better location (57.5 percent of respondents). A generous 57.2 percent noted they’d agree to swap simply to help a parent sit with a young child.

After that, goodwill dropped off. Only 33.4 percent mentioned they would swap so a family could sit together, and fewer (28.5 percent) would do it to allow a couple to sit together. Another 12.1 percent said it’s never acceptable to ask a stranger to swap seats. The takeaway for families traveling together, especially during busy travel days, is to spend the extra money to book seats together rather than counting on the kindness of a stranger at the gate.

Photo: fotogurmespb/Shutterstock.

Sources indicate that sixty-two percent of respondents stated they use the call button to get a flight attendant’s attention. But younger travelers were far more likely to avoid asking for help at all. Among survey participants under age 40, 18.9 percent said they’d rather not ask for anything, though that applied to just 8.5 percent of people over age 46. Women were also more likely to avoid asking flight attendants for help at all, at 13.4 percent versus 8.6 percent.

When asked about the most frustrating in-flight scenarios they may encounter while traveling, 43.5 percent mentioned it would be having to carry their carry-on bag 20 rows behind their seat to find storage space. A messy airplane bathroom came in second at 23.3 percent, followed by a broken seatback entertainment screen (18 percent) and a flight without Wi-Fi (7.1 percent).
