#428. Industry News: The Only Ski Pass Question That Matters: Are You a Local or a Traveler?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1739 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Matadornetwork ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Only Ski Pass Question That Matters: Are You a Local or a Traveler?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1739 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I live in Palisade, Colorado, and ski Powderhorn, 30 minutes from my house, on a pass that still costs under $500 per year.
  • For a long time the answer was “an Ikon or Epic pass you don’t fully use.” The substantial passes are built for people who ski 25 days at an owned resort and treat the partner mountains as a bonus.
  • Every pass on the market answers one of two questions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I live in Palisade, Colorado, and ski Powderhorn, 30 minutes from my house, on a pass that still costs under $500 per year. My daughter’s pass there is $29. This covers much of my resort skiing for the season, but what happens when its time to pack up the gear bag and head out on a trip?

For a long time the answer was “an Ikon or Epic pass you don’t fully use.” The substantial passes are built for people who ski 25 days at an owned resort and treat the partner mountains as a bonus. If you ski 10 days a season at your local and six on the road, you are paying $1,100 to $1,500 for the travel days. There’s a better way to structure that season, and it starts with the pass that most skiers forget exists.

Every pass on the market answers one of two questions. Unlimited passes (Epic, Ikon, your home mountain’s own) reward frequency at one or a handful of resorts. Days-per-resort passes (Mountain Collective, Indy) reward range. Buy the first kind for the mountain you drive to and the second kind for the mountains you fly to.

A full Epic Pass at five days works out to about $229 a day, which is roughly a walk-up ticket. At 20 days it’s a steal. It’s vital to consider, however, whether you frequently ski a full day or, as many passholders do, you often call it early afternoon or show up late. There are also those who, like me, frequently get out for a few laps before work and then head back to town.

Industry observers note that the Mountain Collective pass has been around since 2012, and it has stayed deliberately small while Epic and Ikon grew into conglomerates. For 2026-27 it covers 27 resorts, and the structure hasn’t changed: two days at each partner, then 50 percent off any additional days, no blackouts. Eighteen of the 27 are direct-to-lift. Jackson Hole and Taos still require a reservation. Fresh this year is a referral program that gives passholders a bonus day at a resort of their choosing when a friend buys in.

Todd Burnette, CEO of the Mountain Collective, describes the pass as built around destination trips rather than one home mountain.

“One pass, a whole season of trips,” he told Matador.

Recent findings suggest that that’s the pitch, and the price makes it work: the adult pass is $759, which is roughly half of a full Ikon. Burnette says it can pay for itself in a Salt Lake City long weekend.

Recent findings suggest that “Fly to Salt Lake City, ski two days at Snowbird, two at Alta, two at Snowbasin,” he states. “The possibilities are really endless.” Six days at 3 resorts where walk-up tickets run north of $200, on one pass, with the remaining 24 resorts still untouched.

In a recent development, I’ve done numerous ski trips to Utah and can confirm that this will work, provided you’re willing to drive north to Snowbasin, where it’s better to base yourself in Ogden than Salt Lake City. As a snowboarder, I must also add that we’re screwed at Alta, which bars our kind from its mountain.

Where the pass earns its keep is the mix. If I were on Mountain Collective’s marketing team, I’d build a campaign around a different pitch: where would you ski if money weren’t an object? The website reads like a dream trip, and while you only get two days at each spot, you can take one trip to Utah or Colorado or British Columbia and get your money’s worth. A second trip is effectively free skiing.

Photo: AlbertoGonzalez/Shutterstock.

Storm chasers. Alta averages 543 inches of snow per season. Grand Targhee averages more than 500. Panorama, in British Columbia, had its snowiest December in 30 years last winter. Burnette’s line is “no blackouts, so you can follow the storm,” and that is the first time a pass marketing line has described my intended behavior. The real trick is that the pass includes Alta and Snowbird, which otherwise require either an Ikon or a mortgage.

According to recent reports, big-mountain trips. Jackson Hole’s 4,139 vertical feet is the longest continuous rise of any US ski area. Aspen Snowmass is on the pass, and so is Sun Valley, which hosted the first chairlift in 1936 and is opening two fresh ones this December: a six-passenger Lookout Express that cuts the ride to the top of Baldy to about eight and a half minutes, and a new high-speed Christmas quad. Sun Valley is the resort on this list I’d point a traveling skier to first, because it still works like a ski town rather than a resort complex.

According to recent reports, you fly into Hailey or drive up from Boise, the lift lines on Bald Mountain are shorter on a Saturday in February than those on a Tuesday in Summit County, and Ketchum has a bakery, two good bars and a free bus that runs up and down the valley. Two days on Baldy and a third at half price, with the pass already paid for by the Utah trip, is a cheap week by any current standard.

Sources indicate that massive overseas trips. Niseko United in Japan got 244 inches in January 2026 alone, has a new gondola, and now is served by nonstop service to Sapporo from San Francisco and Vancouver. Chamonix is on the pass. So are Thredbo and Mt. Buller in Australia, Coronet Peak and The Remarkables in New Zealand and Valle Nevado in Chile, which is why Burnette says the pass makes a ski trip possible almost any month of the year. Banff Sunshine opened for 16 days of summer skiing in 2026.

“It’s always snowing somewhere on the Mountain Collective pass,” Burnette remarked, and he’s not wrong, though I’d note the Southern Hemisphere flights are on you.

In a recent development, families and beginners. Sun Peaks in BC has four kids’ adventure zones. Sun Valley’s Sunny’s Adventure Park is built for first-timers. Sugar Bowl, near Tahoe, has a upcoming eight-passenger village gondola and a redesigned main lodge. Snowbasin, outside Ogden, is the Utah resort with the fewest people per acre. It also boasts Lone Tree, a run that is only slightly behind Jackson Hole’s Corbett’s Couloir in reputation.

It has been revealed that east Coast. Whiteface has 3,430 feet of vertical drop, the most in the East. Bromont, outside Montreal, is the largest illuminated ski area in North America, with 90 lit runs, which means an after-work ski day is on the table. Sunday River and Sugarloaf cover Maine. And Jackson Hole and Grand Targhee now have nonstop flights from Boston, which makes a Wyoming week from Fresh England a two-flight problem instead of a three-flight one.

The move Burnette recommends is the one I’ve been making.

“A Mountain Collective pass can work alongside a local pass,” he said. “Ski local and use the Mountain Collective pass for trips.”.

Recent findings suggest that the full Ikon Pass was $1,529 for adults by late October, up from its $1,399 launch, and the Ikon Base ran $1,099. Full passholders get unlimited days at Alterra-owned resorts (Steamboat, Winter Park, Palisades Tahoe, Mammoth, Deer Valley) and 7 days at each of the partners. Base adds blackouts and 5 days at Aspen Snowmass this year, a change from last season. Ikon added Lutsen, Granite Peak and Snowriver in the Midwest and SilverStar in BC for 2026-27.

It has been revealed that ikon is the right pass if you live near one of the Alterra mountains and ski it 15-plus days, and it has real overlap with the Mountain Collective: Aspen Snowmass, Sun Valley, Alta, Snowbird, Jackson Hole and Snowbasin are on both. If you’re choosing between them, the question is whether unlimited days at a home hill are worth the extra $700 or so. For a Steamboat local, yes. For someone in Grand Junction or Boise, probably not. Also worth knowing: Ikon’s fresh Squad Pack sells 5 Base passes for $750 each to a group between ages 23 and 28, bought in one transaction.

Photo: Cavan-Images/Shutterstock.

It has been revealed that the Epic Pass was $1,169 for adults 31 and over by late October, $929 for ages 13 to 30 under a new 20 percent Gen Z discount, and $869 for the Epic Local with blackouts. Unlimited at Vail-owned resorts, which means Vail, Beaver Creek, Breckenridge, Keystone, Park City, Whistler Blackcomb, Heavenly, Northstar, Kirkwood, and Stowe, plus limited days at partners.

It has been revealed that epic is for the Summit County, Tahoe, and Park City regular, and for families whose kids are in Vail’s lesson programs. If you ski five days a season at a Vail resort, skip the pass and buy an Epic Day Pass in the spring, which brings a Vail day into the roughly $100 range. Just don’t buy a full Epic for a single trip to Whistler and four days at Breck. That’s the pass equivalent of buying a truck to haul one couch.

Recent findings suggest that the Indy Pass is the Mountain Collective for mountains you haven’t heard of: 300-plus mostly independent ski areas, two days at each, with the no-blackout Indy+ at $399 and the Base at $419 with blackouts at some resorts. It sold out last spring in under an hour, reopened in September with added capacity, and may be gone again by the time you read this. It lost Lutsen, Granite Peak, and Snowriver to Ikon this year. A $269 add-on version exists for anyone who holds an unlimited pass at an Indy partner resort.

Indy pairs well with the Mountain Collective for a skier who wants the legends and the oddballs in the same winter, for less than one Epic. Mountain Capital Partners’ Power Pass starts at $549 and covers the Southwest (Purgatory, Arizona Snowbowl, Brian Head, and small resorts in the four corners states) plus 10 days in Chile. The Cali Pass is $679 for a handful of California resorts. Walk-up tickets at the big names are projected to hit $344 to $392 on peak days this season, so nearly any pass pays for itself in four to six days. Beyond a pass to your local mountain, the pass to buy is the one that gets you where you want to be in the second week of February.

In a Buddhist temple in the northeast of Thailand, not far from the border with Laos, one can find the World's Only Dinosaur Pulpit.

Recent findings suggest that having been the site of Thailand’s first dinosaur fossil discovery, Khon Kean boasts a variety of dinosaur-related sites. Dinosaur imagery is scattered throughout the entire region, giving a nod to this history. Among these references is the World's Only Dinosaur pulpit. The pulpit is shaped like a giant Phuwiangosaurus, Thailand’s native sauropod dinosaur. The dinosaur was originally discovered in the hills of Phu Wiang outside the city, and officially named in 1994 in honor of Her Royal Highness Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn.

Recent findings suggest that monks reportedly stand inside the dinosaur to give sermons at times. Wat That Phra Aram Luang temple is a stunning sight to behold on its own, resplendent with numerous golden peaks and facades painted in bright shades or red.

As with all Buddhist temples, be sure to remove your shoes and cover your shoulders and knees before going inside.

4 of the Most Common Jobs in Ancient Rome

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that not everyone in ancient Rome could be an emperor or a gladiator.
  • Work evolved significantly over the 1,228 years between Romeâs founding in 753 BC and the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 AD.
  • For most of ancient Romeâs existence, work was inextricably tied to social class, and the vast majority of people were lower-class laborers who spent their days in fields, markets, and shops.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that not everyone in ancient Rome could be an emperor or a gladiator. Instead, most inhabitants of this legendary society spent their days doing the manual labor that made the gears of society turn.

Work evolved significantly over the 1,228 years between Romeâs founding in 753 BC and the fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 AD. In ancient Romeâs earliest years, most people farmed and worked their own land. As society evolved, many farmers flocked to the cities, professions like smith, baker, and butcher became increasingly common, and social hierarchies became more regimented.Â.

For most of ancient Romeâs existence, work was inextricably tied to social class, and the vast majority of people were lower-class laborers who spent their days in fields, markets, and shops. While some people did hold jobs in government, the arts, and the church, the average ancient Roman would most likely have held one of the following positions.Â.

Sources indicate that the most common profession by far in ancient Rome involved working the fields, growing food, and taking care of livestock. Most members of Roman society worked in agricultureâsome sources say up to 80-90%âand the most commonly grown crops were grain, olives, and grapes. Agriculture was generally seen as an honorable profession, and involved complex processes that began with choosing soil and included plowing, sowing, and many other steps. Most farms also kept animals including cows, which provided milk, as well as sheep and goats for wool, cheese, and meat and oxen that helped with heavy farm labor. The majority of farms were family-owned until around the 2nd century BCE, when wealthy landowners began displacing plebeian farmers in high numbers and hiring slaves to maintain their large holdings, causing many landless farmers to travel to the city.

Bread had long been a staple of the Roman diet, but it was typically made by farming families at home until around the 2nd century BCE. Around this time, baking techniques were spreading from Greece to Rome and bakeries were becoming more common in Roman cities. In Pompeii alone, archaeologists have identified a total of 35 bakeries. These operations required massive amounts of labor to function, and typically included grain mills powered by donkeys and large ovens that blazed all day long. In ancient Romeâs later years, commercial bakeries were typically run by members of the corpus pistorum, a formal guild of commercial bakers.

Industry observers note that in the last two centuries BCE, Rome attracted huge numbers of people from around the world, and markets began to thrive in the city. Roman peddlers supposedly became known for their aggressive selling tactics, and shopkeepers sold everything from food and wine to oil, medicine, and imported goods. Typical Roman shops that opened onto the streets were known as tabernae, and these stores provided Romans of all socioeconomic classes with all of their needs. Many sold prepared food that poorer Romans would buy to avoid the laborious process of cooking at home, and others repaired shoes and clothes, packaged goods, made pottery, or sometimes offered many of these services at once. Booksellers, apothecaries, and bankers also often operated storefronts on Roman streets. Shopkeepers could be freeborn citizens, freed slaves, or even slaves working for their owners. Some elite Romans did look down on shopkeeping and commerce, favoring landownership and political and military service. But ultimately, if you werenât a member of an elite class, selling goods was one of the more reliable ways to make money in the substantial city.

Sources indicate that rome wasnât built in a dayâand it also required many hands over the centuries. Ancient Rome is well-remembered for its amazing engineering feats, which include aqueducts, domes, arches, bridges, and of course, endless expanses of road. Each of these innovative creations relied on immense amounts of human labor. Roman building projects involved on a mix of patrons, engineers, architects, tradespeople such as stonemasons and fresco painters, hired laborers, soldiers, and slaves. Constructing structures like the Pantheon required an estimated 100 to 240 men per day, and Roman military legions of up to 5,000 men built countless roads and bridges alongside their campaign duties. Construction was undeniably one of Rome's biggest industries, and it employed a great many people (along with many unpaid workers).

  • To caw is to gawp or to stare foolishly or empty-headed, while to mag is to chatter incessantly or pointlessly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in 16th-century English, at the height of the English Reformation, an abbey-lubber was a derogatory term for a monk or clergyman who lived a life of blissful idleness and self-indulgence. The first part of the word understandably refers to a place of worship, but lubberâthe same tag youâll hear in a landlubberâis an old English word for a silly, clumsy person.Â.

Recent findings suggest that based on an abbey-lubber, though, in the later 1500s describing someone as âabbey-lubber-likeâ meant that they were habitually lazy according to the Oxford English Dictionary. Nor is that the only obscure and old-fashioned word for being lazy thatâs long fallen by the linguistic wayside.Â.

To caw is to gawp or to stare foolishly or empty-headed, while to mag is to chatter incessantly or pointlessly. Put the two together, and youâve the adjective caw-magging, according to the English Dialect Dictionary, which is to be habitually idle or lazy.Â Â.

Recent findings suggest that if youâre clumpsed, then youâre numb with coldâor, more figuratively, slow-witted, dumbfounded, or somehow rendered unable to move or speak. Derived from that, to be clumpst is to be lazy in 19th century Yorkshire dialect.Â.

In medieval times, a draw-latch was a thief who would let himself into peopleâs homes by âdrawingâ up the âlatchâ of their door by some kind of nefarious means. Confusion with the old verb latch, which once meant to slacken a horseâs reinsâand therefore to dawdle or walk slowlyâultimately led to the word being reinterpreted in the 1500s as a nickname for someone who lags behind. And that makes the adjective draw-latching another word meaning idling, acting lazily, or falling behind the others.Â Â.

Sources indicate that gert and Daisy were characters played on British radio in the early 1900s by comic actresses and sisters Elsie and Doris Waters. The duoâs popularity led to their names falling into use in English rhyming slang: Gert and Daisy is a 1960s way of saying someone is lazy.Â.

Just as illogical is the opposite of logical and illegal the opposite of legal, illaborious is a seldom-used and long-obsolete opposite of laboriousâor, in other words, an early 17th century word meaning workshy or sluggish.Â.

According to recent reports, kipper-kaper is a Scots adjective meaning lazy or sluggish, recorded in the early 1900s, which is intended to sound like the clomping of a horseâs hooves. The connection between the two is, according to the Dictionary of the Scots Language, that kipper-kaper describes someone who is âeasy-going, as of a tired or lazy horse.âÂ.

In English folklore, Ludlam was the name of a supposed witch who dwelt in a cave near the town of Farnham in Surrey, around 30 miles south of London. A host of bizarre and often quite quirky stories emerged around her, including a joke that her familiar, a large dog, was so lazy that it would lean against the cave wall to barkâbut if anyone approached the cave, it was so lazy that it wouldnât even bark at all. âAs lazy as Ludlamâs dog,â ultimately, became a popular simile for laziness in 18th century English.

Scowbanker is an 18th-century word for a loafer, while the related adjective scowbanking has been recorded in both Scots and northern English since the early 1800s to mean lazy, oafish, or idling. Quite where the word comes from is a complete mystery, but given that a scow is a large flat-bottomed boat, this may be one of a number of bizarre English words that come from maritime slang.Â.

First recorded as far back as 1639, if you were âsick of the idlesâ in 17th and 18th century parlance then you were âexceedingly lazyâ or âidle without the will to work,â according to one definition. You could also be âsick of the Lombard fever,â if you were habitually lazy (a play on the old dialect word lomber, meaning to idle around or drag something heavy), or in an even more extended version, âsick of the idle crick and the belly-work in the heelââa made-up medical complaint used as a jokey excuse for acting lazy in 17th-century English.Â.

To slotter is to spill or slop something messily, or to make something foul or dirty. From there, perhaps in allusion to someone wearing soiled clothing or not making an effort in their appearance, the same word came to be used to mean to be slothful or indolentâand derived from there, the adjective slottery means lazy.

Recent findings suggest that goodbye to metasearch having its own ad budget and scorecard. Google lets hotels place ads in its price-comparison results, but is changing how they place those ads. Will the fresh process make ad buys harder to scrutinize?

Google is retiring its standalone hotel ad campaigns and folding paid booking links into its main search advertising product, a shift that changes how hotels budget for, bid on, and measure metasearch (meaning, the platform's price-comparison listings).

The advertising line item hotels have budgeted for years for "Google Hotel Ads" must now be bundled into all of their work on Google Search. That leaves hotel commercial chiefs with a question: what counts as success once metasearch and paid search share an ad campaign?

A Google spokesperson told Skift the change brings bidding, reporting, and tools such as AI Max, its suite of automated campaign features, onto one platform. The enhancement reflects only how advertisers buy ads, the spokesperson remarked, so free booking links are untouched.

A Google migration guide that appeared in recent days says that hotel ad campaigns will be converted automatically into "Search campaigns for Travel" in the firs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve mentioned it before, I’ll say it again: Every holiday table needs a salad. This one was dreamed up for Hanukkah, my family’s second-favorite special occasion after Thanksgiving. Serve it with roast chicken or salmon and you have an objectively perfect meal. It’s bright, crunchy, and decked out with little “latkes.” Potato croutons have popped up in a few places over the years, like The Salad Lab’s own Hanukkah-inspired salad (great minds!), Daniel Humm’s salmon rösti salad from Made Nice, and Ore-Ida’s cutely named CrouTots. My take is as lazy as it gets: frozen tater tots, smashed. The result is ultra-crisp, like the tiniest potato pancake in the world. A salad spinner is a godsend for washing the lettuce and herbs. Any type of apple works (I like Honeycrisp or Fuji) and the fresh horseradish on top is optional. But if you can find it, get it!

More festive Hanukkah recipes this way.

Preheat oven to 425°. Mix together ½ cup sour cream, 3 Tbsp. drained prepared horseradish, 1 Tbsp. distilled white vinegar, a massive pinch of kosher salt, and 1 tsp. water in a small bowl, adding more water a little at a time if needed until dressing it drizzle-able. Taste and season with more salt if needed.

Sources indicate that bake 1 lb. frozen tater tots on a large rimmed baking sheet for half the time of package directions (about 10 minutes).

Sources indicate that meanwhile, place 1 small white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, in a small bowl; pour in cold water to cover and add a few ice cubes. Set onions aside.

Industry observers note that tear pull apart leaves from 1 lb. romaine lettuce (about ⅔ head) and/or Little Gem lettuce (4–5 heads) and tear large leaves in half. Place in a large bowl. Remove tough stems from 1 bunch dill and 1 bunch parsley; discard. Coarsely tear remaining leaves and tender stems. Add to lettuce.

Recent findings suggest that remove tater tots from oven and, using oven mitts for safety, lay another baking sheet directly on top; firmly press down on tots to flatten. (If you don’t have a second baking sheet, use a heatproof measuring cup or mug instead.) Return tater tots to oven and bake until deep golden brown and crisp, 10–20 minutes.(If your oven has a convection setting, now is a great time to use it.).

Drain reserved onion and pat dry. Thinly slice 2 large apples (about 1 lb.). Add both to bowl with lettuce and herbs.

Industry observers note that drizzle 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and add a big pinch of flaky sea salt. Toss to combine, then mound salad on a platter. Evenly scatter tater tots and ¾ cup pomegranate seeds over.

Serve salad with remaining dressing for drizzling over and peeled fresh horseradish (if using) for grating over.

Recent findings suggest that six months of weak trading has exposed how lopsided Gulf hotel management agreements are, with owners carrying the losses while operators keep collecting fees. For now, both sides would rather renegotiate than fight, but that patience depends on a recovery that hasn't come yet.

It has been revealed that gulf hotel owners have begun to reassess their hotel management agreements (HMAs) with operators, as the U.S.-Iran war that began in late February continues to weigh on the region’s hotels. So far, they are busy renegotiating terms rather than heading to arbitration.

Under an HMA, an owner pays a brand to run the property, typically through a base fee tied to revenue that gets paid even when the hotel loses money. This leaves owners carrying most of the downside when performance falls short.

And many hotels in the Gulf have been underperforming for more than six months. Dubai hotel occupancy, for example, fell to 68.4% in October, down 16.5 points from 84.9% a year earlier, according to CoStar’s STR. Average daily rate dropped 28.1% to $181 and RevPAR fell 42% to $124.

Dubai received 9.7 million international visitors in the first 10 months of 2026, down 38% from 15.7 million a year earlier, said Issam Kazim, CEO of the Dubai Corporation for Touri.

Since 1984, the dragon-like Wasserspeier ("Water Spitter") on Bern’s Münstergasse has been delighting and fooling locals and tourists alike. Every spring, artist Luciano Andreani (*1947) and homeowner Tinu Mühlethaler install the spout on the roof of the historic Old Town building.

Anyone who lingers too long while bending down to pick up one of the five-franc coins scattered below is in for a surprise and gets a refreshing splash of water from above. The art installation sprays water into the street periodically. Beware - a refreshing shower is guaranteed!

The Wasserspeier is particularly popular with children and the young at heart.

The art installation is installed in spring and not available in winter.

AirAsia’s Q3 Shows Why Fernandes Pushed the Comeback to 2028

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1036 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skift

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Industry observers note that airAsia has shown it can charge more.
  • AirAsia Group posted a smaller third-quarter loss on Monday as higher fares made up for most of the jump in fuel costs, but the results show why Tony Fernandes pushed the comeback to 2028: a smaller AirAsia costs more to run, and it is still losing money.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that photo Credit: An AirAsia A320 neo jet, manufactured by Airbus. AirAsia Group.

Industry observers note that airAsia has shown it can charge more. It hasn't shown it can make money at its new, smaller size. Until the $1 billion debt financing lands, the balance sheet, not demand, decides when the comeback starts.

AirAsia Group posted a smaller third-quarter loss on Monday as higher fares made up for most of the jump in fuel costs, but the results show why Tony Fernandes pushed the comeback to 2028: a smaller AirAsia costs more to run, and it is still losing money.

In a recent development, airAsia Group, the listed organization that now houses all of AirAsia’s airlines, posted a loss attributable to shareholders of RM175 million ($43 million), according to its third-quarter results. That’s about a third of its second-quarter loss. Most of the improvement came from charging more, helped by jet fuel easing from its second-quarter peak. Planes stayed nearly as full as fares rose sharply, and that won back much of what the jet fuel spike had taken earlier in the year.

Including minority interests, the loss after tax was RM381.3 million ($93 million). Revenue fell 11% from a year earlier to RM4.66 billion, and 8% from the second quarter.

Sources indicate that “Our third quarter performance suggests that the worst is behind us,” CEO Bo Lingam remarked in a statement. AirAsia is a smaller airline than it was a year ago, and a smaller low-cost airline is an expensive one to run. It still spends more to fly each seat than it earns from it, and its equity cushion is thin, with shareholders’ equity of RM362 million. The refinancing it needs to steady the balance sheet, which AirAsia targeted for this quarter and as recently as last week expected by December or January, is now due to conclude in the fourth quarter or early 2027.

It has been revealed that the results came the same day Thai Airways reported its own third-quarter loss on fuel costs. If jet fuel eases as AirAsia expects in 2027, higher fares could start turning into profit across the region. For AirAsia, the question is whether that comes fast enough.

Sources indicate that airAsia consolidated its Malaysian, Thai, Indonesian, Philippine and Cambodian airlines with AirAsia X in January. This was the first quarter in which the merged group had almost no seats left that were sold before the fuel shock, which let it reprice. Average fares rose by almost a quarter from a year earlier, while the share of filled seats barely moved.

It has been revealed that the group suspended 76 routes in the third quarter, mostly fuel-heavy international flights to India, China and Australia, and kept most of its flying close to home, where demand held up best. The retreat has cost it ground. Malaysia Airlines this month overtook the AirAsia group as the largest operator between Malaysia and India for the first time since 2021, though Fernandes has dismissed suggestions that rivals could take the lead for internal Malaysia flights.

Recent findings suggest that airAsia cut what it spends on staff, airport charges and leases, but its remaining fixed costs were spread over far fewer seats, so the cost of flying each one rose. Higher fares more than covered the extra fuel bill. The rise in other costs per passenger then took back part of that gain.

Not every market pulled its weight. Malaysia and Cambodia were profitable at the operating level, Indonesia and the Philippines lost less than a year earlier, and Thailand had a weak quarter. Currency losses added to the damage further down the income statement.

Recent findings suggest that fuel is squeezing AirAsia’s regional rivals too. Cebu Pacific’s management said this month it has pretty much no chance of making money this year, and Thai Airways’ finance chief warned that if current oil prices become the new normal then its third-quarter loss could be a guide to performance in the fourth.

AirAsia is handing back older, more expensive aircraft: 25 of them this year and most of them early. And it claims it may return more in 2027. That move cuts lease bills but leaves less room to grow, six months after the group placed a record order for 150 Airbus A220s. Many of the planes it keeps aren’t flying either. About 31% of the 234 aircraft in the group’s main fleet were out of service at the end of September, mostly for scheduled maintenance, with engine problems among the other causes.

In a recent development, that trade-off worries some analysts. Handing back jets now could slow AirAsia’s eventual comeback, analysts told Skift this month, because new narrowbody delivery slots are scarce until around 2033.

The pressure point is funding. AirAsia ended June with far less cash than it owed within the year. It is working on up to $1 billion in debt financing and indicates talks with creditors are progressing.

The strain has been visible for months. In September, Endau Analytics’ Shukor Yusof questioned the airline’s financial resilience, citing its balance sheet and reports of delayed rental payments. Fernandes insisted that no aircraft had been grounded over nonpayment, and he has denied reports of a government-backed contingency plan. Malaysia’s transport and finance ministries remain in talks with the airline.

According to recent reports, for now, management is betting on the year-end peak. It intends to add back capacity in the fourth quarter, restore some routes and keep pushing fares higher — and claims forward bookings are running in line with last year, at elevated yields. The Q3 presentation called 2026 and 2027 a “reset” and 2028 the “rebuild,” when newly introduced fuel-efficient jets begin arriving. It gave no passenger targets for 2027.

Fernandes has been somewhat blunter. In a LinkedIn post last week, he called 2027 “a period of consolidation” and warned of “more painful decisions” on costs, without repeating his September target of 80 million passengers next year. Expansion elsewhere is on hold too: the group’s Bahrain hub is now targeted for March 2027, should conditions in the Gulf allow.

Sources indicate that combine ¼ cup Diamond Crystal or 2 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. Morton kosher salt and 10 cups water in a large pot.

In a recent development, peel 1½ lb. Yukon Gold potatoes (about 3 large or 4 medium). Quarter if potatoes are large, halve if medium, adding to pot as you go. Potatoes should be covered by at least 2" water when finished; add more if needed.

Transfer potatoes to a large shallow bowl to serve.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Historic Park Theatre’s most famous feature was born from heartbreak. Its tower, added by owner Ralph Gwynn in 1929, is known locally as the Tower of Love — not for the romance it celebrates but for the one that fell apart. Legend has it that Gwynn was left at the altar, and he built the tower as a tribute to the woman who broke his heart. Decades later, when a new Estes Park sign ordnance threatened the glittering neon that outlines it, residents took the matter to a ballot and won the theater a variance. So the Tower of Love kept its glow.

Construction on the theater itself began in 1913. The architect Joseph R. Anderson designed the building in the Classical Revival style, with parts of it fabricated in the city of Longmont and hauled up to Estes Park for assembly.

It has been revealed that gwynn, a projectionist from Denver, bought the theater in 1922 at the height of the silent-film era and ran it until his death in 1963. He added the lobby in his first year, the tower in 1929, and the neon lights in 1938.

Recent findings suggest that mickey and Ola Stanger began running the theater in 1967, initially on a lease from businessman Vic Walker before eventually buying the building. What started as a two-person operation eventually became a family affair, stretching across multiple generations, with a Stanger granddaughter, Jenna MacGregor, running it today. The theater was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1984.

Industry observers note that today the Park Theatre operates year-round, screening classics, documentaries, independent films, and first-run blockbusters alongside live music and other events. The concessions offerings have recently been updated, and adult visitors are encouraged to enjoy their movies with a cold beer. The projection technology has also come a long way from Gwynn’s era: A digital projector, Dolby 3-D, and Dolby 5.1 surround sound arrived in 2013, a new screen in 2015, and new auditorium seating in 2024. A historic designation, it turns out, doesn’t require you to sit in the original seats.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s no exaggeration to say that xawaash is at the heart of Somali cuisine. It is Somali history on a plate—a culinary reminder of Somalia’s centuries of global trade, particularly along the Indian Ocean. Xawaash is what makes many Somali dishes taste distinctly Somali. While every household’s xawaash recipe is its own, typically seven core spices—cumin, coriander, black pepper, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and turmeric—are toasted until their fragrance blooms, then blended into an earthy golden-brown powder. Xawaash stores very well and for a long time in an airtight container, though it’s at its peak shortly after it’s made. If you use it often, you can double or triple the recipe for a big batch.

In a recent development, like all suqaar, this chicken suqaar features xawaash and bright peppers, but it skips the potato found in hilib (beef) suqaar. It has a hint of heat thanks to the black pepper and optional jalapeño. Suqaar is cooked covered to keep the meat juicy and moist. Serve with the flatbread of your choice (canjeero, muufo, or sabaayad) for a light lunch or over plenty of rice for a more filling dinner.

More tasty chicken thigh recipes here.

Sources indicate that toast 1 cup (100 g) whole cumin seeds, 1 cup (70 g) whole coriander seeds, ¼ cup (35 g) black peppercorns, 1 small-to-medium piece of cinnamon bark, 2 Tbsp. green cardamom pods, and 1½ tsp. whole cloves in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring constantly so the spices don’t burn. The spices are toasted when they have a slightly darker color and become fragrant, 1–2 minutes. Transfer the toasted spices to a blender or spice grinder and blend until they become a fine powder. Transfer to a bowl and mix in ¼ cup (30 g) ground turmeric until it’s fully incorporated and the spice mix is golden brown. Allow to cool completely, then store in an airtight container.

In a medium bowl, combine the juice of ½ lemon, 1 tsp. xawaash, 1 tsp. fine sea salt, ½ tsp. paprika, and ⅛ tsp. ground black pepper. Add 1 lb. (450 g) boneless, skinless chicken thighs, cut into bite-sized pieces, and mix everything together to coat the chicken. Set aside.

In a large skillet over medium-high heat, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil until loose. Add 1 large yellow onion, halved and sliced, and cook, stirring occasionally, for 8 minutes, or until the onion is softened. Add 6 garlic cloves, minced, and 1 medium jalapeño, halved, and stir for another minute, then add the chicken in a single layer. Allow it to cook undisturbed for 5 minutes, then turn the pieces over and cook for 3 minutes more, until fully cooked through.

Industry observers note that add the remaining 1½ tsp. xawaash, ¾ cup (12 g) coarsely chopped cilantro leaves, 1 medium red bell pepper, sliced, and 1 medium yellow bell pepper, sliced, and stir to combine. Cover the skillet and turn the heat down to medium-low; cook until the peppers have softened, 10 to 15 minutes. Serve hot.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At Macdonald Book Shop, a cozy and beloved store in the Colorado mountain town of Estes Park, selling books began as a side hustle.

J. Edward Macdonald bought a small log cabin in Estes Park in 1908 and opened a hardware and general store next door — with one corner full of books for sale. When he retired, his wife Jessica turned the parlor of their home into a proper bookstore, also selling magazines, stationery, and school supplies. That was 1928. Books have been the focus ever since.

Over the decades, the shop expanded to claim more of the original house. Four generations of Macdonald women kept it going. After J. Edward died in 1932, Jessica ran the store on her own until her death in 1957. Ownership passed to their daughter Louise, and when Louise died in 1971, her daughter Paula Steige took over. Steige retired from teaching in 1976 and reopened the shop year-round — it had been a summer-only operation.

In a recent development, then, in July 1982, the Lawn Lake Dam failed. Four feet of water tore through the bookstore, destroying two-thirds of the inventory. But the community indicated up to help: More than 100 volunteers helped rebuild the foundation, rip out and replace the floor joists, paint, clean, and shelve upcoming stock. The store reopened 18 days later. Steige later called it “a blessing in disguise” — the old house needed renovation anyway.

The Macdonald name is still on the door, though ownership changed again in 2020, when Anastacia Galloway Reed and Kevin Reed, who also own the neighboring Inkwell & Brew, bought the shop.

The bookstore still operates in the same cabin on Elkhorn Avenue, still stocks around 15,000 titles, and still does what it’s done since Jessica first set up in the parlor: It gives people a place to find a book and a welcoming vibe to those who want to sit down and read.

#404. Is mental illness universal?

Is mental illness universal?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4196 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that on a November day in 1994, a 14-year-old girl in Hong Kong named Charlene Hsu Chi-Ying collapsed on a busy sidewalk, in broad daylight, in her school uniform.
  • Recent findings suggest that local journalists scrambled for an explanation of this tragedy, and rapidly found a template ready-made: a Western account of what anorexia was, what it felt like, who got it, what caused it.
  • Before Charlene’s death, the psychiatrist Sing Lee had been quietly studying a small number of women in Hong Kong who were starving themselves to dangerous degrees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that on a November day in 1994, a 14-year-old girl in Hong Kong named Charlene Hsu Chi-Ying collapsed on a busy sidewalk, in broad daylight, in her school uniform. She had starved herself to death. Charlene had never been diagnosed with anorexia, not because her self-starvation went unnoticed, but because the diagnosis, in its Western form, was mostly unknown in the East. Her death changed that overnight. Splashed across the front pages were stark headlines such as ‘Girl Who Died In Street Was A Walking Skeleton’.

Recent findings suggest that local journalists scrambled for an explanation of this tragedy, and rapidly found a template ready-made: a Western account of what anorexia was, what it felt like, who got it, what caused it. The ideas spread rapidly – particularly that anorexia involved distorted self-perceptions about one’s body (dysmorphia) and an intense, borderline delusional, fear of gaining weight, often cued by prevailing beauty standards (notably, a cultural fixation with slender female bodies). Mass public education campaigns followed. Hotlines opened, celebrities spoke out. Anorexia became part of the zeitgeist.

Before Charlene’s death, the psychiatrist Sing Lee had been quietly studying a small number of women in Hong Kong who were starving themselves to dangerous degrees. Most of these women did not obsess over their bodies, nor fear becoming fat. They instead complained of somatic (bodily) ailments: uncomfortable bloating, a profound lack of appetite. The cognitive hallmark of Western anorexia – a distorted body image – was largely absent. Lee seemed to be documenting a distinct form of self-starvation with its own local logic. The situation has changed dramatically since then. By 2007, more than three-quarters of the anorexic patients Lee treated cited ‘fat phobia’ as a central motivation. Today, anorexia in Hong Kong is terrifyingly common, affecting roughly one in 200 schoolgirls – comparable to trends in the United States.

Recent findings suggest that we do not know the form that Charlene’s illness took. What we do know is that her death became a catalyst for the rapid importation of a Western conceptual framework that reshaped how Hong Kong understood and experienced disordered eating in young women.

According to recent reports, anorexia is just one example from a compendium of curious cases in which culture seemingly shapes mental disorders. For example, anthropologists have documented how cultures sculpt ‘idioms of distress’ – socially learned and sanctioned ways of communicating unusual mental episodes and patterns of psychological suffering. Hallucinations and dissociative states are routinely interpreted as forms of spiritual possession across the globe, as with Zār in northeast Africa and the Middle East.

It has been revealed that these cases are not fringe oddities. Even depression – arguably the most common psychiatric condition in the world – seems to look strikingly different depending on when and where it appears. In China, patients who meet Western criteria for depression present mainly with bodily symptoms, such as fatigue, insomnia and headaches, rather than psychological symptoms, like low self-esteem and apathy. Delusions, multiple personality and social anxiety also take different forms in different cultures.

Cultural variation in psychiatry raises fundamental and increasingly urgent questions about abnormal minds. What precisely can culture shape? We usually think of mental disorder as something going wrong inside a person, and of culture as shaping how that internal problem is expressed and socially understood. Can culture penetrate deeper, to reshape the internal problem itself? What would that even look like?

Sources indicate that the suggestion that cultural variables can significantly shape the internal mechanisms of mental disorders, including brute neurobiological hardware, may seem counterintuitive, even radical. But I’ll make the case that culture may possess a more substantial ability to do so – in some disorders, to some degrees – than is generally acknowledged. The basic reason is that the brain, the organ of the mind, is plastic and has functions of representing and adapting to a rich social world.

This could well allow cultural ecosystems to inculcate ‘local’ kinds of disorders – ones that may look similar to their cross-cultural counterparts, but differ in their psychological and even neurological profiles in ways consequential for scientific classification and treatment. ‘Anorexia’ or ‘depression’ in one cultural context may then be best understood as a different condition altogether in another. Mental disorders are already notoriously heterogeneous: one study of 3,703 patients diagnosed with depression found 1,030 distinct combinations of symptoms. One source of this variation may be cultural environments, including subcultures within a country’s borders. These possibilities hinge on unsettled questions about how plastic the mechanisms of mental disorders really are, and whether cultural factors have the right kind of causal access to them.

Sources indicate that to begin, let me distinguish three widely accepted ways that culture can shape mental disorders, before investigating whether it can also shape their internal mechanisms. When I say ‘culture’, I mean a broad class of sociocultural factors, including social roles, norms, values, institutional and political structures, even particular medical beliefs and practices. By ‘shape’, I mean causally influence.

Hearing God speak seems a textbook case of psychosis. Yet many US evangelicals cultivate the experience.

The first widely accepted way is by shaping our concepts of disorder. Here I am accepting a basic distinction between our various concepts of mental disorder (including lay and scientific theories of what disorders are, and what explains them), and the actual nature of those conditions. Historians have long shown that psychiatric concepts can be covertly shaped by social forces. What counts as ‘normal’ versus ‘eccentric’ versus ‘pathological’ behaviour is often prescribed by prevailing cultural norms and scientific authorities (whether legitimate or pseudo). A particularly dramatic example from 1851 is the diagnosis ‘Drapetomania’, which was given exclusively to Black slaves who fled their captors. The warped logic – which rested on the widespread and pernicious belief that God had ordained Black people to be enslaved – was that slavery was so beneficial, only a mentally ill person would cut and run. In this case, the concept was culturally shaped and pseudo, because it did not refer to a genuine condition, only mentally competent agents acting rationally.

Industry observers note that but culture can legitimately inform psychiatric concepts, such as notions of harm and thresholds for ‘appropriate’ behaviour. Answers to questions like How much despondence or apathy is pathological? and Is this person’s gambling significantly interfering with their life? are partly scientific and partly cultural. For example, hearing God speak seems like a textbook case of psychosis. Yet many US evangelicals actively cultivate the experience and consider it a sign of closeness to God. Psychiatry’s own guidelines recognise that such experiences can be a normal part of religious life.

Sources indicate that the second accepted form of cultural shaping is by modulating mental health outcomes, through various pathways, including the social determinants of health. Poverty, discrimination, social isolation, stigma and access to care comprise psychosocial risk factors that can significantly impact disorder prevalence, treatment success, even mortality rates. For example, migrants and their children develop schizophrenia at three times the rate of native-born populations, a gap that researchers have linked to discrimination and social exclusion.

According to recent reports, the third way involves culture shaping the lived experience of mental disorder. Medical anthropologists distinguish between a ‘disease’ – a biological pathology that explains medical symptoms – and an ‘illness’ – how the symptoms of disease are experienced, expressed and socially understood. Culture can significantly shape illness. For example, an HIV infection may be the same disease everywhere, but the experience of AIDS (the late stage of the HIV infection) can differ considerably across cultural contexts – eg, where there is widespread belief that AIDS is a form of divine punishment.

The changing form of self-starvation in Hong Kong is commonly explained as an interaction of two of those types of cultural shaping. First, a Western theory of anorexia reshaped the concept of anorexia in Hong Kong, as understood by both clinicians and laypeople. Second, that conceptual uptake induced new ways of understanding, experiencing and expressing anorexic distress, thereby producing new symptoms. Culture shaped medical concepts; concepts shaped illness. The philosopher Ian Hacking argued that this situation can create a complex feedback loop, where concepts and illness-experience continuously remake each other. In The Social Construction of What? (1999), he called this the ‘looping effect’.

Can culture penetrate deeper, to shape diseases themselves? By shaping disease, I mean creating fresh pathologies, or altering an existing one enough that it becomes a new condition, one we must classify, explain and treat differently. In somatic medicine, the answer is generally ‘no’ for culture, but ‘yes’ for chemical and biological factors. If we expose a case of tuberculosis to antibiotics, it can evolve inside a patient into multidrug-resistant TB, which calls for a distinct diagnosis and treatment strategy. Environmental toxins, genetic mutations, infections and diet can all reshape pathologies. Cultural variables may play an upstream role, for example, by disposing doctors to overprescribe antibiotics. But the cultural content – the beliefs and meanings behind such practices – makes no difference to the disease itself. Culture seems to lack the right sort of causal connection to underlying pathologies.

According to recent reports, A crisp distinction between ‘illness’ and ‘disease’ seems appropriate for most somatic disorders: cholera, cancer and cirrhosis are the same diseases whether they appear in Beijing or Boston, even if illness profiles can vary wildly. Does the distinction hold for psychiatry?

There are two reasons to suspect it does not. First, the paradigmatic features of mental disorders – abnormal thoughts, feelings, behaviours – overlap massively with features of illness, which can be shaped by culture. A cardiologist does not consult their patient’s beliefs to diagnose or explain a leaking heart valve. But psychiatrists make diagnoses based on mental ‘signs’ (outwardly observable behaviours, like disorganised speech) and ‘symptoms’ (self-reports about lived experience, such as low self-esteem or a fear of fatness). These features are also thought to partially explain disorders: in anorexia, a fear of fatness is sometimes thought to drive self-starvation.

Recent findings suggest that second, it is not obvious that mental disorders depend on biological diseases, at least in the familiar medical sense. There is no identified pathophysiology for anorexia, depression, schizophrenia or any other mental disorder – no clear account of system dysfunction, no ‘chemical imbalance’. The picture instead is far messier: the brains and bodies of mentally ill people differ from unafflicted populations in myriad subtle ways. Psychiatry is left with diverse theories of disorder pitched at different explanatory levels – some plausible, all partial and piecemeal, none yet mature enough to revolutionise our understanding.

Mental software is not cleanly separable from its neural hardware.

Even so, psychiatric institutions conceptualise mental conditions as disease-like. The American Psychiatric Association (APA), which writes and publishes the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), defines mental disorder as a pattern of disturbance reflecting ‘a dysfunction in the psychological, biological, or developmental processes underlying mental functioning’ – a ‘dysfunction in the individual’. More daringly, the National Institute of Mental Health’s (NIMH) research framework explicitly formulates mental disorders as ‘disorders of brain circuits’.

Industry observers note that what’s going on here? The APA and NIMH are making an empirical bet that disease-like explanations will earn their keep in psychiatry, once we’ve learned all we want to know about the mind and its maladies. That is, they assume there are deeper internal structures that explain why signs and symptoms tend to hang together. This need not amount to a crude biological reductionism; the relevant structures need not be hidden brain diseases. But the brain’s ability to process information – which supports thinking, feeling and acting – is inextricably entangled with its physiological functions. Mental software is not cleanly separable from its neural hardware.

We need a general term for the internal structures that might explain why symptoms hang together. Let’s call them ‘neurocomputational mechanisms’, or NCMs for short. ‘Neuro’ plus ‘computational’ means these mechanisms could be described at the neural level, the information-processing level, or both.

In a recent development, for example, some specific phobias are thought to depend on a learned threat-association that stubbornly resists updating. Phobic responses are characteristically sticky: arachnophobia can persist despite the patient earnestly believing that spiders are harmless and wanting to tame their fear. The mechanism sustaining that association would be an NCM: an internal structure that partly controls the excessive fear responses and avoidance behaviours typical of phobias. Phobias are usually treatable by exposure therapy, which is thought to work on that mechanism by supplying latest learning that overpowers the original, obstinate association.

One view – let’s call it ‘universalism’ – assumes that the NCMs relevant to psychopathology are culturally invariant. In conceptualising disorders as disease-like, the DSM and NIMH view them as breakdowns in a shared bio-psycho human nature, insulated against cultural influence. Universalism thinks of mental disorders like hydrangeas, which take on different forms in different environments. A hydrangea growing in acidic soil rich with aluminium blooms sky-blue flowers; in chalky soil, its flowers are pastel pink. But it is still the same plant, with the same internal pigment, moulded by interactions with its ecosystem. In this, universalism preserves a crisp distinction between illness and underlying NCMs that fix a disorder’s scientific identity.

In contrast, the view I want to develop – call it ‘deep shaping’ – accepts the distinction between illness and the underlying NCMs, but hypothesises that culture can causally shape both (to some degree, in some cases).

This deep-shaping picture is importantly different from a social constructionism about mental disorder. As I’ll use the term, social constructionism is the view that a mental disorder can be almost fully explained by social factors, with no need to posit internal mechanisms specific to a disorder.

To see the difference, consider Hacking’s perceptive study of the transient mental illness that came to be known as resignation syndrome. This mystifying condition occurred almost exclusively among child refugees in Sweden, who became despondent and apathetic to the point of turning mute and refusing to eat (some children required feeding tubes). Hacking explained the condition as a general trauma response interacting with highly local cultural variables. The children began to express their profound distress in new ways, which caught on via imitation; Swedish psychiatrists responded by crafting and broadcasting a new diagnosis, which covertly created a ‘script’ that children unconsciously internalised. The behaviours co-evolved, and stabilised each other. The children acquired a ‘new psychic state’ that was ‘not so easy to remove’.

Anorexia’s symptoms seem held in place by something more than just cultural scripts and general distress.

This view gets quite close to social constructionism, as the bulk of explanation falls to cultural factors. Hacking thinks there are general psychological processes – trauma responses, social imitation and internalisation – that allow specific cultural content to create and sustain abnormal behaviours. But these processes are not quite NCMs. Internalisation, for example, is a general process by which behaviour that begins as a performance becomes real to the person doing it. An analogy Hacking uses, borrowed from the historian André LeBlanc, is hypnosis: subjects initially say they are just playing along, yet begin to find the instructions ‘more and more compelling’. Hacking does not think resignation syndrome involves an abnormal nor distinctive form of internalisation: it is just the same process as in hypnosis. As the philosopher Dominic Murphy argues in The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Medicine (2025), Hacking’s view requires ‘no distinctive machinery beyond that of ordinary cultural transmission and social learning’. The same explanations, he quips, could be offered ‘to show why my son and his friends are covered in tattoos’. It is in this sense that Hacking is a constructionist. There are no internal NCMs pulling strings, so there is no need for a science of abnormal minds, nor for treatments or classifications aimed at internal structures. The dynamics of socio-cultural shaping is, as Hacking puts it, ‘where the action is’.

Industry observers note that constructionism is plausible for resignation syndrome, and other conditions that are especially transient and culturally peculiar. But it does not adequately explain conditions like schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, which are highly heritable. What about conditions like depression, anxiety and anorexia?

In a recent development, twin studies suggest that anorexia, too, is substantially heritable. So its symptoms seem held in place by something more than just cultural scripts and general distress. One interesting possibility is that patients systematically misperceive their own bodies: they literally see their figures as larger than they are. The source of these distorted perceptions would be an abnormal, scientifically tractable NCM – one we could use to improve classifications, explanations and treatments.

Sources indicate that I think we can make progress by keeping NCMs in the picture, while exploring the possibility that culture can shape them too. What would it take for this view to be right? NCMs would need to satisfy two conditions: they would need to be appropriately plastic, and appropriately coupled to the cultural environment.

Industry observers note that A mechanism is plastic if it can be reconfigured. Gold atoms are not plastic in this sense: change a gold atom’s structure and you no longer have gold, but some other element. Gold is fixed. In the biological and mind sciences, however, we find many plastic systems – especially those involved in adaptation, learning and regulation. For example, covering a kitten’s eye during a critical period of development reorganises its visual cortex. Neurons that used to respond to both eyes rewire to respond only to the open eye, and this persists even after the closed eye is reopened. Experience reconfigures the NCMs that allow kittens to see. Plasticity is a graded property: some systems are more stable across contexts and timescales, others more plastic.

Sources indicate that but plasticity alone is insufficient. An NCM may be plastic but insulated from cultural inputs. The experiences that shape kittens’ visual systems are not cultural experiences. So coupling is a tougher condition to satisfy. We need the relevant NCMs to be responsive to cultural content.

In a recent development, consider literacy. Reading is a cultural practice, only about 5,000 years old, too recent for evolution to have installed a specialised reading mechanism into the brain. Yet when people learn to read, even as adults, a patch of visual cortex that otherwise responds mainly to faces and objects becomes selectively tuned to written words. Here, cultural content shapes neural mechanisms: English and Hebrew readers’ brains become tuned to different letters, because their cultures write differently.

The uptake of emotion concepts and words – like ‘fear’ and ‘joy’ in a community – shapes those models.

Literacy demonstrates that cultural inputs can reorganise NCMs, in some cases. But are the mechanisms involved in mental disorders like this? Psychiatric disorders are vastly complex and difficult to study. So, it is helpful to find a simpler case study to test for plasticity and coupling. Emotion provides a case, and is especially relevant because many mental disorders are thought to be disorders of affect, motivation and emotion.

It has been revealed that affective scientists are split between two warring theories of emotion. On the one side are ‘basic emotion theorists’, such as the psychologist Paul Ekman who argues that a small set of basic emotions – including fear, anger, joy and disgust – are sculpted by evolution, cross-culturally stable, and powered by specialised neural circuits. In our terms, emotions depend on universal NCMs.

On the opposing side are ‘psychological constructionists’ (not to be confused with social constructionism) such as the neuroscientist Lisa Feldman Barrett. Barrett argues that there are no dedicated circuits for emotions. Instead, brains build each emotion on the spot, by mixing general ingredients such as bodily signals, past experience and, most notable here, concepts learned from one’s culture. Constructionists view the brain as continuously generating models of what to expect from the world and our bodies, and emotions emerge when incoming signals are unconsciously categorised according to those models. One striking claim is that the uptake of emotion concepts and words – like ‘fear’ and ‘joy’ in a community – shapes those models, and thereby shapes the mental and even physiological properties of emotions. This suggests a pathway through which cultural content can penetrate deep into the skull, and become entrenched in neural wiring.

Recent findings suggest that that is, constructionists view even the paradigm ‘basic’ emotions as plastic and culturally coupled: emotion-mechanisms partly built by adaptation and learning satisfy plasticity; cultural factors causally shaping those mechanisms satisfy coupling. Constructionism thus predicts that people reared in different cultural environments have differently wired emotion systems, at least to some degree.

Industry observers note that the emotion debate is far from settled. Constructionists are correct that emotional mechanisms appear far more variable and culturally idiosyncratic than basic emotion theorists predict. But conversely, emotions do seem to have pancultural characteristics: beta-blockers quell the racing heart and trembling hands of anxiety by blocking adrenaline’s effects on the body, and the brain circuits for learning fear are largely shared across mammals.

To settle the debate, we need more detailed data and experimental measures, but also better-differentiated theories. Presently, each theory can accommodate the same evidence. Basic emotion theorists explain cross-cultural similarities as the outputs of universal NCMs, and variations as culture modulating those outputs (similar to the illness/disease distinction). Psychological constructionists, by contrast, explain cross-cultural variations as the output of culturally varied NCMs, and explain similarities as similar cultural environments pushing those internal mechanisms to converge. This parallels the situation in psychiatry: we cannot settle debates about cultural shaping until our theories of brains, culture and mental disorders are better developed. Those debates turn on the degree to which the internal mechanisms of disorder are plastic and coupled.

Let’s briefly return to the case of anorexia in Hong Kong. If anorexia is appropriately plastic and coupled, then the Western anorexia script that arrived in 1994 may have done more than change how distress was expressed and experienced. It may have reshaped the NCMs that partly sustain its symptoms. That might warrant changes to how cross-cultural disorders are classified, explained and treated – perhaps as fresh subtypes, perhaps as new conditions. The anorexia Lee documented before 1994 and the anorexia he documented after may not be the same disorder after all.

Sources indicate that in 2013, Thomas Insel, then director of the NIMH, gave a TED talk promoting the institute’s new commitment to biomedical explanations. He ended with an optimistic remark from Bill Gates: ‘We always overestimate the change that will occur in the next two years and underestimate the change that will occur in the next 10.’ Only four years later, however, Insel conceded that his 13 years spent spearheading research into the neuroscience and genetics of mental disorders, at a cost of some $20 billion, had produced plenty of interesting papers, but had not ‘moved the needle’ for patients. More than 10 years later, psychiatry has still failed to produce robust biomedical explanations of almost any mental disorder. (The clearest exceptions are DSM categories that reference known neurological diseases, such as ‘major or mild neurocognitive disorder due to Alzheimer’s disease’; other medical conditions, such as hypothyroidism producing a ‘depressive disorder due to another medical condition’; or substances, such as alcohol producing a ‘substance/medication-induced psychotic disorder’.).

Against sceptics, I don’t think this shows that biomedical-style explanations of mental disorders are wrongheaded. I do think this shows that biomedical frameworks cannot be easily transported from somatic medicine into psychiatry, because the crisp distinction between illness and disease may not hold for psychopathology. In that case, biomedical-style explanations need updating. If mental disorders are plastic and culturally coupled, then explanations must synthesise the insights of biological psychiatry and cognitive neuroscience with those of cultural anthropology and cross-cultural psychology. In turn, for social explanations to do informative work in psychiatry, they need to be made into testable hypotheses – especially those that can be hooked up to NCMs. Psychological constructionists offer a promising (albeit incomplete) way of doing this, by hypothesising rich social environments engaging equally rich and empirically tractable mechanisms.

If deep shaping is right, what does it imply about psychiatry? One implication is a ‘particularism’ about mental disorder. As Murphy puts it, this particularism predicts that neurological systems ‘are so shaped by cultural structures that we should expect to see psychological theories that do not generalise but obtain only within different human populations’. This does not entail that we abandon general classifications, or that we cannot identify scientifically useful kinds of disorders. But it does take seriously that disorders might be ‘local’: explanatorily stable only within certain cultural contexts. On such a view, the underlying mechanisms explaining anorexia or depression in China might be importantly different from those explaining their counterparts in the US. There is much work to do to develop this view, both theoretically and empirically.

Psychiatry should not uncritically accept universalism as its default assumption. It rests on an analogy with somatic medicine that may be premature. Deep shaping is a live and promising alternative hypothesis – one that avoids both overconfident claims of universalism, and the excesses of social constructionism.

This essay was shortlisted for the inaugural Aeon Philosophy Prize.

Skift Global Forum East: Five Decisions in the Room

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (982 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skift

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The most ambitious growth story in global tourism is being tested on every front as multiple wars fester throughout the Middle East.
  • One of the most enduring narratives in travel over the past decade has been built around a clear set of assumptions: Global aviation will flow through Gulf hubs, international travelers will discover and then visit the Middle East repeatedly, and major events and attractions will reap the rewards of that demand well into the next decade and beyond.
  • According to recent reports, war across the Middle East over the past 9 months has called all of those assumptions into question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The most ambitious growth story in global tourism is being tested on every front as multiple wars fester throughout the Middle East. Every decision travel executives make today has to consider the long-term impact when these conflicts resolve.

One of the most enduring narratives in travel over the past decade has been built around a clear set of assumptions: Global aviation will flow through Gulf hubs, international travelers will discover and then visit the Middle East repeatedly, and major events and attractions will reap the rewards of that demand well into the next decade and beyond.

According to recent reports, war across the Middle East over the past 9 months has called all of those assumptions into question. Airspace disruptions have rerouted traffic, leading to suspended service for some airlines. Demand has significantly weakened, and hotels have leaned more heavily on domestic, regional, and short-haul travelers.

According to recent reports, the historically ambitious growth vision for Gulf tourism is facing an existential crisis. Every Middle East destination and travel executive that operates in the region has a decision to make: How much of 2026 is a temporary disruption, and how much do our long-term travel strategies need to be rewritten now?

Standard Pass – AED 2,920 Complimentary registration available (subject to approval) for senior leaders – email events@skift.com.

The Gulf’s aviation strategy depends on being one of the easiest places in the world to connect, and Gulf carriers are still planning for substantial long-term growth. New aircraft, larger airports, and expanded networks assume the region will retain its central role in global connectivity.

However, recent airspace closures and airline suspensions gave travelers and competing hubs a reason to find alternatives. Some of that traffic will return as operations normalize. It’s much harder to predict how much actually does. The decision is how to win back displaced traffic while planning for a future in which geopolitical disruption may remain part of the operating environment.

Emblematic of the air traffic disruption around the Gulf, Turkish Airlines cut Middle East capacity 26% year over year in the third quarter of 2026 while increasing East Asian capacity 18%. [1].

The Gulf has spent years building a hospitality proposition around luxury. The next phase of growth will also depend on domestic, regional, Asian, business, religious, and event-driven travelers with a wider range of budgets and trip types.

Recent findings suggest that development has continued through the disruption. The decision is whether the mix of rooms being built still matches the travelers expected to arrive, without overreacting to a difficult 2026 or leaving the region short of the mid-market supply needed for 2030 and beyond.

Sources indicate that the Middle East had a record total hotel construction pipeline of 771 projects at the close of the third quarter 2026, up 17% year over year. Luxury, upper-upscale, and upscale projects account for 78% of that total. [2].

Recent findings suggest that asia has become centrally vital to the Gulf’s growth story. India is already one of the region’s largest source markets. Coupled with Europe’s decline, China’s resurgence is even more critical. Gulf airlines, hotels, and destinations are adapting connectivity, products, and marketing around both.

The opportunity comes with constraints. India’s aviation market remains capacity-constrained, while Chinese demand can be interrupted quickly by safety concerns and airline suspensions. The decision is how much Gulf operators should invest now in Asian-market product, air access, and distribution before near-term demand becomes more predictable.

According to recent reports, india’s outbound travel market is projected to reach $55.4 billion by 2034, while Chinese is one of the top source markets for the UAE, representing 5% of inbound volume. [3] [4].

Major events create urgency, global attention, and exceptional demand. Permanent cultural, entertainment, and leisure assets give travelers reasons to visit and return throughout the year. The strongest destination strategy needs both working together.

Sources indicate that abu Dhabi shows what a mature recurring event can contribute, while destinations across the Gulf are also investing in museums, entertainment, attractions, and experiences designed to raise the annual baseline. The decision is how to connect event-driven peaks with a broader calendar that sustains demand between them.

Sources indicate that abu Dhabi’s Formula 1 race week has pushed average daily hotel rates close to $900, compared with roughly $200 during off-peak periods, while occupancy reached 93% during the 2025 race week. [5].

Gulf operators are moving promptly on AI at the same moment destinations and airlines need to rebuild international demand. AI assistants can reduce a long list of destinations, airlines, or hotels to a handful of recommendations before a traditional search result, OTA, or supplier website enters the journey.

Booking volume remains small, but commercial infrastructure for AI agents is already being built. The decision is whether travel companies in the Gulf region use their early-adopter advantage to help shape connectivity, customer ownership, payments, and servicing now, or wait for proven volume and enter a market whose terms were established elsewhere.

Recent findings suggest that the Gulf region is more exposed to and more ready for AI booking than any other market. 70% of MENA travelers have used AI tools for trip planning, ahead of North America. [6].

According to recent reports, the Gulf is still building for 2030 and beyond. The assumptions behind that investment are under intense scrutiny.

Aviation leaders have to determine which traffic will return. Hotel developers have to build for the travelers who will actually fill a growing room supply. Operators and destinations must decide how deeply to invest in Asian demand. Tourism authorities need events and permanent attractions to reinforce each other. Every part of the industry must prepare for AI to change how travelers discover and book trips.

The question connecting all five decisions is how much of the current disruption will fade as geopolitical conditions improve and which changes should now be treated as structural.

#401. In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King
