In Alison Roman's World, Curation is King

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (669 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished.
  • The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder.
  • In a recent development, what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With only weeks before opening, Alison Roman’s Brooklyn brick-and-mortar is still unfinished. “Today they’re doing up the walls and putting in the floors,” Roman says. In short, it does not yet look like a dreamy European-inspired grocer. There are still a mountain of calls to be made, meetings to be had, speed bumps to overcome.

The chaos doesn’t seem to be getting to the cookbook author, chef, and aspiring empire-builder. “It’s been so fun,” Roman, a Bon Appétit alum, states of the process. Perhaps that shouldn’t be a surprise; this breezy effortlessness is at the bedrock of the Alison Roman universe. You know the kind of nonchalant magic I’m talking about: chilling wine bottles in a bathtub of ice, buckets of take-out fried chicken at dinner parties—I mean, this woman was one of the foremost proponents of brothy beans.

In a recent development, what Roman has built has grown beyond recipes and bean propaganda. The ever-creeping edges of her lifestyle brand now encompass a jarred tomato sauce brand, once cheekily titled A Very Good Sauce, now renamed Roman’s. There’s also the new podcast, Having People Over, where she hosts guests for a meal and a yap, plus the speaking tour she’s calling “Food, Life and Other Strong Opinions.” There are the shoes (sleek mules and chunky clogs) she made in collaboration with New York–based footwear brand Margaux. And now First Bloom, the grocery store–slash–wine bar–slash–café that—as of mid-November—is on track to open in December.

The Brooklyn shop is an extension of the original Catskill’s location of the same name. Roman states this latest outpost is “a totally different proposition of what we are offering people.” There’s more budget to work with, there’s more staff, there’s more space, and there’s more food.

In a recent development, whereas the upstate location’s function is closer to utility—meat and produce from local farms are a major feature—in Brooklyn (where specialty grocers abound) Roman is focusing on something more akin to world-building. But do not call First Bloom a shoppy shop, those whimsically designed boutiques that seem to pop up everywhere selling the same $45 squiggly candlesticks and squeeze-bottle olive oils everyone seems to have. “I think ‘shoppy shop’ is derogatory,” Roman notes. “In a world where you can buy anything from anywhere, sometimes it’s nice to be told what to do.”.

At Brooklyn’s First Bloom, the shelves will be stocked with products that Roman herself deems “hyper-defensible.” There’s a reason they’re stocked, and a reason for how they’re priced. They’re best in class or a personal favorite of Roman’s. “Perspective and curation is a really special thing to be able to convey,” she indicates.

The vision for First Bloom is set, but with the opening just a month out, Roman doesn’t have all the details nailed down. “We are going to have a rotisserie chicken,” she says. “I don’t know how much it’s going to cost yet,” she follows up quickly, before I can ask. There will also be a couple salads and a couple sandwiches on offer—plus another secret off-menu sandwich for the neighborhood regulars and the real Roman-heads who know to ask for it. “I’m very if-you-know-you know,’” she says. But Brooklyn’s First Bloom isn’t just for popping into—you’ll be able to lounge with a glass of wine or relax with a snack and a coffee.

Sources indicate that alison Roman’s world is organic, craft-centered, and easy but considered. To step into it is an enticing foil to the AI-fueled tasteslop tilt-a-whirl on which we find ourselves. It’s a vision of a slow, steady, wabi-sabi life that many of us only aspire to. A life where one can even somehow enjoy, say, a monthslong commercial renovation project in one of America’s most competitive real estate markets. That’s the draw of First Bloom. The hard-to-find tinned fish, yes, but also the ease of living in Alison’s world if only for an hour.

And if not, well, it seems like there’ll be a pretty good rotisserie chicken, at least.

#399. Charred Cabbage With Yogurt and Hot Sauce

Charred Cabbage With Yogurt and Hot Sauce

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (437 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you think cabbage is boring, this dish will absolutely change your mind.
  • According to recent reports, in a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp.
  • Preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you think cabbage is boring, this dish will absolutely change your mind. Charred aggressively, it takes on a smoky, almost meaty quality—it’s the main event. A drizzle of hot sauce, crispy breadcrumbs, and a cooling yogurt sauce round it out. Treat cabbage like a protein, and it will reward you.

More showstopping cabbage recipes here.

According to recent reports, in a blender, combine 9 pickled Fresnos, stems removed and roughly chopped, plus 2 Tbsp. brine, 1 small shallot, roughly chopped, 3 garlic cloves, 3 Tbsp. red wine vinegar, juice of 1 navel orange, and 1 tsp. kosher salt. Blend on high, taking a pause to scrape the sides, until smooth. With the blender running on low, slowly pour in 1 cup extra-virgin olive oil until the sauce is silky and runny. Transfer the sauce to a bottle or jar and refrigerate for up to 2 weeks.

Preheat the oven to 425°F and set racks in the center and top of the oven. Line a sheet tray with parchment paper.

Make the Cabbage: Cut 1 large head green cabbage in half, then slice each half into four wedges. Arrange on the prepared sheet tray, drizzle generously with extra-virgin olive oil and kosher salt, and massage it into all those craggy layers. Roast on the center rack for 20–25 minutes, until a knife slides through easily. Set the broiler to high and slide the cabbage to the top rack. Broil for 2–4 minutes, until the edges are deeply charred and irresistibly crispy.

While the Cabbage Roasts, Make the Breadcrumbs: In a small skillet over medium heat, melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter with 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Stir in ½ cup panko breadcrumbs, 1 garlic clove, finely grated, and ½ tsp. kosher salt, then toast, stirring constantly, until golden and fragrant. Remove from the heat and mix in ¼ preserved lemon, store-bought or homemade, peel only, finely diced, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, and 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley. Set aside to cool.

According to recent reports, make the Yogurt: In a small bowl, whisk together 1 cup full-fat Greek yogurt or labne, zest and juice ½ lemon, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh dill, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh parsley, and 1 tsp. kosher salt until smooth and creamy.

It has been revealed that when the cabbage is ready, swoop the yogurt across a serving plate. Arrange the cabbage wedges at dramatic angles. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils.
  • More difficult is choosing a material to commit to.
  • Upcoming in this enhancement: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve ever scraped a black fleck off a melted spatula into your pasta and wondered what exactly you just ate, congratulations: You’ve already arrived at the case for nontoxic utensils. Swapping out your plastic-handled, mystery-material kitchen tools is one of the easiest upgrades you can make.

More difficult is choosing a material to commit to. Walk through any kitchen store and you'll encounter wood, silicone, stainless steel, bamboo, and any number of hybrid constructions. Each has its advocates and its limitations. But after thinking through the tradeoffs and cross-referencing what professionals actually reach for day to day, we landed on a clear answer: Silicone is the best material for a nontoxic utensil set, and a five- to six-piece core collection is all most home cooks need to start.

Upcoming in this enhancement: We added more information about the pros and cons of each of our winning non-toxic utensil sets.

Food-grade silicone is heat-resistant up to around 450°–600°, depending on the manufacturer, which means it’s unlikely to melt against the side of a hot pan or leach chemicals into your food the way that plastic utensils can when exposed to prolonged heat. It's also nonreactive, meaning it won't interact with acidic ingredients like tomato sauce or citrus the way that some metals can. Unlike wood, it's fully dishwasher-safe and nonporous and it won't harbor bacteria or crack over time with repeated washing. And—critically—it won't scratch your enameled cast iron.

Industry observers note that there are some things silicone doesn't do especially well. It can feel slightly grippy or drag-heavy compared to a thin fish spatula, for instance, and some silicone utensils pick up odors over time. (The odor issue is real—I've had cheaper silicone spatulas that smelled faintly of dish soap for months.) One other issue you might find is that you can’t scrape a pan very effectively with silicone in a situation where you might want to blend fond into a sauce for flavor (that’s a case for keeping a wooden spoon around). But for the vast majority of everyday cooking tasks—stirring, folding, sautéing, serving—high-quality silicone outperforms the competition on the merits that matter most.

Material: Platinum-cured siliconeSet size: 5 pieces (also available in 3- and 10-piece sets)Heat resistance: Up to 425°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

In a recent development, what we love: GIR (Get It Right) makes some of the best silicone utensils on the market. Its tools are made from 100% platinum silicone, which among other things, is a method that keeps odors off the utensils. It also makes them fully heat-safe and more durable than most other sets. That matters more than it might sound: Many budget silicone utensils use a nylon or fiberglass core to add rigidity, which can become a problem if the silicone outer layer ever cracks or peels. With GIR, what you see is what you get all the way through.

Recent findings suggest that the handles are weighted and ergonomic without being bulky, and the heads are thin enough to actually get under food—like a delicate omelet—which is a genuine problem with thicker silicone spatulas. GIR's tools also hold up unusually well over time. The silicone doesn't discolor, doesn't absorb odors the way cheaper versions can, and doesn't degrade with repeated dishwasher cycles.

It has been revealed that the brand offers a range of set configurations, but its core five-piece collection gives you exactly what you need without the extras: a spatula, a flip turner, a spoon, a ladle, and GIR's signature spoonula—a hybrid tool that functions as both spoon and spatula that’s particularly useful for scraping the sides of a pan or transferring food cleanly from pot to bowl. The spoonula in particular gets more use in my kitchen than I expected—it's become the default tool for anything that needs to be scraped, scooped, or transferred.

What we'd leave: It's a bit pricier than other silicone sets, but we think it's well worth it.

Good Grips 3-Piece Silicone Utensil Set.

Material: SiliconeSet size: 3 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: Yes.

What we love: Oxo's kitchen tools have been a reliable standard for years, and the brand’s silicone utensil line earns that trust at a lower price point. The set includes a ladle, a cooking spoon, and a turner, with flexible edges designed to get every last bit from pans and bowls. The handles are comfortable and grippy even when wet, and the one-piece silicone construction makes cleanup straightforward.

What we'd leave: It's a leaner starting point than our top pick, but that's not necessarily a bad thing—if you're building a collection piece by piece, this is a smart, low-commitment way to start with utensils you'll actually use.

Sources indicate that what we love: Wooden spoons are gentle on cookware, they don't conduct heat, and they have a tactile warmth that silicone can't replicate. The Essentials Set, made by a small wood shop out of Kempton, Pennsylvania, includes a large spatula, a stirring spoon, tongs, a medium serving spoon, a ladle, and Jonathan’s signature Original Spootle—plus a jar of their own SpoonWax to keep everything conditioned.

Material: WoodSet size: Wide range; medium set has 7 piecesHeat resistance: Not listed on siteDishwasher safe: No.

It has been revealed that what we'd leave: The wood requires more upkeep (and will eventually crack or warp) compared to silicone, but a quick hand-wash and occasional wipe-down with wax takes about 30 seconds. It's not cheap, but it's a premium product. Just keep it out of the dishwasher. For cooks who prefer the feel of wood, Jonathan's Spoons makes some of the most thoughtfully crafted wooden utensil sets available.

5-Piece Stainless Steel Kitchen Utensil Set.

Material: Stainless steelSet size: 5 piecesHeat resistance: 600°FDishwasher safe: Yes.

Industry observers note that what we love: Stainless-steel utensils are indestructible and oven-safe to high temperatures, and they look sharp hanging from a rail or stored in a stylish crock. So why make silicone the top recommendation instead? Bare stainless can scratch nonstick and enameled surfaces, so these are best suited for cooks who primarily use uncoated cookware (carbon steel, stainless steel, cast iron). All-Clad's 5-piece set includes a ladle, a solid spoon, a slotted spoon, a turner, and a storage caddy, all crafted from heavy-gauge stainless steel with ergonomic handles long enough to reach into deep pots. The set is heat-safe up to 600°, dishwasher-safe, and backed by All-Clad's limited lifetime warranty. If you're already cooking on All-Clad stainless-steel pans, this is the obvious companion set.

What we'd leave: If you don't have uncoated cookware, this isn't the set for you.

Recent findings suggest that once you have your core set, it's worth considering what other tools you'd need. Whether you're pescatarian, a deep-fryer, or an avid wok user, there's a tool out there that'll help you achieve your highest cooking goals. None of these need to come from the same brand—this is where building piece by piece, based on what you actually cook, makes more sense than buying a bigger bundle. Here are a few of our favorites.

It has been revealed that if crisping salmon skin is your game, a fish spatula is a must. The Lamson Flexible Stainless-Steel Slotted Turner ($53) is a longtime favorite, but Winco’s Fish Spatula ($10) is an inexpensive alternative with a wooden handle that's still flexible enough for delicate fillets.

Medium Stainless Steel Fish Spatula.

If steak is more up your alley, you can't be without a pair of tongs. Of course it's great for turning the steak in a skillet and holding in steady while you slice, but this tool is also helpful for a boatload of other tasks, like removing corn cobs from a pot of boiling water and shifting sheet pans around your oven. Oxo’s 12" Locking Tongs ($20) with silicone tips are gentle on nonstick and enameled surfaces while still giving you a confident grip.

Whether you're a deep-fry fanatic or a dumpling enthusiast, a spider strainer is a great tool for removing crisped or boiled items from hot pots and pans. We like this stainless-steel version for its sturdiness and extra-long handle.

Open Kitchen by Williams Sonoma.

According to recent reports, A from-scratch dressing, a silky cream sauce, or a fluffy whipped cream is made possible because of a good whisk. You can splurge on the editor-favorite Matfer Bourgeat Piano Whisk or opt for a silicone-coated Oxo Good Grips version.

According to recent reports, the same logic that makes a 7-piece cookware set a better starting point than a 15-piece one applies here: More isn't always better, and the average home cook will reach for the same handful of tools repeatedly. A well-considered five-piece silicone set typically covers a large spoon (for stirring sauces, soups, and grains), a slotted spoon (for draining and serving), a flexible spatula (the workhorse for eggs, fish, and pancakes), a turner or solid spatula (for heavier tasks like flipping burgers or moving proteins), and a ladle or tongs, depending on what you cook most.

Sources indicate that with five tools, you can execute most stovetop and baking tasks without reaching for anything else. That mentioned, not every set breaks down exactly this way—and that's fine. A three-piece set that covers your everyday tools beats a five-piece set with two pieces you never touch. Think of five as the target, not a hard rule.

Are silicone utensils actually nontoxic?

Recent findings suggest that high-quality, food-grade silicone is considered one of the safest materials for kitchen utensils, with FDA-approved versions specifically tested to ensure they don’t leach harmful substances into food. It's nonreactive, doesn't leach chemicals into food, and is stable at high temperatures. However, the quality of silicone utensils is much more all over the place. Cheaper sets often use filler materials or nylon cores that can degrade over time. Look for utensils made from 100% platinum-cured or pharmaceutical-grade silicone—the kind GIR uses—and you can feel confident about what's touching your food.

How do I take care of my utensils so they last?

It depends on the material. Silicone is the lowest maintenance—most sets are dishwasher-safe and require no special treatment. Wood needs more attention: hand-washing, drying thoroughly after each use, and oiling periodically with food-safe mineral oil or wax. Stainless steel is virtually indestructible, but hand-washing will keep it looking better longer. Regardless of material, avoid soaking utensils for extended periods and store them somewhere with good airflow rather than sealed in a drawer while still damp.

Do I need to match my utensils to my cookware?

Not exactly—but it's worth thinking about. If you cook primarily on nonstick or enameled cookware, silicone is your safest bet since it won't scratch delicate surfaces. If you cook mainly on stainless steel or cast iron, you have more flexibility and can use metal utensils without worry. Also, you may need a little more leverage to get food off, and metal can help with that. Wood works well across the board but comes with its own maintenance tradeoffs. The most practical approach for most home cooks: Start with a silicone set as your everyday workhorse, then add a stainless fish spatula or tongs as your cooking demands them.

Industry News: Why Weed Is Now a Family Thanksgiving Tradition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (736 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable.
  • The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries.
  • According to recent reports, it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting stoned in America has never been more socially acceptable. In the 14 years since Washington and Colorado first legalized recreational cannabis, a majority of states have followed suit by relaxing restrictions as well. While policy has a ways to go, the social stigma attached to the substance has dissipated into a skunky haze. If you’re not convinced, just look at the sheer number of Americans lining up to buy weed each Thanksgiving.

The day before Turkey day—dubbed Green Wednesday by the cannabis industry—might soon outpace 4/20 as the busiest day of the year for dispensaries. News outlets have covered this phenomenon in recent years with varying degrees of sincerity and snark, but the through line is always the same: People are getting high on Thanksgiving not only to improve the meal, but to make spending time with family more bearable—and apparently it’s kind of working.

According to recent reports, it makes sense: For many Americans, the fourth Thursday in November is for reuniting with relatives who, were it not for blood, might be the last people you’d ever choose to sit next to on a public bus. Thanksgiving is precision engineered for passive-aggressive ideological bickering and wrenching open old emotional wounds. It’s the day when adult siblings remind each other of their deepest insecurities while loading the dishwasher together, and when drunk aunts across the country engage in the time-honored tradition of casually outing their gay nephews to the table.

While this aspect of Thanksgiving provides plenty of material for movies, comedy specials, and sitcom bottle episodes, the lived reality is often less entertaining. The Reddit threads and advice column queries that crop up around this time each year tend to frame the holiday as a problem to be dealt with—a time for wielding the skills gleaned from cognitive behavioral therapy. Sometimes, in more dire terms, it’s a day one must try to survive. No wonder so many people are opting for a predinner edible.

But getting high merely as a means to dissociate through it all isn’t what all of these people seem to be stepping outside for. When Lisa Bonos reported on the phenomenon back in 2019, she spoke with several people who found that getting stoned with family members had a transformative impact on their relationships. Weed helped high-strung parents chill out, impart a “cozy atmosphere” for the stoned and sober alike, and most significantly, it dissolved intergenerational communication barriers. As Bonos pointed out, “getting high together can help equalize a historically unequal relationship—at any age.”.

Industry observers note that this is all anecdotal, of course, but there’s research to back it up. Humans have used cannabis for thousands of years socially through ritual and celebration, and the endocannabinoid signaling system plays an key role in how humans process social interactions by easing anxiety and fostering feelings of connectedness. Granted, this depends on dose and context.

I don’t mean to suggest that cannabis is a miracle substance that will heal the American family. It goes without saying that a whole lot of stuff is far too painful, complex, or irreconcilable to resolve by passing a joint. Opting for an alternative celebration, such as Friendsgiving, chosen family’s-giving, or DINKs-go-out-to-a-nice-restaurant-instead’s-giving, is for many, the safest way to go.

Sources indicate that but for the rest of Americans already imbibing this holiday to deal with more casually dysfunctional matters, it might be time to take the “cousin walk” out of the shadows and invite other cautiously interested members to partake. Since dosage really matters, I’d forgo slathering the Turkey in cannabutter and instead opt for a tin of one of those little low-THC, high-CBD edibles as an option for the inexperienced. Lest we forget when famous Upcoming York Times columnist Maureen Dowd ate too much of a THC infused chocolate bar, causing her to hide in a Denver hotel room in fear that she was both dead and wanted by the police.

Industry observers note that smoking weed with your family may not lead to a miracle, but at the very least, the odds of getting into a heated debate with your uncle regarding the directional shift of the Overton window are less likely if he’s zooted on the couch, reading the Wikipedia page on pecans. And maybe, just maybe, as Thanksgiving continues to get greener, it might become—for some—a day to look forward to rather than a day to endure.

I Planned a Wellness Weekend in Banff. It Totally Changed My Definition of Wellness.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • My first swing bounced off the ice; I hadn’t swung nearly hard enough.
  • It has been revealed that I tried again with less arm and more wrist.
  • According to recent reports, I’ve rock climbed with various degrees of dedication over the years, but I’d never climbed anything that could shatter under me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My first swing bounced off the ice; I hadn’t swung nearly hard enough. The pick hit with a dull clunk, skittered sideways and left a white scar about the size of a thumbnail. I was maybe six feet up a frozen waterfall outside Banff, front points of my crampons kicked into ice the color of snow. The column in front of me clearly didn’t care that I don’t lift, and holding the three-pound axe was already taxing.

It has been revealed that I tried again with less arm and more wrist. The pick sank in with a satisfying thunk, and for the first time, I actually felt secure.

According to recent reports, I’ve rock climbed with various degrees of dedication over the years, but I’d never climbed anything that could shatter under me. After another 10 minutes, I was sweaty and sore, almost 20 feet up the ice column. Hanging there with my forearms burning, I realized I hadn’t thought about anything else in 10 minutes, making ice climbing feel almost more meditative than physical. It was an unexpected twist during a weekend of unexpected winter wellness in outdoorsy Banff, Alberta.

Recent findings suggest that it was early winter, and I was on a long weekend retreat in Banff to get my head on straight before the fresh year. The year had been fine, but busy in the way that leaves you tired without a clear reason why. I wanted a few days to reset and think about goals and the new year before the rush of Christmas and New Year’s.

So I planned the trip the way most wellness weekends get planned. There was a yoga class at a new studio in town. There was time set aside to look after my sore back and shoulders with a massage. I didn’t proposal on any late evenings or huge meals where I’d feel stuffed. I even signed up for a winter forest meditation class. The agenda was something close to a spa brochure: calm, restorative, and gently active (yes, I planned to ski a day or two).

In a recent development, but Banff is world-famous for ice climbing, so I decided to give it a try, even though it didn’t perfectly fit into my calm, light activity trip. But ice climbing ended up being one of several experiences that taught me, by the end of the trip, that “wellness” can mean a whole bunch of things — including decadent dinners.

A beginner climber, no doubt. Photo: Suzie Dundas.

According to recent reports, I went out with Yamnuska Mountain Adventures, which has been guiding in the Canadian Rockies for decades. We met early, drove out to a canyon where the waterfalls had frozen into pale blue columns, and spent the first half hour on the ground learning to walk in crampons without stabbing my own ankles.

I quickly learned that ice climbing demands extreme focus. When your whole body is hanging off two picks and two crampon points, there’s no room to think about email, deadlines, or the work conversation you’ve been dreading. There’s just the next swing, the next kick and the small, specific sound of a pick that’s actually in the ice. My hands went numb, then warm, then numb again. I didn’t think about anything beyond the next move ahead of me and whether my legs could keep holding me up when I reached behind my head to swing.

When I unclipped from the rope for the last time, I felt the way you’re supposed to feel after a good meditation session. My head was clear, my shoulders had dropped about two inches, and I felt energized (if tired). It was like I had just finished a meditation session or hatha yoga class, but I’d gotten there with an ice axe instead of a yoga mat.

In a recent development, the yoga class was the item on my itinerary that looked most like wellness. I took it at Flow State Yoga, a one-room studio in downtown Banff, and spent most of it thinking about a different class on the schedule: “Flower with Flow,” where students are encouraged, though not required, to microdose before class. “The goal is to be microdosing so that you feel more uplifted and aware rather than high off your seat,” owner Coleman Rodrigues told me.

Recent findings suggest that most people don’t put smoking weed and wellness in the same sentence. I certainly hadn’t. But holding a long pose, I kept coming back to it, and it cracked open something I hadn’t questioned: wellness didn’t have to fit in a neat box. If a microdose before savasana could count, I started to wonder what else I’d left off my list.

The next day, I drove up to Lake Louise to snowboard. I’d wanted to ride there for years, mostly because I’d seen too many photos of its back bowls under fresh snow. There was no goal for the day and nothing to learn. I rode until my legs burned, managed to make some sick pow turns despite heavy afternoon clouds, and generally had a good, refill-filled day.

But on my way back, I stopped at the lake itself. I’d been there to hike in the summer, but in the winter, staff at Fairmont Chateau Lake Louise clears a rink on the frozen surface, and skating is free once the ice is thick enough. It’s a cheesy experience that’s been blasted left and right across Instagram, so I almost skipped it. But instead, I decided to apply my new, looser sense of wellness to the idea: I wanted to do it and I decided not to make myself feel like a dork for wanting my own fun ice skating pics and views of the mountains.

Sources indicate that I can skate just fine, but rarely do it, and I’m pretty sure I fell a decent amount on snowy bumps here and there. But still, I spent the next hour doing slow laps among families, couples and a few kids (who were much better than me, of course). It had no purpose at all, and I was one of probably half a dozen people out there staging photos. Instead of being embarrassed, I leaned in and enjoyed myself immensely. If letting go of feeling self-conscious about my own fun doesn’t count as wellness, I’m not sure what does.

According to recent reports, food was where my old idea of wellness had the firmest rules. A wellness weekend, I’d assumed, meant grain bowls, green juice, and limiting oneself to the kind of food you’d find health influencers touting on Instagram. That idea lasted as long as my first dinner in town. One night, I found what I’m still convinced is the best poutine in Banff: fries that stayed crisp under a heavy pour of veggie gravy, with cheese curds that actually squeaked. Normally I’d have filed something like that under “treat,” a little splurge to balance out with a salad later. This time I just ate the whole thing standing at a counter and enjoyed every bite.

The next night, my husband and I went all in at Hello Sunshine Sushi, ordering more rolls, tempura, and sake than two people need, and finishing with dessert anyway. Yes, it was decadent, and yes, it was a lot of food. But it was made from scratch with fresh fish and ingredients sourced with care, not pulled from a freezer bag of preservatives. That felt like a version of wellness too.

None of it would show up on a spa cafe menu, and I didn’t spend a second feeling guilty about that. Enjoying a great meal without wondering whether it was “good for me” felt like a small mental victory — and a tiny rejection of social expectations, which always gives you a little boost.

Sources indicate that who’s to say what is or isn’t “wellness” if it makes you feel better? Photos: Suzie Dundas.

My trip to Banff didn’t drastically change how I live. We still try to eat pretty healthily, I’ve got a 15-minute stretch and strength routine I do most nights, and I’m certainly not one to turn down the occasional massage. But it did help me realize that wellness is as much mental as physical, and that the traditional activities associated with “wellness travel” are definitely not the only ones that can push you in a healthier direction. I even swung by the Whyte Museum, and in a way, that felt like wellness — giving my brain time to just focus on art and aesthetics instead of stressing about work or my to-do list.

Now, when I plan a trip meant to recharge me, I start with how I want to feel when I get home (rested, confident, like I did things that really make me happy), and work backward from there. Sometimes that means a massage or a yoga class, but just as often it means a hard day outside, a long dinner I don’t second-guess, or an afternoon spent simply looking at art.

#394. I Came to Steamboat to Ski. I Stayed for Everything Else.

I Came to Steamboat to Ski. I Stayed for Everything Else.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve spent my whole life on Colorado snow, and somewhere along the way I stopped judging ski towns by just the size of their mountains.
  • Part of it is just getting there, and I don’t say that the way people usually complain about a long drive.
  • In a recent development, you feel the history here before you can explain it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve spent my whole life on Colorado snow, and somewhere along the way I stopped judging ski towns by just the size of their mountains. In Colorado, that’s the easy part. Any place with enough vertical and a decent snow year can sell you a good day on the hill. What I pay attention to now is what’s waiting when I clip out of my bindings at the bottom, and by that measure, Steamboat Springs has slowly become one of my favorite ski towns in the state.

Part of it is just getting there, and I don’t say that the way people usually complain about a long drive. Getting to Steamboat means skipping the I-70 corridor — the stretch of interstate that can turn a Denver ski day into four hours of brake lights and ski racks. Instead, you point the car northwest out of Denver and drive about three hours up and over Rabbit Ears Pass. The pass gets hammered when a storm rolls through, so I’ve learned to check conditions before I leave and give myself the extra time rather than try to beat the weather over the top. But the payoff on the far side is a town that still behaves like the ranching community it’s always been, one that happens to have a ski area attached, rather than a resort that showed up and bought the whole valley.

Photo: Joshua Lehew/Shutterstock.

In a recent development, you feel the history here before you can explain it. Steamboat leans hard into the “Ski Town USA” nickname, and it has sent more athletes to the Winter Olympics than any other town in the country. It’s easy to see why that is when you’re standing at the base of Howelsen Hill. Howelsen has been running since 1915, making it the oldest continuously operating ski area in Colorado, and it was built by a Norwegian ski jumper named Carl Howelsen, also known as the Flying Norseman. It’s small and weathered and sits next to downtown, and on any given winter afternoon, it’s full of local kids throwing themselves off the jumps, training the exact way Steamboat kids have trained for more than a hundred years. You don’t have to just watch, either. It’s open from late November into April with night skiing until 8 PM, and lift tickets are free on Sundays if you reserve a spot ahead of time. I can’t think of another place where you can ski the hill that produced a town’s worth of Olympians for the price of showing up.

Photo: Erica Meier Creative/Shutterstock.

In a recent development, the ranching side of Steamboat highlights up on the snow, too. Every January, the Cowboy Downhill turns the mountain into something I still can’t quite believe is real: a ski race for working rodeo cowboys from the pro circuits who come to town for the National Western Stock Show and point themselves downhill in full Western gear. It’s basically a rodeo on the slopes, and it tells you everything about how this town sees itself. The same spirit runs through the Winter Carnival, a Steamboat tradition going back more than a century that spills onto Lincoln Avenue downtown, and the Tread of Pioneers Museum keeps all of it straight in its Ski Town USA exhibit if you want the full lineage.

Photo: David A Litman/Shutterstock.

Industry observers note that the town also keeps its legends close. At the top of Mount Werner, where Buddy’s Run comes off the shoulder, there’s a bust of Buddy Werner, a local Olympic racer who died in an avalanche in 1964. The tradition is to grab a handful of snow and toss it on him as you go by. I’ve always liked that Steamboat built its memorial into the fall line instead of bolting a plaque to a lodge wall. You pay your respects mid-run, in motion, which feels like the right way to remember someone who skied.

Recent findings suggest that but here’s the part I wish somebody had told me years ago: you don’t have to ski a single turn to get up on that mountain. The gondola is open for sightseeing, and on Thursday afternoons, Thunderhead Lodge throws a gondola happy hour with the sun dropping west over the Yampa Valley. It happens in summer and winter. Down at the base, locals and visitors gather at Slopeside Grill for pub food and beer beginning in the early afternoons. A short hike uphill from Slopeside is the T-Bar, as close to a Euro-style après-ski vibe as you’ll find this side of the Atlantic. Grab a chair outside, watch the skiers fly by, and maybe dance on your seat to 1990s rock, hip-hop, and dance classics.

Industry observers note that if Steamboat were only the mountain, I’d still make the drive. But the food is what snuck up on me and changed how I think about the place. This is the town that gave the outdoor world brands like Big Agnes, Honey Stinger, and Smartwool, so there’s a tinkering, build-it-better streak running through it. And lately, that same energy has landed on the plates. Table 79 Foodbar, at the south end of downtown, runs a modern Western menu with vegetarian options that are actually dishes rather than afterthoughts.

Sources indicate that I celebrated my engagement with a small crew over homemade pasta and cocktails at Mambo Italiano on Christmas Eve 2014. The spot is classic mountain town fine dining — think “The Inn” from the movie “Out Cold,” but with Italian food. The staff is on point, the food is excellent, and its Lincoln Avenue location is walkable from anywhere downtown. If you want a good night, this is the spot. Laundry Kitchen & Cocktails does shareable, tapas-style plates inside a building that used to be an actual laundromat, and the name stuck. It’s also worth a leisurely evening.

When dinner’s done, the town doesn’t fold up. Schmiggity’s brings in local and touring bands, with a dance floor for anyone with the legs left for it. More often, though, I end up at Sunpie’s, a local dive bar on Yampa Street that has somehow kept its soul. I’ve spent many evenings in here over cold draft beers, recounting a day on the hill. It’s a local spot that’s friendly to visitors like me, and what’s a ski town trip without a good dive bar?

Photo: Teri Virbickis/Shutterstock.

In a recent development, however, between the skiing and eating, there’s a spot I never miss: Strawberry Park Natural Hot Springs. It’s a series of sulfurous, stone-lined soaking tubs, with cabins and campsites if you want to make a night of it. It becomes clothing optional after dark, but only if you want, and there’s a specific kind of comfort that comes from lowering yourself into hot mineral water with cold Colorado air on your face and the smell of sulfur and pine around you. On my first visit, I sat in the upper pool in board shorts for a good 20 minutes, working up the nerve to switch to my birthday suit until I realized I was the only person in the water wearing anything at all. Once my trunks got tossed on the rocks with everyone else’s towels, the whole calculation flipped. Nobody cared. It’s dark, the steam is thick, and the only thing anyone is actually watching is their footing on the icy stone between pools. I’ve never bothered with the shorts again, which I realize is a strange thing to brag about in a travel article, but there it is.

In a recent development, that’s the thing about Steamboat that took me years and a lot of other ski towns to understand. The mountain is genuinely great — the kind of terrain that would be worth the drive even without the town at its base. But I don’t keep going back for the terrain. I go back for the three hours of quiet it takes to get there, for the handful of snow I throw on Buddy Werner on my way down, for the laundromat that turned into one of the better dinners in the valley, and for the long soak in the dark at the end of it all. The skiing is the reason everyone comes to Steamboat, but by now, it’s hardly the reason I keep coming back.

  • According to recent reports, whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp.
  • In a recent development, lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is pretty clever, if we do say so ourselves—using roasted chicken thighs to create a Caesar salad, all in the same sheet pan. The wedges of lettuce, tossed in the leftover juices, soften and then everything melds in a comforting way. It’s a family favorite, with kids finding the dressing to be the closest possible thing to a “ranch” that hasn’t come premade in a bottle.

More sheet-pan dinner favorites this way.

According to recent reports, whisk together 1 cup/115 g mayonnaise, ⅓ cup/80 ml buttermilk or kefir, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, 2 green onions, finely chopped, ½ tsp. ground onion, ½ tsp. ground garlic, ½ oz./15 g parmesan, finely grated (2 Tbsp.), and ¾ cup/15 g dill, finely chopped, in a small bowl, along with 1 tsp. fine sea salt and a few grinds of black pepper. Set aside.

In a recent development, lay 6 chicken thighs, skin on and bones removed (about 1¾ lb./800 g), out flat on a parchment-lined baking sheet and season with ½ tsp. salt and a good grind of pepper. Add 1 lemon, very thinly sliced (about 12 slices), drizzle with 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and bake for 30–35 minutes, until the chicken is crispy and the lemon slices have started to caramelize.

Transfer the chicken and lemon to a shallow bowl and let rest for 10 minutes. Keep the baking sheet and parchment paper with all the pan juices. Finely chop half the lemon slices and add them to the dressing. Cut the chicken into ½"-/1-cm-thick slices and toss in the bowl with the rest of the lemon slices.

Add 2–3 heads of romaine lettuce, quartered lengthwise (14 oz./400 g), to the baking sheet, season with a pinch of fine sea salt and some black pepper, and turn them a couple of times in the pan juices. Spoon half the dressing over the lettuce and scatter the chicken on top. Finish with the rest of the dressing, a handful of croutons, store-bought or homemade, the extra parmesan, and a few sprigs of dill.

#391. The Future of Techno Is Being Forged in Monterrey

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1388 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Atlasobscura ↗ Open Full Page

The Future of Techno Is Being Forged in Monterrey

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that on a mild November evening in Monterrey, Mexico, the city’s largest urban park flashed from green to pink to blue, pulsating with the rhythmic beats resounding from a 360-degree sound system.
  • Recent findings suggest that for one weekend in 2026, Monterrey, a city best known for its international corporations and industrial history, became a glowing metropolis of the future — more specifically, the new second home of FuturFestival.
  • According to recent reports, within the park’s open-air steel and concrete structures, the Turin festival became a singular addition to Europe’s house and techno scene: a celebration not only of electronic music but also of the technological progress it represents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on a mild November evening in Monterrey, Mexico, the city’s largest urban park flashed from green to pink to blue, pulsating with the rhythmic beats resounding from a 360-degree sound system. Beneath a steel walkway, in a concrete depression once used for piling steel, thousands of people swayed, trancelike, to DJs’ ethereal mixes. As the sun set over a giant steel furnace, crowds continued to spill through the gates, leaving glitter in their wake as they flocked to the stages.

Recent findings suggest that for one weekend in 2026, Monterrey, a city best known for its international corporations and industrial history, became a glowing metropolis of the future — more specifically, the new second home of FuturFestival. Established in Turin, Italy, in 2006, Futur began as an arts association honoring the tenets of Italian Futurism: namely, youth, urban industrialism, and modernization. By 2012, it had become a full-fledged house and techno music (EDM) festival and found its permanent home in Parco Dora, a former Fiat factory turned 110-acre urban park.

According to recent reports, within the park’s open-air steel and concrete structures, the Turin festival became a singular addition to Europe’s house and techno scene: a celebration not only of electronic music but also of the technological progress it represents. By 2025, Kappa FuturFestival (named for its sponsor, the Italian sportswear brand Kappa) was welcoming more than 120,000 attendees from more than 150 countries; the same year, it was ranked the sixth-best festival in the world by DJ Mag. As the event grew year by year, it put Turin on the global map, marking it as a hub for innovative, avant-garde art.

When Futur chief innovation officer and co-founder Gianluca Brignonen floated bringing the event to his adopted country, Mexico, Carlos López — CEO of the event firm Lostnights — immediately knew the festival would thrive at Parque Fundidora. The massive Monterrey park was a site remarkably similar to Parco Dora, from its historical significance down to its very name.

Now Mexico’s eighth-largest city, Monterrey developed into a major business hub shortly after the Mexican War of Independence and, with the establishment of the Monterrey Foundry in 1900, emerged as the country’s primary industrial center. The first of its kind in Latin America, the foundry took advantage of the city’s easy access to iron and coal deposits to become the backbone of the entire region’s economy.

From structural steel to railways, wire rods, and train wheels, the foundry contributed to some of Mexico’s most notable 20th-century engineering projects and counted the country’s wealthiest families among its investors. However, shortly after it was nationalized in 1977, its fortunes reversed, and it was forced to shut down in 1986.

The people of Monterrey refused to let the foundry’s towers and furnaces simply sit in obscurity, and only two years after it ceased operations, the government unveiled aims to repurpose the site into a public park and recreation space.

In a recent development, as construction began and stretched into the 1990s, Parque Fundidora evolved into much more than just green space. Additions included a convention center, children’s museum, steel museum (inside the former blast furnace), contemporary art center, and restaurant. A “Plaza of the Visionaries” was also added, paying tribute to those who helped establish the foundry over a century ago.

According to recent reports, “All the premises, all the areas are unique. Just to feel and to dance in this place with a lot of heritage — there’s a feeling of greatness,” López indicates. Whether Parque Fundidora would feel right never concerned him because it so clearly had everything: the same industrial spectacle and local reverence as Parco Dora transposed into a new cultural setting.

Getting the 360-acre park festival-ready was a years-long process. (“You could spend days in there doing different things,” Lostnights COO Yalia Bailleres observes.) The team at Lostnights needed to determine not only which sections of the massive space to use but how to let it shine — with lighting, stages, and layouts that would make its mechanical remains as compelling as the artists headlining.

After putting out an open call to audiovisual artists around the world, the Lostnights team selected a handful of moving digital artworks to play on giant LED screens throughout the park and even on one of its stages, “Voyager.” The open call’s theme, “Envision the FUTUR,” encouraged exploration at the intersection of art, technology, and electronica, reflecting Futur’s message that any festival is only as memorable as its environment.

Industry observers note that lópez, Bailleres, and their colleagues also took advantage of the park’s inconspicuous nooks and crannies, turning an area between old towers into a midsize stage for techno funk and a small brick building into a “secret” stage that nevertheless attracted a long line out the door. The festival’s premier stage, “Nova,” sat underneath a long steel bridge, the peaks of the Sierra Madre Oriental just visible behind its beatmakers and record-spinners.

“We wanted to find the perfect location that could give the same atmosphere as [Parco Dora], but at the same time, something a little different,” says Gabriella Botte, project manager of Kappa FuturFestival. “The park has such a strong identity. People know it from how the venue looks in pictures and in videos.”.

The Turin festival’s steampunk setting had become inextricable from Futur itself, making it recognizable even to non-techno fans. Incorporating Parque Fundidora’s architecture into the event as much as possible meant keeping Futur’s brand alive while, at the same time, honoring Monterrey’s cultural and economic history.

Recent findings suggest that “Monterrey is really like [Turin],” Futur CEO and co-founder Maurizio Vitale observed on opening night, Nov. 13, from inside one of the old furnace rooms. “The mountains around, the industry that we see here, and the smiles of people on the welcoming day. There’s a special energy. The people, the venue, the nation itself.”.

It has been revealed that when choosing the event’s lineup, Futur’s organizers sought to maintain its international variety while also spotlighting Mexican techno artists. As Botte explains, “The festival has to be connected with the territory in order to grow. It’s important to represent the locals.”.

Among the Mexican artists who took the stage were betterxfly (Daniela de la Garza), LABIBE (Labibe Bujaidar), and Opuntia (Camila de Laborde), as well as Monterrey up-and-comer SADA, whose unique blend of EDM and cumbia (a dance genre that originated in Colombia) has made him a rising star of the city’s growing music scene.

Recent findings suggest that it was thanks in part to this scene that more than 24,000 people revealed up for FuturFestival Mexico — a turnout that Bailleres views as a huge achievement. Past festivals held in Parque Fundidora, while attracting larger crowds, have centered on traditional Mexican music or more general arts-and-culture fare; FuturFestival is the first to introduce techno music to the mix.

“For us, having electronic music this big — for locals, it’s like ‘What is that?’ because it’s something latest,” Bailleres says. “But then we’ve started getting all this engagement, and people love this space.”.

Recent findings suggest that the team now looks ahead to the 2027 festival, with intends to increase the number of stages and take over even more areas of the park. Botte is already dreaming of a DJ atop the 230-foot-tall blast furnace, while Bailleres has her eyes set on the small river that runs through the park, imagining boats floating, lazy-river-style, past a colorful stage.

In a recent development, A place where thousands of workers once poured and molded molten steel is now a testing ground for what’s possible in electronic music exhibition and, just as importantly, a symbol of what’s next for Monterrey. “Everybody states a long-term plan, but this is more than long. This is a lifetime plan. We are here to stay,” Vitale says.

Once night set in, spotlights illuminated the foundry itself, bathing its pipes and winding staircases in neon against the dark sky. Artists mingled over drinks next to old machinery in the green room, while audience members swarmed past mill halls, cranes, and smokestacks to get to the front row for their favorite artists’ sets. Even far beyond Parque Fundidora’s gates, music echoed through the city. The future had come to Monterrey, and there was no going back.

7 Things You'd Find in a 1950s Grocery Store That Have Disappeared

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mentalfloss

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shoppers from the 1950s would probably be in awe of all the modern conveniences we have to get groceries.
  • According to recent reports, grocery stores still market products that promise convenience for busy lives, but the whole experience has become impersonal.
  • Here are a few things that were common in '50s grocery stores but have vanished today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shoppers from the 1950s would probably be in awe of all the modern conveniences we have to get groceries. The internet and Instacart would be completely mind-blowing. Convenience and saving time were a key focus for grocery stores in the '50s, so products and store features all catered to making shopping an easy and pleasant experience.

According to recent reports, grocery stores still market products that promise convenience for busy lives, but the whole experience has become impersonal. You might not even speak to another person at all if you grab what you need and head to the self-checkout. Some of the features and items of the 1950s disappeared to make way for more profit and technology, and the old ways of grocery shopping disappeared with them.

Here are a few things that were common in '50s grocery stores but have vanished today.

Beginning in 1950, "self-service" meats, pre-packaged in cellophane, became quite the trend, but enough people still preferred ordering custom cuts from the butcher that the meat counter at the grocery store kept its line of patrons. You used to order specific cuts of meat, including how fatty you wanted it, and then the butcher would measure, cut, and weigh your meat. Then, they would wrap it carefully in paper before handing it to you.

Recent findings suggest that at an A&P grocery store in the 1950s, you could grind your own coffee beans in the coffee aisle. The coffee beans were in barrels or containers, and you could scoop out the amount you wanted. Then, the grinder was right there, ready for customers to use. If you loved the smell of coffee, this aisle was heavenly, and you would walk down it even when you didn't need to buy any beans.

Industry observers note that do you ever wish, as an adult, that you could find a fun surprise like the toys that came in cereal boxes? Well, in the 1950s, you could. Duz brand laundry detergent gave a free dish with each box purchased, and families bought laundry soap weekly to collect an entire dining set. There were even gravy boats and platters! If your parents or grandparents have a set of dishes with pictures of golden wheat on them, they likely collected them from laundry soap boxes.

Recent findings suggest that another collection people got from the grocery store were stamps, though not postal stamps. These "Green Stamps" were part of a rewards program, and if you collected enough stamps, you could trade them in for a prize. S&H was not the only company to feature a loyalty stamp program, but it was the most popular. By the end of the 1950s, S&H gave out more stamps than the United States Postal Service. And the prizes weren't cheap either; you could get a bicycle, luggage, or even furniture with enough stamps.

According to recent reports, TV dinners can still be found in the frozen section of the grocery store, but they have changed a lot from the originals. Before microwaves, people heated their frozen meals in the oven, so TV dinners came in aluminum trays. They were so convenient and allowed the family to watch their new televisions together while eating. And housewives loved not having to prepare and cook a full meal every night.

According to recent reports, franco-American brand of canned pastas operated under Campbell's Soup Organization, and while they had several meals that people miss, the most famous was the macaroni and cheese. It was technically long macaroni-type noodles in a cheese sauce, but it was a popular canned meal in the 1950s. It was so popular that Campbell's didn't discontinue it until 2004, and there have been petitions to bring it back.

You can still find boxes of hair dye at the grocery store, but the at-home perms have, thankfully, faded from popularity and store shelves. In the 1950s, though, the Toni Home Permanent for women and the Tonette Home Permanent for girls were all the rage. Not needing to go to a salon for a perm was a massive plus for many women and their pocketbooks. But after many perms that just came out wrong and a lawsuit involving a little girl losing all her hair, the perm in a box lost its status as peak beauty care.

Caviar from an all-inclusive might sound like an oxymoron. With an ounce of mid-tier caviar running about $200âroughly the cost of a night at a resort of the same caliber in the Caribbeanâyou wouldn't expect to find it on a menu. But the kind I dared to try at Secrets MoxchÃ© Playa del Carmenâ"Mexican caviar," which isn't actually fish eggs at allâmost definitely changed my mind on the matter.

Sources indicate that buttery, slightly nutty, and a perfect match for toasted pumpkin seeds, escamoles are the edible larvae and pupae of ants. Unlike sturgeon roe, acquiring these delicate orbs requires conquering colonies of venomous ants rather than the belly of the beast. The name comes from the Indigenous Nahuatl words azcatl, meaning "ant," and molli, meaning "stew," which gives surprisingly accurate insight into how escamol is still prepared all these years later.

Sources indicate that while the caviar you now eat with a mother-of-pearl spoon started off as peasant food in 12th-century Russia, the "caviar of the desert" (another moniker for escamoles) was once a celebrated delicacy among Aztec emperors. From the protein's prestigious history to its current place on high-end tasting menus, its value all comes down to how the food is foraged.

In a recent development, as its upwards of $100-per-pound price tag suggests, harvesting escamoles can be tricky. The process leads straight into the underground tunnels of the velvety tree ants of Central Mexico, Liometopum apiculatum. Although these nests sit surrounded by the roots of agave and maguey plants, getting your hands on escamol is a lot more challenging than harvesting tequila or mezcal. When done sustainably, the ants and nest are preserved while the larvae are carefully scraped out by traditional escamoleros in the springtime.

While this wasn't my first dance with ants on the dinner plate, trying the escamol taco in Playa del Carmen made it much harder to ignore the reality of eating insects than the ground-up chicatana ants blended into the chile mayo on the famous baby corn dish at Pujol, a Michelin-starred institution in Mexico City. Back at the resort, sautÃ©ed and paired with epazoteâa pungent Mexican herbâand pepitas on a warm corn tortilla, it was just one bite of the seven-course taco tasting at its Mexican restaurant, Dos Almas. Yet getting past the anthill my mind had turned into a mountain to taste a centuries-old traditionâway outside my usual taco orderâstuck with me.

The rest of the tasting menu leaned just as heavily into local Mexican flavors without playing it safe. Alongside the ant eggs, the meal moved through a crisp taco dorado stuffed with pork and potato and topped with hamachi tartare and green onion oil, a smoky taco brasero piled with lobster and chipotle mayo, rich pork belly under an Oaxaca-style manchamantel mole, and my favorite, a steak taco on a queso-encrusted flour tortilla topped with charred avocadoâeach paired with regional spirits from mezcal to licor de elote (corn liqueur).

Industry observers note that it was the kind of meal I usually associate with "traveling" over "vacationing"âhunting down hard-to-get reservations and street food instead of settling for whatever is on the hotel buffet. Over a decade ago, my first trip to a Cancun-area all-inclusive cemented the idea that subpar food was just part of the deal. So when I found Secrets MoxchÃ© through Apple Vacations, I expected the usual perks of an easy beach tripâbundled flights, airport transfers, zero legworkânot food I'd actually write home about.

Aside from the few pounds I gained over the long weekend, what actually surprised me was how much Indigenous history and culture made it onto the property, rather than getting watered down for an American palate. Beyond the upgraded tasting dinners, the resort runs a year-round program called "Roads Through Mexico" that brings regional folk art, live music, and local bites onto the immaculately manicured grounds. Catching it during DÃ­a de los Muertos drove the point home: you don't always have to leave the resort gates to get a real taste of where you are.

Indianola, Texas a coastal town that was once the second largest port in Texas next to at the time Galveston.In 1956 the port received a shipment of camels as part of the United States Camel Corps experiment to replace horses and mules as the primary work animal for southwestern America.

Sources indicate that during the Civil War, it was occupied by the Union army, once in 1862, then again a year later. Part of that regiment later drowned moving from Indianola to Matagorda island.

The island was later hit twice again, this time by hurricanes, in 1876 and 1886. The second hurricane was accompanied by a major fire and also submerged most of the town, killing hundreds.

Now basically no sign of the town is left other than a few plaques (one being a marker of where the courthouse used to be). It is however valued as a great spot for fishing for local trout, redfish and flounder.

The first Thanksgiving took place in the fall of 1621. It honored the harvest and gathered the Pilgrims and the Wampanoag people in Plymouth County for three days of food and togetherness. Their relationship was not entirely conflict-free, more like temporarily cordial, and peace did not last.Â.

54 years later, King Philip's War ended with the Wampanoag tribe losing their land and freedoms to the colonists.

The tradition all but disappeared (give or take a few gatherings) until President Abraham Lincoln issued a proclamation in 1863 making Thanksgiving a national holiday on the last Thursday in November. In 1939, President Franklin D. Roosevelt declared it the third Thursday, but that only lasted two years. In 1941, Congress permanently made Thanksgiving the fourth Thursday in November. And thatâs how weâve celebrated it ever since!Â.

Introduced in 2014, Nespresso’s Vertuoline modernized the brand’s original pressure brew method and marked the true beginning of Nespresso espresso and coffee machines. Most Vertuo machines feature just one button and brew both coffee and espresso-style shots using a centrifugal method. Once you choose your preferred pod based on style, roast, and cup size, the machine takes care of the rest. That’s because the rim of every dome-shaped Vertuo capsule features a barcode that tells the Nespresso Vertuo machine how much water and what extraction speed to use for each pod—and can brew everything from a single and double espresso shot to a 14-ounce cup of coffee. Some Vertuo machines can even fill an 18-ounce carafe from a single coffee pod.

The very first Vertuo machine released more than a decade ago is still kicking, and it's one of the best values you can get.

It has been revealed that enabled with Bluetooth and Wi-Fi connectivity, the Nespresso Vertuo Next can brew 18 ounces of coffee from a single pod. If you’re intrigued by the tech or pod yield, it’s worth a try—especially considering Nespresso’s 30-day return policy, warranty, and reputation for maintenance and machine repairs.

Vertuo Next Coffee with Aeroccino Milk Frother.

Modeled on the Vertuo Next, this compact cutie is one of the newer Vertuo machines. It’s perfect for someone who’s short on space but still wants the convenience of the Vertuoline. The Pop Plus machines have slightly bigger water reservoirs than the Pop models, and they can hold more used capsules, but all of the machines have small-kitchen-friendly footprints.

Nespresso Vertuo Pop + Aeroccino Milk Frother.

Industry observers note that released earlier this year, the Vertuo Up is Nespresso's newest machine, and brews the one-touch Vertuo pods. This compact machine heats up in just three seconds (which, is really, really, ridiculously fast for any coffee maker to heat water) and depending on the specific model you get, it can brew six or seven different cup sizes, ranging from a single shot of espresso to a full carafe from a single Vertuo pod. Like the Next and Pop machines, the Vertuo Up is Wi-Fi enabled and you can use the companion app for maintenance alerts and to customize how the machine brews your favorite pods, if you'd like tweaks to the pod-specific presets.

The Vertuo Creatista is the first machine in the Vertuo line with a built-in steam wand. It’s not quite a one-touch cappuccino machine because brewing espresso from a pod and steaming the milk are two separate processes. But if you want the look of a real espresso machine (well, if you don’t look too closely) with the convenience of Nespresso Vertuo capsules, the Vertuo Creatista is a great option. This is the machine that I’ve been using at home for years and it works sort of like a super-automatic espresso machine.

The newest Vertuo machine, the Vertuo Lattissima is a one-touch machine that makes coffee, espresso, cappuccinos, and latte macchiatos at the push of a button.

Until the Vertuoline was introduced in 2014, the OriginalLine machines were simply known as Nespresso machines. These models brew either single or lungo (Italian for "long") espresso-style shots from any compatible pod using a pressure-driven method. The Original Line features a collection of compact pod-only machines (Nespresso CitiZ, Nespresso Essenza Mini, and Nespresso Pixie) as well as a variety of pricier Creatista and Lattissima models, with built-in steam wands or other automatic milk frothers. We rarely see the compact Original machines go on sale, but here are the Nespresso Original Line models you can find for a steal ahead of Black Friday.

These one-touch espresso and latte machines make a variety of one-touch milk drinks and have built-in milk cleaning functions that do a lot (but not all) of the daily maintenance so you don’t have to.

Airports are places of departures and arrivals, but what happens to those who never seem to leave? At Terminal 1 of Madrid-Barajas Airport, a bronze man sits quietly, apparently waiting for a flight that may never come. Known as El Vagamundos (The Wanderer), this 1996 sculpture by Spanish artist Casto Solano captures the peculiar feeling of being suspended between destinations.

Sources indicate that the seated figure has acquired a life of its own through local folklore. Some people believe it commemorates those who have turned airport terminals into temporary homes, stranded by immigration bureaucracy or personal circumstances. One popular story connects the sculpture to a Cuban traveller who allegedly spent 18 months wandering around Barajas in 1992 while trying to secure permission to return to his homeland.

Whether or not the legend is true, El Vagamundos perfectly embodies the strange limbo of airport life: the endless waiting, the transient encounters, and the feeling of belonging nowhere and everywhere at once. Among hurried passengers dragging their suitcases, this traveller has nowhere else to be.

You can find the statue of El Vagamundos on the corridor that links Terminal 1 of the airport with the metro station.

Industry observers note that in a village of just sixty inhabitants in the heart of rural Catalonia, you’d expect to find stone buildings, farmland and perhaps a church. And sure enough, that’s exactly what you get. What you wouldn’t expect, though, is to stumble upon three Soviet fighter jets in someone’s garden. But there they are. And alongside them, an American fighter jet, completing what must be the strangest aviation museum in the entire country.

Sant Pere dels Arquells lies right next to the motorway, just over an hour’s drive from Barcelona. Like many other places in the area, it is an old walled village, dating back to the time when Muslims and Christians were fighting over the region, a thousand years ago. There isn’t much to see here, really, apart from its bizarre collection of aircraft, clearly visible from above and on Google Maps.

Sources indicate that the four aircraft on display are three Mikoyan-Gurevich (MiG) fighters, models 15, 21 and 23, and a Lockheed F-104 Starfighter. According to the local press, their owner, Xavier M., is a military history enthusiast who bought them as scrap after the dissolution of the Soviet Union and the fall of the Iron Curtain. Despite being left outdoors, exposed to rain and sunshine, they are in surprisingly good condition. The Starfighter, in fact, was recently repainted and restored, and looks as though it could take off at any moment.

The aircraft are clearly visible from the village’s main street, as well as from behind the 15th-century church. Amateur pilots taking off from and landing at the two nearby airfields use them as a landmark. Over the years, they have become so well known in the area that the village is now popularly known as Sant Pere dels Avions (Saint Peter of the Airplanes).

Public transport to the village is virtually non-existent. The easiest way to get there is by car; under normal traffic conditions, the drive from Barcelona takes around an hour and ten minutes. Alternatively, you can take a taxi from Cervera. Access to the grounds is not permitted, and you cannot get up close to the aircraft, but they are clearly visible from the street.

Industry News: Summit House/Prospect House in Hadley, Massachusetts

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the 400-plus-acre Skinner State Park adjoins the 3,000-acre Mount Holyoke Range State Park, where visitors can enjoy scenic vistas, picnic areas, and more than 40 miles of trails open year-round.
  • During its heyday, the hotel welcomed an impressive array of notable guests.
  • Sources indicate that one of the Prospect House’s most remarkable features was its mountain railway.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the 400-plus-acre Skinner State Park adjoins the 3,000-acre Mount Holyoke Range State Park, where visitors can enjoy scenic vistas, picnic areas, and more than 40 miles of trails open year-round. At the heart of Skinner State Park stands the Prospect House, better known as the Summit House, a hotel that opened in 1851 and rapidly became a fashionable destination for wealthy travelers from eastern Massachusetts and New York City.

During its heyday, the hotel welcomed an impressive array of notable guests. Jenny Lind, the celebrated opera singer known as the “Swedish Nightingale,” visited in the year the hotel opened, and Alexander Graham Bell was a regular guest. Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, and Emily Dickinson were also among the writers associated with visits to the summit.

Sources indicate that one of the Prospect House’s most remarkable features was its mountain railway. In 1854, the hotel installed what is often described as Fresh England’s first tramway, initially to transport supplies up the mountainside and soon afterward to carry guests. At a time when train travel itself was still a relatively novel experience, a mechanical railway climbing a steep mountainside was an extraordinary attraction. The tramway operated until 1942, and visitors driving past the sign for Track 6 may still catch a glimpse of the cut through the mountainside where the tracks once ran.

In a recent development, reaching the hotel was an adventure in its own right. Guests arriving by train at Smiths Ferry, on the western bank of the Connecticut River, crossed the river by steamboat ferry. A stagecoach then carried them to the tramway, which transported them partway up the mountain before they continued to the summit. The journey offered a memorable combination of river travel, carriage rides, and pioneering mountain engineering.

In a recent development, the hotel’s story is also one of ambition and perseverance. John and Fanny French were instrumental in establishing and expanding the Prospect House. Fanny was only 19 when she and John began building their lives on the mountain. They spent their first winter in the original 1851 house, but the conditions proved so harsh that they built the Half Way House as a more practical winter residence.

The hotel expanded substantially under their proprietorship. An addition in 1861 was followed by a much larger annex in 1894, bringing the hotel to 44 guest chambers and a dining room that seated 200 people.

Industry observers note that by the early 20th century, however, the Prospect House faced mounting challenges. In 1908, following the deaths of the hotel’s owners, local industrialist and philanthropist Joseph Allen Skinner and a group of like-minded businessmen formed the Mount Holyoke Firm. Their interest increasingly centered on preserving the property rather than operating it as a commercial venture. Skinner eventually took sole ownership in the 1910s and introduced modern conveniences, including indoor plumbing, electricity, and a upcoming road for automobiles.Despite these improvements, the hotel’s popularity declined. Automobiles gave vacationers more destinations to choose from, while the economic hardships of the 1930s put a stay at the hotel beyond the reach of many travelers.

The final blow came with the devastating hurricane of 1938. Although the original 1851 and 1861 sections survived, the storm severely damaged the 1894 annex, which Skinner subsequently had demolished.

Recent findings suggest that in 1940, Skinner donated the hotel, its associated outbuildings, and 375 surrounding acres to the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. He asked for nothing in return except that the park bear his name. At the dedication ceremony, he expressed his hope that the property would become a “thing of beauty and a source of joy to the people of the Commonwealth.”.

Recent findings suggest that skinner’s legacy extends beyond the mountain. Visitors can learn more about his life and interests at the Joseph Allen Skinner Museum in South Hadley, which displays his extraordinary collection of nearly 7,000 objects.

Recent findings suggest that mount Holyoke’s appeal predates the hotel itself. In 1836, landscape painter Thomas Cole sketched the Connecticut River valley from the summit, inspiring his celebrated painting The Oxbow. Ralph Waldo Emerson also visited, according to the hotel guest book. It is intriguing to imagine these figures making the arduous climb when the only structure at the summit was a simple shack.

The mountain continues to inspire visitors today. Since 1838, Mount Holyoke College has celebrated its annual Mountain Day, when the ringing of the bells at Abbey Chapel unexpectedly cancels classes and sends students hiking to the summit.

Even the deteriorating Summit House has acquired a folklore of its own. During the 1970s and 1980s, visitors reportedly spotted the ghosts of John and Fanny French: John standing on the porch and Fanny appearing in the windows.

Sources indicate that from its pioneering railway and celebrated guests to the people who built their lives on the mountain, Mount Holyoke’s Summit House offers a fascinating glimpse into an era when reaching a mountaintop could be an adventure in itself. Today, the park preserves not only a remarkable historic building but also a landscape that has drawn travelers, artists, and nature lovers for nearly two centuries.

How many strikes are too many? With almost all of the country's flights grounded on Monday, many of Belgium’s travel leaders have had enough.

Belgium’s airline and travel sector is demanding stronger safeguards against strike-related disruption after air traffic controllers helped bring the country’s airports to a standstill on Monday.

The Board of Airline Representatives in Belgium (BAR Belgium) described it as the 11th strike affecting Belgian airspace in 11 months and accused public-sector workers of repeatedly undermining the country’s international connectivity.

Air navigation provider Skeyes said it could not safely provide regular air traffic control from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time after some of its staff joined a nationwide demonstration against government austerity measures. Only emergency and other safety-critical flights would be supported, it said.

Brussels Airport said all arrivals and departures scheduled within that 14-hour window would have to be canceled, while Charleroi Airport said disruption would affect its entire Monday schedule.

Industry observers note that experiential attractions in busy destinations can grow without drawing bigger crowds.
