Sources indicate that since the mid-1920s, department store giant Macyâs has held an annual Thanksgiving Day Parade to ring in the holiday shopping season. While many of the paradeâs beloved traditions have remained, the celebration has made some pretty significant changes over the course of the last 100 years.

While the parade has by now solidified itself as a Thanksgiving staple across the United States, the extravaganza was originally designed to be a Christmas celebration. When Macyâs first envisioned the parade, it was intended to be a celebration of Christmas staged on Thanksgiving morning to kickoff the holiday shopping season.Â.

After the parade debuted in 1924 to celebrate the opening of their flagship store in Herald Square, Macyâs decided to continue the tradition annually, later changing the name from the Macyâs Christmas Parade to the Macyâs Thanksgiving Day Parade.Â.

When the parade first debuted in 1924, Macyâs borrowed live animals from the Central Park Zoo for the occasion. Elephants, lions, tigers, bears, and even camels marched the six mile route from Harlem to Macyâs in Herald Square alongside clowns, marching bands, and Santa Claus himself.Â.

Macyâs continued featuring live animals in their parade for a few years afterward, but eventually phased them out of the line up when the well-known balloons became the main attraction.Â Â.

Industry observers note that when Macyâs tasked puppeteer Tony Sarg with designing some of their very first balloons, the giant balloons were filled with air instead of helium, requiring them to be propped up by poles instead of floating on their own. By 1928, helium had become more widely commercially available and the balloons were filled with the lightweight gas instead.

During those first few years, the balloons were released into the sky at the end of the parade, but the practice was stopped after a pilot chasing after one nearly crashed.Â.

It has been revealed that in the more than 100 years Macyâs has held its annual parade, the retail giant has only taken a few years off between 1942 and 1944 on account of the United Statesâ ongoing participation in World War II. Being that rubber and helium were tightly rationed to support the war effort, Macyâs decided to forgo its annual parade in the early 1940s and instead donated rubber from their retired balloons to the U.S. military.Â.

By 1945, the war had officially ended and the Macyâs Thanksgiving Day Parade returned.Â.

In a recent development, in November 2020, Macyâs held a scaled back, COVID-conscious iteration of their Thanksgiving Day Parade. Instead of their usual two and a half mile route through Manhattan, the parade festivities all took place just outside Macyâs Herald Square location with a significantly reduced crowd and streaming to audiences quarantining at home.

Sources indicate that alongside pre-taped musical performances, the paradeâs balloons were pulled by specially outfitted vehicles instead of the customary team of handlers. Thankfully, by 2021, the parade was back to its normal standard of spectacle.Â.

#373. Industry News: A colossal oscillation

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4224 w)

Industry News: A colossal oscillation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4224 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As I write these words, surface water temperatures across a great swath of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have been rising for months.
  • Industry observers note that it’s still uncertain how the warming ocean will reshape global weather in the months to come, let alone how ecosystems – and human populations – will respond.
  • Global sea-surface temperature anomalies in November 2015, at the peak of the 2014-16 El Niño event, one of the strongest recorded by meteorological instruments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As I write these words, surface water temperatures across a great swath of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean have been rising for months. El Niño is the name for the recurring and sustained warming of this part of the Pacific. And temperatures are soaring to such highs, relative to their long-term averages, that the El Niño of 2026 may be the strongest in 1,000 years.

Industry observers note that it’s still uncertain how the warming ocean will reshape global weather in the months to come, let alone how ecosystems – and human populations – will respond. The future is always murky. Still, when it comes to El Niño, the past could teach us what to expect. And not just the recent past, but also the deep past recently recovered by scientists, historians and archaeologists.

Global sea-surface temperature anomalies in November 2015, at the peak of the 2014-16 El Niño event, one of the strongest recorded by meteorological instruments. Courtesy NOAA.

According to recent reports, I’m an environmental historian. I work with climatologists to understand how climates have changed in the past. I study how communities understood and adapted to the climate’s changes. And my research suggests that history can help us understand even the most extreme events in today’s rapidly warming climate.

Industry observers note that the past can help us see why El Niño is so hard to forecast, for example, or even define. It can show us that, while El Niño has contributed to the deaths of millions of people in the past, it has also enabled others to amass wealth and power.

El Niño indisputably scrambles worldwide weather patterns, but history teaches us that it’s as much a human creation as a natural reality. And this context may help us weather not only the effects of the 2026-27 El Niño in the months to come, but also El Niño’s future on a warming planet.

According to recent reports, A vast current of cold water snakes up the western coast of South America. In December each year, that current breaks down for about a month. An influx of warm water delivers tropical fish and – because warm water evaporates more readily than cold water – abundant rainfall.

According to recent reports, it’s impossible to know when people first noticed this annual reversal of water temperatures and precipitation. We do know that, sometime after the 16th-century Spanish conquest of the Inka Empire, fishermen named it El Niño, meaning literally ‘the boy’ or, when capitalised, ‘The Christ Child’. At least the reason for the name seems clear: the reversal of current happens around Christmas.

The colonised heartland of the Inka Empire, now known as Peru, won its independence in the 19th century. Towards the end of that century, Peru’s government joined many of its counterparts by establishing a society of geographers to describe the country’s environment and to catalogue its resources. In 1892, the society’s vice president, Camilo Carrillo, introduced the annual switch in water temperatures – and the term El Niño – to the scientific community.

When it entered scientific nomenclature, El Niño was therefore a cycle that was small in time (involving just one month every year), space (affecting only the Peruvian coast), and perceived importance (interesting only to a handful of local scientists).

El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific.

Only gradually did researchers detect a much bigger oscillation in Pacific Ocean temperatures, one that happened every two to seven years. This oscillation was eventually branded as El Niño. By the end of the 20th century, the effort to forecast its onset and worldwide impacts became a quintessential example of big, state-supported science.

The modern version of El Niño seems easy to define. It’s a dramatic warming of the central and eastern Pacific Ocean – a warming that’s confined to the tropics, lasts for many months, and tends to peak around the end of the year. It transfers a stupendous quantity of heat and moisture into the atmosphere, which the tropical jet stream redistributes, reshuffling weather patterns from one region to another.

According to recent reports, but what causes these recurring warmings of Pacific Ocean water? And how, exactly, do they affect regional weather patterns?

It has been revealed that only recently have scientists been able to answer those questions. It turns out that El Niño is actually the oceanic expression of a colossal seesaw of atmospheric pressure over the Pacific Ocean, known as the Southern Oscillation. When air is tightly packed together over the eastern Pacific – when atmospheric pressure there is high, in other words – and when it’s low over the western Pacific, the pressure difference reinforces persistent winds that blow west along the equator.

These trade winds, as they’re called, can push so much warm surface water into the tropics of the western Pacific that they allow deeper, colder water to reach the top of the eastern Pacific. This is called La Niña. But when the difference in Pacific Ocean pressure dips, the trade winds falter, and the warm water of the western Pacific surges east. This we call El Niño.

Recent findings suggest that scientists have learned that the Southern Oscillation involves reinforcing relationships, known as feedbacks, between the air and sea. Usually, hot water in the western Pacific evaporates in towering storms, releasing heat. The air flows east, cools down, grows denser, falls, then surges back to the west, warming up.

Industry observers note that this pattern, known as the Walker Circulation, strengthens the pressure differences of the Southern Oscillation and fuels the trade winds. But during an El Niño, warm water, evaporation and rains shift to the eastern Pacific, weakening transpacific differences in pressure and, in turn, the trade winds. This pattern helps explain the most crucial weather associated with El Niño: torrential rains across parts of the Western Hemisphere, and drought in Australasia.

Today, El Niño seems less like an event, and more like one end of a seesaw that perpetually teeters across the Pacific. But why does the seesaw behave as it does? There is still no scientific consensus, but the historical traces of both human societies and the natural world provide us with clues.

The most key questions about El Niño concern its impacts on global weather patterns – or in other words, the teleconnections that form between the warming of the equatorial Pacific and droughts, floods, storms or heatwaves around the world.

According to recent reports, these teleconnections are usually presented as predictable and consistent from one El Niño to the next. They’re visualised in maps that supposedly depict how regional temperatures or precipitation change as El Niño intensifies in the Pacific Ocean.

Typical rainfall patterns during El Niño events. Courtesy NOAA.

Industry observers note that but no two El Niño events have exactly the same teleconnections. One reason is that the extent, intensity and duration of unusually warm water in the tropical Pacific differs from one El Niño to the next. Another is that El Niño is only one of many influences on regional weather, and its effects generally weaken with distance from the tropical Pacific.

Because El Niño’s impacts on regional weather are never identical, it’s impossible to predict exactly how a future El Niño will impact most of the world’s people and ecosystems. But it’s even harder to piece together the history of El Niño before the beginning of the 20th century, when ships began to regularly measure sea-surface temperatures. And it’s harder still before the middle of the 19th century, when scientists began to systematically gather data from rain gauges where El Niño reliably generates heavy precipitation.

Decades of research now reveals broad patterns in El Niño history that could give a rough sense of what’s in store.

It’s a challenge, but not impossible. Climatologists – and a handful of historians and geographers – estimate the timing, strength and impacts of El Niño before the mid-19th century by consulting what they call the ‘archives of society’ and the ‘archives of nature’.

Sources indicate that the archives of society were created by the people of the past. They include surviving texts that describe weather directly, such as the logbooks that sailors wrote aboard ships. They also include diverse sources of evidence – not only documents but also artefacts, ruins, even oral traditions – that record human activities so dependent on the weather that they can serve as proxies for it.

It has been revealed that unlike the archives of society, the archives of nature were created by Earth itself (even if they are, of course, interpreted by people). These archives are parts of the natural world that responded either to changes in the water temperature of the Pacific Ocean, or to the regional extremes in temperature and precipitation that can be associated with those changes. The responses leave a mark in natural archives, changing the composition of growth rings in trees or corals, for example. Each mark serves as a proxy for El Niño conditions in the distant past.

Neither societal nor natural archives can provide direct measurements of sea-surface temperatures or weather, so histories of El Niño are inevitably full of uncertainty. Trees, for example, can only grow (or stop growing) so much. It’s one reason why their rings can’t precisely measure the strength of past El Niño events (and one reason why we can’t easily pin down whether this year’s El Niño really is the strongest in a millennium).

Still, decades of research can now reveal three broad patterns in El Niño history that could give us a rough sense of what’s in store – not only in the coming year, but in our future on a warming world.

Above all, El Niño shaped humanity’s past by suddenly changing where water was available, how much there was, and how people could use it.

The foundations of human life – food, shelter and movement – depend to varying degrees on water. Human populations can use water in many different ways, so they have learned to thrive in very different environments. But it seems to have been much harder for them to adapt to the sudden disruptions in water that a strong El Niño – or that a trend towards stronger El Niño conditions overall – could bring about.

This is the first pattern in El Niño’s human history.

We can already see its outlines a little more than 4,000 years ago, when the first states and empires established themselves. At that time, El Niño conditions seem to have grown more frequent, intense and long-lasting. The reason may have been a multimillennial cycle in the wobble of Earth’s rotation that altered the amount of sunlight associated with different seasons, weakening the trade winds.

It all sounds convincing until – inevitably – newly introduced evidence emerges.

Natural and societal archives suggest that some communities withered as El Niño intensified. In Peru, for example, populations appear to have deserted temple mounds, giant platforms that supported elaborate buildings and plazas. It’s easy to imagine that torrential floods sparked by strong El Niño conditions made it impossible to maintain these structures. But archaeological evidence hints at other changes that might have been partly responsible for population movements, including upcoming trade networks and newly cultivated plants. How much can the coincidence of two trends really tell us about causation?

According to recent reports, maybe quite a lot, if similar coincidences pop up elsewhere. And it seems they do. A little under 3,000 years ago, for example, settlers established a community at Teouma, on the island of Efate in today’s Vanuatu. Chemical traces of human waste and leaves in nearby swamp sediments show that the settlers cultivated taro, a root vegetable, during a period of increasing rainfall. By around 2,600 years ago, however, a trend towards stronger or more frequent El Niño conditions seems to have made local rainfall more erratic. The trend appears to correlate with a decline in settlement and cultivation on Efate.

You’ll notice a lot of conditional language about possible changes and potential correlations. Deep history is like that. Natural and societal archives can let us identify probable trends, figure out roughly when they happened, and craft convincing theories for how one trend caused another. It all sounds convincing until – inevitably – upcoming evidence emerges that compels us to re-date a trend, or propose another cause for it.

In general, evidence from the archives of nature and society is more abundant and precise the closer it dates to our present. Evidence from the previous millennium lets us identify not just trends in human and El Niño history, but discrete events.

Catastrophic famines partly linked to strong El Niño conditions appear to have killed millions.

By the 16th century, for example, cave formations, tree rings and reports written by government officials let us reconstruct the likely impacts of individual El Niño years on the Indian summer monsoon. They reveal a series of devastating droughts across India in the late 16th century, the middle and end of the 17th century, and the late 18th century.

It may be that a series of explosive volcanic eruptions were partly responsible for these droughts. The cooling effect of the sulphur they rolled out into the upper atmosphere altered temperature differences between latitudes, and between land and water. These differences in temperature help create the winds that bring monsoon rains; when they changed, the rains did too.

But the droughts also coincided with El Niño conditions. In fact, there may be a connection, because the upcoming wind patterns created by powerful eruptions seem to warm the eastern Pacific, relative to the west. Regardless, El Niño can also weaken the Indian monsoon by shifting warm water and rising air eastward across the tropical Pacific.

In a recent development, when the monsoon rains failed, harvests could too. Of course, rural populations and states had many ways of protecting themselves. Wells and granaries stored water and seeds, for instance, while trade networks could allow for emergency food imports. Still, these systems broke down when droughts lasted too long – and especially when states waged war.

In some El Niño events and in some parts of India, droughts provoked widespread famine only when armies demanded food from the already depleted countryside. In other Indian regions, the death toll soared when widespread malnutrition joined migration from drought-stricken regions to encourage the spread of epidemic disease. All told, catastrophic famines partly linked to strong El Niño conditions appear to have killed millions across 16th-, 17th- and 18th-century India.

It has been revealed that everywhere El Niño sparked extreme weather, communities suffered. Yet some prospered at their expense, and this is the second pattern we can discern in El Niño’s history.

Industry observers note that the collapse of China’s Ming dynasty in the 17th century seems to provide a striking example. Growth rings in trees and corals indicate that El Niño conditions repeatedly contributed to a weakening of the East Asian monsoon in the late 16th and early 17th centuries. At first, droughts afflicted both northeastern China – home of the loosely connected Jurchen peoples – and northern China, the Ming heartland.

Recent findings suggest that in the diverse environments of northeastern China, the Jurchen hunted, fished and farmed, a varied subsistence strategy that gave them some protection from drought. They also raided across the Great Wall into Ming territory, where they seized stockpiled grain. Eventually, droughts intensified in northern China, where soaring food prices and famine helped to destabilise the Ming regime. But drought seems to have yielded to above-average rainfall in Jurchen territories. Food provided by plentiful rain may have aided efforts to consolidate Jurchen communities into a united ‘Manchu’ state that was strong enough to exploit the Ming dynasty’s weakness, conquer China, and establish a newly introduced Qing dynasty.

Indeed, conquest and colonialism created a means by which the impacts of El Niño could be amplified for some communities, but alleviated or even exploited for others. This redistribution of vulnerability was never clearer or more catastrophic than in the late 19th century, when exceptionally strong El Niño conditions coincided with a global age of imperialism.

The exact connection between colonialism and crisis differed from place to place.

It has been revealed that in 1876, drought spread across India, then intensified with a strong El Niño in 1877-78. It was the heyday of the British Raj. Colonial officials had upended lives and livelihoods in many Indian farming communities by forcing them to plant cash crops such as tea or cotton. Now, there wasn’t enough food to go round. What grain could be harvested was either redirected from the poorest communities to areas where people could pay more, or exported out of India by colonial administrators who scorned market interventions.

Tens of millions died in the ensuing famines.

‘The Last of the Herd’ by Horace Harral from the October 1877 edition of The Graphic. Courtesy Wikimedia.

Similar tragedies played out wherever El Niño sparked drought in the late 19th century, though the exact connection between colonialism and crisis differed from place to place. In Eritrea and Ethiopia, for instance, Italian invaders arrived with cattle infected by rinderpest, a deadly disease that spread to local cattle before the arrival of another strong El Niño in 1890-91. Widespread mortality among cattle intensified food shortages, as did the arrival of immense locust swarms.

Perhaps a third of Ethiopia’s population perished.

The United States, however, often benefitted from El Niño conditions. As worldwide droughts drove up grain prices in 1877-78, US farmers exported enormous quantities of wheat to Europe. The resulting inflow of gold-backed credit strengthened US finances, and helped the government manage its Civil War debts. A century later, during another strong El Niño in 1972, the collapse of the Peruvian anchovy fishery, owing both to warming water and years of overfishing, deprived poultry producers of fishmeal. But that allowed US farmers to profit by planting soy, a substitute. In the even stronger 1982-83 event, torrential rains devastated California and other southern states, but overall, the US economy received a powerful stimulus from mild winter weather.

It was around this time – the late 20th century – that scientists and journalists created the modern concept of El Niño as a global event that recurred every few years to cause predictable disasters. This is the third pattern in our history. El Niño is not just an environmental reality; it’s also a cultural reality: a manufactured threat that is a unique product of our time.

According to recent reports, in some respects, that threat was a creation of the 1957-58 International Geophysical Year (IGY). During the IGY, a global campaign to observe Earth and near-Earth space served as an arena for scientific and technological competition between the US and Soviet governments. The IGY fortuitously coincided with an El Niño, and unprecedented observations helped scientists begin to understand the true dimensions of Pacific Ocean warming.

It turned out that different El Niño events strengthened in different ways.

Recent findings suggest that cold War politics continued to shape El Niño science. The 1959 Cuban Revolution joined the growing importance – for poultry farmers – of the Peruvian anchovy fishery to spur US support for collaborations between US and Latin American scientists. These collaborations, many of which focused on the study of El Niño, were supposed to demonstrate the value of partnership with US institutions.

When navies deployed nuclear submarines to reinforce newly developed nuclear arsenals, they began to fund oceanographic research partly to better understand the underwater battlespace. Until then, oceanographers had been able to visit marine environments only occasionally, in ships. Beginning in the 1950s, new funds and technology allowed them to deploy instruments to monitor environments continuously, for months or years at a time.

According to recent reports, the launch of Sputnik 1 during the IGY also heralded a new age in which weather satellites kept the oceans under constant supervision from above. And computer models soon seemed capable of forecasting not just global warming, but also the state of the Southern Oscillation. By the early 1980s, prominent scientists believed that El Niño could finally be predicted months in advance.

Yet the strong El Niño of 1982-83 came as a shock to the overwhelming majority of meteorologists and oceanographers. It turned out that different El Niño events strengthened in different ways, and each had distinct impacts on regional weather patterns. Because the unanticipated El Niño led to floods, droughts and storms that killed thousands of people, inflicted billions of dollars in damage, and cost the global economy trillions in estimated lost growth, scientists redoubled their efforts to forecast El Niño and its teleconnections.

The concept of El Niño as a global disaster had deep roots in the history of US mass media.

Industry observers note that in 1985, the World Meteorological Organization – a United Nations agency – introduced a decade-long project to scatter ocean-monitoring buoys across the tropical Pacific. Scientists also began to use both societal and natural archives to reconstruct the deep history of El Niño. In early 1997, they had learned enough to successfully predict another ocean warming months before it happened. Scientists from the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) alerted US journalists, and they created a media sensation: an El Niño reimagined as a looming, worldwide catastrophe.

It’s ironic that American journalists developed this threatening newly introduced view of El Niño. In the US, the economic benefits of the 1997-98 El Niño would again far outweigh the damage. But the concept of El Niño as a global disaster had deep roots in the history of US mass media.

Recent findings suggest that since the 19th century, US reporters had thrilled audiences by portraying natural phenomena as sensational, often threatening events – events that could be understood only by plucky scientists. A close but routine approach of a comet or planet to Earth, for example, became a brush with death recorded by swashbuckling scientists in far-flung observatories.

Sources indicate that it was journalism that resonated in a culture shaped by religious concepts of a purifying apocalypse. And it helps explain why, in the 20th century, the scientific investigation of changes in the atmosphere – not just global warming, but also nuclear winter, the ozone hole, acid rain, and even the potential consequences of asteroid impacts or volcanic eruptions – relied on US funding and institutions, while coming to particularly alarm US citizens.

Industry observers note that now, some US journalists used the Spanish name of El Niño to conjure an image of a foreign menace that several compared to migrants from South America. As the 1997-98 El Niño warmed into the strongest event since the 19th century, ‘Blame it on El Niño’ and ‘Don’t blame me, blame El Niño!’ were common slogans on everything from bumper stickers to T-shirts. That was true even though scientists couldn’t predict exactly how El Niño would affect weather in most parts of the world, let alone how populations would react.

It was in 1997 that today’s understanding of El Niño – part Cold War relic, part scientific achievement, and part media monster – was born.

Sources indicate that the patterns in El Niño’s past teach us that the warming of the tropical Pacific can be disastrous for communities exposed to droughts and floods. But they also reveal that El Niño disasters are caused less by the severity of weather extremes, and more by the brutality of how some communities are exploited by others. They suggest that today’s imagined El Niño – a global threat, with predictable impacts on weather – is less an accurate reflection of reality than a creation of modern science, media and geopolitics.

In a recent development, in the coming years and decades, it’s likely that El Niño’s impacts on populations will be shaped primarily by human relationships and ideas, not by nature. But human actions now include greenhouse gas pollution on such a scale that Earth has warmed by about 1.5°C, relative to its average temperature in the late 19th century. This pollution is supercharging the impacts of El Niño on weather. Heatwaves are growing hotter, and intensifying evaporation means droughts are getting worse. Partly because a warm atmosphere holds more water, downpours are ever more intense.

NOAA’s CFSv2 seasonal climate model demonstrates what sea-surface temperatures could look like in December 2026, based on 1984-2009 model climatology. Revised from Tropical Tidbits.

Recent findings suggest that global warming doesn’t seem capable of ending the Southern Oscillation, and with it the age-old seesaw of El Niño and La Niña. Still, it could lead to even more intense El Niño events that cause even more extreme weather.

It’s never been more urgent to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. But El Niño’s past also teaches us a deeper lesson about adapting to climatic extremes. Today, the world seems increasingly shaped by renewed great power competition: by militarism and colonial relationships between superpowers and their patrons. History suggests that such a world could be one in which millions die unnecessarily, not just through war but in preventable climate disasters.

It’s a warning from the past that today’s governments would be wise to heed, as El Niño reshapes environments from one end of the world to another in the months and years to come.

#372. The Mythological Monsters in ‘Percy Jackson’ Season 3, Explained

Sources indicate that from finding human figures in the stars to creating prehistoric cave art, we’ve been anthropomorphising our world for millennia. Now, machine-learning technologies can generate photorealistic images, synthetic voices that laugh and pause for breath, and chatbots that crush the Turing test. We’re seeing the first generation in history for whom the line between humans and their representations could all but vanish.

In this video essay for the digital publication Fully Human, the UK animator and filmmaker Lewis Heriz interrogates where this is taking us. We inevitably build our world through symbols, he says, but the hall-of-mirrors reality we’re rapidly creating may be leading us down a perilous path. However, he argues, we’re not without agency. Instead of submitting to a world where data and people are indistinguishable, we should be thinking critically and imaginatively about how we might use AI in ways that preserve our humanity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes, when we are going through difficult times, we can wonder what the point of a celebration is. Parties and feasts are all well and good when all our needs have been taken care of, but they seem too frivolous in times of hardship. But having something that raises spirits and gives hope is just as vital as enduring the struggles.

Thanksgiving dinner looked different in the 1930s because the Great Depression had practically decimated the economy. People could barely afford regular food, let alone a typical Thanksgiving meal. But they made the best of what they had and celebrated the holiday as a bright spot during dark days. Even without the staples we think of today, American families used creativity and resourcefulness to make their Thanksgiving special during the Great Depression.

A traditional turkey was too expensive for Depression-era families, so they improvised with whatever meat they had available. Ironically, some of the poorest families could get turkey if they went to soup kitchens or charities that provided Thanksgiving dinners. Most people, however, made old hen, mock duck, or porcupine meatballs as their Thanksgiving entrÃ©e.

Industry observers note that rather than actual porcupine meat, porcupine meatballs were made by sticking rice into the ground beef as a way of making it more filling. Mock duck was similarly created to spread the meal further. It was actually flank steak wrapped around stuffing and roasted. It was a pretty good imitation of a fancy dish, making it feel more like a Thanksgiving meal. An old chicken that could no longer lay eggs could also do in a pinch, but you had to cook it carefully so the meat wasn't too tough.

Speaking of stuffing, that was one dish that was cheap and easy to come by because all you needed was stale bread and some herbs. People in the 1930s would add more to their stuffing, like apples, raisins, or chestnuts they foraged. Dandelion salads were popular side dishes as well, since it was easy to gather the plants from your yard.

Canned vegetables were also a staple for a Depression-era Thanksgiving. The radio show Aunt Sammy's Homemaker's Half Hour often included recipes to liven up canned foods. Some of the most popular were creamed pearl onions and candied sweet potatoes. Mashed potatoes were also easy to make, as potatoes were inexpensive.

According to recent reports, thanksgiving wouldn't be Thanksgiving without dessert, but it got a little tricky when sugar and other baking ingredients were luxuries. Pumpkin pie was only made for dessert if you could get your hands on an actual pumpkin in the 1930s. The canned pumpkin purÃ©e was not easy to access, and if it was sold near you, it was probably out of your budget. People made do with other sweet treats, using canned foods once again.

Thanks to sweetened condensed milk, families could make a sugar cream pie for Thanksgiving dessert. Tomato soup was also a main ingredient for an easy dessert: tomato soup cake. It might sound gross to modern foodies, but it was surprisingly sweet and rich, and it used simple ingredients families were sure to have on hand. If all else failed, you could pop open a can of B & M Brown Bread, which was sweet and dense like a cake.

This flavorful bowl reminds me of Dig Inn's glory days—only I can enjoy it without elbowing my way through midtown lunchtime mobs. Roasted broccoli and shrimp sautéed with lemon and plenty of garlic are spooned on top of large couscous pearls. Chili flakes add an extra kick.

Sources indicate that you'll need to grab olive oil, butter, salt, and pepper from your own pantry; everything else is included in your delivery. In a recent development, true to the recipe card's promise, the meal cooks in less than half an hour. Prep your mise (chop the broccoli, garlic, and parsley; slice your lemon; rinse the shrimp), then get your broccoli in the oven and couscous on the stove. While they do their thing, you cook the shrimp so that everything finishes around the same time.

I found the instructions incredibly clear to follow, including when to add water and butter to your shrimp, and when to reduce the pan's heat. I don't often cook shrimp at home, and was pleasantly surprised how easy it was and how promptly they pinked up.

In a word: delish! Garlic can cover a multitude of sins, and there's a generous amount used when cooking both the couscous and shrimp, the latter also includes garlic powder, for good measure. Lemon and parsley give the dish a nice freshness; the flavors remind me of my favorite clam pie from a local Brooklyn pizzeria.

According to recent reports, this is a great dish for pescatarians, those looking to cut back on red meat, and health-conscious eaters. It has been revealed that finnish writer and artist Tove Jansson's Moomin tales are about as magical as you could wish for. For those who've yet to encounter these fairy tale wonders, the Moomins are a family of creatures who resemble upright white hippos. They dwell in Moominvalley and interact with many other wonderful characters, including the Snork Maiden, Snufkin, and Little My. Jansson wrote nine books in the series between 1945 and 1970, along with several picture books and a comic strip. All are well worth seeking out.

British writer C. S. Lewis penned this fabulous series of books between 1950 and 1956. Once you dive in, you'll be sure not to regret a single moment spent in the realm of Narnia and you will become enchanted by its many wonders.

John Masefield's evocative 1935 novel hits all the right notes. Here, a young Kay Harker, returning from boarding school, becomes embroiled in a tug-of-war over the possession of the titular magical object. When Harker is tasked with the box's safekeeping, he must battle against the sinister magician, Abner Brown, while discovering the artifact's many unusual powers along the way. This is one of those rare books that effortlessly conjures up a cozy yet adventure-filled world of ancient secrets and remarkable goings-on.

Many generations have been thrilled by Wilder's semi-autobiographical tales of her childhood in Wisconsin during the early 1870s. While later entries in the series don't shy away from difficult issues and tough times, this particular book is a perfect read for a cozy winter's day. It chronicles the Wilder family's preparations for the harsh weather to come, as food is harvested and fuel is gathered. The young Laura begins to learn her domestic duties, family comes to visit, and evenings are spent by the fire, wrapped up in music and love.

It didn't take long for Allsburg's highly imaginative and delightful 1985 picture book to establish itself as a modern classic. Allsburg both wrote and illustrated the work, which follows the fortunes of a young boy who inexplicably hears the sound of a train outside of his house one Christmas Eve. It's revealed to him that this is the famous Polar Express, on its way to the North Pole, and, of course the boy jumps on board. He finds himself in the company of many other children, dressed in pajamas. As the magical train rattles towards a meeting with Santa, the children sing songs and slurp hot chocolate, each hoping to be the first to receive a present from Father Christmas. There is a deep reverence for traditional fairy tales at the heart of this beautiful work, and adults will find themselves just as moved by it as their children.

Industry observers note that writer Susan Cooper turned to English folklore and history for this deeply evocative novel, the first in a series of five, which features an eleven-year-old boy named Will Stanton as he slowly discovers the world is far stranger and more magical than he had ever imagined. Stanton learns he is an Old One, part of an ancient group of protectors of the Light tasked with fighting back the ever-rising tide of the Dark. There follows an epic quest to find four magical talismans and secure victory. Cooper's writing brilliantly conjures the wonder and mystery of Christmastime and remains just as engrossing fifty years on from its 1973 debut.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Suzanne Collins never had to invent a word for the country at the center of The Hunger Games: she borrowed one. Panem is Latin for "bread," with Roman ties, and the same word used for "daily bread" in the Latin Lordâs Prayer.

On its own, it's a fitting name for a nation where kids go hungry, but Collins took the word out of a much nastier sentence.

Recent findings suggest that around the year 100 CE, the Roman poet Juvenal wrote his 10th satire, a long, sour poem about how badly people choose what to wish for, and partway through it he takes a swing at his fellow citizens. "Romeâs voters once handed out military commands and consulships," he complains, "but now theyâve stopped caring about any of it": in G.G. Ramsayâs 1918 translation, the public âlongs eagerly for just two things,â bread and games. In Latin, the two things are panem et circenses, and Mental Floss has counted the phrase among the Latin you should be using.

The translation comes in Mockingjay, the third novel, when Plutarch Heavensbee, the former Head Gamemaker, tells Katniss itâs âa saying from thousands of years ago, written in a language called Latin about a place called Rome.â As he puts it, âThe writer was saying that in return for full bellies and entertainment, his people had given up their political responsibilities and therefore their power.â.

Collins has mentioned the bread in her books cuts both ways. Asked in an interview for the seriesâ 10th anniversary why she made Peeta a baker, she said that when he throws a starving Katniss a loaf, âheâs keeping her alive long enough to work out a strategy for survival,â which made him âa life giver.â But, she added, âthereâs a dark side to bread, too. When Plutarch Heavensbee references it, heâs talking about Panem et Circenses, Bread and Circuses, where food and entertainment lull people into relinquishing their political power.â.

Recent findings suggest that panem isnât the only Roman name Collins borrowed. Plutarch is named for the biographer Plutarch, whose Lives Collinsâs father used to read to her: when Spartacus came on TV, heâd get out the âLife of Crassus,â since Spartacus, a slave, âdidnât rate his own book.â And in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, the District 2 boy Sejanus Plinth is named for Lucius Aelius Sejanus, who rose to enormous power under the emperor Tiberius and was executed for conspiring against him.

That last one ties back to Juvenal, who wrote his âbread and circusesâ line in the middle of a scene about the real Sejanusâs fall. In Ramsayâs translation, his statues come down, the head of âthe darling of the mobâ goes into the furnace and comes out as frying pans and slop pails, and âSejanus is being dragged along by a hook, as a show and joy to all!â The same crowd, Juvenal claims, would have hailed Sejanus as emperor if things had gone the other way, because it âfollows fortune, as it always does, and rails against the condemned.â A public execution staged as a show for a crowd that cheers whoeverâs winning is about as Panem as it gets, and it was sitting right next to the name the whole time.

Lake Charles, near the Gulf of Mexico, opens onto the Creole Nature Trail, sprawling wetlands, and a cultural scene shaped by diverse communities. About 75 miles east, Lafayette anchors Acadiana, where music, food, and tradition are not attractions but daily habits.

The Creole Nature Trail All-American Road, often called Louisiana’s Outback, threads through coastal wetlands, grasslands, and Gulf-front communities. Alligators sun along the waterways, and the area’s position on major migratory routes makes it a draw for birdwatchers.

According to recent reports, at Sabine National Wildlife Refuge, the Wetland Walkway carries visitors into the habitat, past freshwater impoundments, canals, ponds, bayous, and wooded ridges. Anglers come here too: its 26,000 acres of freshwater impoundment make it a top fishery, and bank fishing along Louisiana Highway 27 stays open year-round. Nearby, Cameron Prairie National Wildlife Refuge’s Pintail Wildlife Drive loops three miles through open grassland and wetlands, with alligators year-round and different bird species depending on the season.

Then the trail reaches the Gulf. Holly Beach, nicknamed the Cajun Riviera, and Rutherford Beach are rustic stretches of shoreline for beachcombing, fishing, and watching shorebirds, valued for what they lack: elaborate development. Before setting out, travelers can stop at Creole Nature Trail Adventure Point in Sulphur for free, hands-on exhibits and visitor information.

The Creole Nature Trail All-American Road, known as Louisiana’s Outback, is a 180-mile scenic byway through Southwest Louisiana. Photo: Charles Warren.

It has been revealed that bayou Glamping trades the hotel lobby for a riverside setting. Kayaks slide into the water, lines go out for fish, and modern comforts wait back at camp.

Grosse Savanne Lodge goes deeper into the wetlands, built around guided fishing and hunting. Anglers target redfish, flounder, and trophy bass, and landing a redfish, speckled trout, and flounder in a single day earns what locals call the Cajun Grand Slam. Fall is peak saltwater season, when flounder begin their run in Calcasieu Lake, and teal season sends hunters out in the dark to call in ducks at dawn.

That sporting tradition is the draw of Garden & Gun’s Cast & Blast, held in September at the lodge since 2018. The weekend pairs two guided fishing outings with two morning teal hunts, plus game dinners from head chef Matt Whitney rooted in Southwest Louisiana’s culinary traditions.

Just north of Lake Charles, Sam Houston Jones State Park spreads across about 1,100 acres of longleaf pine forest, cypress-tupelo swamp, hardwood stands, and tree-lined lagoons. Established in 1944, it is one of Louisiana’s oldest and most visited state parks, with hiking, birdwatching, and two boat debuts onto the west fork of the Calcasieu River. Ten cabins with screened porches let guests fall asleep to the sounds of the swamp.

Getting back to that took six years. Hurricane Laura knocked down roughly 80 percent of the park’s trees in August 2020, and the gates stayed shut until Memorial Day 2022.

Industry observers note that the park is now also the focus of a major restoration effort, confirmed in June 2026 by Louisiana State Parks, Woodside Energy, ecological restoration firm RES, and McNeese State University. Woodside is funding the project exclusively, committing $5 million over six years to restore more than 800 acres of forest habitat, the largest corporate donation ever received by a Louisiana state park. Lieutenant Governor Billy Nungesser said the aim is to keep the park a place for future families to enjoy.

In a recent development, RES, founded in Louisiana in 2007, will remove invasive species, plant about 245,000 native flora, and use prescribed burns to help longleaf pines regenerate. The goal is a more resilient forest, one that reduces wildfire risk and better withstands storms after hurricanes and years of invasive plant growth took their toll.

McNeese State University will lead biodiversity research, supporting four postgraduate students, and visitors can follow along through volunteer activities, educational outreach, and a project story map reachable by a QR code posted in the park. These landscapes, the project makes clear, are living ecosystems that need sustained care.

In a recent development, the Mardi Gras Museum of Imperial Calcasieu opened in 2026. Photo: Kathryn Shea Duncan.

Industry observers note that back in the city, the Mardi Gras Museum of Imperial Calcasieu is the place to start. Its 6,000-square-foot space opened in 2026 and showcases elaborate headdresses, gowns, king cake traditions, and the Courir de Mardi Gras, a rural celebration associated with the Cajun community. With more than 60 Mardi Gras krewes in Southwest Louisiana, some more than 70 years old, Carnival culture runs well beyond the weeks leading up to Fat Tuesday.

For families, Port Wonder on the waterfront houses the Children’s Museum of Southwest Louisiana and the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries’ Nature and Science Center. Exhibits explore the coastline, fisheries, barrier islands, and regional waterways, while aquariums hold native species from freshwater bayous to the Gulf.

Recent findings suggest that the city’s food tells its story in miniature. At Area 337, a family-owned restaurant, Cuban, Spanish, Venezuelan, and Dominican dishes share a menu, while Cousin’s Lebanese Cuisine gives Lebanese fare a Louisiana twist. After dark, Panorama Music House stages live performances in historic buildings that were extensively renovated after Hurricanes Laura and Delta in 2020.

According to recent reports, vermilionville. Photo: Hannah Thorn.

East of Lake Charles, Lafayette is Acadiana’s hub for food, music, and tradition, and Rouler Bike Tours puts it all at street level. Guides weave local history, art, music, and nature into two routes: the 3.5-hour Cajun, Creole & Beyond tour ($95) digs into the cultures that shaped the city, while the 2.5-hour Bike Like a Local ride ($60) gives a street-level look at the Hub City.

Acadian, Creole, and Native American cultures all have history in Lafayette. Photo: Hannah Thorn.

At Vermilionville Living History Museum and Folklife Park, the region’s past takes center stage. Set on 23 acres along Bayou Vermilion, the site interprets Acadian, Creole, and Native American cultures from 1765 to 1890. Costumed artisans, traditional crafts, cooking demonstrations, and music bring historic buildings to life.

In a recent development, lafayette’s food scene runs on the same spirit of reinvention. Scratch Farm Kitchen began as a pop-up and food truck at a farmers market, rooted in owner Jamie Harson’s family farm in Duson, and now serves breakfast and lunch from a daily menu posted beside the register. The Boudini, a biscuit stacked with boudin, cheese, egg, pesto, and kimchi, sums up Acadiana’s habit of making old traditions new.

East of Lafayette, the Atchafalaya Basin is where the region’s folklore feels most at home. Here live the rougarou, a werewolf-like figure in Louisiana French tradition, and the feu follet, mysterious lights tied to local legend. Airboats skim the basin’s waterways and swamps, gliding past cypress trees, wetlands, and wildlife.

The broader Atchafalaya National Heritage Area stretches across 14 parishes in south-central Louisiana and marks the 20th anniversary of its federal designation in 2026. Its landscape ranges from sugarcane and cotton fields to ancient live oaks and towering cypress, and its communities include people of Cajun, European, African, Caribbean, and Native American descent. Alligators, raccoons, bears, and more than 270 bird species inhabit the wider area.

Industry observers note that southwest Louisiana rewards travelers willing to look beyond its most familiar destinations. From the coastal wetlands near Lake Charles to Lafayette’s living traditions and the vast Atchafalaya Basin, the outdoors here is not separate from the culture. It is one of the places where that culture takes root.

Finding Stillness at The Vessyl in the Jungle of Costa Rica

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before I ever set foot in Costa Rica, Svetlana Parmar wanted to know what I hoped to carry home.
  • Recent findings suggest that on a pre-arrival Zoom call, The Vessyl’s Lead Facilitator and Program Specialist sent me a questionnaire: birth date, time, and location.
  • Industry observers note that the road from Guanacaste Airport in Liberia runs about two and a half to three hours, and somewhere past the pineapple fields, glossy in their rows, the jungle thickens until your phone begins to sound like a rumor from another country.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before I ever set foot in Costa Rica, Svetlana Parmar wanted to know what I hoped to carry home.

Recent findings suggest that on a pre-arrival Zoom call, The Vessyl’s Lead Facilitator and Program Specialist sent me a questionnaire: birth date, time, and location. The answers would feed an astrological reading and introduce the systems woven through my stay, Human Design and numerology among them. When I told her I was a Triple Cancer, she let out a sigh so emphatic I half expected the planets to shift. I had no tidy answer to her question, so I arrived open, letting the days decide. The days, it turned out, had a method. They kept sending me back to my body.

Industry observers note that the road from Guanacaste Airport in Liberia runs about two and a half to three hours, and somewhere past the pineapple fields, glossy in their rows, the jungle thickens until your phone begins to sound like a rumor from another country. I thought I knew this corner of Costa Rica. The previous August I’d based myself in La Fortuna, hiking the flanks of Arenal Volcano and sinking into thermal pools while steam curled into the evening air. Returning for The Vessyl showed me a country I hadn’t yet met.

My lodging was called a tent, a name that undersells it: a luxury cabin of wood and screen with a bird’s-eye view of Arenal, the volcano’s silhouette rising through the canopy. Other guests slept differently. One stayed in a lush treehouse. Another, because of medical conditions, stayed in a two-bedroom villa with a private pool, where a waterfall cascades from the roof of the outdoor space. Parrots and toucans crossed the sky, monkeys worked the branches, and frogs sang the night in and out. One afternoon torrential rain drummed the wooden walls and filled the air with the smell of wet earth. I stayed in and did absolutely nothing, and it felt entirely legitimate. Stillness, I learned, is only the doorway at The Vessyl.

It has been revealed that everything beyond that doorway begins with the founder, Josh Stanley, one of the brothers behind the CBD organization Charlotte’s Web, whom I interviewed in a studio booth attached to the Frequency Dome. Calm and charming, he carries an easy magnetism. He grew up poor in Oklahoma, in a devoutly Christian household where Sunday church was law. “My father was hyper-religious,” he told me. “I was dragged from church to church. I couldn’t miss a Sunday service. I was the first kid to run to the pulpit because this fear had been ingrained in me that I would burn in fire for all eternity. That’s no way for a kid to live.”.

His uncle Larry, a pipe carrier for the Lakota, handed him World Scripture: A Comparative Anthology of Sacred Texts when Stanley was 14. He devoured it and wandered toward Eastern mysticism and other traditions. “In 2015,” Stanley recalled, “I had an indescribable event that changed my life forever.” He offers few details, and he speaks only for himself. He also believes that “telepathy is the next form of communication for humans.” At dinner one night, a guest joked that if Stanley ever started a cult, she’d be first in line. Several people agreed, and we all understood why.

Industry observers note that all that curiosity gets a floor beneath it in the Dome. In the lobby, facilitators Ashley Marie and Dylan Baird introduced me to the Bio-Well scan. I rested my fingertips on a small camera that captures a faint glow from the skin, and software turned it into charts of stress, balance, and energy. My report came back in the optimal range, and I took the compliment. Bio-Well frames the glow as an energy field, an idea mainstream science does not recognize, and the report itself claims it is no medical instrument. Later in the Dome, the yoga floor hummed, so the practice traveled through my bones and settled in my chest. Within a few hours I had been read by a machine and played like an instrument.

Recent findings suggest that the next day, the earth took its own measurement. On October 9, 2026, a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck Panama’s Azuero Peninsula, and the boards of my tent trembled beneath me. I assumed construction workers were busy somewhere on the property. An hour later, in the dining and lobby area, everyone was talking about it. Remote places carry their own trepidation, the quiet arithmetic of how far help might be, and I felt mine rise. So I did what the week was teaching me to do. I stopped, noticed my body, and lifted my eyes to the horizon. Arenal stood there in all its majesty, a single cloud hovering over its peak like a halo. The volcano, no stranger to upheaval, offered respite and ease, and something in my chest unclenched.

Industry observers note that two days later, Josephine Clausen, a Costa Rican facilitator, sat with me for nearly two hours, moving between Spanish and English as the conversation asked. Her tool was Human Design, which she describes as a blend of astrology, the I Ching, Kabbalah, and the chakra system. I asked the skeptic’s question: does everyone born at the same moment and place share the same chart? They do, she stated. A chart is a map, and a map is flat; the territory of a life belongs to the person walking it.

According to recent reports, she had noticed me nodding and making small sounds as she talked, none of it routed through my head first. Those sounds, she mentioned, were my gut speaking, a voice that answers yes or no and never explains itself. She sketched my profile as a volcano hike with three trails to the summit. A person like me tries all three and returns with a report: one muddy, one long and full of obstacles, one steep with the best views. Her homework was simple. Ask yourself a yes-or-no question and notice the first response in your body. If a “because” arrives, that is the mind talking.

In a recent development, svetlana’s question circled back. Josephine’s words touched what I already knew about myself: I’m deeply inquisitive, and I take myself a little too seriously. I skipped an evening program to let that settle. Human Design is an esoteric system, and if you prefer evidence, treat the sessions as prompts for reflection.

If Josephine taught me to listen to my gut, the horses showed me how loudly my body already spoke. Horse master Enrique Molina led our group and four horses into a sandy ring and matched each of us by temperament. Mine leaned its full weight against my side, and the exercise asked what I would do and what my body was saying without me. Horses respond to what we project, Molina noted, whether hesitation, confidence, or fear. Something that Stanley said at the studio came rushing back to me. “It’s up to us how much we want to struggle. Our greatest struggle is not to struggle.”.

Sources indicate that my horse’s name was Negro. In Spanish, the word is simply a color. I am a Black man, standing in a sandy ring in Costa Rica with a horse named Negro leaning into my ribs. I asked whether the pairing was deliberate. Molina noted the horses choose their riders. I’m still turning that answer over. The next day, came the sight I’ll keep longest: horses swimming in a river, powerful bodies yielding to the current, the line between human and wild suddenly thin.

Sources indicate that even the kitchen made its case for listening to the body. I’ve followed a plant-based diet for 13 years and survived many sad side plates, and here the chefs built vegan dishes from the ground up. A smoked beet salad arrived bright and light, aromatic with herbs and avocado puree, delicate in a way I had never tasted. The seared Portobello was earthy and balanced with a subtle sweetness. Coconut sorbet closed the meal, and long communal tables let strangers trade the day’s stories.

It has been revealed that svetlana asked what I hoped to carry home. After days of listening, I can answer. I wanted hope, a fullness that rises from within, and the fire to finish a novel I began long ago. That fire is what I carried out of the jungle, steady as a pulse. I found myself wishing I’d stayed longer. That may be the most honest review I can offer.

In a recent development, where: The Vessyl sits in Altos de Monterey, near La Fortuna in Costa Rica’s Arenal Volcano region. It opened in 2026 across 118 acres of rainforest, with 13 adults-only accommodations — tents, villas, suites, and a tree house — built around the sound installation the property calls the Frequency Dome.

Getting there: The drive from Guanacaste Airport in Liberia takes about two and a half to three hours. We rode with Relaxury RLX Costa Rica.

Rates: From $350 per person, per night, with a three-night minimum.

What’s included: Stays include all meals.

Breaking: 5 Name Traditions in the 'Hunger Games' Franchise, Explained

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mentalfloss

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With the newest cinematic addition to The Hunger Games franchise releasing on November 20, the franchise's fans are more active than they have been in years.
  • In a recent development, one element of the world of Panem that has garnered discussion in recent years is the naming traditions Suzanne Collins uses for her characters.
  • Here are the five naming traditions at the heart of The Hunger Games, and what they say about the characters and the world they live in.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the newest cinematic addition to The Hunger Games franchise releasing on November 20, the franchise's fans are more active than they have been in years. The original trilogy of books (and quartet of movies) undoubtedly made a splash in the 2010s, but the series has received greater attention with the release of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes (novel released in 2020; film in 2023) and Sunrise on the Reaping (novel released in 2025, with the film arriving this November). What was once seen as just another entry in the YA book-to-movie pipeline is now being discussed as one of the most successful entries into the dystopian genre this century.

In a recent development, one element of the world of Panem that has garnered discussion in recent years is the naming traditions Suzanne Collins uses for her characters. While characters with names like Glimmer, Wiress, and even Woof may seem ridiculous on first glance, they actually tell us a lot more about the districts and the Capitol than audiences might realize. Character names tell us what each region knows and values, which are important factors in their role in the rebellion.

Here are the five naming traditions at the heart of The Hunger Games, and what they say about the characters and the world they live in.

In a recent development, anyone with a passing interest in classical history or literature can see the many ways that Greek and Roman names dominate the Capitol. The characters who are most strongly associated with the Capitol mindset are often marked by names associated with Roman history. Prominent figures in the Games have names like Caesar, Seneca, and Pliny, and the most significant Capitol-born characters bear names like Coriolanus (popularized by William Shakespeare in his take on the life of Gnaeus Marcius Coriolanus) and Plutarch (famous for his biographies of Roman leaders).

In contrast, more sympathetic Capitol citizens often have Greek names, perhaps as a nod to the way that Greek culture was absorbed by the Romans. Particularly during the early years of Capitol dominance, we see names drawn directly from Greek mythology and theatre, such as Persephone, Iphigenia, and Lysistrata. Interestingly, Effie Trinket likely gets her name from the Greek Euphemia (meaning well-spoken), but her sister Proserpina has a Roman name (which emerged as a Latinization of Persephone). While neither character actively rebels against the Capitol and its ideologies, Effie sees the Tributes as people more than her sister does, justifying their contrasting names.

It's worth noting that there are also characters with Greco-Roman names that were not born in the Capitol. However, nearly all of these characters come from districts that have close relationships with the Capitol. This is most common in District 2, where there are multiple characters with Roman names like Brutus and Cato. In-universe, their parents likely gave their children Capitol-like names in hopes that it would help them gain Capitol approval. This certainly seems to fit Sejanus Plinth, whose wealthy father hoped to transform him into a Capitol citizen to improve his prospects.

Industry observers note that while some of these names seem to exist only to contrast the more down-to-Earth names of those from the districts, main characters with classical names often find themselves facing fates similar to their namesakes. For example, the historical Lucius Aelius Sejanus was born into the equestrian order but was able to gain power and a close relationship with the emperor through his father Strabo's connections. He was the emperor's closest confidant and advisor for a time, but he eventually pushed too far and was executed for treason. Sejanus Plinth, while far less conniving than his historical namesake, followed a strikingly similar path.

It has been revealed that in stark contrast to the Capitol residents, whose names seem to symbolize their dominance and abundance, many District citizens have names that are much more simplistic, based on their occupations and industries. While this frequently shows up in real-world surnames like Baker, Taylor, and Miller, The Hunger Games drives the point home by using vocational words as first names.

Sources indicate that we see this most in districts that don't receive much attention in the books, including Districts 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, and 10. But while their names define them in the same way that the Capitol doesâby what they produceâthey also offer a nod to how the characters might survive the Hunger Games. As Suzanne Collins explained, "Finnick's trident and Johanna's ax skills develop as part of their districts' industries"âso their exploitation can be used to keep them alive.

Some of those names and their possible meanings are included below:.

These names are likely derived from units of measurement: BTU and Ampere.

Short for "circuit" or "circuitry".

Short for "diode," a device used for conducting electricity.

Short for "hydro" and "solar," two methods of generating electricity.

A negatively charged ion used to conduct electricity.

Likely derived from "potential," as voltage is determined by potential energy.

A measurement of distance still used in Panem.

A variant of "auto," short for "automobile".

A play on "tread," the pattern on tires.

May be connected to the Latin for ship sails or the French for bicycle.

A type of dead wood in the center of a tree that is resistant to decay.

A form of injury or disease that often kills plant life.

A spool used when producing thread and feeding it into a sewing machine.

Small objects used when making clothing, such as buttons, pins, and thread.

"Weft" and "Woof" are two words for the horizontal threads used when weaving fabric.

Associated with branding animals to mark their owners.

The male version of many animals, including deer and rabbits.

A person who makes leather out of animal hides.

While most of these examples feel overtly rural, the pattern continues with a twist in District 1. Their industry is luxury products, and many of their children are either named after types of fabric (Cashmere, Silka, Velvereen) or characteristics of gemstones (Carat, Facet). While these names feel more absurd and superficial, they are still associated with the district's industry, highlighting that District 1 children are as much products built for the Capitol as their actual exports.

It has been revealed that while a few of the names from District 11 are vocational, like Thresh and Seeder, several seem to be more focused on elements of nature that don't impact their industry. The most significant of these is Rue, a plant that is technically edible but is so bitter it's rare to see cultivated as food. Instead of being named after something that they grow for the Capitol, Rue was named after a common flower that her parents likely saw growing in the wild.

Industry observers note that of course, Rue is not the only prominent flower name in Panem. Primrose Everdeen is the name that sparks the rebellion, and her name comes from a plant known for its beauty and its medicinal properties. Â This firmly ties her to her mother, a known beauty and a healer, but it also grounds her in the meadow that her father took Katniss to. Other characters with names like Blossom, Hull, and Chaff highlight parts of nature that would have been considered useless to those in the Capitol, but which were significant to the people in the Districts.

It has been revealed that district 4 also follows this trend, naming their children after parts of their daily life that, while connected to their district industry, seem more personally significant. For example, one of the tributes in the 10th Hunger Games was named Coral, after an inedible aquatic lifeform. The name Mags is likely a variant of Margaret, which means "pearl." Yet again, these names highlight the world that the characters live in, but they seem to focus on the beauty in their world, rather than its consumability.

It has been revealed that the line between names associated with nature and names associated with food can be hazy, but it's worth mentioning due to how it manifests in the story. Like her sister, Katniss is named after a plant, but Suzanne Collins has highlighted the additional meanings that her name carries. In addition to the white flowers that grow from the katniss plant, Collins pointed out "the edible tuber roots she could gather, [and] the arrowhead-shaped leaves" that tie into her skill as an archer. While the celebration of nature is a rebellion against the Capitol's authoritarian ideologies, names based on food are an active reclamation of power.

As Collins explained in the same interview, food is one of the most significant symbols in the franchise, as the Capitol can manipulate people both within the arena and in their day-to-day lives based on their access to food. This is why Peeta's name, which can be read as a reference to pita bread, refers to more than just his family's profession as bakers. In Collins's words, he is "a life giver," providing Katniss with both the literal bread she needed to survive in her youth and the strength and support she needed to keep going during the rebellion.

It has been revealed that on a metatextual level, characters named after nature are frequently positioned as needing protection, while the ones named after food seem more capable of taking care of themselves. In addition to the contrast between Katniss and Primrose, we can see this trend in the fates of minor characters. While dill is technically edible, it is primarily used for flavoring, not sustenance. Likewise, the character Dill was unable to support herself in the arena. On the other hand, chicory, a plant with multiple culinary purposes, is the namesake for a character who was able to survive multiple devastating events.

Although there are obviously many naming traditions used throughout Panem, the only ones explicitly stated belong to the Covey, a community of nomads that was forced into District 12 after the Dark Days. As Maude Ivory explains in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, "We each get our first name from a ballad and our second from a color." The ballads in question typically come from famous poems, while the colors are based on meaningful parts of their lives, like the ivory of piano keys or the gray of a winter sky.

Like many of the Capitol and Capitol-adjacent names, the Covey's names seem to be somewhat prophetic. This is most noticeable with Lucy Gray and Lenore Dove, whose ultimate fates mirror their poetic namesakes. However, fans have also speculated about what happened to Maude Ivory and Barb Azure between the prequel books based on what happened in their name poems.

It has been revealed that this naming tradition helps to maintain the Covey's culture, even when they cannot practice it freely. It highlights the poetry, music, and art that they value most, and it allows them to stand out from the other residents of District 12. Unfortunately, the surviving members of the Covey gave up their naming system by the time of the main series, perhaps as a way of escaping persecution. Fans have theorized about whether characters from the trilogy might have had subtle Covey names, but it seems more likely that they actively abandoned the practice, mirroring the many historical cultures that have been forced to assimilate for their own safety.

It has been revealed that while a name in the real world rarely determines a person's fate, it often holds more weight in literature, where the author has to select each name deliberately. In The Hunger Games franchise, names function as symbols of the social hierarchy. The Capitol names their children after classical history, while the districts name their children after the labor that defines their lives. But as in the real world, every system has its cracks. Characters named after nature, food, and art defy the idea that district children exist as laborers and sacrifices, proving that rebellious sentiments were alive and well long before Katniss became the Mockingjay.

The Thanksgiving Accident That Created TV Dinners

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

American history can be split into two definitive eras: before and after TV dinners.

Sources indicate that all gobbles and giggles aside, Thanksgiving 1953 was pivotal to the rise of pre-made meals. All it took was 260 tons of turkey and one salesman with an idea to change the way Americans ate dinner forever.Â.

In the last week of November 1953, Swanson had an equation to solve: roughly 160 million Americans plus 260 tons of excess turkey presented the need for a solution, and fast, lest precious meat go to waste.

So the company turned to salesman Gerry Thomas, who couldnât have predicted that his brilliance would still be stocking supermarket freezer shelves in 2026.

Industry observers note that according to Smithsonian Magazine, Thomas had 5,000 aluminum trays and a dream. After setting up an assembly line and a few sides to go with the turkey (sweet potatoes, peas, cornbread, and dressing with gravy, of course), Swanson had officially created the first TV dinners. Better yet, the refrigerated railroad cars full of turkeys didnât have to be discarded as holiday scraps.

By 1954, ten million of these new-age meals had sold for just 98 cents a pop to Americans eager to stuff their faces in front of a screen; a revolutionary concept.Â.

Sources indicate that what started as a solution to excess turkey swiftly upended the traditional dinner table as we know it, rendering it no legs to stand on. Â.

Before TV dinners, meals were enjoyed at the dining-room table; food was prepared, conversation was shared, and dishes were passed from person to person. All of that changed in 1953.

Sure, many households still insisted on eating at the table to instil proper manners, but others took full advantage of the convenience of these flashy TV dinners, initially marketed as a fancy grocery item.

Sources indicate that gone were the days of women preparing food hours in advance, meticulously spreading it out on the table, and then facing the inevitable task of washing and drying all the plates and utensils afterward. The no-muss, no-fuss trays could be popped in the oven, heated in under half an hour, and savored while watching your favorite program (in color, if you had an RCA or Westinghouse TV). And when you were done eating, all you had to do was toss the tray in the trash!Â.

Because TV dinners were so popular, special tray tables eventually hit the market, and when microwaves (and microwavable trays, thanks to Campbell's) became widespread, there was no going back. Over time, Americans were spoiled with both single-serving and family-sized options: Banquet's Salisbury steak, Stouffer's pasta, and, in 2024, Blue Zones Kitchen's more health-conscious alternatives. There was even a version marketed to children: Kid Cuisine, with its chicken tenders, macaroni and cheese, and brownie: a meal '90s kids all but begged for in the frozen-food aisle.

Whether a time-saver, the beginning of the end of dinner table conversations, or maybe both, TV dinners are infinitely baked into American culture; just donât forget to take off the plastic wrap.Â.
