According to recent reports, prison takes almost everything away from a writer except time, and over the centuries, a surprising number of them have used it. Mental Floss has already looked at the letters Nelson Mandela wrote from prison. Here are 10 more books that started behind bars, written by everyone from a Roman official waiting to be executed to a Kenyan novelist writing on toilet paper.

Industry observers note that boethius had about as successful a career as a man could have in sixth-century Italy, rising to become the Ostrogothic king Theodericâs âMaster of Offices,â one of the most senior officials at court. Then he fell out with his colleagues, was accused of treason and of practicing magic, and was imprisoned and, probably in 524, executed. In between, he wrote a dialogue between himself, âsitting in his prison-cell awaiting execution,â and a woman who personifies Philosophy. Chaucer translated it into Middle English, and its 1897 translator, H.R. James, called it the medieval âscholarâs familiar companion.â.

Sources indicate that during the war between Venice and Genoa, Marco Polo ended up in a Genoese jail, where he began dictating the stories of his travels. This book owns up to its origins in its prologue, which says that Polo, âbeing thereafter an inmate of the Prison at Genoa, he caused Messer Rusticiano of Pisa, who was in the said Prison likewise, to reduce the whole to writing; and this befell in the year 1298.â The strangest part is the language: Henry Yule, who translated and edited the book in the 19th century, concluded that a Tuscan took it down from the dictation of a Venetian âin French, a language foreign to both.â.

This 15th-century retelling of the King Arthur legend ends with a request: its author, who calls himself Sir Thomas Maleore, asks readers to âpray for me while I am alive, that God send me good deliverance,â and indicates he finished the book between March 1469 and March 1470. The only knight of the time with a name like that, Thomas Malory of Newbold Revell, was jailed on and off in the 1450s, and a Thomas Malorie who may have been the same man was left out of four of Edward IVâs general pardons in 1468 and 1470. No record puts him in a cell when he wrote that last line, but Britannica reads it as a prayer for deliverance from prison.

Miguel de Cervantes was collecting taxes for the king of Spain when he handed the money to a merchant who, in translator John Ormsbyâs words, âfailed and absconded.â The shortfall landed Cervantes in jail in Seville in September 1597, and he spent two stints there. His prologue to Don Quixote calls the novel âjust what might be begotten in a prison, where every misery is lodged and every doleful sound makes its dwelling.â Ormsby noted that those words are âgenerally held to be conclusiveâ evidence that Cervantes came up with the book, and wrote at least the start of it, behind bars.

Sources indicate that sir Walter Raleigh had already done time in the Tower of London over a secret marriage when he was convicted in 1603 of plotting against King James I. He got a last-minute reprieve from the death sentence and went back to the Tower, where he undertook The History of the World. Published in 1614, it runs from the Creation to the 2nd century BCE and carries warnings, meant for James, that âthe injustice of kings is always punished.â James got the last word: in 1618, he invoked the old sentence, and Raleigh was executed.

Sources indicate that john Bunyan was arrested in 1660 for holding a religious service outside the Church of England, and he refused to promise he wouldnât do it again, which kept him in the county jail for 12 years. The Pilgrimâs Progress, once second only to the Bible in popularity, was largely written while he was imprisoned, and it opens with a clue: âI lighted on a certain place where was a Den, and I laid me down in that place to sleep.â In a 1679 edition, Bunyan identified the den himself as âthe gaol,â and historians have argued ever since about which one he meant.

Oscar Wilde served most of his two years of hard labor at Reading Gaol. Prisoners couldnât write plays, novels, or essays, but they could write letters, and as the novelist Colm TÃ³ibÃ­n told the BBC, âthe regulations did not specify how long a letter should be.â Wildeâs, to Lord Alfred Douglas, ran to tens of thousands of words, and Mental Floss has already covered how that relationship went. His friend Robert Ross published about two-thirds of it in 1905 as De Profundis, and the full, correct text didnât appear until 1962.

Antonio Gramsci was head of the Italian Communist Party and a member of the Chamber of Deputies when Mussoliniâs Fascists outlawed the party and he was arrested in 1926. At his trial, the prosecutor argued, âWe must stop his brain from working for 20 years.â It didnât take: despite rigorous censorship, he filled his prison notebooks with a wide-ranging study of Italian society, including his ideas about cultural hegemony. He died in 1937, not long after being released for medical care, and the complete Quaderni del carcere werenât published until 1975.

Jean Genet was a thief long before he was a novelist, and he started writing in 1942 while serving time for theft at Fresnes prison. The result, Notre-Dame des Fleurs (1943), a portrait of the Montmartre underworld, got the attention of Jean Cocteau and, later, Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir. His literary friends came in handy: in 1948, he was convicted of theft for the 10th time and faced an automatic life sentence on the next conviction, so a delegation of writers appealed to the president of France, and Genet was âpardoned in advance.â.

It has been revealed that in 1977, NgÅ©gÄ© wa Thiongâo co-wrote a play in Kikuyu, Ngaahika Ndeenda (I Will Marry When I Want), and its performance got him detained for a year without trial. Inside Kenyaâs Kamiti Maximum Security Prison, he wrote a novel in secret on toilet paper, which came out in 1980 as Caitaani Mutharaba-ini, or Devil on the Cross. As he later put it, âThe writing of the novel has been one way of keeping my mind and heart together.â.

Two New England states top the list for the percentage of their populations over 65.

Maine came in first place with 23.5% of the population over 65, followed by second-place Vermont with 22.9% over that age. For Maine, that equates to around 330,000 residents, while Vermont has 148,000 Vermonters above that age. Nearby Newly introduced Hampshire ranks seventh with 21.5% of its population over that age.

Recent findings suggest that florida is well known as a place for retirees who want to move somewhere warmer when they get older, and that's reflected in the population. The state ranks fourth by percentage, with 21.8% of its population checking in as 65 or older. That equates to 5.1 million Floridians over 65. The only state with a higher population over 65 is California, with 6.5 million senior residents. However, that's only 16.5% of its total population, ranking it 45th overall.

In a recent development, the District of Columbia came in second place with only 12.9% of its population over the age of 65. Because of its small population, that only equates to 91,000 residents, which is the smallest number of 65- and older residents in the U.S. by count.

In a recent development, more gods from the Greek pantheon are making an appearance in Percy Jackson and the Olympians season 3. Chief among them is Artemis. Sources indicate that in Greek mythology, Artemis holds dominion over the wilderness and wild animals. She is associated with the moon and considered to be both a harmonious and opposing force to her twin brother, Apollo, the god of prophecy and music who is associated with the sun.

Recent findings suggest that most know Artemis by her hunting bow and quiver of arrows, though sheâs sometimes draped in a deerskin cape complete with a hood or crowned with a diadem. Famously, she is a virgin goddess whose followers pledge chastity and are held to living pure lives under penalty of severe punishment.

But what might you not know about her? Letâs get into some of the long-held and most disputed beliefs behind the goddessâ origins, meaning, and actions, according to ancient Greek stories that have stood the test of time.

The Titaness Leto is the mother of Artemis and Apollo. Her affair with Zeus, which produced a pregnancy, angered the goddess Heraâthe Queen of the Gods and Zeusâ wifeâso violently that she forbade Leto from giving birth on land or in water. To ensure Leto adhered to her order, the giant serpent Python was commanded to pursue Leto throughout her pregnancy. She was given no leave to rest as nowhere was safe.

It has been revealed that fortunately for Leto, she came upon Delos. The floating island allowed her to stay within the bounds of Heraâs words. First, she gave birth to Artemis. Then, according to some versions of the myth, her daughter served as her midwife and delivered her twin into the world. That is why Artemis is a goddess of childbirth along with her many other duties.

Recent findings suggest that artemis is primarily thought of as a huntress. Her youth, athleticism, and vigor are typically visible in depictions of her, and she is also often portrayed alongside animals, her trusty silver-and-gold bow and quiver of arrows in hand. But, like Apollo, she also loves music, and that includes dancing to it with the nymphs in her retinue.

Her worshippers often honor her through choral dance, a style of rhythmic movement that is coordinated and done in unison. It includes singing and vocalization, and participants often run and mimic animals in devotion to the goddess.

In antiquity, Artemis was portrayed as a maiden because she is considered to be the protector of girls up until they marry. While her charge is their safety, that does not mean she always keeps girls from harm.Â.

It has been revealed that as is true of the rest of the Grecian gods, Artemis can be fickle. She can act in favor of one mortal, healing their wounds and ending their suffering, while bringing ruin through sudden death or disease to another.

Recent findings suggest that though the prevailing belief is that Artemis has never fallen in love, she had a close companion in Orion. The giant huntsman skilled with weaponry had earned her respect so deeply that Apollo grew jealous, and tricked his sister into shooting her friend. Grief-stricken, she laid Orion to rest among the stars.

Some stories suggest Apollo betrayed Artemis to protect her vow of chastity as she was in love with Orion. Others claim that she purposefully shot the giant because heâd attempted to assault her or one of her attendants, and in these stories, there is no mention of her making him a constellation.

Blessed with the power to transform herself and anyone she chooses into an animal, Artemis has also been noted to use her abilities to punish those who incur her wrath.Â.

According to recent reports, when her handmaiden Callisto was seduced by Zeus after he took the goddessâs form, Artemis turned her into a bear after learning of Callistoâs pregnancy. She then banished her to the wild.

Sources indicate that the hunter Actaeon suffered a worse fate. Artemis transformed him into a stag after she caught him watching her bathe in a spring with her nymphs. She set his hounds on him, and they tore Actaeon apart.

There was also Niobe, queen of Thebes, whose children and husband bore the consequences of her boastfulness. She had compared her 14 children to Letoâs twins, and the slight drew Artemis and Apolloâs ire. They killed all seven of her sons and her seven daughters as well. The pain of the loss resulted in Niobeâs husband also dying, though itâs disputed whether he killed himself or was slain to ensure he didnât try to avenge their children.

Niobe was turned to stone, either in pity by the gods or because her devastation was so great that it literally petrified her. However, the transformation didnât stop her tears, which continued to fall from her eyes.

#349. When Your Winter Trip Has No Snow, Find Your Inner Daredevil Instead.

When Your Winter Trip Has No Snow, Find Your Inner Daredevil Instead.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1641 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I’ve never understood the appeal of roller coasters or similar thrill rides.
  • Industry observers note that so imagine my surprise — or horror, or maybe a bit of both — when I found myself willingly, eagerly even, climbing into an Olympic bobsled, knowing I’d soon be barreling down an icy track at nearly 80 miles per hour, experiencing up to five times the force of gravity.
  • Sources indicate that it happened on a ski trip that barely involved skiing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’ve never understood the appeal of roller coasters or similar thrill rides. The stomach-dropping plunges and screaming passengers who stumble off, then immediately get back in the perpetually long line? No, thank you. I’ve tried enough of them throughout my life to know they’re just not my thing.

Industry observers note that so imagine my surprise — or horror, or maybe a bit of both — when I found myself willingly, eagerly even, climbing into an Olympic bobsled, knowing I’d soon be barreling down an icy track at nearly 80 miles per hour, experiencing up to five times the force of gravity. Even more surprising? It turned out to be one of my favorite travel experiences to date.

Sources indicate that it happened on a ski trip that barely involved skiing. An unusually warm, dry winter had left the mountains in rough shape, and I’d gone hoping to improve my mediocre technique. Instead, I came home with a upcoming appreciation for the kind of thrill I’d spent most of my life avoiding.

At the base of the Utah Olympic Park in Park City. Photo: Taryn Shorr-Mckee.

I visited Park City, Utah, with a group of friends for four days in early February 2026, in what’s typically prime ski season. I’d been looking forward to two full days on skis, maybe even squeezing in a bonus run on our last morning. Instead, we arrived to temperatures warm enough for short sleeves and no snow on the ground around town or at the resort bases. We knew it was bad, as the dismal ski conditions throughout the western US had made headlines for months. But seeing it in person was jarring.

Up on the mountain, crews worked hard to make snow, but Mother Nature wouldn’t cooperate. By mid-morning of our first full day, conditions had deteriorated into a treacherous combination of slush and ice with exposed rocks and roots. Most of our group, myself included, managed a couple of laps or a lesson, but it didn’t take long before we threw in the towel. The two more advanced skiers stuck it out a little longer, but nobody was having the ski trip we’d envisioned.

It has been revealed that on our second day, I managed a single run before deciding I’d had enough. But rather than spend another morning struggling and cursing the conditions, I headed to Utah Olympic Park for a guided tour. It was, after all, gorgeous weather for being outside – just not for skiing.

Built for the 2002 Winter Olympics, the park is home to ski jumps, a tubing trail, and a museum showcasing Olympic history. I was enjoying the tour, but didn’t expect to discover anything really out of the ordinary. Then our guide casually mentioned that visitors could ride in an actual Olympic bobsled on select evenings. She glanced at her watch. “Oh,” she remarked. “Tonight.”.

Looking down the bobsled track. Photo: Taryn Shorr-Mckee.

That was all it took. I didn’t stop to wonder why someone who sits out roller coasters was jumping at the chance to ride an Olympic bobsled. People who aren’t professional athletes can ride bobsleds at only a handful of tracks worldwide, just two of which are in North America. I was very literally in the right place at the right time. (The other place is Whistler, British Columbia.).

In a recent development, I didn’t know what it cost or whether anyone else would join me – just that I was going. As soon as the tour ended, I raced to meet the rest of our group for lunch. I shared the news, and a couple of other women were immediately on board. Within minutes, we’d reserved our spots for that evening.

The writer and her fellow bobsledders getting ready to roll. Photo: Taryn Shorr-Mckee.

Only after committing did I start researching what, exactly, bobsledding entails.

I’m a ’90s kid, and Cool Runnings was practically required viewing, so I was loosely familiar with bobsleds. But I’d never even imagined I’d be anywhere near one, much less inside one, so I’d never had a reason to look too deeply into it.

What I didn’t realize was how similar the experience is to a roller coaster. The sled reaches about 80 miles per hour as it navigates a track with 15 curves, taking on forces of up to five Gs — all in less than a minute. My spontaneous decision suddenly seemed a lot more consequential.

According to recent reports, I don’t fear roller coasters: I just genuinely don’t enjoy them. Every couple of years, I try a new one, waiting for that magical “aha” moment to see what makes people think they’re so fun. It’s never come. What does come is that distinctive queasiness that others seem to relish. That part gave me pause, but only for a moment. But nothing was going to stand in the way of my newfound dream of becoming the world’s newest bobsled rider.

Recent findings suggest that the view from the top of the Utah Olympic Park. Photo: Taryn Shorr-Mckee.

Industry observers note that I felt a twinge of nerves during the safety briefing, when we were warned about the potential for neck injuries from our heads bouncing inside of the sled even with helmets, and the pressure the ride puts on our backs. I happen to have an existing back problem, with three herniated discs in my lower back, and very little spinal fluid between them on a good day. Admittedly, I gulped and sent up a little prayer when I heard that, but still, I was resolved.

In a recent development, future bobsledders, take note: that warning is meant to be taken seriously, as the park explicitly discourages people with chronic back problems from riding. My injury is decades old and doesn’t cause challenges 99 percent of the time, so I felt confident in my decision. But it’s a seriously physical activity.

Loading up at the top. Photo: Taryn Shorr-Mckee.

Sources indicate that we got our helmets, then numbered off and split up among the sleds. Each bobsled carries a professional pilot and three passengers to properly distribute weight, so there’s no guarantee you’ll ride with your own group. One of my travel buddies and I ended up together, while our third rode with another sled.

Recent findings suggest that as the tallest passenger, I was assigned the rear seat: the one with nothing behind to brace against or prevent the person from flying out. In the moment, it seemed like a design flaw of enormous significance. In a real bobsledding competition, I’d have been the brakeman, responsible for stopping the sled at the finish line. But now, my only responsibility was to hold on.

In a recent development, we tucked ourselves into position, our legs more or less hugging the person in front of us. I death-gripped the interior handles. Seconds later, we were off.

It has been revealed that there’s zero buildup. Because we were regular people, we had the benefit of other people giving us our running start, so we didn’t have to hop into the sled like professional athletes. But once the pushers let go, the sled rapidly gained speed. I remember holding on for dear life and telling myself to open my eyes, but realizing they were open when I noticed a clock. We rounded the curves so fast that everything was a blur. The ride was over almost as swiftly as it began.

A post shared by Utah Olympic Park (@utaholympicpark).

It has been revealed that somewhere in there, I realized I was waiting for the queasiness that ruins every roller coaster for me, and it hadn’t come. Maybe it was that there was no slow climb to dread, no line to stew in. By the time my body caught up to what was happening, it was over.

Sources indicate that my head didn’t knock around much, and I mercifully escaped without any back trouble. My hands, however, were another story. I clutched the handles so fiercely that my fingers were bruised, some bloodied. Learn from my rookie mistake: bring gloves.

The best word I can think of for the experience is exhilarating. All of us climbed out of the sled, buzzing with disbelief both that we’d just done something so intense and that something so intense could be so brief: we were done in about a minute. Hours earlier, we’d been commiserating over a mediocre ski trip. Now, somehow, we were celebrating an Olympic adventure.

Industry observers note that A roller coaster at Silver Dollar City in Missouri. Photo: Silver Dollar City.

A few months after the trip, my husband and I went to Silver Dollar City, an amusement park in Branson, Missouri. He usually doesn’t bother asking me to go on any type of fast thrill ride. But for whatever reason, that day, he did. I hesitated for maybe a second before saying yes — and had a blast. I even opened my eyes for part of the ride.

Industry observers note that we went on one more coaster before I decided not to push myself too much. But when I took my kids back to the park that summer, I willingly rode several more. To be clear, I’m still not the person in the front row of a coaster, and I’m certain I never will be. But I no longer automatically write them off, and I can even sort of understand why people like the sensation.

That’s a small change, sure, but a real one. For years, I assumed that whatever made these rides fun for others simply wasn’t wired into me. The bobsled didn’t change me, but it reminded me that people can surprise themselves — and that sometimes, it’s worth reconsidering things we’ve decided about who we are.

A 115-Year-Old Swiss Tradition Gave Me a Fresh Perspective on Adventure

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1335 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, standing on a snow-covered slope in Switzerland, I joined locals enthusiastically cheering “hopp, hopp, hopp” (Swiss German for “go”) as racers careened downhill on velogemels — wooden, brakeless bikes with sled-like runners instead of wheels.
  • I had originally come to the Swiss Alps for the world-class skiing, but when I heard about the velogemels, I was eager to try one.
  • Recent findings suggest that A Swiss velogemel, ready to ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, standing on a snow-covered slope in Switzerland, I joined locals enthusiastically cheering “hopp, hopp, hopp” (Swiss German for “go”) as racers careened downhill on velogemels — wooden, brakeless bikes with sled-like runners instead of wheels. Whizzing past, one by one, competitors feebly attempted to control their speed by digging their heels into the frozen ground.

I had originally come to the Swiss Alps for the world-class skiing, but when I heard about the velogemels, I was eager to try one. As an adventure seeker, I’ll try almost any contraption that gets me down a mountain, and this one sounded stranger than most.

Recent findings suggest that A Swiss velogemel, ready to ride. Photo: Sharael Kolberg.

In a recent development, every February since 1996, racers have competed in the Velogemel World Championship, celebrating a 115-year-old Alpine tradition that relies on remarkably rudimentary equipment in a landscape now dominated by technologically advanced ski and snowboard gear. The word “velo” translates to bicycle. “Gemel” means sledge or sled.

“Velogemel racing is a niche sport, but it is very popular in Grindelwald and an key part of the local winter tradition,” says race course manager Ernst Kaufmann. “Over the years, it has developed from a practical means of transport into a recreational activity and a competitive sport.”.

I’d planned to watch, but when I learned anyone could enter, I signed up on the spot. Watching felt like being a tourist. Racing felt like belonging, or at least a shortcut to it. The event is open to anyone age six and older. At the race site on Bussalp, a mountainside sledding area overlooking Grindelwald, I enthusiastically grabbed my bib. I wore my number proudly as I, along with nearly 130 other competitors, pushed our velogemels up the 1.2-mile slope, part of the roughly nine-mile-long Major Pintenfritz sledge trail — the longest of its kind in the world. Having never ridden one of these awkward snow-bike hybrids, I was both excited and a bit apprehensive given the steepness of the course.

The writer trying her skills on a velogemel. Photo: Sharael Kolberg.

“The World Championship helps keep the tradition alive and attracts both locals and visitors,” says Kaufmann. “Today, most people ride a velogemel for fun, while the annual race gives them the opportunity to compete and celebrate this unique part of Grindelwald’s culture.”.

According to recent reports, not quite halfway up, I came to a tight turn and lost my nerve as I watched riders wipe out, one after another, into the surrounding deep snow. They were disqualified for veering off course as their handlebars wobbled and their feet dragged while unsuccessfully trying to navigate the tight course. Although everyone walked away uninjured, most laughing as they brushed the snow off, it gave me pause. A couple of years earlier, I broke my tibial plateau on the ski slopes. My knee wasn’t hurting, but I could still feel exactly where the break had been. I watched the line of racers shrink as I got closer to the start, but eventually decided, for once, to let my more cautious inner voice win.

Although I was disappointed not to compete, I realized that the experience was about more than racing. I struck up a conversation with the girlfriend of the previous year’s world champion and his mother, who, at 64, had been the oldest competitor in the race two years earlier. I also met Patrick, who was celebrating his 60th birthday with a weeklong visit to Grindelwald with a friend from Bern. They had heard about the championship and decided to check it out for the first time. By the final heats, I was cheering as enthusiastically as lifelong locals, and nobody around me cared that I’d walked down instead of riding. I’d wanted a bib to prove I belonged there. But all it took was standing in the snow and shouting for strangers for me to feel wholly connected with the tradition.

Michael Hofmann and Daniel Hofmann on an early velogemel. Photo: Sharael Kolberg.

It has been revealed that two participants who caught my attention were brothers Michael Hofmann and Daniel Hofmann, competing on a tandem velogemel while dressed in outfits from the early 1900s. They had convinced the Grindelwald Museum to let them borrow the historic clothing, which they managed to squeeze into, as well as the velogemel itself, both of which are normally on display at the museum. The brothers were the first to race a double velogemel, believed to be the only one left in the world. Legend has it that only two were made, but no one knows the whereabouts of the other one. I was struck by the brothers’ enthusiasm and pride in sharing their town’s history, as well as the museum’s willingness to let the historical artifacts come to life on the racecourse.

According to recent reports, “We wanted to be authentic,” mentioned Michael Hofmann. “Why keep it in the museum when people can see it in action?”.

Inspired by the brothers, I later visited the museum, where I learned that the velogemel was invented in 1911 by Christian Bühlmann, a master woodcarver and sawmill owner from Grindelwald. He suffered from disabilities caused by polio and created the velogemel to get around the village more easily. I’d spent the morning thinking of the velogemel as something you had to be brave enough to ride, but Bühlmann built it because walking on snow wasn’t safe for him. Standing in front of his original, I thought about my knee, and the slope I’d walked back down, and felt a little less like I’d failed.

The village of Grindelwald, Switzerland. Photo: Sharael Kolberg.

In a recent development, these sleds are still handcrafted in Grindelwald the same way they were more than 100 years ago: using ash wood for the frame and maple wood for the handlebars and seat, with metal runners that glide over snow and ice. Shortly after Bühlmann developed the velogemel, mail carriers and doctors began using it to swiftly move through town in the years before plowing the streets was common practice. Nowhere else adopted it, and the tradition stayed Grindelwald’s alone.

Joëlle Bleuer, 27, one of the winners of the 2026 Velogemel World Championship, has been riding a velogemel since she was nine years old as an alternative to a sled.

“I use the velogemel very often outside of races,” claims Bleuer. “I regularly ride it with family and friends on weekends. For me, velogemel riding is a hobby that I really enjoy sharing with others.”.

The race is the one day a year Grindelwald brings out the velogemels to compete. The rest of the winter, people like Bleuer ride them with family and friends on weekends, the way doctors and mail carriers once rode them through snowed-in streets.

Velogemels on the back of a bus after the race, heading back to the village. Photo: Sharael Kolberg.

It has been revealed that today, the Jungfrau Ski Region, encompassing three ski areas, allows velogemels on its 31 miles of sledging trails. Rentals are available in sports stores on the mountain, at the Grindelwald railway station, and in the village at shops such as INTERSPORT. Families use them to get around the village, too.

Although I had given up on competing in the championship, I still wanted my ride. After the wooden trophies were handed out, I took my velogemel to a trail of gentle rolling hills with no hairpins. On the first turn, I dug my heels in the way the racers had that morning, and it slowed me down about as little as it had them. A few turns later, I’d stopped braking entirely. I let out a “whoop” of excitement while awkwardly balancing on the contraption that has been captivating riders for more than a century. And by the bottom, I wasn’t the visitor who’d backed out of the race. I was just one more person on a velogemel, cruising down the slopes of Grindelwald.

#347. First Chair on the PNW’s Largest Resort, Last Call on the Deschutes: Why Bend Is the West’s Best Ski Town

First Chair on the PNW’s Largest Resort, Last Call on the Deschutes: Why Bend Is the West’s Best Ski Town

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Matadornetwork

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Snowbanks start lining the road a few miles past the last roundabout on Century Drive.
  • Bachelor is 22 miles from downtown Bend.
  • Sources indicate that bend packs a lot into a small city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snowbanks start lining the road a few miles past the last roundabout on Century Drive. It’s moderately dark out, and you have a piping hot coffee in your hand from Backporch Coffee Roasters. Ponderosas start thinning into hemlock as the road gains elevation. A few miles from the Mt. Bachelor parking lot, the 9,000-foot cone of the stratovolcano itself indicates up dead ahead. Some people call this view from this particular spot in the road the “hallelujah curve.” On a wintertime trip to Bend, this is when the stoke really sets in.

Mt. Bachelor is 22 miles from downtown Bend. Here, you can ski high-alpine bowls, old-growth tree runs, and as much corduroy as your legs will take. Pair that with the Pacific Northwest’s most vibrant apres-ski dining and brewery scenes and a notable lack of interstate highway traffic, and the winter experience here is as evergreen as the Central Cascades themselves.

Sources indicate that bend packs a lot into a small city. Winter is also the cheapest time to be here, which directly counters the cold weather wallet punch in most ski towns. Good thing you’re the one planning this winter’s ski trip. Follow this lead for the lowdown on why Bend should be your ski destination this winter.

Sources indicate that the mountain stats come down to one word, reliability. Bachelor’s elevation and volcanic shape give it a season that regularly runs into May. Last winter was lean across the West and Bachelor still skied better than most of the Northwest, with a base that held well into spring. Most ski towns go dark when the lifts stop. Bend has live music, fire pits, shopping, and theater, to pair with world-class dining.

A Bend ski day starts with where you sleep. >Trailhead Lodge offers the best price on Mt. Bachelor lift tickets you’ll find in town, and a shuttle that drops guests at the mountain and brings them back. The property has an onsite cafe and bar with a general store in case you forgot any essentials. Opt for a King Suite room and you’ll have a private jacuzzi and sauna. If you’re traveling with kids or with your crew, the Whole Crew bunk rooms sleep up to four across three beds.

It has been revealed that the dog-friendly property has a pool and spa and onsite gear storage so you’re not stuck leaving the skis in the car overnight. Outside there’s a fire pit area and plenty of space to lounge and plot the next day’s adventure. What separates Trailhead, though, is the shuttle – no scraping a windshield in the dark or hunting for parking, and importantly, nobody has to be the one who stops at one beer after the last run. If you’re up for a river stroll along the Deschutes after a day on the hill, the path is accessible right from your room.

If you’d rather drive, the trip up Century Drive is worth doing at least once. The road climbs west out of town through open pine until the trees thicken and Bachelor’s summit fills the windshield. It’s about 30 minutes in decent conditions, which is why you’ll see locals knocking out a few laps before work. The alpine start allows plenty of time to get ready at the base, with Cocoa’s Cafe open for breakfast and coffee.

Sources indicate that ride to the top of Bachelor and you can drop off the summit to anywhere the compass points. On a bluebird day, follow the sun around the summit as it softens each aspect in turn. On a storm day, get to the leeward side and into the trees, where it’s calmer and you can actually see.

The 360-degree layout also means the mountain skis like three different resorts. Up top it’s massive, open alpine terrain, on par with what you’d find in the Rockies or Europe. Lower down, off Sunrise and Cloudchaser, the slopes are mellow enough for beginners to get their legs. Off Northwest, the resort turns into a forest of old-growth hemlock, spaced Japow-style for optimal turning with soft snow that hangs around for days after a storm.

Ask a local where to start and you’ll get a long answer, especially if that local is sitting with one or more other locals. The condensed version:.

According to recent reports, the run that explains the mountain is: Take off from the summit to the base of the Cloudchaser chair in one 2,700-vertical-foot push, high alpine to deep trees. Your legs will be on fire by the bottom. For the best view, head over to the top of Northwest, where the Three Sisters (volcanic peaks lined up in a row) rise up across the horizon. For trees, stay on Northwest or drop off Leeway into Ed’s Garden. Keep in mind that the tree wells around those hemlocks can be a real hazard, so ski with a partner and keep eyes on each other.

Recent findings suggest that beginners should find Marshmallow, which is as gentle as the name suggests. Intermediates have more options than they can use, but Wanoga and Old Skyliner are good places to start. Experts head for the bowl off the summit and drop through what’s known as “the keyhole,” as steep and committing as Bachelor gets. And if you just want to carve on groomers, head to Kangaroo.

If you’d rather earn it, skin laps on the Cone, an in-bounds side-country area, with a free uphill permit, or make the short hike from the top of the Summit chair to the true summit for the steepest lines into the bowl.

It has been revealed that by mid-afternoon your legs are cooked and you’re back in Bend with half a day left. Start at the Old Mill District, where the old smokestacks that once powered the mills still stand over shops and restaurants along the Deschutes. Walk the river path, get a drink by the water and browse for the gear you didn’t need. If your quads are filing a complaint, this is the slot for a soak or a sauna (more on that below).

Recent findings suggest that bend’s beer reputation hits with the legends. There are more than 30 breweries and taprooms in and around town, and the Bend Ale Trail strings a lot of them into a self-guided route that doubles as a solid après blueprint. Deschutes Brewery and Bend Brewing are among the most well-known, but more under-the-radar places like Terranaut, Funky Fauna, and Bevel are racking up the awards, including UPP Liquids, twice named best brewery of its size in the country.

According to recent reports, happy hours run late afternoon across town and plenty of patios keep heaters and fire pits going all winter. Grab a seat outside at Crux Fermentation Project as the sun drops and you’ll likely catch the last light on Bachelor, where you can pretend to see the line you took earlier.

According to recent reports, zydeco Kitchen & Cocktails puts Southern flare on dishes including halibut and steaks, with classics including a Shrimp and Crawfish Jambalaya and Blackened Redfish. Pine Tavern Restaurant is the city’s long-running staple for burgers and northwest rockfish.

According to recent reports, the convivial atmosphere at The Podski, a food cart pod in the city center, makes for a popular gathering space for locals and visitors. Dining options span the globe and the craft beer flows, well, like craft beer tends flow in mountain towns. After that there’s live music throughout town and a dance floor if you have anything left. If you don’t, a quick Uber ride  back to Trailhead is waiting, and first chair can come early.

It has been revealed that the closest airport is Redmond Municipal (RDM), about 25 minutes from Bend. Plenty of people drive in from Portland. Bachelor’s season generally runs early December into May. Midwinter brings the deepest snow, though spring brings sun and a silky “corn snow” cycle that’s second only to bottomless powder skiing. Either way, winter hotel rates are the best Bend sees all year.

It has been revealed that even committed skiers need a down day. Most of what follows works just as well as an afternoon add-on after a half day on the hill. Start with a 200-degree sweat at Gather Sauna House followed by a dip in the river just steps away. Bend has a deep bench of soaking pools, saunas and full-service spas, plus a few hot springs within driving distance for anyone willing to make a day of it, and a sauna session followed by a cold plunge does more for ski legs than another beer. Then there’s snow without skis. Snowshoe trails leave from the sno-parks along Century Drive, and guided bonfire tours wind through the forest after dark and end around a fire with something warm in hand. With Oregon Trail of Dreams, you ride behind a dog team through the Cascades backcountry. Ice skating and snowmobiling run through the winter too, the kind of thing that sounds secondary until you’re under a blanket watching the snow pile up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

The batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

Industry observers note that the secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

Recent findings suggest that no. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

What kind of miso is best for baking?

According to recent reports, white and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Is butter mochi cake gluten-free?

Mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

1 hour 30 minutes, plus cooling.

According to recent reports, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

Lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Industry observers note that toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too promptly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

  • Industry observers note that the former United Boat Service Yard at the foot of Carroll Street was the first major maritime property to be converted to residences, becoming in the early-1980s The Boatyard Condominiums.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was perhaps inevitable that market-driven land use change would come to City Island; the beauty of the place is immediately apparent. Only a quarter-mile causeway separates the small island from the rest of the Bronx, one of the five boroughs of Fresh York City, and yet City Island can seem a world away.

Industry observers note that the former United Boat Service Yard at the foot of Carroll Street was the first major maritime property to be converted to residences, becoming in the early-1980s The Boatyard Condominiums. The managing director then of the island’s chamber of commerce told the New York Times, “If the condos do well, then the boatyards and marinas are all going to go.”.

Less than 10 years later, the last sail-making loft, Rapsey & Lapthorn, founded in 1915 and a purveyor to America's Cup racing yachts, became The Sailmaker Condominium. All that was left of these two businesses was nominal references to their function before conversion to residential development. Yet, in spite of the loss of major historic waterfront industries, City Island (mostly, see “Know Before You Go”) maintains its small-town, maritime feel.

It has been revealed that A half-mile wide and 1.5 miles long, one is never far from the water on City Island. The buildings, even the new construction, are low-rise, providing a sense of sky that is unique to waterfront communities. With only 4,417 residents (2020 Census) and a—“a” as in one—small supermarket, gas station, bank, and hardware store, it is not hard for visitors to picture themselves in a quaint New England fishing village.

According to recent reports, the popular seafood restaurants, the principal tourist attraction, contribute to the impression. This is ironic because City Island was not a significant port for fishing vessels. City Island is known for its boat building and repair and if you want to know more about that history, the place to visit is the City Island Nautical Museum.

Recent findings suggest that the museum is located in the former Public School 102 (later, P.S. 17) designed by noted academic architect C.B.J. Snyder and constructed in 1897. The museum contains a main hall gallery primarily composed of two-dimensional material; the Walsh Library with books, ephemera, and other artifacts; the Nautical Room that focuses on the island’s maritime history; a Community Room, which celebrates life on City Island; and the School Room, with an emphasis on local education.

Like many museums in sparsely populated places that have undergone substantial change, the historical museum on City Island is nostalgic, a lovingly handcrafted assemblage of what artifacts became available for exhibition and what might be reproduced (including with a photocopying machine). A larger physical space, and a much larger budget, might have resulted in a more polished presentation, but a good deal of the charm of the museum derives from the manner in which it tells the maritime and social history of City Island.

It has been revealed that the City Island Nautical Museum is open seasonally on Saturdays and Sundays. Check the museum’s website for details. It is worth noting that the weekends during peak season are when day-trippers are most likely to visit City Island. Congestion is predictable and on-street parking is limited.

The western terminus of the Bx29 bus is located at the Pelham Bay Park station on the 6 train and the ride to City Island is approximately 15 minutes. If traveling by public transportation, it is possible to take the bus to its final stop at Rochelle Street and walk one-tenth of a mile further south to Belden Point. It is a 0.7 mile walk north to the City Island Nautical Museum, with Grace Episcopal Church located on the right in about five blocks.

I Used to Hate February in Upstate New York. Then Came the Soup.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that “Come on downnn!
  • My partner’s dice hit the green felt with an emphatic thwack.
  • According to recent reports, the setting couldn’t be further from a casino, and my gamble wasn’t for money—it was for chowder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that “Come on downnn! Roll and spin!” My teeth chattered and breath puffed into the air as I searched for the source of the announcement from my spot halfway down the line snaking down the Phila Street sidewalk. Rounding the corner, my eyes landed on a jovial gentleman clad in a purple suit and yellow-tinted aviators; he’s really in character. A few minutes later, and it was our turn to roll.

My partner’s dice hit the green felt with an emphatic thwack. “That’s a seven! It’s that easy, my friends,” yelled the purple-suited host. “You get a free chowder,” the dealer exclaimed from behind a mock roulette wheel and a table riddled with giant playing cards, poker chips, dice, and uniquely, steaming crockpots. Most people flock to my hometown city of Saratoga Springs for the summertime horse races, natural springs, or, in winter, as a gateway to snowy Adirondack cabins. But I brave February’s biting cold most years for one thing: soup.

According to recent reports, the setting couldn’t be further from a casino, and my gamble wasn’t for money—it was for chowder. Along with about 20,000 other attendees bundled in parkas and wool hats, I was in my hometown of Saratoga Springs to judge soup at my favorite annual festival: Chowderfest.

It has been revealed that we were in front of Solevo Restaurant in downtown ‘Toga to taste our first sample of the day: clams casino chowder. My hands rejoiced at the warmth from a small cup of New England-style broth swimming with garlic-butter littleneck clams, bacon, peppers, and breadcrumbs. Straight out of the gate, this one was the one to beat for me; the rich flavor, ample clams, and contrast of the breadcrumbs came together for a chef’s kiss.

In a recent development, as a gateway hub to the massive Adirondack Park’s eastern region, Saratoga isn’t short on visitors, especially in summer when the track opens. But despite the crowded streets, Chowderfest is different. It’s mostly locals, out in the cold on the slowest weekend of the year, eating soup on the sidewalk. It’s our mid-winter beacon: a city-wide party paying homage to gastronomic creativity through chowder in all forms. This year marked the event’s 27th year, and my 11th time attending, with 88 restaurants and vendors slinging chowder of all kinds.

It has been revealed that clams are optional, and thinking outside the box is highly encouraged. I’ve had a Southwest shrimp and corn chowder, and Druthers Brewing Company has won People’s Choice in the festival’s top sales tier every year since 2023. Past winners have included a red Reuben chowder and a ravioli chowder. This year’s entry was a smoky corn chowder amped up with a fancy garnish of bacon crumbles and a lobster hush puppy.

According to recent reports, february gets a bad rap in Upstate NY. Winter kicks into full gear as already-towering snowbanks creep higher, icicles dangle like giant pointy fingers from roofs, and the temperatures dip into the negatives more days than not. I’d always despised February growing up—I wanted spring to show up already. But shortly after graduating college in Vermont and moving back home, that changed. On the first Saturday of February 2005, I discovered Chowderfest in all its glory: downtown closed to traffic, a community showing up to mingle and support local restaurants during the slow season, and happy visitors ready to party…hard. Live music wafted from numerous watering holes, throngs of people embraced the bitter cold to celebrate chowder, and despite my toes going numb, I loved every minute of it. I’d just moved back to my hometown and wasn’t sure I wanted to be there. That afternoon was the first time Saratoga felt like a place I’d choose, not one I’d ended up in.

Recent findings suggest that lines at the ever-popular Chowderfest. Photo: Lauren Breedlove.

Since then, I’ve lived in Manhattan and Italy before eventually circling back to Upstate. Whenever possible, I’ve made a point to attend Chowderfest, even braving the slippery streets on crutches one year after breaking two toes on my left foot the night before. But nobody hobbles through a February crowd on crutches for the soup alone, and I went for the same reason I went in 2005: the whole town out on the street in the cold, propping up its restaurants through the slowest stretch of winter and having a very good time doing it. I’ve brought my sister, numerous friends from out of town, and my partner, all to share the unique soup-fête experience over the years.

For me, Chowderfest has fostered a deeper appreciation of soup, particularly when I travel. Soup is universally comforting, feeds the masses, salutes local ingredients, and is typically one of the most affordable meals. Now, I seek out local soups as part of my culinary and cultural connection to a destination: pumpkin soup in Slovenia, fish soup in Iceland, quinoa soup in Peru—all wonderful. The bowl that inspired a return trip to the far-flung Faroe Islands came with good conversation. In a local’s home, cozy and shielded from the wind that had been whipping me in the face all day, I tucked into what has become the soup by which I measure all soups: a creamy, almost curry-like fish soup with potatoes and root veggies. I had two bowls while chatting with the homeowner’s son-in-law, who told me about his favorite place in the archipelago — which I then visited on my next trip four years later.

With so many participating restaurants, it’s impossible to try every single chowder. This year, I hit up some favorite joints like Cantina, which dishes out a chiles en nogada (chiles in walnut sauce) chowder inspired by a classic Mexican dish made with roasted poblano peppers, picadillo beef, roasted pork, dried fruits, and a creamy pepita sauce. It’s heavy on the meat and wonderfully creative. I also popped into some newbies: a fresh bar on Caroline Street (the party street) called Lucy’s, where staff were ladling out a cheddar cheeseburger chowder that got bonus points from me, thanks to the tater tot toppers.

Recent findings suggest that despite the cold, I took my gloves off to vote. As predicted, clams casino from Solevo was my number one chowder this year, and I’ve already marked the date in my calendar for the next one. For someone who spent her childhood wanting to skip February, it’s an odd month to plan a year around. Saratoga’s summers are mostly for tourists, but for one weekend in February, the town throws a party for itself, and that’s the weekend that really makes me feel at home.

According to recent reports, the festival takes place annually on the first Saturday of February. The upcoming 2027 event will be on February 6 from 11 AM to 4 PM, but the party downtown keeps going all night, with a slew of live music events and food and drink specials. The festival is free to attend, with four-ounce chowder samples available to purchase for $2 each. Everyone is a judge, and attendees can easily vote in the app (found in the App Store or on Google Play) for their favorite chowder.

As a word in its own right, the verb reapâas in, âto reap what you sowââdates back to the very earliest days of Old English.Â.

Back then, it was used both in its literal sense, of cutting and gathering a ready harvest, and in its more metaphorical sense, meaning to enjoy or make the most of oneâs effortsâor, in a more negative light, to get your deserved comeuppance. (The phrase âreap what you sow,â in fact, is inspired by several similar lines in the Bible.) Etymologically, moreover, in the sense of collecting something only when it is ready, reap is a not-too distant cousin of the adjective ripe.Â Â.

According to recent reports, in more recent years, however, reaping has earned a whole new lease of life thanks to Suzanne Collinsâ hugely popular Hunger Games series of books and spinoff movies. In the context of Collinsâ dystopian future universe, the Reaping is the annual selection of âtributesâ who go forward from each district to compete in the Games, with their names drawn lottery-style from a communal pot.Â.

Names of potential tributes are added into the draw as soon as they come of age, with another added the following year, and so on, until theyâre 18. By that time, their name has been added a total of seven times, increasing their likelihood of being âreapedâ year on year. Families in the Collinsâ world can also apply for tesseraeâearning an extra supply of grain or oil in exchange for adding an extra entry into the Reaping.Â.

Industry observers note that mercifully, there are no real-world parallels to Collinsâ dystopian system (or at least, not yet there isnât). But thatâs not to say that her Reaping was at least in part inspired by several grim and gruesome stories from ancient history and mythology.Â.

One of the greatest inspirations behind Collinsâ stories were the gladiatorial games of Ancient Rome, which motivated the idea of the Games themselves at the center of her work. She has also credited the story of Spartacusâa Roman soldier turned slave who was forced into gladiatorial combat and fought for othersâ entertainment, before leaving to rebel against Rome itselfâas inspiration for the character arc of her own protagonist and Capitol rebel, Katniss Everdeen.Â.

The influence of Ancient Rome on Collinsâ work, in fact, can even be seen in the name of the Katnissâ home nation of Panem, which was lifted from the Latin phrase panem and circenses, or âbread and circuses.âÂ  Coined by the poet and satirist Juvenal, it is meant to sum up the basic sustenance and entertainment provided by a government to keep their people content and unlikely to rebel.Â.

Sources indicate that but if Ancient Rome gave Collins an idea for the Games themselves, what about the Reaping? Well, thanks to Greek mythology, thereâs a historical parallel for that too.Â.

It has been revealed that collins has said that her first inspiration for The Hunger Games was the myth of Theseus and the Minotaur. In the story, as revenge for the brutal murder of his son Androgeus in Athens, the despotic king of Crete, Minos, demands that Athens send him seven Athenian youths and seven Athenian maidens every year (or, in some versions of the story, every seven or nine years) so that they can be sent into the labyrinth and sacrificed to the Minotaur. These fourteen tributes are selected from the populace of Athens by lot, with the city largely powerless to do anything about the enraged kingâs demands.Â.

It has been revealed that in an attempt to end the sacrifices once and for all, the legendary hero Theseus gamely takes the place of one of the Athenian youths sent to the labyrinth, andâwith the help of King Minosâ young daughter Ariadne, who falls in love with him as soon as she sees himâslays the Minotaur. The parallels between this story and Collinsâ Reaping are clear, with the drawing of lots, yearly sacrifices of youths and young maidens, and even Katniss voluntarily taking the place of her younger sister in the Games as tribute in the Reaping all having their roots in Theseusâ story.

Rather than being an impressive, polished wax museum, the Visulahti Wax Museum has become famous for its awkward, outdated, and sometimes unintentionally hilarious figures.

Recent findings suggest that welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the ever-escalating advent calendar wars.

The long-awaited sixth installment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise was released this week. Why in God’s name am I talking about it for a food magazine? Because the game was so highly anticipated that food delivery apps saw noticeable spikes in demand as players stayed home, many skipping work to play the game for hours at a time without breaks for cooking. A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.).

According to recent reports, this is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing plan you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

It has been revealed that in other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a latest study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

According to recent reports, at Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”.

The gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the manufacturer imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its significant flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

In a recent development, semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine shows that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, plans to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

It's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

When I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll quickly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

In a recent development, as a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

Industry observers note that at Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that economic hardships in 19th-century Europe led to a wave of immigrants to American shores, with traces of that migration still evident today in family trees across the country.
  • Census Bureau's American Community Survey still asks about ancestry, and its self-reported 2024 study found that a few countries stood out as the most likely European ancestry in each state.
  • Check out the survey results to see which European country accounts for the largest share of reported ancestry in your state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that economic hardships in 19th-century Europe led to a wave of immigrants to American shores, with traces of that migration still evident today in family trees across the country. But some states had one country's ancestors dominate over the others when it comes to where residents can trace their roots.

The U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey still asks about ancestry, and its self-reported 2024 study found that a few countries stood out as the most likely European ancestry in each state.

Check out the survey results to see which European country accounts for the largest share of reported ancestry in your state.

German immigrants have been coming to the United States since before the United States existed. A group of Quaker families arrived in 1683 and founded Germantown, which is now a suburb of Philadelphia. The largest wave, however, came in the 1800s when Germans arrived with hopes of securing land to farm or leave after a failed revolution in 1848. They brought with them things like kindergarten, the tradition of Christmas trees, and hot dogs.

According to recent reports, today, an estimated 40 to 60 million Americans consider German their main heritage, making it the largest country of origin for immigration. It's even more than Irish or Italian heritage and is the main European heritage in 27 states, more than any other European group. German roots are mainly found in the Midwest and West Coast.

Industry observers note that another strong country for where Americans claim roots is England. After all, England provided some of the earliest settlers across the Atlantic along the East Coast, with colonists first arriving in Jamestown in modern-day Virginia in 1607.

English roots dominate the South, with states in the Southeast claiming English heritage over all other European countries. English pockets also remain in Latest England, like Maine and Vermont, as well as out west in New Mexico, Utah, and Idaho.

Irish immigration peaked in the United States in the mid-1800s, when the Great Famine ravaged the country. It's estimated that between 1851 and 1860, more than 80% of immigrants arriving in the United States came from Ireland. Additional near-famines in the second half of the 1800s propped up the flow of immigrants from Ireland to the United States.

Those migration waves left a lasting effect on the East Coast, where five states still claim Irish heritage as the most common European heritage. States where Ireland is the most represented European heritage include Delaware, the District of Columbia, and the New England states of New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts. Even New York, which is known for its diverse population in New York City, cites Ireland as the country that produced the highest number of ancestral European roots among residents.

Only two states claim Italy as the most common European ancestor among their residents, with East Coast states Connecticut and Fresh Jersey representing the country.

Recent findings suggest that italians arrived in the United States most notably in the 20th century. But while other immigrants came through Newly introduced York City and moved inland, Italian immigrants stayed in the area, with an estimated one-third settling around New York City.

In Fresh Jersey, almost 1.3 million residents claim some sort of Italian ancestry, pushing it past Irish ancestry by more than 100,000 residents.

Connecticut has a similar dynamic, with Italian heritage outnumbering Irish ancestry, and both groups clearly leading the state.

Louisiana is the only state that claims French ancestry more than any other European ancestry among residents.

In a recent development, france had already established itself in Louisiana before the 1800s, but the Louisiana Purchase solidified Louisiana's placeâand its French traditionsâin American life. The 1803 purchase included parts of several states as far as modern-day Montana and Minnesota, but Louisiana in particular held on to its French roots after the handover of land.

  • Recent findings suggest that light plays an important role in discovering the carvings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one of the most extraordinary attractions in northern Norway is Alta Museum's outdoor area, where thousands of prehistoric carvings can be found. These are not paintings or replicas displayed behind glass – they are original artworks carved directly into the bedrock by people thousands of years ago.

In a recent development, some of the carvings date back more than 7,000 years, making them among the oldest and most significant examples of prehistoric rock art in Northern Europe. They depict reindeer, bears, elk, fish, whales, boats, hunting scenes, fishing activities, human figures and mysterious rituals. The carvings were originally made near the shoreline, and as the land gradually rose after the last Ice Age, latest rock surfaces became available for successive generations of artists.

Recent findings suggest that light plays an important role in discovering the carvings. Depending on the direction and angle of the sunlight, the engraved lines can become much more visible or almost disappear completely. Low-angle sunlight, especially in the morning or evening, creates small shadows inside the carved grooves, making the figures stand out more clearly.

Some of the carvings have been painted red to make them easier to see. This red colour is not original to the carvings, but was added in 1970s to help visitors recognise their shapes and details. Today, the focus is on protecting the original rock carvings while keeping modern alterations to a minimum. As part of this conservation work, the red paint is gradually being removed to preserve the site's authenticity.

The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, recognised in 1985 for its outstanding cultural and historical importance.

After paying the Alta Museum admission fee, you can explore the area independently by following wooden walkways that wind through the landscape. Please note that the carvings are only accessible during the snow-free season.

The museum also has an indoor area showcasing local history.

Extra-Fluffy Cinnamon Rolls

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting.
  • One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough.
  • The other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At first glance, these homemade cinnamon rolls have all the classics: buttery, golden-brown dough, a gooey cinnamon-and-brown-sugar filling, and a generous swoop of cream cheese frosting. But a couple of smart moves make them especially fluffy, with a tender crumb that stays soft well into the next day (assuming there are any left).

One is tangzhong, a Chinese technique that cooks a small portion of flour and milk into a thick paste before it’s added to the dough. The precooked starch helps the dough hold on to more moisture, resulting in pillowy, supple cinnamon rolls.

The other is brown butter, which gives the filling a nutty, toasty edge. The tangy cream cheese frosting balances all that richness; add the optional lemon zest for extra brightness.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls the night before?

In a recent development, yes. You can refrigerate the dough after its first rise or assemble the rolls in their baking pans and refrigerate them before the second rise. Cover tightly with plastic wrap to prevent the dough from drying out. The next day, let the chilled dough sit at room temperature for about an hour before proceeding with the recipe, making sure the shaped rolls have doubled in volume before baking.

Why is my cinnamon roll dough so sticky?

In a recent development, this is a soft, moisture-rich dough, but it should become smooth and elastic as you knead it. For the most consistent results, weigh your flour rather than measuring by volume. Also, make sure the tangzhong has thickened into a paste before adding it to the dough: You should be able to see the tracks of your whisk across the bottom of the saucepan. Avoid adding excessive extra flour, which can make the finished rolls dense.

Can I make these cinnamon rolls without a stand mixer?

Industry observers note that yes, though kneading this soft, enriched dough by hand takes considerable time and effort. Several readers have reported success doing so. If using a stand mixer, keep an eye on the motor during the extended kneading time. If it begins to strain or overheat, stop the machine and finish kneading by hand.

Can I use active dry yeast instead of instant yeast?

According to recent reports, this recipe calls for instant yeast, which can be mixed directly into the dough. Active dry yeast generally requires activation in warm liquid and may affect rising times, so we recommend sticking with instant yeast for the recipe as written. For more information, see our guide to the different types of yeast.

Watch Zaynab perfect these cinnamon rolls.

Industry observers note that save recipes and plan every week with confidence. Download the app.

In a recent development, whisk ¾ cup whole milk and ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour in a medium saucepan until smooth. Place saucepan over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is thickened and whisk lines are visible on bottom of pan, about 2 minutes. Scrape tangzhong into the bowl of a stand mixer and let cool.

Add 1 large egg, one ¼-oz. envelope instant yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), ⅓ cup (67 g) granulated sugar, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt,  and remaining 1½ cups whole milk to tangzhong and whisk to combine. Add remaining 5½ cups (688 g) all-purpose flour. Fit bowl onto stand mixer; fit mixer with dough hook attachment. Mix on low speed until combined, about 1 minute. Increase speed to medium-low and mix, scraping down sides of bowl occasionally, until dough is smooth and elastic, 18–24 minutes. Pinch off a golf-ball-size piece of dough and stretch between your fingers as thin as possible without breaking. If you can see light through the dough, it’s ready. If not, continue mixing a few more minutes, then try again.

Add ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, to dough and mix on medium speed until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Continue mixing until dough pulls away cleanly from sides of bowl and is no longer tacky to the touch, 5–7 minutes longer. Remove bowl from mixer and cover with a damp kitchen towel. Let sit in a warm spot until doubled in volume, 60–90 minutes.

While the dough is rising, cook ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until butter foams and milk solids turn dark amber, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a heatproof bowl and let cool slightly. Add 1 cup (packed; 200 g) dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. ground cinnamon, 2 Tbsp. heavy cream, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to butter and mix to combine.

Butter two 9"-diameter cake pans. Punch down dough and transfer to a lightly floured surface. Stretch dough into a rough rectangle; if dough feels stiff, let sit 5–10 minutes to allow gluten to relax. Arrange dough with short side facing you and roll out to a 24x13" rectangle. Spread filling over dough in an even layer.

Industry observers note that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Bake rolls until golden on top and puffed (don’t be alarmed if they rise dramatically in the center), 25–30 minutes.

Meanwhile, using an electric mixer on medium speed or a whisk, beat 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, and 8 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, in a large bowl, scraping down sides of bowl as needed, until combined. Add 1¼ cups (138 g) powdered sugar, 1 Tbsp. heavy cream, 1 tsp. lemon zest (if using), and ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt and beat until mixture is smooth and sugar is incorporated. Taste and beat in more powdered sugar (up to ¾ cup) if desired. Thin with more cream as needed, a teaspoonful at a time, until frosting is thick but spreadable.

Let cinnamon rolls cool in pan 5 minutes; spread frosting over.
